Thirdly; the very origin of this Mover, as previously described, displays something nobler and more majestic than a mere bodily form. For if it is an abstract form <note>original: *species abstracta*; here meaning a non-material influence or "image" emanating from a source</note>, or one flowing out from the First Moving Cause which initiated this motion from the outside—namely, from God Himself—what else could it be than the Prime Mover, which is itself immovable: that is, the Soul. For in this way, God is, in a supereffential way <note>original: *supereffentialiter*; meaning existing beyond the nature of created things</note>, the first moving and creative cause; and thus He Himself is transcendently essential motion—that is, eternal generation—of which all souls and spirits are shadows, carrying His likeness in some way, just as shadows represent bodies.

Fourthly, the function of this mover points to the same conclusion. Let it be granted that the regularity and duration of rotation do not require anything else besides a brute natural cause; even its very slight increase and decrease in speed, tempered by the sun’s approach and retreat, is a geometric matter and a characteristic of physical matter. Yet, there remains that very slow inclination, whether of the axis or the movement of the middle circle <note>likely referring to the precession of the equinoxes or the change in the Earth's axial tilt</note>; concerning which we are uncertain (at least in this branch of astronomy) whether it might not require the guidance of a Mind.

*What you said about the constancy of motion seems to be weakened by the example of animals, which, although endowed with a soul, nevertheless grow tired?*

Animals have clear causes for their fatigue in the condition of their bodies, which undergo their own cycles of change; this is not the case for the soul that moves them. Such causes are absent in the globe of the Earth, which is perpetually and equally disposed toward motion—or rather, toward rest <note>Kepler describes the Earth as having a natural "inertia" or "laziness" (moles) that the Mover must constantly overcome</note>. For the passive qualities in matter are more durable than the positive ones, which are the offspring of forms that can expire.

However, the testimony of our eyes teaches us that this principle cannot be understood or granted universally for all circular motions. For experience bears witness: just as the eagle glides through the clouds, not merely for exercise, but primarily to catch its prey; so too does the <term>first motion</term> <note>original: "primum motum"; this refers to the apparent daily rotation of the stars and planets around the Earth from east to west.</note> happen so that all parts of the Earth may successively enjoy the sun’s heat. Otherwise, if this motion did not exist, one of the Earth's hemispheres would be scorched, while the other would be stiff with perpetual frost.

Now, it is not credible that the entire machinery of the heavens should revolve—either around the Earth, from which it receives nothing, or even around the Sun placed in its own central bosom—for the sake of its own private necessity. Indeed, the hollow shape of the machinery speaks against it; from this we understand that whether it rests or moves, it enjoys the sight of the Sun (and, if you like, the Earth as well) equally either way. Therefore, if the heavens and the sun within them are moved by the "first motion," they would be revolved not for their own sake, but for the sake of the Earth. 3. One could also argue from the principles of the philosophers—who teach that the heavens are a perfect body and the Earth is <term>elemental</term> <note>Composed of the four changing elements: earth, air, fire, and water, as opposed to the "aether" of the heavens.</note> and imperfect—that rest, which is the negation of the <term>primary motion</term> <note>The daily rotation of the celestial sphere.</note>, belongs to the heavens, while motion itself belongs to the Earth. This is because motion belongs to the category of things that are not static but are in a state of "becoming." Therefore, motion does not pertain to those things which possess a perennial degree of perfection within themselves, but rather to those things which, unless they are moved, grow sluggish with inactivity and decay—such as the Waters and Air on the Earth itself, and the many bodies living within these elements. This argument was used by Origanus <note>David Origanus (1558–1628), an astronomer who proposed a system where the Earth rotates but does not orbit the sun.</note>.

*7. What argument do you have for the Earth's motion based on the effect of that motion itself?*

It has been discovered through nautical experience that it is more difficult, and takes a longer span of time, to navigate the African Ocean <note>The South Atlantic, then often called the Ethiopian or African Ocean.</note> toward the East than toward the West. This is because the ocean rushes in a perennial motion toward the setting sun, where it is hindered by no barriers of coastlines. Similarly, in the Spice Islands <note>The Moluccas in modern-day Indonesia.</note>, it is reported that there is a perpetual flow from the Eastern Ocean into the Indian Ocean, swifter than any arrow. This occurs because an immense mass of water, accumulated from the East against this barrier of islands, presses upon and drives forward from the outside. In the Southern Ocean, along the shores of America facing East, there is almost no ebb and flow <note>Tides.</note> of the sea, because the ocean is carried away from those shores continuously toward the west, not encountering any obstacle to its course for two thousand German miles <note>A German mile was roughly 7.5 kilometers.</note>. The same westward motion is also felt at the shores of America facing North; the flow is carried as if striking against them and, following their layout, it swerves toward the north. From there, it leaps back as if toward the East, but by then it is outside the Tropic.

Even though the cause of this motion is manifest—being the same, of course, as that of the reciprocal ebb and flow, with the moon drawing...

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s argument regarding the Earth’s motion, specifically addressing the psychological and physical reasons why humans perceive the Earth as stationary while the heavens appear to move.</meta>

130 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

He who sails downstream, unless previously warned, will think the nearby shores are moving in the opposite direction; and if the ship is carried past a stake that the current washes over while submerged, the passengers will exclaim that an otter is swimming up to meet them. He who is carried forward in a carriage between hedges will swear the hedges on both sides are rushing toward him; he who travels backward will swear the hedges are fleeing. The eyes conceive this impression and retain it deeply even when the person comes to rest. Furthermore, he who is carried away backward in a carriage from a Tower of remarkable height, along a path leading directly from the Tower, will be terrified that the ruin of the tower is falling upon his head. <note>Kepler is describing the "looming" effect where perspective changes make a receding object appear to tilt or fall toward the observer.</note> In the same way, someone observing a gaping, widely spread cloud moving gently from the south to the North will swear that the stars, which fall into the gaps and flash out from them, are moving with a contrary motion from the North to the south.

->*But why, of these two options, does that which is*<-
->*false seem more likely than that which is true?*<-

The cause, sprouting from a single root, stretches out into two branches. For motion is not a proper object of sight, nor does it have a peculiar sense by which it may be perceived; instead, it is judged by the <term>common sense</term>. <note>In 17th-century psychology, the "common sense" (sensus communis) was the mental faculty that integrated data from the five individual senses into a coherent perception.</note> However, the common sense is deceived chiefly in these two ways which can be applied to the motion of the earth. First, a man thinks his eyes are at rest whenever he knows that the motion by which the eyes are carried does not come from his own internal <term>motive faculty</term>, <note>The "motive faculty" refers to the conscious will or biological power to move one's own limbs.</note> or when he does not feel that motion in his own body by the evidence of <term>jolting</term>; <note>original: "succussionis." This refers to the physical vibration or shaking one feels when moving over a surface.</note> as when a man is carried along by a ship, or in the present case, by the very rotation of his place on the Earth.

Next, those things which appear larger, and either exceed the scope of the eye or occupy it widely, are thought to be likely at rest—such as a cloud, or the level surface of the earth bounded by the distant mountains. On the other hand, those things which appear tiny in respect to them, such as the stars between the great volumes of the clouds, or the Sun and the Moon

# Concerning the Calcination of Vitriol

It is essential for the practitioner to recognize that **true medicine is hidden within the crude body** of the mineral. To extract the soul of the vitriol <note>a historical term for various sulfate minerals, likely copper or iron sulfate here</note>, one must proceed with a slow and gentle fire.

Place the green crystals into a broad, shallow vessel. Let them remain in the heat of the sun for three days until they begin to whiten. As the ancient masters observed, "The spirit is drawn out by the heat of the heavens" <note>original: "Spiritus extrahitur per calorem coelestem"</note>.

Since heavy bodies seek the body of the Earth by their own nature, and are sought by it <note>Kepler describes gravity here as a mutual attraction between the Earth and the object, a precursor to Newton's law of universal gravitation</note>, they will therefore move more strongly toward the parts of the Earth that are closer than toward those further away. Since the only question is how much more easily an apple, held by one person, might be knocked away by a companion traveling on the same ship; not how far it goes from the ship or through how much total space between the ship and the shore. For if you consider the shores: to the extent that the ship flees from that higher place where the apple is struck, the strike is nearly that much weaker with respect to the resting shores. This is because the surface beneath the person striking is moving away, which weakens the resistance. Thus, whatever the movement of the ship was going to add to the apple's leap, the yielding of the ship—on which the impact relied—takes away again.

And conversely, what the speed of the ship was going to snatch away from the apple’s downward leap, a stronger resistance to the force of the impact adds back. For the same force strikes downward more powerfully when it is carried along by the ship than when it stands motionless on the shore. But when, as is proper, one considers only the bare forces of the hand grasping the apple and the weight of the apple itself, the force applied is the same on both sides. The magnitude of the effect that occurs outside the ship from a combination of causes contributes nothing to this; even though—relative to the ship alone (and not the shores)—the distance from the ship will be nearly the same.

Therefore, let the same judgment be applied to cannons <note>original: "Bombardis"</note>, with the necessary changes being made <note>original: "mutatis mutandis"</note>. Indeed, a large cannonball, remaining in flight through the air for two minutes of an hour, travels one German mile <term>German mile: a historical unit of distance, roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers</term> westward across the earth. Meanwhile, the earth beneath the equator moves eight miles in the opposite direction. Therefore, with respect to the space of the universe, the ball is still carried seven miles into the opposite region of violent motion—namely, to the east. The explosion in the westward direction provides no other benefit except that it cancels out that eighth mile and makes the ball follow the Earth more slowly toward the east. The gunpowder cannot knock the ball entirely out of the Earth's "hands," as it were; the ball always remains entangled in the Earth's pulling power. If it breaks the grip of the "index finger," it remains caught in the grip of the following "pinky finger." <note>Kepler uses the fingers of a hand as a metaphor to describe how an object never truly escapes the Earth's physical influence or "motive virtue," even when moving through the air.</note>

1. Not at all. Clouds or little birds are in no way comparable to the massive volume of the Ocean waters. Imagine, therefore, a Cloud or a Bird held suspended in the air, not rushing by its own impulse in any direction: that object—just like a stone falling from above—being connected by the **virtue of the Earth** <note>original: "virtute Telluris"; Kepler used the term "virtue" or "power" to describe a magnetic-like attraction that we now call gravity</note> to the fields lying beneath and around it, will be rotated along with the Earth (with respect to cosmic space), always hanging perpendicularly over the same spot. Suppose, then, that an animal’s own impulse is added to it while it is turning in such a condition: it is clear that this impulse will draw the creature out of its perpendicular line toward whatever region the impulse tends; and this happens without distinction, whether toward the east or the west.

*If the Earth were to rotate, would animals and buildings be shaken and collapse, and would growing things be hindered and destroyed by this motion?*

None of these things follow. For the motion is **uniform** <term>uniform motion: motion that travels at a constant speed in a single direction, which Kepler argues is imperceptible to those moving with it</term>, and it does not collide with anything. For all those things are gathered within the innermost bosom and embrace of the **attractive power** <note>original: "virtutis attractricis"</note>, and of the air and mountains moving together with it; being thus carried around, they nevertheless enjoy the greatest tranquility.
Indeed, not even in ships carried uniformly through the swiftest rivers is any restlessness felt, nor are cups full of wine overturned.

*But surely we would at least feel this motion in our own bodies, even with our eyes closed?*

Not at all. For even in Ships, motion is not always felt when they run along uniformly: even though in that case natural bodies are snatched away by their own weight, not toward the ships as ships, but beyond the ships, outward and downward toward the lands lying beneath, which are at rest with respect to the river; yet the ship truly carries those bodies across the path of this line.

This could be granted concerning the highest peaks of the mountains, and from this cooling, a cause could be sought for the perennial snows even under the <term>torrid zone</term> <note>The tropical regions of the Earth near the equator.</note>; likewise for the coldness of the Eastern winds, the pleasantness of the morning, and similar things: provided that both the lower mountain regions and the valleys hidden within those highest peaks, which animals inhabit, were safe; and the air in them remained undisturbed and quiet despite this external friction, allowing freedom for the rising vapors to rush in every direction. ->*What do you think should be answered to the authorities of all ages and all ranks, sacred and profane, which receive without controversy the opposite—that the Earth is at rest in its primary motion, and the sky moves?*<-

**Copernicus** responds thus: 

1. Since the common people are the masters of speech, expressing the sensory perception of the eyes through everyday language, while the Philosopher inquires into the truth that lies beneath the appearing forms of things: it is not absurd for the thoughts of a philosopher to be far removed from the judgment of the common people. 

2. Certain passages of Scripture are wrongly twisted to serve an astronomical purpose: the judgments of those who are accustomed to doing this, however rash, are to be despised. This response can be explained at greater length. For **Astronomy** reveals the causes of natural things and professionally investigates the deceptions of sight; the sacred books, delivering much more sublime teachings, use the common speech of men, so that...

Look throughout this entire first book for traces of popular scriptural expressions regarding the shape of the world and its motions, about which there is no controversy: why, then, do we labor so hard here only concerning the motion of the Earth?

Certain other passages are also dragged into this debate which are not even to be examined by the perception of the eyes, but are clearly foreign to our purpose, as the context of the text proves. This occurs when the scriptures speak not of astronomical state or "rest," but of the physical duration of the Earth, while animals on its surface meanwhile die and are born; or when the firmness of the ground upon which animals walk is compared with their various motions; or when it is an allegory, in which the "strengthening of the pillars of the Earth" <note>original: *confirmationem columnarum Terrae*</note> signifies the calming of wars and public tranquility.

*You said that for the demonstration of the primary motion, a material sphere is necessary. What then is a material sphere, and why is it so called?*

It is called a "sphere" from its globular shape, for a globe is called <note>original: "σφαῖρα"</note> *sphaira* by the Greeks. It is "material" because it is made from some physical matter, such as paper, wood, or metal. It consists of certain specific circles that outline a single spherical surface. In the center, a small globe is suspended from an axis passing through the middle of the sphere. Thus arranged, it is an image of the world as our sight imagines it; it is designed so that the principles of the <term>primary motion</term> <note>This refers to the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky around the Earth, caused by the Earth's own rotation.</note> and those things that depend on the primary motion can be demonstrated to the eye as if by an instrument.

*What is represented by the surface of the sphere?*

The heavens and the stars within them.

*What by the innermost globe?*

The globe of the Earth.

*But you said it is unknown where the outermost surface of the world is; how then can it be represented?*

Just as in geometry a circle is drawn around any point on a plane by "geometrical license," so also in the discipline of optics, every eye imagines some spherical surface cast around itself—whether that surface passes through the middle of the fixed stars, or is above them, or below them. And the likeness of such a surface, at least an imaginary one, is found on the surface of the sphere.

*You stated above that the Earth is insignificant <note>The Latin "insensibilem" suggests the Earth is so small in comparison to the heavens that it has no measurable size in that context.</note> compared to the heavens; this little globe in the sphere is necessarily visible, so is it not then a false likeness?*

This globe represents not the size of the Earth, but only the Earth itself. For it could neither be seen nor manufactured, nor could its parts be distinguished, if it corresponded in proportion to the smallness of the Earth.

*You denied above that the Earth is in the center of the world; why then is its likeness in the center of the sphere?*

Because the Earth, which this globe represents, is the home of our eyes; and indeed every eye, through its imagination, surrounds itself with...

*Since there are so many eyes <note>The "eyes" refer to individual observers or points of view on the Earth's surface.</note>, and just as many imaginary spheres, why is there only one small globe here, the indicator of the Earth's eye, a single sphere?*

Because all imaginary spheres are similar to one another, and thus even equal—that is, they constitute a single sphere. For although there are many eyes, and therefore many centers for that sphere (both because of the multitude of eyes across the entire circumference of the Earth, and because of the various positions of the Earth in its great circle around the sun—which is discussed in the theoretical teaching), nevertheless, all that distance between the centers or eyes vanishes entirely when compared to the vastness of the sphere of the fixed stars. <note>Kepler is explaining that because the stars are so incredibly far away, the "parallax" (the change in appearance from different vantage points) is so small that every observer on Earth effectively sees the same sky.</note>

### Where does the name Horizon come from?

In Greek it is called the *horizōn* <note>original: ὁρίζων</note>, and in Latin it is called the *Finitor* <note>the "Finisher" or "Limiter"</note>, because it terminates or finishes our vision. It divides the upper and visible part of the world from the lower part that is not visible; thus, all things above this boundary or *horos* <note>original: ὅρον</note> can be seen, but those that exist below it can no longer be seen. A star falling upon this circle either begins to be seen by rising, or ceases to be seen by setting.

### What, then, of the World is represented by the Horizon circle of the Sphere?

It is no fixed or constant part of the world; rather, it is that edge of the heavens, in whatever position it may be, where the visible hemisphere ends. That is, it is the place where all straight lines extending from the eye of the observer reach the furthest parts of the visible globe of the Earth—for example, the peaks of mountains or the swell of the sea.

### Since the stars are not on the same spherical surface, is the boundary of what is seen not the edge of a single surface, but rather a flat plane extending from the eye into the depths of the world?

<margin>but
is
[cip]
[ce]</margin> <note>These marginal fragments appear to be truncated guides for the reader or remnants of a previous layout.</note>
The previous answer must be repeated: although it is true that the stars are not on the same spherical surface, our sight nevertheless imagines them all to exist on the same spherical surface. This is because, for those bodies that are beyond the furthest mountains, our sight lacks the tools to distinguish between what is near and what is remote. The material sphere <term>Material sphere: A physical model of the heavens, such as an armillary sphere, used to represent celestial motions</term> is an image of this visual imagination. Therefore, the Horizon represents the limit of those things that are seen, insofar as our sight imagines it as a line, without regard for which thing seen is closer to the eye or further from it.

*How do you prove the <term>Horizon</term> <note>From the Greek "horizōn," meaning "limiting." It is the boundary where the sky appears to meet the earth.</note> is a circle?*

When any spherical surface is cut by a flat plane, the resulting section is a circle. Now, the shape of the world—at least from the perspective of our vision—is a spherical surface. The earthly Horizon is conceived of as a flat plane cutting through that sphere, as judged by our sight <note>original: "visu quidem judice"</note> (as we stated at the beginning). Therefore, it is a circle.

*But that view—the limit of our sight—is not a perfect circle. Instead, it is a winding border that moves through the summits of the farthest mountains, which are naturally not all of equal height. Truly, the lines of sight drawn through those peaks do not align on a single flat plane.*

That is certainly true. However, because this uneven height of mountains varies from place to place—and in some places, like the middle of the Ocean, there is no such unevenness at all—reason suggests we define an "average" in a physical model <note>original: "Effigie materiali"; likely referring to a physical globe or an armillary sphere used for teaching</note>. This allows us to compare the various parts of the World, whether they bulge outward or sink downward, against a consistent baseline.

*What distinction of Horizons arises from this?*

The Horizon is either Visible or Rational <note>The "Rational" or "Astronomical" horizon is an imaginary plane passing through the center of the Earth, parallel to the observer's local horizon.</note>.

*What is the Visible Horizon?*

In Geography, the Visible Horizon is understood as that portion or region of the earth's surface that comes into view at once during a single rotation of the eyes. This area is narrow if the eye is in a valley, and wider if it is on a very high mountain (see the table on page 23). Indeed, such a Horizon would not exist at all if the Earth were perfectly round and the observer's eye were placed exactly on the earth's surface. Therefore, where there is a wide plain, the Horizon is called "free"; where mountains stand in the way, the Horizon is "impeded."

146 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY.
if someone is standing on a very high mountain or promontory, and looking either down the course of a river or toward the far reaches of the sea, the Horizon seems to gape open. These are the descriptors of the Mundane Visible Horizon as compared to the Rational Horizon.

*How does Reason establish the Rational Horizon, if it is deprived of Sight for this task?*

It is not completely deprived of sight, but rather uses it and assists it with an instrument called a <term>dioptra<note>A sighting tube or rod used by early astronomers to align their vision with specific points in the sky or on a scale.</note></term>. For the line of the dioptra, such as AH, when it makes a right angle with the <term>plumb line<note>original: "lineâ perpendiculi" — a cord with a weight used to find a perfectly vertical line toward the center of gravity.</note></term> NA, it directs the eye toward the Rational Horizon; and when rotated around, it describes the plane of the Rational Horizon. Therefore, the rational horizon is everywhere at a distance of a <term>quadrant<note>A quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees.</note></term> of a great circle from the plumb line. The visual ray passing through the dioptra, where it falls upon land masses (K) or mountains, judges those to stand out above the rational horizon; but where it meets the clear sky because the earth sinks away, it judges that, in respect to that lower region, the observer is standing in an elevated position.

*What are the poles of the Rational Horizon?*
The vertical point, called **Zenith** in Arabic, and its opposite, called **Nadir**.

*What is the Vertical point?*
It is the point on the visible sphere upon which the plumb line falls—that is, a straight line imagined to be drawn from the center of the earth through the eye of the observer. For a line from the center of a globe necessarily falls at right angles to the surface of a perfect globe, and is therefore perpendicular to it—that is, to the plane of the Rational <term>finitor<note>original: "finitoris" — a Latin term for the horizon, meaning "that which limits" or "defines" the view.</note></term>.

*Why is it called Vertical?*
Because the human body stands upright according to the plumb line

### Why, then, is there only one Horizon on the sphere?

Because any sphere, in any one of its positions, is an image of a certain and unique view of the heavens. Furthermore, that single horizon on the sphere can be adapted in turn to all the various Horizons in the World.

*If the two worldly Horizons of two opposite places on Earth (or even of the Earth's revolution around the sun) are distinct from one another, separated everywhere by the full diameter of the Earth (or even the orbit of the Earth around the sun), will the whole sky not be divided by them into two visible Hemispheres? Instead, would there not be left in the middle a border of the sky, the width of this diameter, which would belong to neither Hemisphere?* <note>The author is addressing a common astronomical objection: if the Earth is large, or if it moves in a wide orbit, the "horizon" seen from one side should be different from the other, creating a gap in the middle of the sky.</note>

It is true; but that celestial border vanishes due to its immense distance from the eye and its negligible thinness. Indeed, it appears narrower from a distance than one of the fixed stars, as was proven above in Book 1, page 87. Therefore, in this context, a single Horizon used on a material sphere <term>material sphere: a physical model of the heavens, like an armillary sphere, used for teaching astronomy</term> suffices for two parallel lines separated from each other; it is just as if both, passing through the same center, coincided completely.

*I grant that one Horizon suffices for the fixed stars; but what about the planets, which are not as far removed from us as the fixed stars?*

In the primary motion <term>primary motion: the apparent daily rotation of the stars and planets around the Earth from East to West</term>, we consider planets no differently than we imagine them—guided by our sight—to be positioned among the fixed stars themselves. In fact, we do not consider the planet itself at its actual distance from the Earth, but rather use the planet's apparent position among the fixed stars. Moreover, we usually presuppose the Planet to be immobile at a single point throughout an entire diurnal revolution, or 24 hours. For

*Why, however, is the <term>material sphere</term><note>An armillary sphere: a physical model of the heavens made of nested rings representing the great circles of the sky.</note> rotatable around this axis and its poles, while the globe in the middle is fixed to it and remains immobile, since you said earlier that the sphere of the fixed stars stands still, while the earth—of which that little globe is the image—rotates?*

Even though the truth was stated above, because our sight judges otherwise—namely, in a popular manner—that the earth stands still and the heavens revolve, this is expressed in this way in the material sphere, adapted to a single location on Earth. For the sphere is an image of the world such as our vision imagines it for itself, as was said above.

*But how can the true causes of those things that happen in the heavens be handed down through an instrument that partakes in falsehood?*

This deception of the eyes, even when transferred to an instrument, does not hinder us from drawing out the true causes. For most of the <term>circles</term><note>The imaginary lines used for navigation and mapping the stars, such as the equator, tropics, and ecliptic.</note> in the sky and on the earth are the same, and are subordinated to one another in a line drawn from the center of the earth into the sky. It is already certain that parts of the celestial expanse are separated from the corresponding parts of the earth's expanse (through which these circles pass) by the <term>daily motion</term><note>The apparent rotation of the sky every 24 hours.</note>, and after a full circuit is completed, they return to their first correspondence—regardless of whether the sky moves while the earth remains at rest, or the earth moves while the sky remains at rest upon the world-axis. Both of these can be represented in a material sphere.

*Why then, out of two options that provide the same result—namely, the motion of the sky or the motion of the earth—is the one that is true (the motion of the earth) not expressed in the material sphere?*

1. Because it is the Astronomer’s duty to provide the reasons why our sight imagines this or that for itself—for instance, why the sun appears to rise now in this place and now in that on the <term>Horizon</term>, for in truth it does not move. Now, these causes are explained otherwise—

## II. The Meridian.

### 154 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY

->*By what principles is the Meridian established?*<-
   We imagine, on the Earth, a circle passing through our place of habitation and through the poles of the Earth; in the "fixed" stars <note>the celestial sphere of stars that appear not to move relative to one another</note>, a circle drawn through the Vertical point <term>Zenith: the point directly above an observer</term> of each place, and its opposite, or Nadir, and through the poles of the Sphere.
   *In this diagram and the others, F is the Zenith, G is the Nadir,* **B and C are the poles.**

->*What kind of circle is the Meridian?*<-
   It is one of the <term>great circles: a circle on a sphere's surface that shares the same center as the sphere, dividing it into two equal halves</term>; for it is drawn through both poles, and thus its flat surface <note>plane</note> passes through the axis and through the eye—which is the center of the Sphere—and cuts the sphere in half.

->*Why is it called the Meridian?*<-
   From midday <note>original Latin: *meridies*</note>: For since it is erected perpendicularly above the Horizon, it cuts the visible Hemisphere into two equal parts. Therefore the Sun, reaching it by its daily motion, creates midday in the place to which that Meridian belongs. For "Meridies" is used in place of "Medidie," or "mid-day" <note>original Latin: *media die*</note>, because the part of the day already passed is equal to the part remaining. Because of this, the stars are also said to "mediate the sky" <note>reach their highest point or culminate</note> when they reach this circle.

->*Into what parts is the Sphere divided by the Meridian?*<-
   Into two Hemispheres, or into the halves or Quarters of the sky established by the Horizon—the Eastern and Western; or the rising and setting. Since both the Pole and the Zenith are in the Meridian, and the stars move in circles around the pole, they never become closer to the zenith—that is, higher in the sky—except when they are in the meridian.

->*How many Meridians are there?*<-
   In a material sphere <note>a physical model such as an armillary sphere</note> there is only one Meridian, because any such sphere, by its very placement, represents one specific location on earth. But with respect to the Earth, since the sight of the Horizon and the vertical point establish the Meridian, there are as many Meridians as there are locations in one circle of the earth...

It establishes the Meridian's role in dividing the sky into eastern and western halves and determining the highest point of a star's path.</summary>

[Diagram of a celestial sphere with various lines and points labeled with letters: T, L, B, D, O, R, S, P, E, G, Q, n, a, m.]

*How is the equinoctial of the physical sphere established?* <note>The "material" or physical sphere refers to an armillary sphere—a brass or wooden model of the heavens used for teaching.</note>

*What kind of circle is the equator?*

It is one of the "great circles" <term>great circle: a circle on the surface of a sphere that shares the same center as the sphere, dividing it into two equal halves</term>, because it is equidistant from the poles of the Sphere.

*What is the reason for these names?*

By the Greeks it is called *isēmerinos* <note>original: ἰσημερινὸς</note>, meaning "equal-day," and by the Latins it is called the *equinoctial*, because when the Sun reaches it, the days are made equal to the nights. It is called the **Equator**, however, both from this function and from its role in "equating," examining, and measuring the entire prime motion <note>the daily rotation of the heavens around the Earth</note>. Modern sailors call it **THE LINE**, because it is depicted on their flat maps as a straight line.

*Which locations on Earth lie upon the equator?*

The equator passes through the Island of **Saint Thomas** <note>modern São Tomé</note> in the great gulf of Africa, which is called the Ethiopian Ocean. Having crossed Ethiopia—a part of Africa—it passes over the City of **Arim**, celebrated by Jewish and Saracen <note>historical term for Muslim</note> astronomers as the center of the World; from there, it crosses the Indian Ocean and within it the Island of **Taprobane** <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>, the **Golden Chersonese** <note>the Malay Peninsula</note>, and the innumerable **Sporades** <note>scattered islands</note> of the Eastern Ocean. Then, having sailed past the shores of the Magellanic lands <note>a reference to the hypothesized southern continent, *Terra Australis*</note> from a distance—where it takes the name **New Guinea**—it traverses a vast stretch of the Southern Ocean, and finally reaches **Peru**. It passes near Lake **Guajano** and the city of **Manoa** <note>the legendary "Golden City" of El Dorado</note>, and entering the Atlantic Ocean once more, it completes the remainder of the circle back to the shores of Africa.

### IV. The Zodiac.

[Diagram: A celestial sphere or armillary sphere is shown. It features a prominent diagonal band representing the Zodiac, marked with various letters and astrological symbols for the constellations. The Earth sits at the center, surrounded by the rings of the celestial equator and the polar axes.]

**How did it happen that they established the Zodiac in the <term>Material Sphere<note>A physical model of the heavens, often called an armillary sphere, constructed from metal rings to show the paths of stars and planets.</note></term>?**
The Sun, Moon, and Planets appear to mark a certain path in the starry sky by their motions or their appearances. This path circles the middle of the "Sphere of fixed stars" as we observe it, placed so that we are in its plane. For one part of that path, occupying the east, and another part in the west, are always seen by us in one and the same straight line; never are both parts seen from the same side of the sky at once. The representation of this path, which is called the Zodiac, in a physical model is that wide Band <note>original: "Limbus"</note> tilted at an angle to the <term>Equinoctial<note>The celestial equator; the circle in the sky directly above the Earth's equator.</note></term>.

In this diagram and the others, **L M Q N** represents the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>the belt of the heavens through which the sun and planets appear to move</note> and its <term>poles</term> <note>the fixed points around which the celestial sphere rotates</note> are **O** and **P** in this instance.

Why, however, does this circle alone among all those of the <term>material sphere</term> <note>a physical model of the heavens, often called an armillary sphere, used for teaching astronomy</note> possess such great width?

Because only the sun, by its center, is observed to trace the middle line of it and to travel perpetually along it; the other planets rarely stay exactly on that line. Instead, they usually wander out to its sides by a distance that determines the width of this "rim" or band as it is constructed on a physical globe.

How great is this width?

The ancient astronomers, looking primarily at the motion of the Moon, set the width at twelve degrees. However, if this width must encompass the <term>evagations</term> <note>the "wandering" or deviation of a planet from the central path of the sun</note> of all the planets, including Mars and Venus, it must be larger. Since the deviation for Mars is seven degrees and for Venus is ten degrees from the center, the Zodiac would need a total width of 14 or 20 degrees <note>doubling the deviation to account for movement on both sides of the center line</note>.

V. VI. The Tropics.

*What is the origin of the Tropics?*

The <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun through the sky over the course of a year.</note> is at an angle to the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and is thus oblique to the <term>first motion</term> <note>original: "primum motum" — the daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note>. Imagine, therefore, a line drawn from the center of the earth to two points of the Ecliptic among the fixed stars which are the furthest distance from the equinoctial, one toward the north and the other toward the south. Imagine also that the earth meanwhile revolves while this line remains still; this line, as it is carried around, will therefore cut the surface of the earth on both sides in a circle—not a "great circle" <note>A circle that divides the sphere into two equal halves, like the equator.</note> but a smaller one, positioned at the side of the equator. The representations of these two circles are usually depicted on the small globe of a <term>material sphere</term> <note>An armillary sphere, a physical model of the celestial coordinates.</note>. Next, imagine this line fixed at some point of this terrestrial circle, and nevertheless extended as far as the fixed stars, going around with the earth—or even remaining still with the earth while the heaven of the fixed stars revolves. That line therefore describes a circle in the highest heaven of the fixed stars, corresponding to the previous circle on the earth, and this occurs in both regions of the sky. The representations of these two circles, therefore, are those two collateral circles in the material sphere.

*In the diagram on page 156. LS. and RQ.*

*Where does the name "Tropics" come from?*

From the Greek word <note>original: "τροπὴ" (tropē)</note> *turning*: For the Sun, coming to the points of the Ecliptic through which these circles pass—namely, to the beginnings of Cancer and Capricorn—turns its course to some extent. Previously, it had always wandered further and further from the equator toward the side while proceeding, and thus, in the position of our sphere, outside the Tropics...

Since the sun had been rising higher in the sky each day at noon toward the **Tropics** <note>The tropics are the latitudes marking the northernmost and southernmost points where the sun can be directly overhead.</note>, it now begins to turn its course back toward the **equator** again, and each day it appears lower at noon. The opposite occurs at the opposing point of the **Ecliptic** <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the sun across the sky over the course of a year.</note>. Because of this, the seasons in Greece also change; these changes are therefore called *tropai* <note>original Greek: τροπαὶ, meaning "turnings."</note>. They are called the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, each named after the specific point on the Ecliptic which it touches.

**How else are they named?**

They are called **Solstitial** because before that turning of the sun's course—or rather, the turning of its <term>declination</term> <note>Declination is the astronomical term for the distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the midline of the equator—is perceived, the sun meanwhile is found at the same distance from the equator for several days. Consequently, it is also found at the same height during the noon hours, and so, in respect to this unchanging declination and height which it reaches daily at noon, it seems in a way to "stand still" <note>The word "solstice" is derived from the Latin *sol* (sun) and *sistere* (to stand still).</note>. Lucan, in Book 9 of the *Pharsalia* <note>A famous Roman epic poem by Lucan regarding the civil war between Caesar and Pompey.</note>, calls the Tropic of Cancer the "circle of the high solstice," and says that it "strikes"—that is, touches—the middle of the **zodiac**... <note>The Latin text cuts off at "fign," likely for "signiferi," meaning the "sign-bearing" circle or zodiac.</note>

BOOK THREE. 365

...according to Copernicus, the mundane Horizon: but here we will treat the appearance and disappearance of stars, which is caused by the Sun and by the light of day.

*How are the risings and settings considered in this place named?*

They are commonly thought to be called **Poetic**, for the reason that Poets use them in their descriptions of the seasons <note>The author refers to "Poetic risings," a traditional method used by ancient authors like Hesiod or Ovid to mark the time for farming or sailing based on when certain stars first appeared in the sky.</note>: to me, this name does not seem to belong to the whole class, but only to one specific type.

*In what sense, then, are the words "to rise" and "to set" or "to depart" used here?*

The sense of these phrases is twofold, even in this context. The first is the popular sense: when night approaches and the light of day is extinguished, all the stars indiscriminately are said to "rise"—those which were previously present but hidden under the light of day. Conversely, when light arises at the Sun's approach, the stars are said to "depart"—those which, though they were previously shining and visible, are now hidden by the light of day, so that although they are still present in the high heaven, they can no longer be discerned.

The other meaning is more restricted and specific to the <term>art|The "art" refers specifically to the science of astronomy</term>, and is used for those stars which, because of the Sun's annual motion through the <term>Zodiac|The circle of twelve constellations through which the Sun appears to move annually</term>, undergo cycles of Rising and Setting.

*How many types of such Risings are there?*

Today, three types of poetic rising and setting are commonly counted: **Cosmic**, **Acronychal**, and **Heliacal**.

*What do they call the Cosmic rising and setting?*

Modern astronomers designate with the epithet **Cosmic** the *beginning*...

# 366 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

...the beginning of the day, for an obscure reason: as if that star rises **Cosmically** <note>original: "Cosmicè"; from the Greek *kosmos*, here referring to the physical world or the horizon</note> which rises when the sun is rising, and sets **Cosmically** which sets when the sun is rising.
    I define the **Cosmic rising or setting** simply and generally as that which occurs when a star emerges above the Worldly Horizon, or descends below it, without regard for the position of the Sun.

->*What is the **Acronychal** rising or setting?*<-
    An **Acronychal rising** <note>original: "Acronychus"; from the Greek *akros* (edge) and *nyx* (night), referring to the boundaries of the night (dusk or dawn)</note> is when a star emerges above the Horizon at one "edge" or boundary of the night—that is, at its beginning—while the Sun sets in the opposite region. To Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a famous Roman naturalist and author</note> this is the **Evening Rising**.
    *The common people of today add this definition of the **Acronychal setting**: when a star sets as the Sun sets—that is, together with the Sun.*
    I define the **Acronychal setting** as occurring when the star sets at the other "edge" or boundary of the night—that is, at its end. To Pliny, this is the **Morning Setting**.

->*What is the **Heliacal** Rising and Setting?*<-
    A star rises **Heliacally** <note>original: "Heliacè"; from the Greek *helios* (sun)</note>—that is, it begins to appear—when a star that was previously hidden under the rays of the Sun (so that it rose and set at almost the same time as the Sun) emerges from the Sun's rays on the following day to such an extent that, while the Sun stays hidden below the Horizon, the star can first be seen, just as it is about to sink below the Horizon or be extinguished (if it had risen from the Horizon) by the arrival of daylight.
    A star sets **Heliacally**, or is hidden, when it was previously seen above the Horizon while the Sun was submerged not far below it, but now hides itself so far within the Sun's rays that on the following day, whether rising from the Horizon or about to sink below it, it can no longer be seen. The former would be more rightly called an **Appearance** or **Emergence**, and the latter an **Occultation**. Pliny, Book 18, Chapter 25.

BOOK THREE. 367

Either by the Sun’s arrival stars are hidden and cease to be seen, or by its departure they reveal themselves. Custom would have better called this "Emergence" <note>original Latin: *Emersum*</note> rather than "Rising": and the other "Hiding" <note>original Latin: *Occultationem*</note> rather than "Setting." Thus the Greeks call it an *Appearance* <note>original Greek: *Epitolēn*</note>, not a *Rising* <note>original Greek: *anatolēn*</note>; likewise they call it a *Phasis* <note>a "showing" or "appearance" of a celestial body</note>; and they use *Hiding* <note>original Greek: *krypsin*</note> or *Disappearing* <note>original Greek: *aphanismon*</note> instead of *Setting* <note>original Greek: *dysei*</note>.

I think this type of rising and setting was formerly called by the specific name "Poetic" <note>original Greek: *poiētikēn*</note>, as if it were "fictional"; this is because the stars do not truly rise or set in a physical sense, but only *appear* to rise or set to our eyes.

<margin>*What then shall become of the common "Cosmic Rising" and "Acronychal Setting"?*</margin>

I believe those types, as the common crowd defines them, ought to be named differently—if indeed any place is left for them in this branch of teaching. Certainly they are not "Poetic" in the ordinary sense of that word; for what poets would make use of them, given that they cannot actually be seen? Let them rather be called "Astronomical," and let them be termed <term>risings and settings with the Sun</term> <note>These occur when a star rises or sets at the exact same time as the sun, making it invisible to the naked eye due to the sun's glare.</note>. Pliny calls these "Morning Risings" and "Settings"...

[marginal note: akron] <note>original: "ἀκρ", short for akron, meaning "the edge" or "extremity."</note> "beginning and end," and Ptolemy calls the Planets *Acronychal* <term>Acronychal: from the Greek for "at nightfall," referring to a star that rises as the sun sets.</term> throughout the whole night: specifically, those rising at the beginning of the night as well as those setting at its end. It seems the intention of whoever devised this name was to show that the star then undergoes conditions opposite to the Sun; namely, rising at the start of night while the Sun rises at the start of day; and therefore setting when the Sun rises. 

But what else does the term *Cosmical* <note>original: "Cosmici," meaning "relating to the world" or the horizon.</note> signify than that which is opposed to the Sun, when we ask in respect to what the star rises and sets—is it in respect to the Sun or the World (that is, the Worldly Horizon)? Next, regarding the prominent stars—specifically those that fall within the Zodiac—their *Evening Rising* and *Morning Setting* are joined by reason of time. Why, then, should these be distinguished by different names, so that one is called *Acronychal* and the other *Cosmical*? The same logic applies to *Morning Rising* and *Evening Setting*: why should I get into the habit of calling the rising of the same star "Cosmical" and its setting "Acronychal" on the very same day? 

Thirdly, rising and setting with the Sun are usually surrounded by *Emergence* and *Disappearance* <note>original: "Emersio & Occultatio," referring to when a star first becomes visible or finally becomes hidden by the sun's glare.</note>; what is the need to distinguish these narrow windows of time even more subtly and laboriously through these "cosmical risings" and (in the popular sense) "acronychal settings"? 

Finally, those we call *Heliacal* <note>relating to the sun; when a star is just far enough from the sun to be visible.</note> are seen; those I call *Acronychal* are also seen; they are useful to Farmers, Physicians, Historians, and Poets for common descriptions of the Seasons. But those "spurious" Risings and Settings with the Sun—which some enrich with the names *Cosmical* for the former and *Acronychal* for the latter—are not seen at all. They are not to be sought from the sky but from the books of Astronomers, and are recognized only by those who have studied Astronomy. 

Therefore, I have noted no approved author who used these names in the popular sense, nor even for the purpose of common descriptions. On the contrary, when Pliny and others use these inconspicuous risings and settings in describing the seasons, they use different names (as mentioned before) and do so for a different purpose—not to describe the seasons with common markers, but

*In which parts of the day do **Heliacal Risings and Settings** occur?* <note>A "heliacal" event (from the Greek *helios*, meaning Sun) happens when a star or planet first becomes visible in the dawn sky just before sunrise, or last appears in the evening sky just after sunset, before being lost in the Sun's brightness.</note>

Thus, they are seen emerging in the region of the **Rising** (the East), while in the **Setting** (the West) they are lost, hidden beneath the rays. 

There are exceptions, however: 
1. Always the **Moon**, and also **Mercury** and **Venus** at those times when—like the Moon—they are moving faster than the Sun itself and are in "direct" motion <note>Moving in the normal direction through the zodiac rather than appearing to move backward.</note>. In these cases (like the Moon), they are found to have emerged in the West during the evening, and to have disappeared in the East during the morning, hidden beneath the Sun's rays.

2. Therefore, based on the previously explained teaching, it is necessary to know the degree of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year</term> that rises or sets together with a given star, and the angle that the Ecliptic makes with the Horizon in those parts of the sky. For this reason, the arc of the Ecliptic OS opposite the right angle is also found, which is the arc between the rising or setting point O and the Sun at S.

->*In what order do the various risings and settings of the same fixed star follow one another?*<-

1. A star always rises with the Sun <term>cosmical rising</term> <note>original Latin: "oritur cum Sole"; this refers to the moment the star and Sun cross the horizon at the same time</note> before it rises out of the Sun <term>heliacal rising</term> <note>the first day a star becomes visible in the morning twilight after being lost in the Sun's glare</note>; similarly, it sets with the Sun <term>cosmical setting</term> later than it disappears under the Sun's rays <term>heliacal setting</term> <note>the last day a star is visible in the evening before the Sun's light masks it</note>.

2. When the star's <term>latitude</term> <note>distance north or south of the Ecliptic, the Sun's path</note> is northern, the star first rises with the sun, then reaches the <term>midheaven</term> <note>the highest point in its daily arc</note> with it, and finally sets with the Sun. It follows this same order for its <term>acronychal</term> <note>original: "acronychos"; referring to a star rising exactly as the Sun sets</note> risings and settings. When the star is southern, the opposite occurs. If the star is positioned exactly on the <term>ecliptic</term> itself, all three of these events must necessarily coincide.

3. Heliacal risings and settings also change their order among different stars, both in relation to each other and in relation to the aforementioned risings and settings with the Sun. However, the common boundary for this variation is not the Ecliptic; rather, it is found among those stars that have such a great northern latitude that they can rise and set heliacally on one and the same day. For stars that are further north than these at any given ecliptic longitude, they emerge from the Sun's rays first and are hidden under them later; this happens on days closer to their <term>meridian transit</term> <note>original: "Mediationi cœli"; when the star crosses the north-south line of the sky</note> than their risings and settings with the Sun. But stars that are further south than these limits are hidden first and emerge later, rising and setting with the Sun in the intervening time, so that their heliacal risings and settings are further removed from their transit of the midheaven.

### 378 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

This is the sought-after declination <term>declination: the angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator</term> of a star which indicates a latitude of 12 degrees, 57 minutes North at 0 degrees of Cancer: a first-magnitude star will have such a position that, while the Sun is moving through 0 degrees of Cancer, the star itself rises and sets on that same day.

**Can you show the variation of these appearances using the example of Arcturus?**

Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a famous Danish nobleman and astronomer known for his incredibly accurate astronomical observations.</note> locates **Arcturus** at 18 degrees, 40 minutes of Libra; its Latitude is 31 degrees, 3 minutes North. Therefore its Right Ascension is 209 degrees, 24 minutes. Its Culmination <note>original: "Cœli Meditio," referring to when the star reaches its highest point in the sky</note> is at 1 degree, 34 minutes of Scorpio. Its Declination is 21 degrees, 19 minutes North. From these figures, the types of its Risings and Settings are calculated by Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), a German astronomer and mathematician who was the mentor of Johannes Kepler.</note> as shown in the following table:

| Date | Position of the Sun | Appearance of Arcturus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| March 23 <note>The text lists dates like "13. 23." likely reflecting the 10-day difference between the old Julian calendar and the New Gregorian calendar.</note> | 2 degrees, 24 minutes of Aries | Rises in the Evening |
| June 16 | 25 degrees, 18 minutes of Gemini | Sets in the Morning |
| September 25 | 2 degrees, 24 minutes of Libra | Rises with the Sun |
| Sept 29–Oct 9 | 15 degrees, 40 minutes of Libra | Emerges from the Sun's rays |
| October 25 | 1 degree, 34 minutes of Scorpio | Culminates with the Sun |
| November 25 | 3 degrees, 2 minutes of Sagittarius | Is hidden in the Evening |
| December 17 | 25 degrees, 18 minutes of Sagittarius | Sets with the Sun |

Therefore, from the time of the Equinox until almost the Solstice—specifically from March 23rd until June 16th—the star Arcturus is seen *all night long* <term>pernox: a term used for a star that is visible in the sky from sunset until sunrise</term>. However, its actual rising above the Horizon and its setting below it cannot be observed because of the light of day. For on March 23rd, rising at the very moment of Sunset, it remains above the Horizon for a longer duration than the Sun remains below it. In the following days, as the Sun sets, Arcturus has already climbed above the Horizon, so that it is revealed along with the other stars once the light of day has faded; it is then hidden by the arrival of the following day's light before it has even set.

Meanwhile, the Sun reaches 1 degree, 34 minutes of Taurus; then Arcturus [at the] heaven's [meridian]...

THIRD BOOK. 379

...occupies the <term>middle of the sky<note>The meridian; the highest point a star reaches in its daily path across the sky.</note></term> at the stroke of midnight, and the intervals of its rising above the horizon and its setting below it are equal distances from the beginning and end of daylight.
      Therefore, for other stars located in the <term>South<note>In the original Latin: "Austro". Referring to stars in the southern celestial hemisphere.</note></term>, their stay above the horizon is short; they are not visible all night, but are seen to both rise and set within the same night when the sun is moving in opposition to them. But **Arcturus**, in this position, rises before sunset and sets after sunrise, making it invisible at both of those specific moments. <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin>
      On June 16, although the night is at its shortest, **Arcturus** ceases to be visible throughout the whole night; indeed, it sets at the very moment of sunrise, and thus before that time, while it is still night, it withdraws below the horizon from our sight. Therefore, from June 16 until November 25, the setting of **Arcturus** occurs during the night, passing gradually from the beginning of the night to its end: its setting is thus observed for five full months. <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin>
      Conversely, from October 9, its rising above the horizon emerges from the sun's rays, and its rising remains visible from that day until March 23, when, as stated, it ceases to rise after the end of the day, and thus during the night. <margin><unclear>illegible</unclear></margin>
      Between these intervals, in a shared span of time—which is between October 9 and November 25, lasting 47 days—both events happen during the night: the rising of **Arcturus** above the horizon as well as its setting below it. Thus, both can be observed while the sun passes closest to **Arcturus** and <term>culminates<note>original: "cœlum mediante"; reaching the highest point in the sky.</note></term> with it. But southern stars, by contrast, are not seen at all when they have the sun present with them. And southern stars are indeed hidden earlier by the sun's rays in the evening and emerge later from those rays in the morning; **Arcturus** follows the opposite order, emerging first in the morning on October 9, and being hidden later in the evening on November 25. <margin>Arcturus [in the] sky</margin>

380 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*How do writers use these risings and settings of the stars, and for what purpose?*

The Greek nations, and the Romans following their custom, anciently used a year mixed from both lunar and solar cycles <note>A "lunisolar" calendar, which attempts to reconcile the cycles of the moon with the Earth's orbit around the sun.</note>. From this, it happened that they were sometimes ahead of the Sun and sometimes behind it. Since the seasons of the year do not return according to an erroneous calendar, but rather with the Sun and the solstices, it was necessary to find a better guide. So that agricultural, domestic, and military tasks might each be performed in their proper season, the Ancients put forward the risings and settings of the stars in place of a calendar. 

Some did this out of necessity, and some for the sake of instruction. This was because copies of a calendar could not be obtained in such abundance as they are today. Furthermore, even if calendars were displayed in public, they could not be understood by country folk, who were both illiterate and lived far away in the fields. These celestial signs, however, could be observed even by the unlettered. Finally, some sought to decorate their speech, such as the poets; luxuriating in a flowery style of writing, they used these signs to describe and, as it were, "paint" the seasons through their surrounding circumstances. Indeed, no circumstance is more beautiful than the varied risings and settings of so many stars.

*In how many ways are ancient times compared with modern ones, for the purpose of this marking of time through the risings and settings of the stars?*

The comparison is threefold:
I. By reason of one and the same Roman Calendar.
II. By reason of the motion of the Sun in the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year</term>.
III. By reason of the rising and setting of the stars themselves.

Of these, the first and the last are of little use unless they are brought back to the middle one. For the first comparison is merely historical or political; the last <margin>C m</margin> savors of astrological practice <note>The author suggests that looking at the stars alone, without grounding them in the Sun's path (the ecliptic), leans toward astrology rather than pure astronomical science.</note>.

<summary>This page explains that ancient civilizations used the stars as a practical calendar for farming and war because paper calendars were rare and most people were illiterate. It also categorizes the three ways scholars compare ancient timekeeping with modern systems.</summary>
<keywords>Roman calendar, Greek calendar, lunisolar year, heliacal rising, agricultural cycles, ecliptic, history of astronomy</keywords>

### BOOK THREE. 381

...subtlety; the middle sort, however, is rustic, domestic, medical, and natural.

<margin>*Why do you call only the last comparison "natural"? Do those risings of the Stars, then, accomplish nothing?*</margin>

The ancients were indeed of the opinion that whatever violent storms usually occurred nearly every year around the rising of any particular star were produced, or at least signaled, by the rising or setting of that star. From this arose a peculiar use of the Greek words *sēmainei* <note>original: "σημαινει"</note>, *prosēmainei* <note>original: "προσημαινει"</note>, and *episēmainei* <note>original: "επισημαινει"</note> <note>These Greek terms generally mean to signify, to portend, or to give a sign beforehand.</note>, for which we Germans say: *it weathers before or after* <note>original: "es wittert vor oder nach"</note>; they meant to say that the Star was effective and generated a great disturbance of the air. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman author and naturalist</note> rendered the Greek term into Latin with the same usage, saying it *Signifies* or *Indicates*; hence certain stars were called "Indicating stars" above others, such as the Dog Star <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, associated by the ancients with the "dog days" of summer heat and storms.</note>.

And so the matter reached the point where, through <term>metonymy</term> <note>a figure of speech where a thing is called by the name of something associated with it, such as using "the crown" to mean "the king."</note>, even the fixed seasonal storms themselves were named "Stars,"

It explains the linguistic origins of weather forecasting terms in Greek, Latin, and German, noting how stars like the Dog Star became synonymous with the weather they were thought to predict.</summary>

the stars have departed from their ancient positions in the Zodiac and rise in the months that follow; yet the seasons return with the sun, and today those signs precede their ancient ones. Now it is true what Virgil sings:

*“They know their own sun and their own stars,” that is, any part of the year calculated from the solstice retains its own nature, its own character, and its own weather, even as the fixed stars migrate more and more into the following days.* <note>original: "Solemque suum sua sidera norunt." This quote from Virgil’s Aeneid is used here to explain that while the stars move, the solar seasons—marked by solstices and equinoxes—remain consistent in their weather patterns.</note>

<margin>Teach how to compare modern times with the Ancients regarding the rising or setting of the stars as expressed from the same sign.</margin>

For this task, one requires the longitude and latitude of the star, and an <term>Ephemeris</term> <note>A table providing the calculated positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</note> of the Sun’s motion, adapted to the time of the writer, specifically in the form of the old Julian Year extended backward. Then, if the writer specifies a day of the Roman year and the rising or setting of a star at a certain <term>elevation of the Pole</term> <note>A historical term for geographical latitude.</note>, one must look for the position of the Sun on that specific day in the ancient Ephemeris. Next, one must find the point of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note> that rises or sets along with that star. By comparing the Sun’s position with this rising point, the reliability of the writer will easily be revealed and—if he wrote accurately—the specific type of rising or setting.

Therefore, if we take that same day of the Roman Calendar today, the sum of the political years will be exact, but neither the weather of the year nor the stars will return on that same day. In terms of the <term>Tropical Year</term> <note>The "Year of Turning," or the time it takes for the seasons to repeat; approximately 365.24 days.</note>, we will have gone beyond the intended mark; however, we will not yet have reached the mark of the <term>Sidereal Year</term> <note>The time it takes for the Earth to complete one orbit relative to the fixed stars; it is slightly longer than the Tropical Year.</note>.

Secondly, therefore, to know the return of the goal of the Natural or Tropical year, look for the position of the sun taken from the ancient Ephemeris in the [tables] of our own age...

But the Rising and Setting of the stars, as they are of various types, so they also vary greatly through different climates <note>In ancient and Renaissance astronomy, "climates" referred to specific latitudinal zones of the Earth which determine the length of the longest day and the visibility of celestial bodies.</note>, through their declinations <note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the Sun—which are reduced or increased today—and finally through the positions of the Ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>, where oblique ascensions <term>oblique ascensions: the arc of the celestial equator that rises together with a star or a point on the ecliptic in a non-perpendicular orientation.</term> are longer or shorter today. 386 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

This star, called the Great Dog and Sirius <note>original: "Canis Major, & Sirius dicta"</note>: for it is the largest of the stars and was very frequently observed by the Egyptians for the purpose of making prognostications <note>predictions about the future based on celestial events</note>. Its rising was marked by the blowing of the Etesian winds <note>original: "Etesiarum flatu"; these are the strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow annually</note> in Greece and Egypt, a phenomenon most celebrated among ancient historians. In short, whatever naturally occurred during that part of the year—due to the peak summer heat which was already beginning to fade as the Sun moved away—was attributed to this star: such as the ripening of summer, the "boiling" of the seas, grapes being infested by "carbuncle" disease <note>original: "morbo carbunculari"; likely referring to a type of agricultural blight or rot</note>, the spoiling of wines, dogs being driven into madness <note>the origin of the association between heat and rabies</note>, the onset of diseases, and the treatment of illnesses becoming difficult. Finally, that part of the year has been known for two thousand years now as the **DOG DAYS** <note>original: "DIES CANICVLARES"</note>.

Moreover, another notable star precedes the rising of the "Dog," though it is slightly smaller, which the Greeks call <term>Procyon</term> <note>From the Greek "pro," meaning before, and "kyon," meaning dog</note> and Pliny calls the <term>Canicula</term> or the Lesser Dog; once it has risen, we know the Great Dog will soon follow.

**BOOK THREE. 387**

...the arcs of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year</term> between the Sun and the Horizon are found to be 14° 40' and 15° 33'. The former, when added to the co-rising point, and the latter, when subtracted from the co-setting point, show the locations of the Sun during the <term>heliacal rising: the first day a star becomes visible in the dawn just before sunrise</term> of the star at 28° 12' of Leo, and at its setting at 11° 7' of Taurus.

Therefore, today, with the Sun positioned at 11° 7' of Taurus—which occurs on April 21 according to the Old Style <note>original: "St. V." refers to the Julian Calendar</note> or May 1 according to the New Style <note>original: "St. N." refers to the Gregorian Calendar</note>—the Greater Dog <note>original: "Canis major," referring to the star Sirius</note> is hidden in the evening near the banks of the Danube. On May 7 (Old Style) or May 17 (New Style), it sets with the Sun and remains hidden for three months. In the middle of this period, namely June 18 or 28, it reaches the <term>midheaven: the highest point the star reaches in the sky each day</term> at the same time as the Sun, which is when it is as close to the Sun as possible.

Afterward, on July 27 (Old Style) or August 6 (New Style), it rises with the Sun, and a little later, on the morning of August 11 or 21, it appears again. It follows that for the remainder of the year during which it can be seen, it sets in the morning on November 9 or 19, but rises in the evening on January 23 (Old Style) or February 2 (New Style).

Thus Tycho Brahe <note>A famous Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his accurate planetary observations.</note> recorded the Dog Star <note>original: "Caniculam"</note> in the year 1600 at 20° 19' of Cancer, with a latitude of 50° 57' South. Its Right Ascension was 109° 37', and its Declination was 6° 12' North <note>Note: Sirius is actually in the Southern celestial hemisphere; the author may be using a specific coordinate system or there is a transcription error in the original Latin "Bor." (Borealis).</note>. It reaches the midheaven along with 18° 6' of Cancer. Therefore, under the same polar altitude, the <term>Ascensional Difference: the difference between the star's rising time on the equator versus at a specific latitude</term> is found to be 7° 3', so that the Oblique Ascension is 102° 34', co-rising with 3° 40' of Leo, where the angle is 50° 56'. The Oblique Descension, however, is 116° 40', co-rising <note>The author uses "cooriente" (co-rising) here, though in the context of descension, he likely refers to the point on the ecliptic setting with the star.</note> with 27° 36' of Gemini, where the angle is 36° 17'.

Since the star is ranked by Brahe as being of the second <term>magnitude: a measure of the brightness of a star</term>, the depth of the Sun below the horizon must be set at 13 degrees. Using this with the aforementioned angles, the arcs of the Ecliptic between the Rising and the Sun require 17° 27' and 23° 14'. When the former is added and the latter subtracted, they designate the locations of the Sun at the appearance of the star at 21° 7' of Leo, and at its disappearance at 4° 16' of Gemini.

If, however, we follow Ptolemy <note>An influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer.</note> and categorize the star as being of the first magnitude, and therefore set the Sun's depression at 12 degrees, the star will set heliacally when the Sun is two degrees further back, and rise when the Sun is two degrees further forward.

Therefore, while the Sun moves between 4° 16' of Gemini and 21° 7' of Leo—that is, from May 16 or 26 until August 4 or 14—the Dog Star lies hidden beneath the rays of the Sun. It sets with the Sun on June 9 or 19, rises with it on July 17 or 27, and reaches the midheaven with it...

### BOOK THREE. 391

->Now compare the testimonies of the Ancients.<-

The writings of the Ancients contain much obscurity; either because <term>astronomy</term><note>The study of stars and celestial bodies.</note> was not yet commonly known, or because the variation between different eras had not yet been noticed. For this reason, it happened that even astronomers were not immune to errors, nor did they agree among themselves. Therefore, writers who are unskilled in astronomy—who follow an uncertain guide or are unsure whom to follow—must be read with great attention and discernment.

Nevertheless, **Virgil** agrees with this calculation in these verses:
*When the bright Bull opens the year with gilded horns,*
*and the Dog-star, yielding, sets before the opposing constellation.*
<note>original: "Candidus auratis aperit dum cornibus Annum / Taurus, & adverso cedens Canis occidit astro." — From Virgil’s Georgics, Book 1.</note>

He says that when the Sun is moving through <term>Taurus</term><note>The constellation of the Bull.</note>, the Dog-star sets, "yielding to the opposing constellation." The poet invents a reason for why the Dog-star sets: because, of course, it yields to the approaching Sun. And why does it yield? Because the Sun is a "star" hostile to dogs. He is alluding to the <term>Dog Days</term><note>The hottest days of summer, historically associated with the rising of the star Sirius.</note>, when dogs are driven into a frenzy because of the heat caused by the Sun, as **Pliny** noted.

You see that the <term>heliacal setting</term><note>The time when a star first becomes invisible in the evening sky due to the brightness of the setting sun.</note> of the Dog-star is assigned to the 8th degree of Taurus, which is May 2nd, during the time of **Hippocrates**. This was around the end of April in **Caesar’s** time. Thus, the poet used the word *opens* (*aperit*) to allude to the name of the month in which this setting occurred <note>The Latin word for April, *Aprilis*, was traditionally thought to derive from *aperire*, "to open," as it is the month when flowers open.</note>, or at least to the month in which the Sun enters Taurus.
