*What was the rationale for the Dog Days among the Ancients and what is it today, and what is the cause of their beginning?*

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher</note> in Book II, Chapter XVII, attributes the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: *Canicula*; the star Sirius</note> to the 15th day before the Kalends of August <note>July 18th</note>, on which day he thought the Sun was entering Leo, although it was actually at 22 degrees of Cancer. Therefore, according to the tradition of the ancients, the beginning of the Dog Days <term>Canicular days</term><note>A period of midsummer heat historically associated with the rising of the star Sirius</note> used to be assigned to this day. 

However, from the time of Hippocrates <note>Ancient Greek physician, c. 460 – c. 370 BCE</note> until our own, this position of the Sun has receded from July 17th back to July 1st. For this reason, calendar-makers <note>original: *Calendariographi*</note>—ignoring the transition of the fixed stars into the following signs—have handled it differently. Some fixed this most ancient seat for the Dog Days on July 17th; others, adapting it to the "Seventh Climate" <note>A geographical zone in ancient Greek geography, roughly corresponding to the latitude of the northern Mediterranean or Black Sea</note>, moved it to July 19th, and they still retain it today, just as if either the Sun or the fixed stars returned to the same spot in the Julian year. 

Others, having considered the difference between the natural year and the political Julian year, each in their own age, weighed the rate at which the natural year anticipates the Julian. Disregarding the fixed stars from which the name originated, they made the name "Dog Days" move up along with the Sun itself in the Julian calendar. 

Therefore, in modern calendars, depending on whether the custom one follows is ancient, the Dog Days begin on either the 19th, 17th, 16th, 7th, or 6th of July. For after the Gregorian correction <note>The 1582 calendar reform by Pope Gregory XIII</note>, when 10 days were removed, that most ancient position on July 17th or 16th jumped in a single moment to July 7th or 6th. Leaving the Dog Days on the 17th or 16th of the New Calendar was not a bad move regarding the calculations of the Natural year; indeed, the 17th and 16th of July were pulled back closer to 22 degrees of Cancer, which they once occupied. But others, considering every recent observation in the calendars to be weighty and almost sacrosanct, and not paying attention to its first origin; lest by the removal... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the page turns</note>

the 10-day correction <note>The Gregorian calendar reform of 1582 skipped ten days to realign the calendar with the solar year.</note>, violence was done to Heaven and Nature; that is, the Dog Days of July 16, 17, or 19—as these days have slipped away over so many centuries—they transferred to the corresponding Gregorian days of July 26, 27, and 28. Others, in turn, through the exemption of the 10 days, brought them back to July 6 or 7 on the Julian calendar, and having used them that way for some time, they moved them to July 6 or 7 on the Gregorian calendar, or June 26 or 27 on the Julian. These things, therefore, concern the custom received in the Calendars and the <term>political year</term> <gloss>the civil or legal year used for state and church business, as opposed to the natural solar year</gloss>.

But if we look at the nature of the <term>sidereal year</term> <gloss>a year measured by the position of the stars</gloss> and the natural year, two starting points for the Dog Days are born for us today: one group holds the same heat as the <term>Hippocratic</term> <gloss>referring to Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician who linked health to seasonal changes</gloss> days, while the others share the same star and name. For today, the Sun returns to the 22nd degree of Cancer—the place where the Sun once revealed the Dog Star <note>original: "Canicula", referring to Sirius, the brightest star in the sky</note>—on July 4 or 14; or, if the ancient rising of the star were calculated in our climate, it would be July 6 or 16. But in our climate and our century, the Dog Star is found to emerge, as was said above, on August 4 or 14.

Now it is up to the experts of Nature to decide to which they wish to attribute the power of the Dog Days: to the height of the Sun, or to the Dog Star itself. For if even today, though these two are now pulled apart, they still believe the tempered powers come from an equal interval of days, they will remain at the first seat on July 17 or 19 of the Julian political year, which is the 27th or 29th of the Gregorian.

### 398 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

->When Zeus has completed sixty wintry days, then the star<-
->Arcturus, leaving the holy stream of Ocean,<-
->First rises all-shining at the onset of evening.<-
<note>Original Greek: "Χειμέρι᾽ ἐκτελέσῃ Ζεὺς ἤματα: δὴ ῥα τότ᾽ ἀστὴρ Ἀρκτοῦρος, προλιπὼν ἱερὸν ῥόον ὠκεανοῖο Πρῶτος παμφαίνων ἐπιτέλλεται ἀκροκνεφαῖος." This is a quote from Hesiod’s "Works and Days," lines 564–567.</note>

He clearly expresses the rising of the star above the horizon in the evening, or the **acronychal** rising <term>acronychal: the rising of a star in the east at the same time the sun sets in the west</term>, and adds that this occurs on the 60th day after the winter solstice. You can see, however, that at that time it usually rises in the evening when the sun is in the 5th degree of Pisces—that is, 65 degrees after the winter solstice. Therefore, you have the testimony of Hesiod that the solstice is completed 5 days after the beginning of Capricorn <note>In ancient calendars, the "beginning" of a zodiac sign often shifted due to the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, known as precession</note>, and even more days if we assume a smaller motion of the fixed stars between the ages of Hipparchus and Hesiod, as held by **Hipparchus** and **Ptolemy**. It can be believed that this was also among those pieces of evidence from which **Eudoxus** or **Hipparchus** reasoned that the Solstices are completed in the eighth parts <note>the 8th degree</note> of the signs; but more on this matter in Book VII.

**Pliny** places the rising of the star 11 days before the equinox, which almost agrees with Hesiod's time, because you see the Sun is placed more than 10 degrees before the equinox during the emergence of **Arcturus**. He mentions the setting of the star three times: first on the 8th day before the Ides of June <note>June 6th</note>, which is true today regarding the morning setting, which you see happens on the 6th of June in the Julian calendar. Second, he mentions the same on the 8th day before the Ides of August <note>August 6th</note>, which is clearly incorrect. Third, he mentions the evening setting either on the 1st of the Calends or the 5th day before the Nones of November <note>November 1st or 5th</note>, which is the only one that matches. For **Pliny** is distant from Hesiod by one-third of the time interval, and two-thirds from us. And for us, Arcturus is hidden on November 25th; for Hesiod, on October 25th; therefore, by analogy: for Pliny, it was November 5th.

For the **Antoecians** <note>Those living at the same longitude but opposite latitude (e.g., one north, one south)</note>, the seasons of the year are opposite; for the **Perioecians** <note>Those living at the same latitude but on the opposite side of the world (180 degrees of longitude apart)</note>, the differences of day and night are opposite; for the **Antipodes** <note>Those living at the exact opposite point on the globe, both in latitude and longitude</note>, both are opposite. Indeed, for the Antoecians, noon and midnight occur at the same moment, but summer and long days occur for one group while winter and long nights occur for the others, and vice versa. An exception is the Torrid Zone <term>Torrid Zone: the region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, characterized by a hot climate</term>; there, regarding the days and summer, it is as I have described: they can experience winter at the same time, but not in an equal manner, nor of the same but rather of opposite character. Likewise, there is an exception in the Frigid Zones <term>Frigid Zones: the polar regions</term>, where there is continuous day; because of the Sun's own motion, this happens for a longer duration for some than for the others.

For the Perioecians, days and nights occur at the same time and are of equal length; however, one group has the middle of the day when the others have the middle of the night—be it true night or something analogous to the middle of the night. 

For the Antipodes, all things occur in reverse: Summer and long days (or no nights at all) occur for them when the others have winter and short days (or no days). It is night there when it is day here, and day when it is night here. Furthermore, at the same moment the Sun rises for us, it sets for them; and when it sets for us, it rises for them.

To these points, add from the previous sections that for the Antoecians and Antipodes—since they are inhabitants of the Southern Hemisphere—the patterns of the rising and setting of stars, and the ascending and descending of the signs of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky through the zodiac throughout the year</term>, are reversed. For those stars that are always visible to us are, to our Antoecians...

### 410 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY
#### On the longitudes and distances of places.

*Since you have frequently compared the Right Ascension of the stars with the longitude of places on Earth, and their declination with their latitude, tell me then: what is the purpose of knowing the longitude and latitude of places on Earth?*

1. It is the branch of Astronomy concerning the differences in the longitudes of places on Earth, or the hourly difference of <term>Meridians</term> <note>imaginary lines running from north to south used to measure time and position</note>, so that celestial phenomena <note>such as eclipses or planetary movements</note> can be adjusted for different Meridians. 2. Without the longitudes and Latitudes of places, the distances between those locations cannot be determined through calculation.

*How much time is one degree of longitude difference worth on Earth?*

Since the Sun, having returned to the meridian of the same place from which it departed, marks the boundary of a natural Day and night of 24 hours, it follows that 15 "Times" <note>original: "tempora"; in this context, it refers to degrees of rotation</note> of the terrestrial equator are equal to one hour. One "Time" or degree is worth four minutes of an hour; and so on.

*How is the difference in longitude of places on Earth investigated?*

1. From the altitudes of the pole <note>the latitude of the observer</note> and the distance between places. For if the travel distance of a direct path is known in German miles <note>original: "milliaribus Germanicis"; a historical unit of measurement where 15 miles traditionally equaled one degree of the Earth's circumference</note>, it is converted into degrees of a <term>Great Circle</term> <note>the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, like the equator</note> drawn through both places, taking 15 Miles for one degree. Alternatively, if one place can be seen from the other, the arc of the great circle between the places is investigated by the method handed down in the first book. Then a Triangle SIP is formed between the two places S and I, and the Earth's pole P, with the known...

*How is this time difference to be used?*

Since it is certain that a given celestial phenomenon <note>such as an eclipse</note> occurs at the same moment in all places on earth—for instance, when the moon begins to enter the [Earth's] shadow—then if the time of the phenomenon is known for a specific place, those who are further west than that place always count less time from noon, and those who are further east count more. Therefore, the hourly difference of longitudes must be subtracted for those to the west, and added for those to the east.

*Tell of some strange phenomenon resulting from this cause.*

1. The Portuguese, who were mentioned in Book 1, page 19, after spending three years on their voyage in their circumnavigation of the globe, having returned home, counted it to be Wednesday <note>original: "feriam quartam," the fourth day of the week</note>...

...returned, while Portugal was counting the fifth day: for by following the sun, they carried the meridian of their ship <note>The "meridian of the ship" refers to the crew's local noon, which they reset daily based on the sun's position</note>—from which they numbered the start of the natural day—around the world once, while the Meridian of Portugal had remained in its place. The opposite happens to those who set out toward the East and return home from the West; for by moving to meet the Sun, they finally count one day more than those to whom they return.

2. This question troubles the Jews: if two Jews, one traveling through the West and the other through the East, meet each other in China, which man's Sabbath should prevail? For they will bring together different Sabbaths (a difference of one day), and the one who arrived via the East will be a day ahead. Indeed, even Christians, who are rigid observers of their festivals, will be troubled by the same perplexity; for just as the Jews begin all festivals from the setting of the Sun in any given place, so do Christians begin from its Rising.

->*In what other ways is the difference in longitudes investigated?*<-

There are only two astronomical means: one through the observation of Lunar Eclipses <note>original: "Eclipsium Lunæ"</note> already explained; the other through the visible location of the moon when it is at the <term>Ninetieth Degree of the Ecliptic</term> <note>The "Nonagesimal" is the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon; measuring the moon's position here helps determine longitude by minimizing certain visual errors</note>, about which there is no need to say more in this place; both serve for locations at great distances.

Physicists attempt one method by means of a round Magnet, an image of the Earth <note>Kepler refers here to a "terrella" or little earth, a magnetized sphere used to model the Earth's magnetic field, a theory popularized by William Gilbert</note>; the principles of which are as yet uncertain. For it is required that, just as the axis of a natural Magnet is spontaneously directed into the plane of the Meridian, and just as the Pole of the Magnet sinks spontaneously—deeper or higher—according to the proportion of the location's proximity to the Earth's pole; so also there might be a certain part in the middle circle of the Magnet which spontaneously turns itself toward its native place. Whatever the truth of the matter, it is likely that such an observation cannot be precise enough, and is therefore less useful.

There is also one <term>Chorographic</term> <note>The art of describing or mapping specific regions or districts</note> method for places that are not very far apart: namely, those where one can be seen from the other, so that the altitude of the Pole for both places may be known...

->TO THE READER, GREETINGS.<-
<note>The Latin abbreviation "S." stands for *Salutem*, a standard formal greeting wishing the reader health or prosperity.</note>

**E**LEVEN YEARS HAVE PASSED since I published my *Commentaries on the Motions of the Star Mars*. <note>This refers to Kepler's landmark 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova* (The New Astronomy), where he first proposed that planets move in elliptical orbits.</note> Because only a few copies of that book were produced, and because it had hidden the teachings concerning the causes of the heavens within a thicket of numbers and other astronomical apparatus; and further, because the high price of the book discouraged those of more modest means, my friends felt that I would be acting rightly and according to my duty if I were to write an **Epitome** <note>An *Epitome* is a summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note>. In this summary, the core of both the <term>physical teachings</term> <note>By "physical," Kepler means the actual forces and causes of motion, rather than just the mathematical models.</note> about the heavens and the astronomical theories would be presented in simple and plain language, cutting away the tedious technical demonstrations.

I undertook this task many years ago. However, while various delays interfered with the publication, the little book itself was not only revised several times and—if I am not mistaken—perfected as far as possible, but the very plan of the publication began to waver. To some readers of the *Doctrine of the Sphere* published three years ago <note>This refers to the first three books of this series, published in 1617, which dealt with the basic geometry of the heavens.</note>, I seemed too long-winded in the dispute over the daily motion or rest of the Earth, more so than the nature of an "Epitome" usually allows. Therefore, I began to think: if readers could not stomach that part—which nonetheless is found in every astronomical summary—how much more "unusual" will this **FOURTH** book seem to them, which [discusses] so much about all...

†† 2

420 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;P R E F A C E

...of the whole nature of the heavens, it examines new and unexpected matters—so much so that you might doubt whether you are dealing with a part of **Physics** or rather **Astronomy**; unless, of course, you already knew that speculative astronomy itself is entirely a branch of Physics. <note>Kepler was a pioneer in arguing that the movement of planets was governed by physical forces, not just abstract mathematical models.</note> On the other hand, I considered that this was the very subject matter which my friends urged me to write this booklet about, for the sake of expanding upon it and bringing it into the public eye. These speculations cannot be omitted, unless I should deliberately strive to pour darkness over **theoretical doctrine** <term>Theoretical doctrine: In this context, the mathematical and causal models used to explain planetary positions</term>, which would then be stripped of its very principles. 

Finally, necessity settled that debate—and I wish it were never so troublesome—making what could not have happened otherwise appear as if it were a deliberate plan. The printing press was busy, and the work on the theoretical doctrine was progressing. The official overseer of the work (whom I mentioned in the introduction to the **spherical doctrine** <note>This refers to the earlier books of the *Epitome* dealing with the geometry of the celestial sphere.</note>), was clinging to his old ways, or perhaps dozing off, or maybe even breathing his last breath. Meanwhile, the generosity of a most eminent patron was filling his role. 

Then, suddenly, a reason arose for me to depart and interrupt the work. At that very moment, the typesetters had reached the end of the fourth book, and the **Frankfurt fairs** <note>The Frankfurt Book Fair was the most important event for the European book trade; missing it meant waiting months for another chance to sell the work.</note> were fast approaching. It occurred to me that it would be most appropriate if Book IV—which is written for both Physicists and Astronomers alike—were also published separately. In this way, at the buyer’s discretion, the astronomer could choose either to leave it out or to insert it into the rest of the *Epitome*. 

You have here, kind reader, the reasons for this edition, which I hope will satisfy you.

# APOLOGETICS

424 ->FROM THE LETTER<-

...He builds up his discourse on the Gods and their number; he, I say, who sends his own disciples to the Astronomers; he who grants to the Astronomers the weight of testimony and authority. Truly, he would never have rejected either Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish nobleman and astronomer whose precise planetary observations laid the groundwork for Kepler's laws.</note> or even myself, if that fatal necessity of the ages had brought us together. For he commands us *to inquire from both*, from Eudoxus as well as from Callippus <note>Eudoxus and Callippus were ancient Greek astronomers who developed early models of planetary motion using concentric spheres.</note>, the latter of whom had corrected the former. Today, that would mean inquiring of both Ptolemy and Tycho. He says to follow not the older authorities, but the *more accurate* <note>original: "accuratiores"</note> ones. 

Therefore, if Aristotle is dear to your most just Prince, I present Aristotle himself as a witness that no injury is done to you if an Astronomer—using those arguments which a more recent age has brought forth regarding the Heavens—has indicated that creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to celestial phenomena like comets or "new stars" (supernovae) that appear and disappear.</note> have arisen and then vanished again within the Heavens themselves. This is contrary to what seemed true to Aristotle, because although he did cite experience <note>Aristotle famously argued that the heavens were "incorruptible" and unchanging based on the records available in his time.</note>, his experience was not of a sufficiently long duration.

As for the Academies <term>Academias: Universities and centers of formal learning</term>, they were established to shape the studies of those who are learning; and it is important that the laws of teaching are not changed frequently. In such places, because the concern is the progress of the students, it often happens that things must be chosen not because they are the most true, but because they are the easiest. ### THE FIRST PART OF THEORETICAL DOCTRINE

*What is the subject of theoretical doctrine?*

The <term>proper motions</term><note>Latin: "motus proprii." These are the actual paths planets travel through space, as opposed to the "common motion" caused by the Earth's rotation.</note> of the planets, which we call "secondary motions," and the planets themselves, which we call <term>secondary mobiles</term><note>In traditional astronomy, "mobiles" refers to things that move. The "First Mobile" was the outermost sphere of the heavens; "secondary mobiles" are the individual planets that have their own distinct orbits.</note>.

*In what respect do you call the motions of the planets "proper"?*

1. Because that common motion—shared by both the planets and the fixed stars, and indeed the apparent daily motion of the whole world, which was the subject of <term>spherical doctrine</term><note>The study of the celestial sphere as seen from Earth, covered in the first three books of this work.</note>—seems to travel from the east toward the west. However, the individual motions of each planet are far slower and move in the opposite direction, from the west toward the east. Therefore, it is certain that these planetary movements cannot depend on that common motion of the world which we have discussed up to this point, but must be attributed to the planets themselves; thus, they are "proper" (or belonging) to the planets in general.

2. Although, truly, in these proper motions of each individual—

434 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

In the motion from west to east, there is still something common—not a daily motion, but an annual one—which is external and derives its cause from sight alone, rather than from the actual reality of the matter. This sometimes causes the planets to appear to move backward <note>original: "retrocedere." This refers to retrograde motion, where a planet appears to loop backward in the sky.</note> in their own proper motion, namely from east to west. However, because this common element is so entwined in the individual periods of each of those planets and is transformed in various ways, it cannot be discerned at first glance what is common to all and what is specific to each. Therefore, that entire combined motion of each planet, as it meets the eyes, is also called the "proper" motion of that planet in appearance; especially since that common element shared by many does not originate from the primary common motion of the whole world <note>The "primary motion" usually refers to the daily rotation of the heavens.</note>, but from the proper motion of a single planet <note>Kepler is subtly referring to the Earth here; our movement around the Sun creates the "annual" illusion in the observations of other planets.</note>.

*How many parts are there to Theoretical doctrine?*

Above in the first book on page 15, the entire doctrine was divided into three specific parts: the first on the principles from which Copernicus demonstrates the second motions (the subject of Book IV); the second on manual instruments <term>manual instruments: conceptual or physical models, such as diagrams of orbs, used to visualize celestial math</term> by which these motions are presented to the eyes, namely concerning Eccentric orbs and similar things (the subject of Book V); the third concerning the apparent motions of the individual planets themselves and the common occurrences shared between them (the subject of Book VI); and into a fourth part, common to both Spherical and Theoretical doctrine, concerning the apparent motion of the eighth sphere <note>The "eighth sphere" in traditional astronomy was the outer shell containing the fixed stars.</note> (the subject of Book VII).

<meta>This page transitions from the general principles of astronomy to the specific physical causes of planetary motion that Kepler explores in Book IV of his Epitome.</meta>

436 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*What do you substitute in place of the second principle, and what do you add besides that relates to the true form of the world’s home, or the nature of the heavens?*
Although individual motions must be assigned to individual planets, they do not move by themselves, nor through the rotation of <term>spheres</term><note>original: "sphærarum". In older astronomy, planets were thought to be carried by solid, transparent crystalline spheres. Kepler famously rejected this, arguing for empty space.</note> (of which none are solid). Instead, the Sun, located in the center of the world and rotating around its own center and axis, becomes the cause for each planet to circle around through this rotation of its own body.
Furthermore, even though planets are in fact <term>eccentric</term><note>An orbit where the Sun is not at the exact geometric center, but slightly off-center, making the orbit an ellipse.</note> from the Sun’s center, there are no smaller circles, called <term>epicycles</term><note>Small circles whose centers move along the circumference of a larger circle; a mathematical device used by Ptolemy to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down.</note>, which vary the distance between the planet and the Sun by their rotation. Rather, the bodies of the planets themselves, through an inherent force, provide the occasion for this variation.

*What then will be the subject matter of the Fourth Book?*
This Fourth Book will contain the very essence of celestial physics, or the form and logic of the world’s workings, and the true causes of motions. And this will be that primary duty of the astronomer mentioned in Book I, page 5, namely: the demonstration of his <term>hypotheses</term><note>In Kepler's time, "hypothesis" referred to the physical and mathematical model used to explain the heavens.</note>.

*List the primary parts of Book IV.*
There will be three main parts of Book IV:
The first concerns the bodies themselves; the second, the motions of those bodies; the third, the real <term>accidents</term><note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are properties or characteristics that a thing has (like speed or position) which are not part of its essential nature.</note> of those motions.
For the first part will teach the arrangement of the entire universe, its division into principal parts or regions, the location of the Sun at its center, the number, size, and order (or position) of the planetary spheres, and finally the proportion of all the world's bodies to one another.
The second will present the revolution of the Sun around its own axis and its effect in driving the planets around; the causes of the proportion of the motions to one another—that is, the times—

He rejects the ancient idea of solid crystalline spheres and epicycles, attributing changes in planetary distance to the planets' own inherent forces.</summary>

*What do you think is the arrangement of the primary parts of the world?*

The Copernican philosophy categorizes the primary parts of the world according to the distinct regions of the world’s shape. Since there are three regions in a sphere—which is the image of God the Creator and the <term>archetype</term><note>An "archetype" refers to the original pattern or model upon which the universe was built.</note> of the world (as proved in the first book)—these serve as symbols of the three persons of the Holy Trinity: the center represents the Father, the surface represents the Son, and the intermediate space represents the Holy Spirit. Consequently, three primary parts of the world were created, each in its own specific region of the sphere: the Sun in the center, the sphere of the fixed stars on the surface, and finally the system of planets in the intermediate region between the Sun and the fixed stars.

*I used to think that the primary parts of the world were to be counted as heaven and earth?*

Indeed, to us inhabitants of the earth, our sight cannot show us other more notable parts (as stated in Book 1, folios 8, 9, 10). We tread upon the one with our feet and are covered by the other; both appear to be joined and glued together at the common border of the Horizon, like a palace in which the stars, clouds, birds, humans, and various kinds of terrestrial animals are enclosed. 

But since we are engaged in a discipline that reveals the causes of things, dispels the deceptions of sight, and carries the mind higher and beyond the limits of vision, it should be a wonder to no one that sight learns something new from reason—the disciple from the Master—which it did not know before. Namely: that the earth, when considered by itself in isolation, is not to be held among the primary parts of the great world. Instead, it is to be reckoned as part of one of the primary regions—specifically, the planetary region or the "moving world"—holding a certain foundational role within it. Conversely, the Sun is removed from the list of stars and established as one of the primary parts of the entire universe. However, I am speaking now of the earth insofar as it is part of the world-structure, not regarding the dignity of the <term>ruling creature</term><note>Kepler refers here to humanity, whom he considers the dominant or "ruling" inhabitant of the Earth, regardless of the Earth's physical position in space.</note> who inhabits it.

By which...

# BOOK FOUR. 439

By what properties do you distinguish between these three members of the great world?

The perfection of the world consists in light, heat, motion, and the **harmony of motions**; these are analogous to the faculties of the soul: light to the **sensitive** faculty, heat to the **vital** and **natural** faculties, motion to the **animal** faculty <note>In 17th-century philosophy, 'animal' refers to the 'anima' (soul) as the source of voluntary movement, rather than to beasts.</note>, and Harmony to the **rational** faculty. In light consists the world's adornment; in heat, its life and growth; in motion, its active operation; and in Harmonies, contemplation—in which Aristotle places true happiness. 

Now, since three things must necessarily concur for every affection or state: the cause **FROM WHICH** it comes, the subject **IN WHICH** it exists, and the form **UNDER WHICH** it is organized:

The **Sun**, therefore, through all these stated conditions of the world, performs the role of the **efficient** <note>The 'efficient cause' is the primary source of change or rest; here, the Sun is the 'doer' or 'engine' of the universe.</note> cause; the region of the **fixed stars** holds the role of the **forming**, **containing**, and **limiting** principle; and the **intermediate** space holds the role of the **subject**, according to the nature of each condition. In all these ways, the Sun becomes the most important body of the entire world.

For as far as light is concerned, the Sun itself is the most beautiful and acts as a kind of **eye of the world**. As the source of light or a most brilliant torch, it illuminates, paints, and adorns the bodies of the rest of the world. The **intermediate** space is not luminous of itself, but is translucent and transparent—a stream through which light is dispensed from its source. Within it are the globes and creatures into which the Sun’s light is poured and who enjoy it. The **sphere of fixed stars** performs the role of a riverbed in which this river of light flows; it is like a wall, at once opaque and illuminated, reflecting and doubling the Sun’s light. You might very rightly compare it to a **lantern** which keeps out the winds.

Likewise in animals, the **brain**, the seat of the sensitive faculty, communicates all senses to the whole animal. By the action of the **common sense** <term>Common sense (sensus communis): A theoretical faculty that was believed to collect and integrate the data from the five individual senses into a single conscious perception.</term>, it causes the presence of all those senses, as if exciting them and commanding them to remain awake. To put it another way in this comparison, the Sun behaves like that very common sense, while the globes in the intermediate space—

Here the region of the fixed stars, standing everywhere on the opposite side, assists this vegetation by **concentrating the heat**, as they say, like a certain skin of the world.

Regarding **motion**, the Sun is the first cause of the motion of the universe's planets, and the **first mover**, even by reason of its own body. In the intervening space, the mobile things travel, namely the globes of the planets. The region of the fixed stars provides a place and a certain base for the mobile things, upon which the mobile things might lean, as it were, and by comparison to which—since it is immobile in itself—motion is understood to occur. Thus in animals, the **cerebellum** is the seat of the motive faculty, while the body and its members are that which is moved; the earth is to the animal body, the body to the arm or head, and the arm to the finger, a base upon which, as if on something immobile, the motion of each part occurs.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the physical structure of the universe, specifically addressing why the heavens are not a single uniform mass and whether planetary "spheres" are physical solids. It is page 442 of the Epitome of Copernican Astronomy.</meta>

442 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*...the Sun and the fixed stars, does it not seem that everything is set in motion?*

Indeed, the most fitting response is indicated by the three parts of the world. Since a mathematical point <note>In Euclidean geometry, a point has no dimension; Kepler is arguing that the Sun, though a physical body, acts as the "point" at the center of the universe.</note> cannot be "clothed" or expressed except through a physical body, the body located at the center falls short of the indivisibility of a true point. In the same way, it was appropriate that the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "fixarum"; referring to the distant stars that do not move relative to one another.</note> should fall short of being a continuous spherical surface, and instead should break apart into the tiny, individual points of the innumerable fixed stars. Finally, the intermediate space between them is not entirely occupied by motion and other influences; it is not perfectly transparent, but a little denser, because it could not be completely empty <note>Kepler refers to the "ether" or "aura," the substance he believed filled the space between planets.</note> but had to be filled with some form of matter.

*Are there solid orbs in which the planets are carried, and are the intervals between them empty of orbs?*
<term>Orbs: historically, astronomers believed planets were embedded in physical, transparent "crystalline spheres" that rotated like nested Russian dolls.</term>

Tycho Brahe <note>A famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose precise observations provided the data Kepler used to discover the laws of planetary motion.</note> disproves the existence of solid orbs by three arguments. The first is from the motion of Comets; the second from the lack of refraction of light; and the third from the proportion of the orbs themselves. 

Regarding the first: if the orbs were solid, Comets would not be seen crossing from one orb into another, for they would be blocked by the solidity; but they do cross from one to another, as Brahe demonstrated. 

Regarding the second: since these orbs are eccentric <note>off-center relative to the Earth.</note>, and the Earth and its surface (where our eyes are) is not located at the exact center of every orb, it follows that if the orbs were solid—and certainly denser than that most clear celestial air—then the rays of light from the stars would reach our own air only after being refracted <note>original: "refracti"; the bending of light as it passes from one medium, like glass or water, into another.</note>, as the science of Optics teaches. Consequently, a planet would appear irregularly, appearing to be in a very different place than what an astronomer would predict.

The third reason is Brahe’s own, adapted from the principles of the system: both his own observations and those of Copernicus testify that Mars sometimes becomes closer to the Earth than the Sun is. Brahe could not believe this overlap was possible [if the spheres were solid]...

<summary>Kepler explains why the universe is divided into distinct stars and space rather than being a solid mass, and recounts Tycho Brahe's evidence that planetary "spheres" are not physical solid shells.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, solid orbs, planetary spheres, refraction, comets, Mars, celestial matter, Johannes Kepler</keywords>

# II. On the location of the Sun in the center of the world.

*By what arguments do you establish that the Sun is situated in the very center of the world?*

Some of these arguments are supplied to us by the most ancient Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, whose mathematical and mystical views on the universe influenced early science.</note> and the Italian philosophers in Aristotle, Book 2 of *On the Heavens*, chapter 13. They are derived from the dignity <term>dignitate|In this context, "dignity" refers to the perceived importance, nobility, or ontological rank of a thing.</term> of both the Sun and its location, and from the Sun's duty in the world for giving life and light.

*State the first argument based on dignity?*

The reasoning of the Pythagoreans, quoted word-for-word from Aristotle <note>Kepler is referencing Aristotle’s summary of his predecessors' views, even though Aristotle himself disagreed with them.</note>, goes like this: a more worthy location is owed to the most worthy and precious body. Now, the Sun—for which they used the word "Fire" <note>original: "Ignis". The Pythagoreans believed a "Central Fire" was the heart of the universe, which Kepler here identifies as the Sun.</note>, hiding their doctrines according to the custom of their sect—is indeed more worthy than the Earth, and the most precious and worthy thing in the entire world, as was shown a little earlier. Furthermore, the surface and the center (or midpoint) are the two boundaries of a sphere. Therefore, one of these must belong to the Sun. It cannot be the surface, for that body which is the most important in the whole world ought to be guarded above all things. The center, however, is perfectly suited for this purpose, which is why they were accustomed to call it the "Guardhouse of Jupiter" <note>original: "Iovis custodiam". In Greek mythology, Jupiter (Zeus) was the supreme ruler; his "guardhouse" at the center of the world represents a place of ultimate power and protection.</note>. Therefore, it is not fitting for the Earth to be in the middle; for that place belongs to the Sun, while the Earth is carried around the center in an annual motion.

*How does Aristotle respond to this argument?*

1. He says they take for granted something not granted—namely, that the "middle" <note>original: "medium"</note> is the same...

# BOOK FOUR. 445

...the center of size (that is, of the sphere), of the object (that is, of the worldly body), and even of Nature itself (that is, of its <term>informing</term><note>Latin: *informatio*; the process by which a soul or "form" gives life and specific structure to matter.</note> or quickening). Just as in animals, the center of life and the center of the body are not the same (for the heart is indeed inside, but it is not at an equal distance from the extremities); so too must we think regarding the heavens. We should not fear for the safety of the entire universe, nor must we place a "guard" at the center. Rather, we should seek what kind of body that heart of the world—or center of quickening—might be, and in what location of the world it is situated.

2. He <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note> wishes to show the difference between the "center of nature" and the "center of place." For he argues that the center of nature—that most noble and precious body—has the character of a first principle. The center of place, however, is instead the "last" thing when quantity is considered metaphysically, rather than being its first or primary principle. For that which is the center of quantity (that is, the innermost part) is what is bounded or circumscribed. But the "boundaries" are that which bound or circumscribe. Now, that which surrounds, limits, and encloses from the outside is more excellent and noble than that which is limited on the inside. For <term>matter</term> is among those things that are limited, terminated, and contained; <term>Form</term><note>In this philosophical context, "Form" is the essential nature or soul of a thing that gives it its "being," as opposed to "Matter," which is the raw stuff.</note>, however, or the essence of each creature, is among those things that limit, circumscribe, and encompass. Thus he <note>Aristotle</note> believes he has proved that the Sun—or as he understood it, the **Fire of the Pythagoreans**—does not belong in the center of the world so much as at the outer edge.

*How do you refute this refutation by Aristotle?*

1. Although it is true that in not all creatures—and least of all in animals—is the most vital part in the center of the whole mass, yet when we discuss the world, nothing is more probable than this very thing <note>i.e., that the vital center is indeed the geometric center.</note>. For the shape of the world is round, but that of an animal is not. Because animals require limbs stretched out beyond themselves, by which they may stand upon the earth, move upon it, and take in food, drink, and outward appearances...

2. While we seek this **Sun** and where in the world it is situated, **Copernicus**, the master of the heavens, points out the middle to us. Others who show it in a different place are not forced to this by astronomical arguments, but by certain others that are metaphysical in appearance, drawn from the contemplation of the Earth and its place. The evaluation of these arguments is common to us and to them, and by these they do not prove, but they themselves also seek the place of the Sun. While we, therefore, seeking the place of the Sun in the world, find the center of the world, we do this in accordance with Aristotle himself, nor is his refutation here against us.

## *Prove from the office of the sun that the center belongs to it?*

This has already been partially done in the dismissal of the Aristotelian refutation <note>original: "elenchi Aristotelici." This refers to the logical counter-arguments used by followers of Aristotle to keep the Earth at the center.</note>. For, first: if the entire world, which is spherical, requires the light and heat of the Sun equally, then it is best for the Sun to be in the middle. From there, these gifts may be distributed equally into all regions of the world. This is accomplished more uniformly and directly by resting in the center than by circling around it. For if the Sun were to move toward some parts for the sake of heating them, it would move away from the opposite parts, and would thus cause <term>vicissitudes</term><note>alternating changes or fluctuations</note>, though the Sun itself is a most simple being. It is a wonder that some people, for the sake of mockery, use the analogy of a light in the middle of a lantern; yet this is a most fitting comparison, and not at all suited to disparage this opinion, but rather uniquely ideal for depicting the force of this argument.

2. Regarding light, a specific demonstration is woven, assuming a sense of fitness <note>original: "concinnitatem." Kepler often uses this to mean a harmonious or elegant "fittingness" in God’s design.</note> rather than absolute necessity. Imagine the sphere of the Fixed Stars to be a concave mirror. It is well known that an eye placed in the center of such a mirror looks upon itself from every side; and if a light is in the center, it is reflected from every part of the concave surface at right angles, and the reflected rays meet again at the center. However, this can happen at no other point of the concavity except the center. Therefore, since the Sun is the source of light and the "eye of the world," the center is owed to it, so that (representing the Father in divine symbolism) it may contemplate itself in the entire concave surface (which bears the symbol of the Son of God), and in that image of itself, it may take delight in itself, and by illuminating itself, it becomes radiant, and by heating itself, it becomes kindled. To this point belong these melodic verses:

->*Reflected from every side,*<-
->*O navel of the ether,*<-

## III. Concerning the order of the moving spheres.

*How are the planets distinguished from one another?*

Into primary and secondary; primary are those whose bodies are carried around the sun, as will be taught below; secondary are those whose own circles are arranged not around the sun, but around one of the primary planets, and which, besides their own motion around the body of the primary, also share in the motion of their primary around the Sun. Saturn is believed to have and lead around with it two such companions <note>original: "duos". At the time of this writing, only a few of Saturn's moons had been identified; the "two" likely refers to early observations before the discovery of the full system.</note>, which sometimes come into view by means of the telescope. Jupiter has four such around itself, labeled **d. e. f. h.** The Earth, **b.**, has one, **c.**, called the Moon. Concerning Mars, Venus, and Mercury—primary planets themselves—it is not yet established whether they also have such companions or a "retinue" <term>satellitium: a Latin term for a group of attendants or followers, used here to describe what we now call satellites or moons</term>.

[Diagram: A celestial diagram showing planetary orbits. In the center is the Sun, labeled 'A'. A small inner orbit contains the Earth 'B' and its moon 'C'. A large outer orbit represents Jupiter's path, with Jupiter itself shown at the top accompanied by four moons labeled 'H', 'E', 'F', and 'D'.]

*How many planets, therefore, are to be considered in Theoretical doctrine?* <note>Theoretical doctrine refers to the mathematical and philosophical study of the heavens as established in textbooks of the era.</note>

No more than seven; indeed, six are called primary: 1. Saturn, 2. Jupiter, 3. Mars, 4. Earth (the Sun, as it appears to our sight <note>original: "Sol ad visum". The author is reconciling the Copernican reality that Earth moves with the traditional perception that the Sun moves.</note>), 5. Venus, 6. Mercury; and 7. the only one from the secondaries, the Moon; because she alone revolves around the Earth, our dwelling place; the other secondaries do not concern us, who belong to the Earth.

<summary>This page defines the distinction between primary planets (which orbit the Sun) and secondary planets (moons), incorporating early telescopic discoveries of Jupiter's and Saturn's satellites. It establishes a list of seven principal celestial bodies relevant to Earth-based astronomy, including the Earth itself as a moving planet.</summary>

<keywords>primary planets, secondary planets, satellites, Jupiter's moons, Saturn's moons, heliocentrism, telescope, Moon, Earth, astronomical classification</keywords>

->*What do you say are the reasons for the arrangement of the spheres, and how does Copernicus excel in them?*<-

Aristotle teaches in the second book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de caelo"</note>, chapter 10, that nothing is more consistent with reason than that the times of revolution <term>revolution: the time a planet takes to complete one full trip around its orbit</term> of each planet should correspond to its height or the size of its sphere. Now, according to the ancients, the highest planet is indeed the slowest, namely Saturn, because it takes 30 years; it is followed in place and time by Jupiter, which takes 12 years, and then Mars, which takes less than 2 years. But then, for the remaining planets, the logic of the ancients is thrown into confusion. For unless you grant the Earth an annual motion around the Sun, it happens that the Sun, Venus, and Mercury—three distinct planets—all have the same one-year period for their circuits; yet the ancients assign them different spheres: the highest to the Sun, the middle to Venus, and the third to Mercury. Finally, they give the lowest place to the Moon, which indeed has the shortest time, namely one month.

Copernicus, however, by establishing that the Earth is carried around the Sun, maintains this same proportion <term>proportion: the mathematical relationship between a planet's distance from the center and its speed</term> of motion and time across all primary planets. For him, the Sun is in the center of the world and is thus the innermost, lacking any circuit of the center—that is, it is immobile in respect to its center and axis; the body of the Sun...

**By what measure does Copernicus determine the distances for each of the planets?**

We must use a proportionate measure here, one to which the other spheres can be compared, and which is closely connected to us and therefore known to us in some way.       But the truer reasoning is that those five figures form as many intervals between the spheres, which enclose one another. If, therefore, there are five spherical intervals, there must necessarily be six spheres: just as for four linear intervals, there must be five fingers.

      *What are those five regular figures?*
      The Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron, and Octahedron. <note>These are the "Platonic Solids," the only five three-dimensional shapes where every face is an identical regular polygon and the same number of faces meet at every corner.</note>

      The Cube, Tetrahedron, and Dodecahedron are **primary**; the Octahedron and Icosahedron are **secondary**.

The latter two take their origin from the primary ones, have an angle made of more lines (which is more complex), and have a borrowed face. <note>Kepler is arguing that some solids are more fundamental than others based on the geometry of their vertices and how they can be nested inside one another.</note>

<meta>This page continues Kepler's discussion on the geometric hierarchy of the Platonic solids, specifically focusing on why the cube is considered the primary or "first" among them.</meta>

458      EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY

In fact, the **Tetrahedron** <note>original: "Tetraëdron"; a pyramid with four triangular faces</note> is less than the **Cube**, and the **Dodecahedron** <note>a solid with twelve pentagonal faces</note> is more than the cube. Or rather: the Cube is the first of the "generated" forms <note>shapes built up from simpler elements</note>; the Tetrahedron is the first of the shapes "cut out" from a cube; and the Dodecahedron is the first of the "composite" forms, produced by enlarging and covering the cube. This hierarchy even dominates their constituent planes: the Square, the Triangle, and the Pentagon. For the Square is produced first of all by the simplest and most uniform movements, as was said in Book I; the Triangle is formed by dividing the square into two; and the Pentagon is composed of three suitable triangles.

->*Explain the origin, primacy, and nature of the cube?*<-

Straight quantities have an origin that is visible to the mind's eye. As was said above, the spherical shape carries a certain character of eternity, or of eternal generation. Once the sphere is established, a point is placed in its center and infinite points on its surface. From the flow of a point toward another point, a **line** arises; from the lateral flow of a line, a **surface** arises; and from the lateral flow of a surface, a **body** <note>a three-dimensional solid</note> arises. 

If the flow is straight and follows the shortest path, a straight line arises, bounded by two points. If the flow of a straight line is such that all its points move equally, a **parallelogram** arises, bounded by four lines. If the parallelogram flows in this same way, a **parallelepiped** <note>a six-sided solid where opposite faces are parallel</note> arises, bounded by six planes. 

Furthermore, if the length of the flow is equal to the line being moved, and the angle of the path of that flow is any angle other than a right angle, a plane called a **Rhombus** arises, whose sides are equal to each other. If the angle is a right angle, it is a **Square** that arises. If a square flows in this same way, the **Cube** is born: a solid whose six planes are all squares and are thus equal to each other. 

Now, the shortest path is prior to the winding path; the equal and self-similar is prior to the unequal and dissimilar; and the straight is prior to the oblique. Therefore, just as the straight line is primary among generated lines (for the circle is posterior to the plane, and the plane is posterior to the straight line), and the square is primary among surfaces, so among quantities, that which is perfect—

->*What is the origin of the secondary figures, and why are there only two?*<-

To these three figures—the **Cube**, the **Tetrahedron**, and the **Dodecahedron**—three others correspond, but one of them coincides with its own primary figure <note>Kepler is referring to the Tetrahedron, which is "self-dual." If you place a point in the center of each face of a tetrahedron and connect them, you simply get another, smaller tetrahedron.</note>; and these are also produced by a "diminishing" of the three primaries. However, this is a different kind of diminishing: here, it is not an edge that is left to represent a plane, but an angle. That is to say, for the surface of the primary figure, the secondary figure receives not a line, but a point, while the number of sides remains the same. At the same time (as before), a plane of the secondary figure is generated in place of an angle of the primary. This plane is triangular because the angle of its primary is <term>trilinear<note>Formed by the intersection of three lines or edges at a single point.</note></term>, created by connecting the three centers of the three planes of the primary that surround that solid angle. Therefore, these secondary-born figures are, as it were, the *internal organs* <note>Original: "viscera." Kepler frequently used biological metaphors to describe the mathematical harmony of the cosmos.</note> of the first ones.

*Why do you make those five <note>The five Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> the most beautiful and perfect?*

Because they imitate the spherical image of God as much as can be done by a rectilinear figure, ordering all angles in the same sphere, and being inscribable in a sphere; and just as the sphere is everywhere similar to itself, so all the planes of each of these figures are similar to one another, and all are also inscribable in one and the same circle, with equal angles.

*Could more figures similar to these be established by some other method?*

By no means. For the solid angle of any figure is constituted by at least three planes. Therefore, equilateral triangles meet in threes, fours, or fives; quadrangles <note>squares</note> in threes; and likewise pentagons in threes to form a solid angle. But six triangles, and three hexagons, fill a flat surface <note>They sum to 360 degrees</note>, and do not rise into a solid. Indeed, more than these—as even three heptagons <note>seven-sided shapes</note>, and any other three—exceed the sum of 4 right angles, which are arranged around the same point in a plane. See the scholium to the last proposition of Book XIII of Euclid: and the second book of my *Harmonics* <note>original: "Harmonicorum meorum", referring to Kepler's 'Harmonice Mundi' (The Harmony of the World, 1619)</note>.

*How is the sphere divided by the Tropics and the Polar circles, or what is the meaning of those different-colored bands on the innermost globe of the sphere?*

The surface of the earth is divided by the two tropics and the two polar circles into five parts; the three middle ones are circular bands; because of this, all those parts are called the five Zones <term>Zones: from the Greek word for "belts," referring to the climatic regions of the Earth</term>. Now, the red color of the middle zone signifies the Torrid Zone <note>original: "Zonam torridam." Historically, "torrid" suggested a land scorched by the sun where life might be impossible.</note>: and it is that stretch of lands which I mentioned above are situated under the equator and the Tropics, along with the intervening parts of the earth. The green color of the two side zones denotes the Temperate Zones; one of these we Europeans occupy, as well as the greatest part of Asia, a significant portion of Africa, and finally half of America above New Granada <note>original: "novam Granatam," referring to the Spanish colonial territory in northern South America, roughly corresponding to modern-day Colombia and Venezuela.</note>.

168 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

The matter does not stand quite so simply. For although we are in the Temperate Zone, we are nonetheless burdened by heat in the summer and by frost in the winter, yet we are not moved from one Zone into another in the meantime. And there are, in this same Temperate Zone, places that are very cold throughout the whole year, such as <term>New Albion</term><note>An early name for the Pacific coast of North America, explored by Francis Drake.</note> in America; likewise, there are flourishing lands in the Frigid Zone, such as Greenland (named in German for its "greenness"); and finally, there are most blessed and temperate dwellings in the Torrid Zone, as in Western Africa, in Peru, and in the islands of the Indian and Eastern Ocean.

*Why then is heat attributed to the torrid regions,*
*cold to the frigid ones, and a mild temperature to the temperate ones*
*through these names and colors?*

Because although heat, cold, and the qualities that accompany them—the fertility or barrenness of lands—have various causes, both celestial and terrestrial: the celestial causes are indeed universal and dominant, while the terrestrial ones are particular and restricted to the narrowness of certain places and times. They do not extend widely, but are seen to be surrounded by the universal cause. Therefore, in this innermost <term>small globe</term><note>Likely referring to a diagram or a physical model of the Earth being discussed in the text.</note>, the pattern of the celestial cause is depicted for us.

Add to this that in our Europe, and in its once-most noble part, Greece, the terrestrial causes were found to harmonize excellently with the celestial causes by the first inventors of these arts. For as they turned their faces toward the East, to their right were Syria, Egypt, and Africa—burning regions—and above those, Arabia, Ethiopia, and Libya, which are stony or sandy regions. Such places assist the heat of the sun immensely. To their left were Thrace, Sarmatia, and Scythia; from their marshes and snow-covered mountains, cold winds blow out, binding the <term>Ister</term><note>The ancient name for the lower Danube River.</note> and neighboring rivers with ice throughout the winter. From there also blow the <term>Etesian winds</term><note>Strong, cool, seasonal winds of the Mediterranean/Aegean.</note> during the summer, which are the primary relief from the heat.

IX. X. The <term>Colures<note>The colures are two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that intersect at the celestial poles and pass through the equinoxes and solstices.</note></term>.

*By what reasoning are two colures established within the sphere?*

Astronomers have imagined one circle passing through the poles of the <term>Equator<note>The celestial equator, representing the projection of Earth's equator into the sky.</note></term> and the <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year.</note></term>; the other passes through the poles of the Equator alone and through the points where it intersects with the Ecliptic. Both are among the <term>Great Circles<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that shares the same center as the sphere, dividing it into two equal halves.</note></term>, so that by their mutual meeting and intersection at the Poles of the Equator, they might form two poles on each side. From these, a physical model of the sphere—with an axis passed through it—could be suspended and rotated. It is also into these circles that the remaining six circles (except for the Horizon and the Meridian) are fixed and joined together.

*In the diagram on leaf 158, BMCN is the colure of the <term>equinoxes<note>The two days of the year when day and night are of equal length.</note></term>, because M and N are the equinoctial points. And OBLDPC is the colure of the <term>solstices<note>The two days of the year when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, marking the start of summer and winter.</note></term>, because L and Q are the solstitial points, and O and P are the Poles of the Ecliptic.*

*What are they called?*

They are called "Colures," a Greek term <note>original: "Coluri graeca voce"</note> derived from the "docking of a tail" <note>original: "à curtatione caudae"</note>, because their extremities near the lower pole were not visible to us, and thus appeared as if they were cut off by the Horizon. The first of these is called the Colure of the Solstices.

170 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY
On the Distinction of the Circles.

*Having explained the origin of each individual circle, say now—for the sake of strengthening the memory—in how many ways are these ten circles distinguished among themselves?*

In six ways: either by reason of their subject <note>the physical body they belong to, like Earth or the heavens</note>, or by reason of their origin, or by reason of their quantity <note>their size or diameter</note>, or by reason of their shape, or by reason of their position relative to motion, or by reason of the motion itself.

I.
*How do they differ from each other by reason of their subject?*

Some are proper to specific and distinct regions of the heavens alone, such as the Zodiac and the two Colures <note>original: "Coluri"; these are the two great circles that intersect at the celestial poles, one passing through the equinoxes and the other through the solstices</note>. Others are proper to specific and distinct regions of the Earth, but are projected <note>original: "tralatitij"</note> into specific and distinct regions of the heavens, such as the Equator, the two Tropics, and the two Polar circles. For it must not be thought that there is any fixed star, wandering star <note>planet</note>, or even the Sun itself, which by its own motion traverses that specific region of the fixed stars into which these circles are transferred. Finally, others belong neither to the distinct regions of the heavens nor of the Earth, but are applied broadly to all things; these belong specifically to the Sphere as an instrument of the primary motion <note>the daily rotation of the sky</note>, such as the Horizon and the Meridian.

Of those assigned to the heavens in this way, some maintain the same positions in it perpetually, such as the Zodiac, which belongs to the heavens not in respect to the daily motion of the Earth but because of the stars themselves and their secondary motions <note>the slower orbits of the planets as opposed to the fast daily rotation</note>. Others, over the passage of centuries, migrate from their positions and pass into neighboring ones; these are the ones that belong to the heavens in respect to the daily motion of the Earth—namely the Colures and all those projected into the sky.

Likewise, of those that belong to the Earth, all of them indeed belong to it unchangeably. However, some are on the Earth only because of its daily motion, such as the Equinoctial <note>original: "Æquinoctialis"; the Equator</note>; others exist because of the comparison of the daily motion with the celestial circle of the Zodiac, such as the two Tropics and the two Polar circles.

Com-

## II.
***Compare them by reason of their origin?***
Some are primary, each having arisen from its own causes; others are secondary, depending on the first ones joined together.
The primary circles have an origin that is either intrinsic to the World—namely, motion; such as the Zodiac, a celestial circle <note>original: "caelestis circulus"</note> [representing] the motion of the secondary movable bodies <note>the planets</note>; or the Equator, a terrestrial circle [representing] the primary motion of the earth. Alternatively, they have an extrinsic origin, such as the Horizon [which depends on] the sight of a human being inhabiting the "machine of the world" <note>a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divinely designed mechanism</note>.
Secondary circles are those which exist through the mutual comparison of the primary circles: on the earth, these are the two Tropics and the two Polar circles, defined by the relationship between the Zodiac, the Equator, and the poles. In the heavens, however, they are the colures <term>colures: two principal circles of the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles and pass through the equinoctial or solstitial points</term>, defined by the relationship of the same. Finally, on a material Sphere <note>an armillary sphere or globe used for teaching</note>, the Meridian: defined by the relationship of the Horizon, the Equator, and the poles; all of which have been explained up to this point.

## III.
***Distinguish the circles by reason of their quantity?***
Quantity, as used here, is understood in comparison to the spherical surface, not indeed to the physical material, whether of the world itself or of a craftsman's sphere <note>an armillary sphere model</note>. Therefore, some are "Great Circles" <note>original: "maximi"</note>, which share the same center as the sphere, such as the Zodiac, Equator, Horizon, Meridian, and the two Colures. Others are "Lesser Circles" <note>original: "minores"</note>, which have different centers than the center of the Sphere, such as the two Tropics and the two polar circles.
***If there are six Great Circles, and therefore equal to one another, why in a constructed sphere is the Meridian made larger than the rest, and the Horizon alone the largest of all?***
This occurs by the necessity of the material: for a physical Sphere could not be constructed and turned by hand unless the Horizon embraced and supported the Meridian from the outside.

*What primarily happens to the circles of the Sphere when compared among themselves, regarding this distinction?*

Since the planes of the circles of the sphere either meet inside or outside the sphere and intersect each other, or do not meet but proceed in parallel: in the case of the **smaller circles**, astronomers carefully consider their parallel position; but in the case of the **greatest circles**, they consider their mutual intersection. For the Greatest Circles <note>term: "Great Circles" are those that divide the sphere into two perfectly equal halves, such as the Equator or the Ecliptic.</note> cannot be parallel to each other, but they either coincide or intersect one another. Smaller circles, however, even if they are not parallel to each other, do not always intersect on the surface of the Sphere: nor is there much use for those intersections.

*What then is the use of the intersections of the Great Circles?*

Three great circles constitute a **spherical triangle**, and two a **spherical angle**: in these consists the doctrine of Triangles; by which all the principles of the First Motion <note>term: The "First Motion" (Primum Mobile) refers to the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky from east to west.</note> are contained, explained, and put into practice.

*How many things are considered in each spherical triangle?*

Six: Three sides—namely, the arcs of three Great Circles—and three angles.

### VI.

*Finally, how do the circles differ among themselves in regard to motion?*

They differ in one way regarding the **material sphere**, and in another way regarding the **universe**. Regarding the <term>material sphere</term><note>A physical model used by astronomers, such as an armillary sphere, consisting of a frame of rings representing the principal circles of the heavens.</note>, the **Horizon** and **Meridian** are immobile, while all the others are mobile, because the sense of sight—which is the author and origin of these immobile circles—judges itself to be at rest. But regarding the universe itself, the opposite occurs: for only the mundane <note>original: "mundani," referring to the circles as they exist in the actual cosmos rather than on a model.</note> **Horizon** and **Meridian** move, while the regions of heaven, to which the other circles belong, remain at rest. Finally, regarding the **Earth**, the **equator**, the **two Tropics**, and the **two polar circles** are fixed to the Earth's Meridian and Horizon; and thus, they are mobile along with the whole Earth. These things were explained more clearly above.

*What is the cause of this discrepancy between the circles of Heaven and the circles of Earth?*

The cause consists in the various and manifold uses of the <term>Equinoctial Sphere</term><note>The celestial sphere as defined by the projection of Earth's equator into space.</note>. For if its only use were that it and the remaining **parallels** might show over which locations on Earth those points of the **Ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note> pass as they move along each parallel, then in the sphere all parallels could and should have been fixed to the Meridian and made immobile. This is just as they are fixed to the same on Earth, since these circles belong first to the Earth, and from there they are transferred into the sky through imagination. For then the eye would imagine for itself another kind of **flooring** or another **vault** outside and above the ultimate sky, under which the sphere of fixed stars would run its course as if the vault were at rest. Then, every point of the ecliptic would inscribe its own parallels onto that outer flooring—in which the **Meridian** and **Horizon** of the Sphere are imagined to exist—corresponding to the parallels of the Earth, likewise as if rest— <margin>qu... ri... fe... q... P...</margin> <note>The marginal notes are partially cut off in the original text, appearing to be fragments of Latin references.</note>

*What name does one of such parts have in any circle?*

The common name throughout all circles is **Part**: but specifically in the **Zodiac**, they are called **degrees** <note>original: *gradus*</note>, because the sun is seen to cross almost exactly such an arc within one day. In the **Equator**, however, they are called **Times** <note>original: *tempora*</note>, because that is the measure of time; in the **Horizon**, they are called by the Arabic word **Azimuths** <note>original: *Azimutha*</note>, which in Latin could be called "Regions" <note>original: *plagae*</note>. But through common usage, the name "**Degrees**" has become the standard for all circles.

*In what sequence of numbers are these parts written in any one circle?*

In the Equator and the Zodiac, the beginning is made from their common vernal intersection <note>The Spring Equinox, where the sun crosses the celestial equator</note>. Those parts that rise first in the Temperate and Torrid zones are numbered first; in the Zodiac, those parts are numbered according to where the sun enters later. In the Equator, the numbering is continuous from 1 to 360 through the entire circle. In the Zodiac, however, the numbering goes from one to thirty, which measure constitutes one **twelfth-part** <term>dodecatemorium: one of the twelve signs of the zodiac, each covering 30 degrees</term>. From there, the numbering returns to the beginning or to unity until another twelfth-part is completed; and so it proceeds twelve times.

And when the numbering or motion proceeds in this order, it is called the **sequence of signs** <note>original: *consequentia*; moving forward through the zodiac signs</note>; in the opposite way, the numbering or motion is said to proceed **backward** <note>original: *in antecedentia*; literally "in the preceding"</note>.

In those circles that pass through the poles of the world <note>meridians or hour circles</note>, the beginning is made from either of the poles in a double fashion: one in one semicircle, the remainder in the other; and it is led through...

->*Why does the numbering in the Equator and the Zodiac begin from the Vernal intersection?*<-

In a circle, by its very nature, there is neither beginning nor end. However, because a beginning must be made somewhere, with nature as our guide we arrive at one of the cardinal points; indeed, these are shown by the intersections or contacts of the <term>Colures</term> <note>The two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that pass through the equinoxes and solstices</note>, the Equinoctial, and the Tropics, and are placed in a clear and conspicuous location.

Of the equinoctial points, however, the first inventors of Astronomy chose the one that brought back light and heat to them in their own region, and opened the beginning of spring, when the face of the earth is renewed and nature lives again. For since all the opposite things happen in the autumn season, they held that intersection which the sun approaches in the autumn in lower esteem.

184 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*How is one part or degree subdivided?*

Into 60 parts, which we call "scruples" <note>original: *scrupula*, a term for small weights or stones used to denote small units</note> or minutes; in Greek, these are called *lepta* <note>original: $\Lambda E \Pi T \alpha$, meaning "small" or "refined" parts</note>. Furthermore, one minute is divided into 60 seconds, one second into 60 thirds, and so on, as far as such precision is required for the work.

*What is the method for writing them down?*

For numbers representing whole parts, it is common to place a small circle above them. For minutes, a single stroke is used; for seconds, two strokes; and so on. In this book, the names for parts such as <term>Degree</term> <note>a unit of measurement representing 1/360th of a circle</note> or <term>Time</term> <note>often used here to mean degrees of the celestial equator as they relate to the passage of time</note>, as well as Minute, First, Second, etc., are either written out in full or abbreviated to the first letter (especially when the strokes are missing), and are placed either before or after the number. If this is not done, the numbers must be distinguished by their order: those in the first position or appearing alone are considered whole parts; those in the second position are first minutes; and those in the third are seconds.

*What is the reason for this sexagesimal division?* <note>a system of counting based on the number 60</note>

There is no reason derived from the nature of celestial movement, nor a rational Geometric reason deduced from the nature of the circle itself—at least not regarding such a small arc. Instead, the reason is purely Arithmetical. There is no other number under one hundred that has more <term>multiples</term> <note>Kepler here refers to divisors, or numbers that go into 60 evenly</note>, making it much more convenient to work with. It has a 60th part (1), a 30th (2), a 20th (3), a 15th (4), a 12th (5), a 10th (6), a 6th (10), a 5th (12), a 4th (15), a 3rd (20), and a half (30). Additionally, this division is related to the previous division of the entire circle into 360 parts. For if a circle is divided by a hexagon <note>a six-sided shape</note>—which is the easiest division because the side of a hexagon is equal to the <term>radius</term> <note>the distance from the center of a circle to its edge</note>, and the same compass that drew the circle can also divide it—then to one-sixth there belongs...

# On the Division of the Zodiac

*By what names are the twelve equal parts or <term>dodecatemoria|From the Greek 'dodeka' (twelve) and 'moros' (part); the twelve 30-degree sections of the Ecliptic</term> of the Zodiac distinguished from one another?*
