->*Since not only astronomers but also other writers are very much occupied with the signs, in how many ways are they usually distinguished?*<-

      They are distinguished chiefly in five ways: three ways indeed because of the intersection of the Ecliptic with the equator and the <term>Colures</term> <note>The Colures are two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that pass through the celestial poles and either the equinoxes or the solstices</note>, where adjacent signs constitute one class; and in two ways where signs that are separated in position are reduced into one class through the inscription of a geometric figure within the circle.

->I.<-
->*How are those signs, or the Ecliptic itself, distinguished by the circle of the Equator?*<-

      Into a semicircle of six northern signs, which decline from the Equator and are raised toward the north, such as Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo; and into just as many Southern signs, which are depressed from the Equator toward the south, such as Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.

->*Should we be careful of any ambiguity here in the words "Northern" and "Southern"?*<-

      Absolutely. For the Ecliptic also divides the whole sphere into two Hemispheres, the Boreal <note>Northern</note> and the Austral <note>Southern</note>. In this way, the first semicircle of the equator, one tropic, one polar circle, and one pole are called Boreal, Northern, or Arctic; the remaining semicircle of the equator, etc., is called Southern. Therefore, one and the same star belonging to a certain sign might be called northern with respect to the equator, but southern with respect to the Ecliptic—and vice versa—if it is located between the Ecliptic and the equator.

II.

*State the distinction of the signs by the <term>solstitial colure</term>?* <note>original: "Colurum solstitiorum"; the solstitial colure is one of the two great circles that intersect the celestial poles and the points where the sun reaches its highest and lowest points (solstices).</note>
Six are called ascending and their semicircle is the Ascending [semicircle], in which the sun and planets ascend from the South toward the North toward the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note> of our zone, such as Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini: the remaining six, or their semicircle, are called descending for the opposite reasons: Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius.

III.

*How is the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note> with its signs distinguished through each colure and the cardinal points?*
Into four quadrants, corresponding to the four parts of the year, from which they are named.
The Vernal <note>Spring</note> signs are: Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, in which the sun, ascending from the Equator into the North, establishes spring; this is the first quadrant.
The Summer signs are: Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, by which the sun, descending from the North toward the Equator, brings about summer; this is the second quadrant.
The Autumnal signs are: Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius, in which the sun, descending from the Equator into the South, completes autumn; this is the third quadrant.
The Winter signs are: Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces, in which the sun, returning from the South toward the Equator, passes through winter. This is the fourth quadrant.

IV.

*What is the fourth division, and what is its use?*
This is more astrological, for three quadrangles <note>Likely referring to the "Qualities" in astrology—Cardinal, Fixed, and Mutable—each of which contains four signs forming a square shape within the Zodiac circle.</note> are numbered in the Zodiac; and in each, four signs are arranged through the Zodiac in a tetragonal form, from which the class takes its name.
It serves, however, for understanding the movements of the Sun and Moon.

# On the Quarters of the Winds.

*How do sailors usually divide the Horizon?*

In the most ancient times, four quarters of the Horizon were recognized, described by the four cardinal points of the world, and marked by the names of the same number of winds. For no more than these four winds are named by Homer <note>The legendary Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.</note>: **Eurus** blowing from the east, **Zephyrus** from the west, **Boreas** from the North, and **Notus** from the South. But later Greeks, dedicated to seafaring, began to divide the Horizon more precisely, dividing the East and West into the Solstitial (or summer), the Equinoctial, and the Hibernal (or winter <term>brumal<gloss>from "bruma," the shortest day of the year or winter solstice</gloss></term>) points. As a consequence of this, the North and South were also tripled, so that twelve winds were created. These intermediate winds in the Greek sea—which is enclosed by continents and is not so vast—were named... <note>The text ends mid-word, likely continuing as "denominati" or "denominantur" (were named) on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the astronomical definitions of zodiac signs and their application to planets and comets, before transitioning into a historical overview of how ancient sailors and the Greeks divided the horizon into four, then twelve, directional winds.</summary>
<keywords>zodiac signs, ecliptic, comets, winds, cardinal points, Homer, Greek navigation, horizon divisions</keywords>

...they named them for the lands lying nearly around them, from which they blow. From this we have **Phoenix**, **Africus**, **Libs**, **Thrascias**, **Hellespontius**, **Olympias**, **Strymonia**, and **Iapyx**. <note>These are ancient Greek and Roman names for winds based on specific geographical directions, such as the Thracian wind or the Libyan wind.</note> **Vitruvius** <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer active in the 1st century BC.</note> doubles the number, so that there are 24 of them.
      After the entire Ocean surrounding the Continents began to be navigated, it was found that neither the summer nor winter rising and setting points of the sun were at an equal distance in all locations; neither were names invented by a single nation suitable for all places, nor were they easy to remember in such a large number. Therefore, the **Germans** <note>The author uses "Germani" to refer generally to Northern European seafaring peoples.</note> introduced a new division of the Horizon into 32 Winds, by a continuous doubling of the four-fold **Cardinal** <note>The four main directions: North, South, East, and West.</note> number, and they gave them names from their own language. The other nations—the Italians, French, Spanish, and modern Latin writers—for the most part imitate these by applying the Ancient Names, but by no means with equal success.
      Each one of these parts, therefore, equally occupies eleven and a quarter astronomical parts or degrees.

->*Explain, by what names are these parts called?*<-

      First, they are usually called <term>Rhombi</term> <note>Rhumb lines or compass points</note> by modern Latin writers, using a common term. For the nautical compass (called a **Bussola**) has a paper disc placed upon a magnetic needle, which is always directed toward the North; on this paper are depicted thirty-two rays or diamond-shaped points <note>original: "Cuspides Rhomboides"</note> of different colors; so that when the magnetic needle, with its painted lily <note>The fleur-de-lis, the traditional symbol marking North on a compass rose.</note>, is directed to its own natural region, every **Rhumb** also indicates its own direction.
      Indeed, all the **Rhumbs** are named from the **Cardinal** points of the world, though the cardinal points themselves are named one way, and the intermediate ones another.

*From where do the Cardinal winds get their names?*

The Homeric <term>cardinal winds</term><note>The "cardinal" points—North, South, East, and West—were traditionally associated with specific winds in classical antiquity.</note> seem to be named according to their qualities: **Eurus** <note>The East wind</note> from a foul moisture or "moist rot"; **Auster** <note>The South wind</note> from "drying," which in Greek is *auein*; likewise **Notus** from mists, which are called *notides* in Greek; **Boreas** <note>The North wind</note> from the "voracity" or "greediness" which its cold brings to our bodies; and **Zephyrus** <note>The West wind</note> from "fervor" or "boiling," which is *zein* in Greek. Others maintain that **Eurus** and **Zephyrus** are named after their regions, following that passage in Homer’s *Odyssey*, book 10:

*For we do not know where the gloom is, nor where the dawn.* <note>original Greek: "οὐ γάρ τ’ ἴδμεν ὅπη ζόφος, οὐδ’ ὅπη ἠώς"</note>

In this view, **Eurus** comes from *eurein* <note>meaning "to find," associated here with the rising sun/east</note>, and **Zephyrus** comes from *zophos*, which signifies "gloom" or "the west" in Homeric language.

# Concerning other Circles.

*Are the ten circles of the sphere sufficient here to explain all the patterns of the <term>primary motion</term>?* <note>The "primary motion" (primum mobile) refers to the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky from East to West.</note>

Others do indeed come into consideration, but they can be easily understood from those already explained.

*Enumerate the more important ones by their types?*

1. Among the **Minor Circles**, there are many—in fact, infinite—**Parallels**. These are usually parallel to the <term>equator</term>, but sometimes also to the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's path</note> or the **Horizon**. For through any point or star on the sphere, one parallel is understood to be drawn to the equator itself, due to the daily motion of the heavens.
2. Among the **Great Circles**, there are the **circles of declination**, which pass through the poles of the sphere.

->### BOOK TWO. 197<-

...of the sphere, the circles of Latitudes <term>circles of Latitudes: great circles passing through the poles of the ecliptic, used to measure how far a star is from the sun's path</term> [passing] through the poles of the Zodiac; the circles of Positions used by astrologers [passing] through the intersections of the Horizon and the Meridian; and finally others, drawn through any two points of the sphere.

*What do you call Longitude and Latitude on the sphere?*

Although the sphere is round, we nevertheless say its **longitude** is extended according to the order of the signs of the Zodiac, and its **latitude** toward either pole of the Ecliptic; because these poles and this circle belong to the heavens. On the earth, however, longitude is reckoned according to the equator, and latitude from one pole of the Earth to the other, because again, the circle and poles belong to the earth. In both cases, longitude is double the latitude, since there are 360 degrees [of longitude] and 90 degrees [of latitude] toward either side. <note>In ancient and early modern geography, "latitude" was often measured as 90 degrees from the equator to a pole, while "longitude" covered the full 360-degree rotation.</note>

*What is the relationship of these circles with those that are usually depicted on a sphere?*

Among the **parallel circles** are numbered the Equator, the two Tropics, and the two polar circles on the sphere. Among the **circles of declination** are the two colures <term>colures: two principal meridians that intersect at the celestial poles; one passes through the equinoxes and the other through the solstices</term> and the Meridian, which takes the place of all those others due to the mobility of the sphere. Among the **circles of Latitude** is the Colure of the Solstices; among the **Vertical circles** is the Meridian, the middle of them all. Finally, among the **circles of position** are the Meridian and the Horizon.

*Which of the many Parallels that are not physically built into the sphere are considered the most notable?*

1. The circles of the **Natural days**, which are discussed in the third book. <note>These circles represent the path a star or the sun travels across the sky in a single 24-hour period.</note> 2. The **Arctic and Antarctic** [circles] of any given location according to the teaching of the ancients; these are smaller circles described from either pole through the intersections of the Horizon and the Meridian, which are also discussed in the third book.

*What else has a relationship with the parallels of the sphere?*

Terrestrial parallels, drawn through the middle and the boundaries of the **Climates** <term>Climates: ancient geographical zones defined by the length of the longest day of the year in that region</term>, which are also discussed in the third book and in the section on Geography.

*What are the parallels of the Horizon called?*
The Arabs, devoted to the **Astrolabe** <term>A historical handheld "analog computer" used for telling time and mapping the stars; it represents the 3D sky on a 2D flat plate</term>, (which is an image of the sphere projected onto a plane), call them in their own language the **Almicantarat** circles <note>original: "Almicantarat". These are circles of altitude that run parallel to the horizon, used to measure how high a star sits in the sky.</note>.

*Are there any others related to the circles of declination?*
Related are the Circles of Latitude of places on Earth, mentioned above as Terrestrial Meridians.

*What name is given to the Vertical circles among the Arabs?*
The Arabs call them in their language **Azimuths**, just as they call the Vertex <note>The point directly overhead</note> the **Zenith**, and its opposite the **Nadir**. Therefore, Azimuthal circles pass through the Zenith and Nadir.

*How do Astronomers use the Azimuth of a star, and in what sense?*
The Azimuth of a star is sometimes a quadrant <note>a quarter-circle</note> of a great circle drawn from the vertex through the star down to the Horizon; this is how the Arabs use it. At other times, it is the means by which these vertical circles are distinguished from one another: specifically, it is the angle which that circle makes with the Meridian, or the measure of that angle, which is the arc of the Horizon intercepted between the vertical circle and one or the other part of the meridian, or even the equator. They speak of Azimuth from the North toward the east or west, from the south toward the east or west, or Azimuth from the east or west toward the north or south as the occasion arises <note>original: "pro renata"</note>, and according to the method of inscribing the number 360 upon the horizon.

*Regarding circles of position, which are the most notable?*
Besides the Horizon and the Meridian, which are represented on the sphere, there are four others which are called by Astrologers (sharing a common name with the others) the circles of the **Celestial Houses**, which divide the entire sky into twelve houses by a certain method. To each of these, the astrologers attribute their own names. Hence these short verses:

*Life, Wealth, Brothers, Father, Children, and Health,*
*Wife, Death, Travel, and Kingdom, Good Deeds, Prison.*
<note>These verses serve as a mnemonic for the twelve astrological houses, which were believed to govern different aspects of human life.</note>

*Are there never more than ten circles depicted on the sphere?*

200 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY
*What circles do sundial-makers use, beyond*
*those that are found in the Sphere?*
Sundial-makers <note>original: *Gnomonici*, those who study the "gnomon" or the shadow-casting blade of a dial</note>, in addition to the planes of the Meridian and of all Horizons sharing the meridian of a single location, recognize three further categories of planes upon which sun-dials <note>original: *sciaterica*, literally "shadow-drawings"</note> must be described: Declining, Inclined, and De-inclined—that is, those that are declining and inclined at the same time. Inclined planes correspond to the same circles that are called "circles of position"; Declining planes correspond to the Vertical circles. Among these, sundial-makers recognize the <term>Primary Vertical</term> <note>Also known as the Prime Vertical, the circle passing through the East and West points of the horizon</note>, which is drawn through the shared intersections of the Horizon and the Equator. Its poles are the intersections of the Horizon and the Meridian, so that it sits at a right angle to the Meridian, facing directly south on one side and north on the opposite side.

This is the circle in whose plane solar clocks—which are called *Regular Vertical Dials*—are drawn. In relation to this primary vertical, the planes of the remaining vertical circles are said to "decline" either toward the east or toward the west, with the exception of the plane of the Meridian itself, which looks directly east and west.

All those planes are considered <term>De-inclined</term> which correspond to great circles that pass through neither the intersections of the Horizon nor the Primary Vertical with the Meridian. However, these are reduced <note>mathematically simplified for calculation</note> back to Inclined planes of a Pole with a higher or lower altitude than that of the given location.

To all types of planes are assigned their own Meridians. These are taken from the circles of declination, corresponding to the circles of latitude of the locations, and are perpendicular to the planes of which they are the Meridians. In any given location, the Meridian of the Sphere itself serves as the Meridian for the Horizontal plane and the Primary Vertical plane—and thus for all other Horizontal and Vertical planes under that same Meridian.

*Why is the study of the sphere presented before the Theory?* <note>original: "Theorica." In the 17th century, "Theory" referred to the specific mathematical models of planetary orbits (the "second motions"), whereas "Spherical" astronomy dealt with the apparent daily rotation of the stars (the "first motion").</note>

Even though the Theory of the planets' own motions can be taught and understood on its own based on established hypotheses, requiring no assistance from the diurnal <term>diurnal motion: the apparent daily rotation of the heavens from east to west, caused by the Earth's rotation on its axis.</term> or "first" motion; and conversely, an accurate explanation of the first motion—one that is perfect in every detail—is only truly completed through knowledge of the "second" motions (especially the movements of the sun) and requires many details borrowed in advance from the Theory: nevertheless, there are fitting reasons why we should begin with the diurnal motion. First, the diurnal motion is more familiar to our senses and more obvious, as it is swift and occurs daily, corresponding more closely to the practical rhythms of our lives; thus, it was also the first to be recognized by the human race. The second motions <term>second motions: the slower, individual orbits of the planets as they move through the zodiac over months or years.</term> are more concealed, further removed from our immediate perception, and because of their slowness and various <margin>A, fe, le, Ho, nu, ve, re, re, ta, zo, M, no, u, M, de, u, ar, un</margin> <note>These marginal notes are fragmentary and appear to be cut off from the edge of the page.</note>

intricacies with the first motion, they required long observation by the most learned men and much more theoretical speculation to establish Hypotheses. Therefore, the teaching of this doctrine rightly follows the order of discovery.

      Furthermore, the first motion <note>The "First Motion" refers to the apparent daily rotation of the entire sky from east to west.</note> requires only the instrument of the sphere <note>A celestial globe or armillary sphere.</note>, which conforms to the visible sky and could, in a way, even be shown in the sky itself without an instrument. The causes and reasons for the secondary motions <note>The "Second Motion" refers to the individual paths of the sun, moon, and planets moving west to east against the background of the stars.</note> are by no means demonstrated in the visible sky, but require entirely flat diagrams, and we cannot easily imagine such a flat surface in the heavens. Nor is it easy to apply those things demonstrated on a flat diagram regarding secondary motions to the sky itself as it appears to the eyes, unless the first mode has first been understood, so that it can be mentally separated from the secondary motions.

      *How many parts are there of spherical doctrine?*

      Mainly five. The first and second are more general and contain the preparation for the rest.

->*What do the words "to Rise" and "to Set" mean?*<-

To **Rise** <note>Latin: *oriri*</note> is to be lifted or to stand up from a flat surface into the heights, to ascend gradually more and more, or to emerge, just as mountains seem to emerge from the waves to those sailing in the Ocean. Thus, you might not be far off in believing that the word is derived from "from the mountain" <note>original Greek: "apo tou orous"</note>, which means mountain, and from "to stir" or "to rise" <note>original Greek: "orsein"</note>. The Greek word for rising <note>original Greek: "anatellein," "anatole"</note> is related to the Latin "to be lifted" <note>Latin: *tolli*</note>; it is used properly of plants when they lift themselves into the air from the moist earth, which is called a "marsh" <note>original Greek: "telma"</note>.

To **Set** <note>Latin: *occidere*</note> and to **Fall** <note>Latin: *occumbere*</note> is to fall forward; it is used for those falling in a line of battle, and from there for all those who perish. The Greek word "to sink" <note>original Greek: "dyein"</note> is used for the act of retreating into some chamber, to go under, to enter, or to be hidden; this is because the stars retreat behind the mountains as if into a bedroom. The German prepositions for **Rising and setting** <note>original German: "Auff und nidergang"</note> are obvious, for they mean "up" and "down": **To go under** <note>original German: "untergehen"</note> is to be submerged, like ships in the waves.

### BOOK THREE 207

I.

*What is "Altitude" of a star to astronomers in this matter?*

The word "Altitude" is not to be understood in the common sense as the length of a perpendicular line dropped from a star to the plane of the Earth, but technically: it is the arc of a vertical circle drawn through the star, intercepted between the star and the rational <term>rational horizon|a theoretical horizon line that passes through the center of the Earth, used for calculations</term> Horizon. The complement of this arc to a quadrant <note>a 90-degree angle</note> is the distance of the star from the vertex <term>vertex|the zenith, or the point directly overhead</term>.

Since the Earth turns around an immobile axis in twenty-four hours, it is necessary that there are two points on the terrestrial globe—the ends of the axis, called poles—where an observer, positioned there and rotating along with his visible horizon, would perceive the heavens and the stars (which are actually stationary) to be swept up in a rotation around the extreme edge of his visible horizon. Meanwhile, throughout the entire circuit, the stars would remain at an equal distance from the zenith <note>The "vertex" or point directly above the observer's head.</note>—insofar as the celestial pole is located there—so that no star in any region appears higher or lower than it was before. <note>original: "stella nullâ in plaga fiat altior vel humilior seipsâ"</note>

As these locations on Earth are driven around, their zeniths also move beneath the immobile sphere of the fixed stars. ->*What is the variety of stars throughout the spheres of those that rise and those that do not rise: and how does this arise from the rotation of the earth around its axis?*<-

For the Horizon, or the boundary of sight, coincides with the equator, cutting the World into two hemispheres, Northern and Southern.

In a **right sphere** <note>The "Right Sphere" refers to the view from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator passes directly overhead through the zenith.</note> all stars rise and set within the space of one day. For the Horizon cuts the sphere—and thus all the **parallels**—through the axis and the poles. Since this rotates with the globe of the earth within 24 hours, it therefore covers all parts of the circles within one day during one of its half-circles, and in turn uncovers them during the remaining half-circle. Because of this, if a star were ever to fall exactly upon the pole itself, it would be visible throughout the whole year and at all hours of the night in the same place on the Horizon.

In **oblique spheres** <note>The "Oblique Sphere" refers to any latitude between the equator and the poles, where the celestial axis is at an angle to the horizon.</note>, just as much as the vertex or **Zenith** <note>the point directly above the observer</note> declines from the equator, so much does the Horizon sink below one pole on one side and rise above the other pole on the opposite side. **BOOK THREE. 213**

Stars within the embrace of the small circle which the horizon describes around the upper pole <term>celestial pole: the imaginary point in the sky directly above the Earth's axis around which all stars appear to rotate</term> at the point closest to its path, appear perpetually, as they do in a Parallel sphere <term>parallel sphere: a view of the sky from the Earth's poles, where the celestial equator aligns with the horizon and stars move in circles parallel to it</term>; all those within the opposite circle, which the horizon traces around the lower pole, remain hidden along with that pole itself; and the stars through which these circles pass touch the horizon once a day, and immediately either hide themselves again or rise back up. These circles, as mentioned in the second book, are depicted in some spheres and are called by the names Arctic and Antarctic. However, all the stars intermediate between these two circles rise and set, as in a right sphere <note>original: *sphaera recta*; the celestial sphere as viewed from the Earth's equator</note>; those closest to these circles and the visible pole mark points on the horizon very near to one another when rising and setting: for as soon as they have hidden themselves, they rise again almost in the same place beneath the pole. Those further away mark more distant locations, yet still from the same visible quarter, all the way to those stars that fall upon the equator; for the rising of these is distant from their setting by an entire semicircle of the horizon. Indeed, if a sighting instrument <term>dioptra: a classical astronomical tool used for measuring the positions of stars or terrestrial objects</term> is pointed toward the East and fixed in that position, the West will be seen through the same instrument from the opposite side, since the eye is the center of the Horizon. Therefore, the locations of the rising and setting of these stars cannot be seen together in a single glance.

[A circular diagram representing the horizon with intersecting lines. Labels include "EAST" at the top, "WEST" at the bottom, "NORTH" with arrows on the left, and "SOUTH" with arrows on the right.] <note>original labels: ORI (Oriens/East), OCCI (Occidens/West), SE (Septentrio/North), ME (Meridies/South)</note>

Stars located beyond the equator—yet by a distance less than the distance of the zenith <note>the point in the sky directly above the observer</note> from the equator—already have the locations of their rising and setting in both regions of the south, notwithstanding the fact that they themselves are seen at their highest point in the northern region. From there, the further the stars are distant from the equator <note>The "celestial equator," which is the Earth's equator projected onto the sky.</note>, the closer the points of rising and setting meet in the southern region. Eventually, you will see some stars that, having barely emerged, immediately hide themselves again, as if in the same place on the horizon toward the region of the midday sun <note>The author is describing how stars far from the equator appear to "graze" the horizon in short arcs.</note>.

*Do all these things appear at the same time every night, for each star?*

Not at all; rather, the observation of these things requires time, diligence, and remaining in one place. For rarely can one and the same star be seen both rising and setting within the space of a single night. This is because, for most stars, the light of day hides one of the two—either the rising or the setting—and therefore another day must be waited for, when that event also falls during the night.

*How then can these phenomena be investigated other than by observation, so that once investigated, they may be compared with the heavens themselves at their respective times?*

We need to investigate the <term>altitude of the Pole</term> <note>This measurement is equal to the observer’s latitude on Earth.</note> in any given place on Earth; the altitude of the Equator, the altitude of any <term>meridian star</term> <note>A star at its highest point in the sky as it crosses the imaginary north-south line.</note>, and its <term>declination</term> <note>The angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the Equator.

*What is the altitude of the Pole, the Equator, or a meridian star?*

It is the arc of the Meridian Circle, captured between the nearest part of the Horizon and the pole, the equator, or the star.

Not always from the region of the south, but from the **meridian circle**—to whose northern part also certain stars are seen to approach—and indeed some of those which do not set <note>original: "non occidunt"; these are circumpolar stars that stay above the horizon</note> approach it twice. From this arises a **double meridian altitude** for certain stars: one maximum, the other minimum.

**Explain this variety of meridian altitudes more specifically?**

<margin><unclear>E coru di vi in lo</unclear></margin>

->[Diagram 1: A celestial sphere showing the path of stars when the Pole (marked P) is at an altitude of 45 degrees (halfway between the horizon and the zenith Z). Several star symbols follow circular paths around the pole.]<-

At a **Pole altitude** of 45 degrees—which is the quantity of half a quadrant <note>A quadrant is 90 degrees; half is 45 degrees</note>—stars that graze the horizon also pass through the **zenith** <note>the point directly overhead, referred to here as the "vertex"</note>. Therefore, all stars closer to the pole than these come to the Meridian twice from the direction of the visible pole. None of those that are further from the pole are seen to approach the meridian twice, for the Horizon hides the lower crossing. Furthermore, none of these stars further from the visible pole approach the meridian toward the region of the visible pole.

<margin><unclear>Pol ud usa</unclear></margin>

->[Diagram 2: A celestial sphere showing the pole at a lower altitude (less than 45 degrees). The paths of the stars are tilted differently relative to the horizon.]<-

At a lower pole altitude, those stars which are between the **zenith stars** and the **grazing stars** approach the meridian once from the pole’s direction; those which are closer to the pole approach it twice from the direction of the Pole.

### 216 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

At a greater altitude of the Pole <note>The "altitude of the pole" refers to the angle of the celestial pole above the horizon, which is equal to the observer's geographic latitude.</note>, whichever stars are closer to the pole than those that just touch the Horizon appear to transit <note>original: "applicare"; referring to the star crossing the meridian line.</note> twice. Specifically, those that are closer to the pole than the Vertical circles <note>Circles passing through the zenith (the point directly overhead) and the nadir.</note> transit twice from the same side; however, those that are between the Vertical circles and those touching the Horizon transit once from the side of the pole and once from the opposite side of the Equator.

->[A circular diagram of a celestial sphere with various intersecting lines. Labels include the letters U, S, A, P, and h at the top, two star symbols, an arrow pointing towards the bottom-left, and a crescent-like shape on the right.]<-

*How is the size of that arc of the Pole's altitude known in any given place?*

In various ways, but the method proper to this section is as follows. When the night is longer than the day, so that more than half a revolution of the earth <note>The author adopts a Copernican perspective here, attributing the movement to the Earth's rotation rather than the stars.</note> can occur within a single night, we then choose a star near the pole of the world which does not set, and which can be observed on the meridian at the beginning and the end of the night: once when it appears at its highest point, and again when it appears at its lowest. Now, the parallel of the vertical point <note>The zenith</note>—by the definition of parallels—shares the same poles with the sphere. Therefore, the Meridian circle, because it passes through the pole, cuts this parallel at two opposite points, one of which (where the zenith point falls) is closest to the star, and the other is farthest from it. Therefore, when that semicircle of the Meridian which passes through the zenith reaches the star, the star appears at its highest; when the opposite semicircle reaches it, then the star appears at its lowest. And then the arithmetic mean <note>The average: (Highest Altitude + Lowest Altitude) divided by 2.</note> between both meridian altitudes of the star is the altitude of the Pole.

### BOOK THREE [space] 217

Let **V** be the Zenith <note>original: *Vertex*; the point in the sky directly above an observer</note>, **P** the pole, and **SI** the small circle <note>the circular path</note> of the movement of an apparent star—for example, the North Star <note>original: *Polaris*</note>. (For the diagrams represent the movement of stars, not the movement of the Zenith point, whose movement would be **VH**). Let the maximum altitude of the star **S** be the arc **SR**, 51° 3'. Let the minimum altitude **IR** be 45° 29'. Subtract **IR** from **SR**, and the remainder **SI** is 5° 34'. Half of this is **PI**, 2° 47'. Add **PI** to **IR**, and it results in **PR**, the altitude of the pole: 48° 16'. The same result would occur if the star **S** were stationary and the Zenith **V** were moving. First, if the semicircle **PVL**, containing the Zenith **V**, passes through the star **S**, the star will be at a distance **VS** from the zenith. Then, let the zenith be at **H**, and its semicircle **PHL** (and the opposite **PVL**) pass through the star; therefore, the star's distance from the zenith will be **HS**. Having subtracted **VS** (or the equal distance **HI**) from **HS**, the remainder is **SI**, as before.

#### How is the Altitude of the Equator obtained?

The altitude of the Pole and the altitude of the Equator, when combined, make a complete Quadrant <note>A quadrant is a 90-degree arc, or one-quarter of a circle</note>. Therefore, by subtracting the altitude of the Pole from the quadrant, the altitude of the Equator remains.

->[A circular diagram representing a celestial sphere. It shows the relationship between the horizon (the horizontal line), the celestial equator (angled), and the North Pole. Points are labeled V, P, H, Q, A, and L to illustrate the geometric proofs described in the text.]<-

# 258 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

To geographers, this is the latitude of a place: for by as much of an arc as the pole is raised above the Horizon, by that same amount of arc is the place distant from the equator. <note>In other words, the angle of the North Star above your horizon is exactly equal to your latitude on Earth.</note>

*What is the latitude of a place?*
It is the arc of the terrestrial <term>meridian</term><note>An imaginary Great Circle on the Earth's surface passing through the North and South Poles.</note>, caught between the specific location and the terrestrial equator.

*Prove that the arcs of the pole's altitude and the latitude of the place are proportional?* <note>original: "proportionalis"—here meaning they have the same degree measurement.</note>
From the equator to its pole is a quadrant <note>A quadrant is 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note>. From the <term>zenith</term><note>original: "vertice"—the point in the sky directly above the observer.</note> to the Horizon is likewise a quadrant in the Meridian circle: therefore these arcs are equal. Subtract the common arc that lies between the zenith and the pole; the remaining parts are therefore equal: in the first case, the distance from the equator to the zenith, and in the second, the distance from the Pole to the Horizon. Furthermore, the celestial and terrestrial arcs of the meridians, defined by two straight lines from the center—the vertical line and the axis—are proportional.
*In the previous diagram, IA or VQ are quadrants and equal; subtract the common segment VP. AT and PQ will be equal; likewise on Earth NL and VD, where NL is the latitude of the place and PQ is the altitude of the Pole.*

*What do <term>Gnomonicists</term><note>Specialists in the art of making sundials (gnomonics).</note> call the Declination of a Plane?*
The arc of the Horizon circle caught between the prime vertical <note>The vertical circle passing exactly East and West.</note> and the circle of the declining plane.

*What do they mean by the Inclination of an Inclined Plane?*
It is the arc of the primary vertical caught between the Meridian and the circle of the inclined plane.

*What is the inclination of a <term>Reclining Plane</term>?* <note>original: "Deinclinati"—refers to a surface that leans back away from the observer, common in sundial calculations.</note>
It is the arc of the Vertical circle perpendicular to the reclining circle, caught between that circle and the Zenith.

# THIRD BOOK 219

### What is required of the <term>Gnomonicist|A specialist in the art and science of constructing sundials</term> regarding a <term>declining-inclining plane|A sundial surface that is both tilted relative to the horizon (inclined) and turned away from the direct East-West or North-South lines (declining)</term>?
That first of all, it should be related back to a simple inclined plane. This is done by finding the specific "altitude of the pole" <note>In modern terms, this refers to the latitude of a location.</note> under which that complex declining-inclining plane can be calculated as if it were a simple inclined plane, as well as finding the angle of inclination relative to that new Pole altitude.

### How can this be done?
A right-angled triangle is formed [on the celestial sphere] between the Horizon, the Meridian, and the circle of the declining-inclining plane. Within this triangle, the side on the Horizon is given, which is the <term>complement|The angle needed to complete 90 degrees (e.g., the complement of 20 is 70)</term> of the plane’s declination. The angle between the circle of the plane and the Horizon is also given, which is the complement of the Inclination. The angle between the Horizon and the Meridian is a right angle [90 degrees]. From there, we seek the side on the Meridian—specifically the arc between the Horizon and the point where the plane’s circle intersects the meridian—as well as the angle of that intersection. This side, when compared with the altitude of the pole at your specific location, reveals the sought-after altitude of the pole.

*How is it truly known that a star is at this moment in the meridian and at its highest point, since the meridian circle is not visible to the eyes in the sky?*

By investigating the <term>meridian line</term> <note>An imaginary line on the ground running exactly north-south, used as a reference for astronomical measurements.</note> and placing a <term>quadrant</term> <note>A fundamental astronomical tool shaped like a quarter-circle, used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies above the horizon.</note> upon it or parallel to it; for when a star is seen falling into this plane, it is judged to be in the meridian.

*How is the meridian line obtained?*

In various ways, but the method most appropriate and convenient for this location is this: On a clear night, look toward the star at the tip of the tail of the Little Bear <note>original: "cauda ursæ minoris"; this refers to Polaris, the North Star</note>, for it is near the pole; therefore, that region is the northern region in our hemisphere, and the region opposite to it is roughly the South. Once the southern region is known, choose a star that is to the left of the South toward the east <note>original: "ortum", the place where the sun rises</note>: take its altitude DE with the quadrant SD and fix the <term>rule</term> <note>The movable sighting arm on the quadrant</note>; then note the position of the quadrant at that time by drawing a line SQ on the plane of the horizon where the quadrant stands.

Then wait until the star has crossed the meridian region; it

[A geometric diagram showing a quadrant instrument with various lines and points labeled with letters: A, C, S, t, k, d, q, P, D.]

### BOOK THREE 225

When this is done, always with the plane of the <term>quadrant</term> <note>A quarter-circle instrument used for measuring angles and altitudes.</note> directed toward the star until the star is seen again through the <term>pinnacidia</term> <note>The "sights" or small brass plates with holes used to align the instrument with a celestial body.</note> of the fixed rule S E, note the position in which this occurs by drawing another line S O on the horizontal plane. Then continue both lines until they intersect each other at S. Once this is done, bisect the angle Q S O between the two lines: and the bisecting line S P will be the **Meridian** of your location.
      There is a similar method by day using the sun, which is more popular and easy. On a plane that is parallel to the Horizon, let a circle A L C be described, and in its center S let a <term>style</term> <note>Also known as a gnomon; the vertical rod of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> S T be erected perpendicularly, of such a length that its shadow some hours before Noon ends at the circumference of the circle C. When this is exactly done, let that place on the circle C be marked, and wait for the time after noon when the shadow of the style again touches the same circle at another place A. Let that place be marked similarly, and by bisecting the arc C A intercepted between both places, let a straight line S L be drawn from the center S through the bisection; this will be the **Meridian line**.

*What is declination?*

      The word **declination** takes its origin from the apparent proper motion of the sun, or from its <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The path the sun appears to follow across the sky over the course of a year.</note> orbit which, since it meets the Equator in two places, gradually turns away and "declines" from the equator after those points. Therefore, declination is properly called the length of the arc of a circle drawn through the poles of the world, by which arc any point of the Ecliptic, as it successively "declines," has moved away from the Equator.
      Later, usage prevailed so that the distance of any star—even one existing outside the Ecliptic—from the Equator, measured on a circle drawn through the poles of the Equator, would be called the "declination" of that star.
      Therefore, in this context, declination is the arc of a circle drawn through the poles of the sphere, intercepted between the equator and the star, or whatever point on the spherical surface whose declination is sought.

### 226 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*How is the declination of any star or point determined from observations?*

If a star reaches the meridian <note>The imaginary north-south line passing directly overhead.</note> from the direction of the equator, the altitude of the Equator and the meridian altitude of the star or point must be compared with one another. For if the altitude of the star is greater than the altitude of the Equator, the <term>declination</term> <note>Declination is the celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring how far north or south an object is from the celestial equator.</note> will be northern; if it is less, the declination is southern. In these cases, subtracting the smaller value from the larger yields the total amount of declination.

But if the star falls on the meridian toward the Northern region <note>Meaning it is between the North Pole and the northern horizon.</note>, the altitude of the Pole must be used instead of the altitude of the Equator. The difference between the Pole's altitude and the star's maximum or minimum altitude, when subtracted from a full <term>quadrant</term> <note>A quadrant represents 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note>, leaves the northern declination of the star—at least here in our Hemisphere.

*How are rising and setting stars distinguished from those that do not rise or do not set by using declination?*

When the declination of a star is greater than the altitude of the equator <note>The altitude of the celestial equator at the meridian is equal to 90 degrees minus the observer's latitude.</note>, the star does not set, provided it is a northern star. This is because the depth of the opposite point of the equator below the northern Horizon is equal to the altitude of the equator in the south. Therefore, a star that is further from the equator than the Horizon is will remain above the Horizon even when it is at its lowest point.

If, however, you find a star in the records with such a great southern declination, you should know that it is one of those stars which, at your specific <term>altitude of the pole</term> <note>The altitude of the celestial pole above the horizon is equal to the observer's geographic latitude.</note>, never rises or comes into view.

Therefore, only those stars rise and set whose declination is less than the altitude of the equator.

Having observed the Azimuth, the altitude of the pole, and the star, its declination is calculated by the computation of Triangles. For a very well-known triangle is established in the primary motion, whose angles are the Pole P, the zenith <term>V</term><note>Original: "vertex". The other side, VS, between the zenith and the star, is the complement of the star's altitude SG, which is called the star's distance from the zenith. For if this side is found to be less than a quadrant <note>A quadrant is 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note>, its complement to the quadrant SE—or if it is greater, its excess above the quadrant SQ—will be the sought-after declination: northern in the former case, southern in the latter. The specific rules for this must be sought from the Geometers; but here you have a model of the work:

When a star rises, this angle is at its smallest, and it never equals the altitude of the equator, unless the rising star happens to be on the equator itself. From that point, this angle <note>This refers to the parallactic angle, also known as the angle of position, formed at the star by the arcs leading to the Zenith and the Pole.</note> increases and becomes a right angle on either side of the meridian. Therefore, in the case of a star whose declination <note>Declination is the celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring how far north or south a star is from the celestial equator.</note> is greater than the altitude of the Pole of the same name, the angle increases until it equals two right angles <note>180 degrees</note> at the Meridian. But if the declination is smaller, or even in the opposite direction, the angle decreases again until it vanishes entirely at the meridian.

->**What is related to the declinations of stars?**<-

->**How do astronomers usually speak of the places on the Horizon in which any given star is seen to rise or set?**<-

    They use the term **Rising Amplitude** <term>Rising Amplitude: The angular distance along the horizon between the East point and the point where a celestial body actually rises.</term>.

->**What is Rising Amplitude?**<-

    It is the arc of the Horizon intercepted between the Equator and the rising point of the star. Although the name seems to have originally derived from whole constellations, asking how "ample" a space of the Horizon any given constellation occupies when rising, along with all the stars assigned to it.

### BOOK THREE 237

...from being inverted. For the parts or limbs of the figures <note>The author refers to the "figures" of the constellations, such as the limbs of Andromeda or the Great Bear.</note> are always oriented toward the celestial pole. Therefore, the top <term>vertex | the highest point or "head" of a constellation figure</term>, located at any point on its own parallel circle, always inclines from the constellation toward the region where the pole **P** is located, whether the constellation appears above or below that pole. Thus, a standing observer views the figures just as if they had the zenith directly under the pole itself in a "parallel sphere" <note>A "parallel sphere" describes the sky as seen from the Earth's poles, where stars move in circles parallel to the horizon.</note>; that is, they see them positioned in the same way whether they are high in the southern region or low in the northern region.

In this case, turning one's face to follow the star prevents the orientation from being inverted.

However, regarding those stars within the span of the **VH** parallel passing through the zenith: they reach the meridian twice in the northern quadrant—once when they are at their highest point **S**, and once when they are at their lowest point **I**. Because the viewer’s face is turned toward the same polar region in both instances, their orientation must necessarily be fully inverted; for when they are high, the parts furthest from the pole are at the top, whereas when they are low, the parts closest to the pole are at the top.

The opposite occurs with stars that rise and set. For the turning of the face by one following the constellation into opposite regions presents their orientation as inverted. For those rising, the leading parts are higher; for those setting, the trailing parts are higher.

Thus, in a "right sphere" <note>The sky as viewed from the Earth's equator, where stars rise and set at right angles to the horizon.</note> a full inversion happens in this manner; in "oblique spheres" <note>The sky as viewed from any latitude between the equator and the poles.</note> it is a partial inversion. For those stars which rise upright, they set laid flat, face-down, or face-up; and this varies according to the greater or lesser obliquity of the sphere, and according to the position of the constellations fixed upon the surface of the sphere.

->240 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY<-

Again, another triangle, SQT, can be formed here—which was described a little earlier—between the declination SQ, the <term>Rising Amplitude</term> <note>original: "Amplitudinem Ortivam"; the angular distance of a rising celestial body from the East point of the horizon</note> ST, and the equator QT. For a northern star, this is below the earth; for a southern one, it is above. For QT produces an arc of the equator, which below will be called the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>original: "differentia ascensionalis"; the difference between the right ascension and the oblique ascension of a celestial body</note>, measuring the excess of the semi-diurnal parallel arc over a quadrant; for the process is the same.

*Review all the varieties of these durations* <note>original: "morarum"; referring to the time spent above or below the horizon</note> *through all three positions of the sphere?*

In a **right sphere** <note>the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's equator, where the poles lie on the horizon</note>, or among those who live under the Equator, the upper arcs of all stars are equal to their lower arcs, such that any star lingers 12 hours above the Horizon and 12 below.

In **Oblique spheres** <note>where the celestial pole is at an angle between 0 and 90 degrees</note>, where each has the same altitude of its respective pole: just as stars that do not rise for one observer do not set for another [at the opposite pole] and vice versa; so also stars grazing the Horizon for one as if about to set (though they do not set), likewise graze the Horizon for the other as if about to rise (though they do not rise). Furthermore, among the rising stars, those with a greater northern declination have longer days and shorter nights here [in the north], while those with the opposite declination [southern] have the opposite there, up until those that fall upon the Equator, which alone have days equal to nights. From there, the greater the declination they have in the opposite region, the longer their night and shorter their day. Finally, those stars that have equal declinations in opposite regions have the proportions and measures of their days and nights exchanged in the same place on Earth, so that the day of one is equal to the night of the other. Again, the same star at the same altitude of opposite poles remains above the horizon in one place as much as it remains below in the other, and vice versa.

In **Parallel spheres** <note>the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's poles, where the equator coincides with the horizon</note>, nothing rises and nothing sets; therefore, half the stars have a continuous day in one [hemisphere], and a continuous night in the other; the remaining half have the opposite.

# BOOK THREE. 241

*You said that the rays of the stars are refracted near the Horizon: does this then not disturb the teaching handed down so far?*

Since stars, through <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, which makes celestial objects appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note>, appear to be raised higher than is correct in the vertical circle—both at their rising and their setting—their declinations <note>The coordinate measuring a star's distance north or south of the celestial equator.</note> in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The view of the sky from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator passes directly overhead.</note> are not changed in any way that can be perceived. However, in <term>oblique spheres</term><note>The view of the sky from any location between the equator and the poles, where the celestial paths appear tilted.</note>, they change significantly. For those stars that share the name of the northern hemisphere, their declinations are represented as greater than they truly are, and for others, they appear smaller. From this it follows that their <term>diurnal arcs</term><note>The path a star takes above the horizon from rising to setting.</note> appear longer than is correct for some, and shorter for others. This difference is greatest in a right sphere and non-existent in <term>parallel spheres</term><note>The view from the North or South Pole, where stars move in circles parallel to the horizon.</note>. Furthermore, the <term>rising amplitude</term><note>The angular distance from due east where a star rises.</note> is altered everywhere; it does not change at all in the right or parallel spheres, yet it changes most of all at a polar altitude of 45 degrees.

*Tell by what means it was brought about that the Ecliptic should decline from the Equator, and for what purpose?*

The genuine and formal cause of this declination is the inclination of that axis around which the Earth rotates (as if on an unmoving point) upon the plane of the Ecliptic, in which the center of the Earth moves in its annual motion as it goes around the Sun. For if the axis of the Earth’s daily motion stood upright upon this plane formed by the Earth's annual motion, the Equator and the Ecliptic would coincide. <note>The author is explaining that the 23.5-degree tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit is what creates the angle between the celestial equator and the path of the sun (the ecliptic).</note> *See the second diagram from here.*

The final cause <note>In the philosophy of this era, the "final cause" refers to the ultimate purpose or "why" a thing exists as it does, often attributed to divine design.</note> of this inclination is, without doubt, for the benefit of humans and living creatures dispersed across the entire surface of the Earth: so that the variety of celestial phenomena <note>Refers to the changing seasons and the shifting positions of the sun throughout the year.</note> might reach every single place on Earth; which will be explained further below in the fourth part.

These things, therefore, are demonstrated most ingeniously with the most delightful reasoning in Copernican Astronomy, such that both the "how" of the matter and its "why" are established within the Earth itself; in common astronomy <note>original: "Astronomia vulgatâ"; this refers to the older Geocentric or Ptolemaic system which placed the Earth at the center of the universe.</note> we are only taught *that* it is so; *why* it is and *how* it happens is there shrouded in much darkness.

Then they subtract the minimum from the maximum; the remainder, cut in half, is taken as the maximum declination.

->*How great is this maximum declination of the Ecliptic from the Equator?*<-

      Astronomers from all ages do not entirely agree on the minute details. Because of this, the most ancient ones established it as precisely 24 degrees, which is the fifteenth part of a full circle. Eratosthenes, dividing the whole circle into 83 parts, stated that eleven of those parts equal twice the maximum declination. Therefore, for him, the maximum declination is approximately 23° 51 1/3', a value that Hipparchus and Ptolemy also kept, following Eratosthenes. Albategnius <note>original: "Albategnius"; the Latinized name of Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> recorded 23° 35'. Arzachel <note>Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer</note> 23° 34'. Almeon 23° 33'. Prophatius the Jew 23° 32'. Tycho Brahe 23° 31 1/2', and by another method 23° 30 1/2'. And according to Peurbach, Copernicus, and other astronomers of these times in the northern world <note>original: "Arctoo orbe"</note>, it is 23° 28' or even 23° 27'. Thus, the entire disagreement fluctuates within 24 minutes, <margin>P</margin> which is no more than the nine-hundredth part of a circle. Nevertheless, <margin>o</margin> today in the astronomy of Tycho Brahe, we commonly use <margin>g</margin> 23° 31 1/2'.

## ASCENSIONS

*What do Astronomers call Ascension and Descension?*

The same thing that the Greeks call by the compound terms *rising-together* and *setting-together* <note>original: συνανατολή (synanatole) & συγκατάδυσις (synkatadysis)</note>, as if you were to say in English "Co-rising" and "Co-setting." These are arcs of the Equator <term>Equator: the great circle of the celestial sphere, lying in the same plane as the Earth's equator</term> which appear to rise above the horizon or sink below it together with some other part of the sky located away from the equator, for which a specific beginning and end is given on the sphere.

*Why are the arcs of the Equator observed as co-rising or co-setting rather than those of any other circle?*

Because among the great circles, only the equator moves uniformly <note>The equator rotates at a steady, constant speed compared to other circles like the ecliptic</note>; the equal parts of the others often move...

*But why does the same thing not also happen to the equinoctial itself, through the Horizons of different places?*

Because that motion of the Earth, by which the risings and settings of the stars are represented, follows the path of the equinoctial, not the path of the ecliptic. From this, it follows that the Horizon and the Equinoctial always intersect each other at the same point of the Horizon <note>original: "in eodem puncto Horizontis"</note>; the Ecliptic, however, intersects the Horizon at various points with its different parts, and these points differ according to the intervals of the places—or the positions of the sphere.

*In how many ways do we investigate the **Ascensions** and **Descensions** of the arcs of the Ecliptic?*

In two ways. For we take those arcs either as **Continuous**—that is, beginning from the common vernal intersection <note>The "vernal intersection" is the Spring Equinox, the point where the sun crosses the equator moving north.</note> with the equator—or as **Discrete**—that is, not beginning from the vernal intersection.

*Do we not also seek the Ascensions of stars or points of the Ecliptic, which are not arcs but the boundaries of arcs?*

Whenever it happens that we speak in this way—for example, "the Ascension of the 23rd degree of Leo," and so forth—then the entire continuous arc of the Ecliptic from the beginning of Aries <note>In traditional astronomy, Aries marks the 0° point of the ecliptic.</note> up to the named 23rd degree of Leo is understood. It is, therefore, merely a shorthand way of speaking. Hold this same rule when we speak of the "Ascension of a star." ...we shall seek the vernal equinox <note>original: "sectionem vernalem," the point where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring</note> and the star and the ascension of its arc.

->*How are the ascensions or descensions of such arcs found?*<-

Once the sphere <note>Referring to an armillary sphere or celestial globe, a common tool for astronomers of this period.</note> has been positioned as the specific location requires, the beginning of the given arc is placed on the rising <term>Horizon</term> <note>The eastern horizon where stars appear to "ascend" or rise.</note>, and the point on the <term>equator</term> through which the Horizon then passes is marked with some sign. The same is done with the end of the given arc. Therefore, the arc of the equator intercepted between those two marks is the **Ascension** of the proposed Arc of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The Ecliptic is the path the sun appears to follow through the stars over the course of a year.</note>. If the same is done on the western part of the Horizon, the **descension** <note>The "setting" or "falling" of a celestial body.</note> of that same given arc will be marked in this manner.

In a continuous arc, only its end point is placed on the horizon. For its beginning and the equator coincide at the same point, and there is no need for the Horizon's indication. Then, the number appearing at the point rising with the end immediately reveals the quantity of the Ascension or descension, in parts or times of which the whole circle has 360.

->*How many types of Ascensions and descensions are there?*<-

There are just as many as there are types of the sphere's position. For just as after the <term>right sphere</term> <note>A "right sphere" occurs at the Earth's equator, where the North Pole is on the horizon and stars rise vertically.</note>, there follow ninety positions of the sphere according to the ninety degrees of the **Elevation of the pole**, and infinite intermediate positions could be named until the last has the pole at the very zenith, with the horizon coinciding with the equator, in a **parallel sphere**: so also the Ascensions begin from the "right" ones, passing through as many "oblique" ones, and end in no Ascension or descension at all. For in a <term>parallel sphere</term> <note>The view from the North or South Pole, where the stars move in circles parallel to the horizon rather than rising or setting.</note> the heaven revolves in the manner of an upper millstone (or the earth revolves with the horizon, as if someone were revolving the lower millstone while the upper one stood still); for nothing there either rises or sets.

BOOK THREE. 253

In the tables of the **prime mover** <term>prime mover; Latin: *primum mobile*, the outermost celestial sphere in pre-modern astronomy that carries all others from east to west</term> by Regiomontanus, Reinhold, Magini, and others, there exist—after one table of Right Ascensions—another 89 tables of Oblique Ascensions for each degree of the Elevation of the Pole <note>the "Elevation of the Pole" refers to the observer's latitude</note>. Others have also constructed specialized tables for the intermediate elevations of the pole.

*Is there some* **ambiguity** <note>original Greek: Ομωνυμία (*homonymia*), referring to a term having multiple meanings</note> *here that might deceive the unwary?*

Indeed. For in one sense, in a "right sphere" <note>an observer's view from the equator where the celestial poles are on the horizon</note> the entire circle is said to rise "rightly," and in an "oblique sphere" <note>an observer's view from any other latitude</note> it rises "obliquely." But in another sense, different parts of the whole circle are compared to one another: one part is said to rise "rightly" and another "obliquely," both in the right sphere and in the oblique sphere.

*In what respect are arcs said to ascend "rightly" and "obliquely"?*

Those arcs of the **Ecliptic** <term>Ecliptic; the apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year</term> which cut the horizon at more right (upright) angles are said to ascend rightly; those that cut it at more oblique (tilted) angles are said to ascend obliquely.

*By what argument do we know the greater or lesser uprightness or tilt of these angles? And which part ascends "rightly" and which "obliquely"?*

<margin>On the Right Ascensions of the points and arcs of the Ecliptic.</margin>

The more oblique the angles are, the smaller the arc of Ascension assigned to them; therefore, the more upright they are, the larger the Ascension. In general, therefore, that arc of the Ecliptic is said to rise "rightly" when it rises alongside an arc of the equator that is larger than itself, and "obliquely" when it rises with an arc smaller than itself.

EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY 256

### More notable and easily remembered rules of <term>Right Ascensions</term><note>Right Ascension is the distance measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox; it is the celestial equivalent of longitude.</note>.

#### I. Compare Right Ascensions with descensions.

*The Right Ascension is equal to the right descension <note>descension: the point or time at which a celestial body sets below the horizon.</note> of the same point: because each semicircle of the Horizon cuts the equator at a right angle, and the arc of the <term>Ecliptic</term><note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note> remains the same, as does the angle between the equator and the Ecliptic. Therefore, since three parts in the <term>spherical triangle</term><note>The author is referring to the geometric triangle formed on the surface of the celestial sphere by the horizon, the equator, and the ecliptic.</note> remain constant, it is necessary that the remaining three also remain the same; among these is the arc of the equator, which in the first case is the Ascension and in the second is the Right Descension.*

#### II. Compare the Ascensions of opposite equal parts and semicircles.

*The Ascensions of these parts are also equal to each other, regardless of where they begin: because the angle of the vernal intersection <note>The Spring Equinox.</note> is equal to the angle of the autumnal intersection, and the other factors are as before. Either they begin from the equinoctial points, in which case the proposition is self-evident, or they do not: in that case, the remaining distance to the neighboring equinoxes on both sides is the same. Therefore, when equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal. Or, if they are semicircles, they are divided by the equinoctial points; and again, the Ascensions of the individual equal parts on both sides are equal. Consequently, the joined parts—that is, the whole semicircles—are also equal.*

#### III. Compare whole quadrants of the Ecliptic with their Ascensions.

**When a whole quadrant <note>A 90-degree segment of a circle.</note> of the Ecliptic starts from a cardinal point <note>A "cardinal point" here refers to the equinoxes or solstices.</note>, a full quadrant of the equator rises along with it.**

*For the Horizon FE, passing through the solstitial points D and also through F, the pole of the Ecliptic: It therefore cuts it at an angle* <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the geometric proof on the following page.</note>

->IV. Compare the ascensions of various<-

->among themselves.<-

Parts of Quadrants are not equal to their ascensions; those that begin from the equinoctial points ascend obliquely <note>original: "obliquè"</note>; that is, they have ascensions smaller than themselves. However, those that begin from the Solstitial points ascend rightly <note>original: "rectè"; this refers to Right Ascension, where the stars rise more vertically compared to the horizon.</note>, and have ascensions larger than themselves.
When one of two Ecliptic arcs, starting from the equinoctial point, is equal to the ascension of the other ending at the Solstice (or vice versa): the difference between the arcs and their ascensions is likewise equal.
The distinct parts, the closer they are to the Equinoctial points, the more obliquely they ascend; the closer they are to the Solstitial points, the more rightly.
*For the angle between the Ecliptic and the Horizon is a right angle at the Solstices, and most oblique (namely, acute) at the Equinoxes: since the angle of the equator and the Horizon is always a right angle, and greater than that; therefore, a larger arc of the Ecliptic is subtended to this than the arc of the equator to that.*

This necessarily occurs near the midpoints of the quadrants.
   *How is this point sought geometrically?*
   <term>Regiomontanus</term><note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a vital figure in Renaissance astronomy.</note> defines it in this way, following <term>Geber the Arab</term><note>Jabir ibn Aflah (c. 1100–1150), a Spanish-Muslim astronomer whose work influenced European mathematics.</note>: the sine of its distance from the pole of the equator is the mean proportional between the sines of the arcs by which the ends of the quadrant are distant from that same pole.
   *The beginning of the quadrant is 90 degrees from the pole; its sine is 100,000. The end of the quadrant is 66 degrees, 28 minutes, and 30 seconds away; its sine is 91,688. These values, when multiplied together, have a square root of 95,754, the arc of which is 73 degrees, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds. This, then, is the distance of the point we seek from the pole. Therefore, it is 16 degrees, 45 minutes, and 24 seconds from the equator. The point that is at this distance is found, according to the teachings above, to be 46 degrees, 14 minutes, and 40 seconds from the intersection of the Ecliptic. Thus, that much of the arc rises obliquely, beginning from the intersection; the remaining arc of 43 degrees, 45 minutes, and 20 seconds rises "rightly" or directly.*
   *When all these values are quadrupled, 184 degrees, 58 minutes, and 40 seconds rise obliquely, while 175 degrees, 1 minute, and 20 seconds rise rightly. However, some who are accustomed to dealing only with whole <term>Signs</term><note>The twelve 30-degree divisions of the Zodiac.</note> favor "right ascensions," saying that eight signs rise rightly and four obliquely. This is because when the right ascensions are distributed, they are found in Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius. Yet they ignore the fact that the outer edges of the signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius actually rise obliquely.*
   *There remains in our triangle the angle between the Ecliptic and the Horizon, the Meridian, or the circle of declination, which the Right Ascension subtends; what observations do you have regarding that?*
   This angle, as has already been said regarding the <term>Right Horizon</term><note>The celestial horizon at the Earth's equator, where the poles lie on the horizon line.</note>, is acute, and it is smaller the closer it is to the equinoctial points. However, it never equals the complement of the maximum <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note>; but at the solsticial point itself, the angle is a right angle (90 degrees). Beyond the solsticial point, it becomes an obtuse angle with respect to the more distant preceding equinox, and acute, as before, with respect to the closer following equinox.

*What is the Right Ascension of a star or point on the sphere that lies outside the Ecliptic?* <note>The Ecliptic is the sun's apparent path across the sky. Right Ascension is the standard way to measure "celestial longitude."</note>

It is the arc of the celestial equator intercepted between the beginning of Aries <note>The vernal equinox; the zero-point of the astronomical coordinate system.</note> and the star's or point's <term>circle of declination</term> <note>A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the star, acting like a celestial line of longitude.</note>, measured in the order of the zodiac signs. More will be said on this below in the fifth part of the spherical doctrine.

*What is the terrestrial counterpart to the star's Right Ascension?*

The longitude of a place on Earth.

*What is the longitude of a place?*

It is the arc of the terrestrial equator (or even of the parallel of latitude drawn through the location) intercepted between the first terrestrial meridian <note>The prime meridian; in this period, it was usually set at the Canary Islands or the Azores rather than Greenwich.</note> and the meridian of the place, measured in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia"; meaning from West to East.</note>. More on this below in part five.

**Regarding the oblique ascensions of points and arcs of the Ecliptic.**

*How are Oblique Ascensions determined?*

One must know the declination of the chosen point, its right ascension, and the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>The difference between the time a star rises at the equator and the time it rises at a specific geographic latitude.</note>. This difference is determined from the declination. By adding this ascensional difference to the right ascension, or subtracting it from it, the <term>oblique ascension</term> <note>The point of the equator that rises with a star or zodiacal degree at a specific latitude.</note> of that point is established.

*What is the ascensional difference, and how is it investigated?*

When the chosen point is placed on the rising horizon, a right-angled triangle is formed by the horizon, the equator, and the circle of declination of the chosen point. In this triangle... [catchword: Triangulo]

*Generally compare oblique ascensions with right ascensions?*

Equal portions smaller than a semicircle beginning from the equinoxes—specifically those starting from the Vernal <note>Spring</note> equinox—are faster during their rising in our hemisphere than in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The "right sphere" refers to the view of the sky from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator passes directly overhead and stars rise and set vertically.</note>, and they rise more obliquely than in that sphere. However, those portions that begin from the autumnal equinox become slower than in a right sphere, and for that reason, they are said to rise "more rightly" than in a right sphere, though this term is used loosely. Indeed, in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>The sky as seen from any latitude other than the equator or the poles, where the stars rise at an angle.</note>, the <term>Ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note> can rarely rise more vertically than it does in a Right Sphere, except perhaps near the Tropics.

Distinct arcs, however—that is, those not starting exactly from the equinoxes—rise more obliquely the closer they are to the vernal equinox (either before or after it), and more "rightly" the closer they are to the autumnal equinox.

*How is oblique descension investigated?*

Since the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>The difference in time between a celestial object rising at the equator versus rising at a specific latitude.</note>, when subtracted, results in the oblique ascension, that same difference when added results in the oblique descension; and conversely, that which is added to create the oblique ascension must be subtracted to determine the oblique descension.

*What analogy arises here between oblique ascensions and oblique descensions?*

1. The amount of the ascension of an arc starting from the beginning of Aries is equal to the descension of an equal arc starting from the beginning of Libra, and vice versa. The same is true for distinct, equal, and opposite arcs. Therefore, no tables are made for descensions, as the tables for ascensions are sufficient.

2. The same parts that rise "rightly" descend "obliquely," and vice versa.
