->264 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY<-

*How many types of positions of the sphere are there, with respect to the equator and Ecliptic joined together, through which oblique ascensions vary?*

There are six positions in either Hemisphere, to which a seventh is added: that of the <term>right sphere</term> <note>A "right sphere" refers to the celestial sphere as seen from the Earth's equator, where the celestial equator passes directly overhead at a 90-degree angle to the horizon.</note>. For the <term>zenith</term> <note>original: "vertex loci," the point in the sky directly above the observer.</note> of a location either falls under the equator, or between the Equator and the <term>Tropic</term>, or under the Tropic itself, or between the Tropic and the <term>Polar Circle</term>, or under the Polar Circle itself, or between the Polar Circle and the <term>Pole</term>, or under the Pole itself. In the first of these positions, the <term>ascensions</term> <note>The rising of celestial bodies over the horizon.</note> are only "right," which have already been discussed; in the last position, there are clearly no ascensions at all. Therefore, five intermediate positions remain in each Hemisphere for <term>Oblique Ascensions</term> <note>Oblique ascension is the arc of the celestial equator that rises together with a star or a point on the ecliptic in a non-right (oblique) sphere.</note>.

*Compare the ascensions and descensions of each Hemisphere with one another?*

1. Just as much as the oblique ascension of any certain sign, degree, or point of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The annual path of the Sun across the sky.</note> is at a certain northern elevation of the pole, so is the oblique descension of that same sign, degree, or point at an equal southern elevation of the pole; and however much the descension is there, so much is the Ascension here.
2. Whatever is demonstrated regarding a certain sign, degree, or point of the Ecliptic in the Northern Hemisphere will also be true regarding the opposite sign, degree, or point in the Southern Hemisphere, with the elevation of either pole being the same on both sides.

*How does the ascensional difference relate to the right ascension through the various positions of the sphere?*

In a right sphere, just as there is no oblique ascension, so the arc of the Ecliptic—whether extended backward or forward from the nearer <term>equinox</term>—retains no value for the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>The difference in time/arc between when an object rises on the equator versus when it rises at a specific latitude.</note>. In <term>oblique spheres</term>, it acquires some value as it deviates from the equator; and as long as it is between the Equator and the Polar Circle, it is less than the <term>right ascension</term>; at the Polar Circle, it is equal to it; and within the Polar Circle, it is greater than it through all...

# EPITOME
## OF COPERNICAN
## ASTRONOMY

->Written in the common form of Questions and Answers, and divided into VII Books, of which these first THREE are concerning the<-

### Doctrine of the Sphere.
<note>The "Doctrine of the Sphere" refers to the traditional study of the celestial sphere, including the coordinates, circles (like the equator and ecliptic), and the movements of stars as seen from Earth.</note>

->YOU HAVE, FRIENDLY READER, IN THIS FIRST<-
part, besides an accurate physical explanation of the Earth’s daily Motion, and the arising from it of the circles of the Sphere, the whole doctrine of the Sphere in a new and more elegant METHOD, expanded by the addition of Examples of all kinds of Astronomical and Geographical Calculations, which encompass the full force of the instructions.

->BY THE AUTHOR<-

### JOHANNES KEPLER
->MATHEMATICIAN TO THE EMPEROR CAESAR<-
->MATTHIAS, AND TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS ESTATES<-
->of the Archduchy of Austria above the Enns.<-

->EPISTOLA<-

...how very expensive editions of this kind are: on one hand, my solitude, and on the other, my meager means, made the beginnings very difficult for me. I struck a deal, compelled by necessity, with a bookseller from Augsburg <note>Augsburg was a major German printing center</note>, so that he might publish a copy of this *Epitome* at his own expense. He agreed to do this, and he even included this *Epitome* in the catalog of the Frankfurt Fair <note>The Frankfurt Book Fair was the most important marketing event for books in early modern Europe</note> more than two years ago. 

But conveniently, a printer came to us, in whose presence—since I retained the right to correct the type and perform multiple proofreadings—I hoped I would present everything in a more perfect and corrected state. Yet, on the other hand, my bookseller complained because the expenses had to be paid in Linz <note>Kepler lived in Linz, Austria, from 1612 to 1626; it was a more remote and expensive location for publishing than major centers</note>, which were both greater and in an inconvenient location. However, he would not release me from our contract, nor would he renounce his legal rights to printing the booklet. 

It happened through various delays that the edition of this *Spherical Doctrine* <note>The "Spherical Doctrine" refers to the first part of Kepler's work, which deals with the geometry of the heavens as seen from Earth</note> alone was not even started until a year and a half after our agreement, and once started, it was dragged out for over another year. Indeed, unless I had supplied part of the costs myself and hired the most convenient workers I could find (though I wished for better), the edition would still be unfinished today. 

However, this repetition of the *Spherical Doctrine* should not seem useless or idle, as if after the works of the ancients—Euclid, Aratus, Cleomedes, Geminus, Proclus, and Theon <note>A list of classical Greek authorities on mathematics and astronomy; Kepler is justifying why he needs to write a new textbook when these "greats" already exist</note>—

# DEDICATION

After the concepts of Theon <note>Theon of Alexandria (c. 335 – c. 405 AD), a Greek mathematician and astronomer</note>, or the works of the more recent Sacrobosco <note>Johannes de Sacrobosco, whose 13th-century introductory astronomy text remained standard for centuries</note> and his infinite commentators—among whom is the most learned and exhaustive Christopher Clavius <note>A key Jesuit mathematician and architect of the Gregorian calendar</note>, as well as Hartmann, Virdung, Wurstisius, and Peucer; Schreckenfuchs, Piccolomini, Brucaeus, Winshemius, Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, the teacher of Johannes Kepler</note>, and the most recent of all, Metius; and following the *Theories* <note>original: "Theoricas," referring to technical models of planetary motion</note> of Peurbach, Reinhold, and Simus; there would seem to be no reason remaining why this concise teaching should be handed down once again. For, in the first place, even if nothing new were added to the teaching of the Ancients, it is still useful for that same material to be delivered by various authors, since the intellects of students are varied. Not all students are suited to the same teacher, nor is the same style or the same method convenient for everyone. No writer deviates so far from the common custom that he does not find his own reader, someone who takes pleasure in the same subjects and style as himself.

It was with this plan that I mixed together not only the well-worn and necessary definitions but also certain higher speculations, as the method suggested. I have presented both types of material in the form of questions and answers <note>This "catechism" style was a popular pedagogical tool for helping students memorize and internalize complex subjects</note>, so that beginners would not lack what their capacity allows them to grasp, and so that advanced students with mature judgment might not suffer the boredom of trite and common definitions without some variation to refresh them; and so that the difficulty of the speculations—

# EPISTLE

...ty, should be discussed as the opportunity for conversation allows.

Next, I believe that <term>experts</term> <note>original: "artificers"; referring to skilled practitioners of astronomy and mathematics.</note> will also judge that the method I have followed has been made more convenient throughout; furthermore, I have omitted several less necessary <term>minor details</term> <note>original: "parerga"; secondary matters or ornamental additions not essential to the core proof.</note>, and in turn added things which others had not yet handed down. I have also presented the rules for astronomical calculations—drawn from the most recent shortcuts of Tycho Brahe, Paul Wittich, Jost Bürgi, and Bartholomaeus Pitiscus—through individual examples in such a way that for practical use almost nothing else is required except for a careful and faithful imitation of the model, simply by changing the numbers.

But the type of philosophy I follow has provided me with more numerous and urgent reasons for reshaping <term>spherical doctrine</term> <note>The mathematical study of the positions and motions of objects on the celestial sphere.</note>. By the single, moderate daily motion of the Earth, this philosophy removes from the universe many other motions which are contrary to the genuine and proper motions of the planets in that same subject—motions of an ineffable and insane speed. Furthermore, by the single annual motion of that same Earth, it casts down all the <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary paths.</note> of the ancients (which were tied to the motion of the Sun by a blind reasoning), and all their <term>eccentrics</term> <note>Orbits that are off-center from the Earth, used in the Ptolemaic system.</note> of eccentrics, as well as all the circles of inclinations, deviations, and reflections; as I shall explain more fully in the section on theoretical doctrine.

And from this it even happens, that however much more absurd it appears at first glance, and however much more difficult it is to believe regarding the Earth...

->### DEDICATION<-

With the axiom of the Earth’s motion, all of Astronomy becomes so much easier to understand and to handle, as soon as one has admitted that the Earth moves.

Therefore, a <term>Hypothesis</term> <note>In this context, a "hypothesis" is a foundational mathematical model used to explain celestial observations.</note> of such excellence is entirely worthy—despite the prejudices of all contemporary astronomers—of being refined and made easier to perceive in all its parts. Let everyone hold it in whatever place they wish; I certainly understand that I owe this duty to it: that since I have inwardly confirmed it in my mind as true, and I enjoy incredible pleasure gazing upon its beauty, I shall also defend it outwardly to my readers with all the powers of my wit. 

However, since there are those who fear that the **doctrine of the sphere** <note>original: "doctrina sphaerica." This refers to the traditional study of the heavens as a series of nested, rotating spheres, a concept central to the older Ptolemaic system.</note>—through the supposition of the Earth’s daily motion—either cannot be taught or will be entirely overturned because we assert that the Earth moves rather than the celestial sphere; they ask, "what need then is there for the sphere, or what use is it?" And since many other things can be objected to in appearance, for which common solutions are not everywhere available: I have judged it my responsibility to provide all these things clearly explained in this **Epitome** (something which has never been done before).

If anyone wishes to accuse me here of being eager for **innovation** <note>original: "novationis." In the early 17th century, "innovation" was often a negative term implying a dangerous or heretical breaking of tradition.</note>: let them know that in philosophy, this is no crime; for indeed, the whole of philosophy is innovation.

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his philosophical and scientific methods, moving from the rejection of ignorance to the pursuit of truth over personal fame.</meta>

->EPISTOLA<-

...in ancient ignorance. The only difference is whether you innovate out of a desire for glory or for truth. And yet, if I were seeking glory, perhaps I would not lack the talent to devise something unique; whereas in this branch of philosophy <note>The author refers to natural philosophy or science, which at this time was shifting from traditional Aristotelian views to new observational methods.</note>, most of the things I follow belong to others. They are not, to be sure, slavishly copied, but are harmoniously arranged from various sources according to how each person seemed to uphold the truth in their own part.

Indeed, it is a pleasure for me to agree with the many, as often as the multitude is not in error. For that reason, I take great pains to persuade as many people as possible of what is inherent in the reality of the matter. By that means, sharing the same view with a great multitude, I might enjoy a greater delight. Meanwhile, just as a good Prince desires peace above all things, but if he cannot obtain it, he seeks Victory; so also I am refreshed amid the troubles caused by the disagreeing common crowd. This is because, for the most part, after the long-lasting clouds of common opinions, the clear beam of truth finally shines forth. Whenever I fight on the side of truth, the victory is eventually mine—a victory that would not exist if there had not been a very long struggle involving great sweat and danger.

That same truth moved and conquered that foremost teacher of the old <term>Astronomy</term> <note>Traditional "Ptolemaic" astronomy, which held that the Earth was the center of the universe.</note> whom Rome borrowed from the heart of our Germany, Christopher Clavius <note>Christoph Clavius (1538–1612) was a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, famous for his work on the Gregorian calendar. Late in life, he acknowledged the importance of Galileo's telescopic discoveries.</note>. So it was that when he was near death, since...

->DEDICATORY EPISTLE.<-

[decorative flourish] I reflect in my thoughts that Peurbach <note>Georg von Peurbach (1423–1461), a pioneering astronomer whose work "Theoricae Novae Planetarum" modernized planetary theory before Copernicus.</note>, the author of the *Theories*, was a citizen of this province; that Winsemius <note>Sebastian Theodorus Winsemius, a 16th-century scholar.</note>, the author of the *Questions on the Sphere* <note>original: "sphæricarum quæſtionum"; a standard textbook topic regarding the geometry of the heavens.</note>, dedicated his little book to the Illustrious Barons of Polheim and Wartenberg. I recall that the High-born Lords, the Hohefelder brothers—who are today the Lords of the town of Peurbach—cultivated the <term>Doctrine of the Sphere</term> <note>The mathematical study of the celestial globe and the positions of stars and planets.</note> through public exercises at Tübingen under the teacher Mästlin <note>Michael Mästlin (1550–1631), the astronomer who introduced Kepler to the Copernican system.</note>. I was there as a student <note>original: "auditore"</note> and, if I am to tell the truth, as a secret rival.

And why say more? Even significant parts of this very book are rightly and deservedly returned through this dedication to their true authors: the leading men from your circle, NOBLES, because of the beneficial advice you have provided. 

Therefore, Reverend, Illustrious, and Gracious NOBLES, accept this little gift—as is appropriate to come from me—prepared with as much care as was possible. Receive it with serene countenances and, as you have long done, continue to protect and defend me and my studies under the shadow of His <insert>Sacred Imperial</insert> Majesty.

At Linz. On the Ides of August <note>August 13th</note>: In the year of the Western Christians, 1617.

->To Your Reverend and Illustrious Lordships,<-
->*Your Devoted Mathematician,*<-
->Johannes Kepler.<-

# A Comparison of Ptolemy and Kepler

Because you move the heaven, Ptolemy, and the burning stars,
      In my judgment, Ptolemy, you achieve nothing great.
The sky is a light thing: light are the stars: lightest is fire:
      And whatever thrives with a similar ease of movement.
Kepler <note>The original uses "Keplerides," a patronymic form meaning "son of Kepler," used here as a poetic honorific for Johannes Kepler.</note> is rightly held much greater than you:
      He who moves the heavy and inert weight of the Earth.
But by this one motion alone, he alone provides and achieves more
      Than you do, Ptolemy, with your thousand cycles <term>cycles: refers to epicycles, the complex circular paths Ptolemy used to explain why planets occasionally seem to move backward</term>.
Feathers, straws, and bubbles are spun by children;
      But he who rotates seas and mountains—that is a man.

## Another

Kepler turns the earth; Ptolemy turns the Heavens <note>original: "Olympum," the home of the gods, used here to represent the entire celestial sphere.</note>;
      The latter rotates a light thing; the former rotates a heavy thing.
Tell me, which of them is worthy of greater honor?
      The serious German <note>original: "Germanus gravis." A pun: "gravis" means both "heavy" (referring to the Earth) and "serious" or "dignified."</note>, or the trivial little Greek <note>original: "Græculus levis." A double pun: "levis" means "light" (referring to the stars) and "frivolous"; "Græculus" is a diminutive, often used disparagingly.</note>?
The dispute remains in doubt. However, a single rule of Law
      Places Kepler in a more noble position.
What is that rule? "Things should never be done by many means,
      When they can be accomplished by a shorter hand" <note>This is a phrasing of the principle of parsimony, often called Occam's Razor. It argues that the simplest explanation—having the Earth rotate once rather than the entire universe rotating around it—is the most likely to be true.</note>.

->F. Saxirupius<- <note>Likely a Latinized surname, possibly "Steinrock" or "Stonecliff."</note>
->of Virginia.<-

[Three decorative fleurons arranged in a triangle]

# EPITOME
# OF COPERNICAN
# ASTRONOMY

## BOOK ONE.

### Concerning the principles of Astronomy in general, and the doctrine of the SPHERE in particular.

*What is ASTRONOMY?*

IT IS the science that teaches the causes of those things which appear to us dwelling on Earth concerning the heavens and the stars, and which produce the changes of the seasons. Once these are understood, we are able to predict the face of the sky—that is, celestial appearances <note>In this context, "appearances" or "phenomena" refers to how the stars and planets look from our perspective on Earth, regardless of their actual physical positions.</note>—for the future, and assign certain times to those of the past.

*From where is the name "Astronomy" derived?*

From the law <note>original Greek: *nomos*</note> or governance of the stars <note>original Latin: *astrorum*</note>—that is, the laws of the motions by which the stars are moved—just as "Economy" comes from managing domestic affairs, and <term>Pedonomus</term> <note>A term for a supervisor or teacher of children, from the Greek *pais* (child) and *nomos* (law/rule).</note> from governing children.

*What is the relationship of this science to the others?*

1. It is a part of Physics <note>In the 17th century, "Physics" or "Natural Philosophy" was the study of all natural phenomena and their underlying causes.</note>, because it investigates the causes of natural things and events; and because among its subjects are the motions of the celestial bodies; and because one of its goals is to investigate the structure of the world's architecture and its parts.

A 2. Geo- <note>This "catchword" at the bottom of the page indicates that the next page begins with the word "Geometry."</note>

<summary>This page introduces Johannes Kepler's foundational textbook on Copernican astronomy, defining the field as a causal science used for predicting celestial events and categorizing it as a branch of physics.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, Copernicus, physics, celestial motions, etymology, Johannes Kepler, natural philosophy</keywords>

## 2 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

2. Astronomy is the soul of Geography and <term>Hydrography</term> <note>The science of surveying and charting bodies of water; essentially maritime mapping.</note> or the Art of Navigation. For those things which occur differently in various places and regions of the Earth and the Ocean according to the heavens are judged by Astronomy alone.

3. It has <term>Chronology</term> <note>The science of arranging events in order of time.</note> as a subordinate, because the celestial movements arrange the times and the political years, and they provide the dates for history.

4. It has <term>Meteorology</term> <note>In the 17th century, this included the study of all atmospheric phenomena and the influence of stars on the Earth's weather.</note> as a subordinate. For the stars move and stir <term>sublunary Nature</term> <note>The realm of the Earth and its atmosphere, literally 'below the moon,' which was thought to be subject to change unlike the eternal heavens.</note> and even humans themselves in a certain way.

5. It encompasses a large part of **Optics**, because it shares a common subject with it: the Light of celestial bodies. It also reveals many deceptions of sight regarding the shapes of the world and its movements.

6. It is nevertheless classified under the category of **Mathematical** disciplines, and it uses **Geometry** and **Arithmetic** as its two wings; it considers the quantities and figures of worldly bodies and movements, counts the times, and through these means carries out its demonstrations—bringing the whole of its speculation into use or practice.

->*How many parts, then, comprise the astronomer’s task and duty?*<-

The parts of the astronomical duty are chiefly five: the **Historical** concerning Observations, the **Optical** concerning <term>Hypotheses</term> <note>In this context, models or systems used to explain the movements of the planets.</note>, the **Physical** concerning the causes of those Hypotheses, the **Arithmetical** concerning Tables and Calculation, and the **Mechanical** concerning Instruments.

->*How do they differ from one another?*<-

Although none of them can do without **Geometric** demonstrations (which belong to Theory) and **Numbers** (which belong to Practice), as these are the very language of geometers, the first three parts pertain more to Theory, and the final two pertain more to Practice.

Of... <note>original: "De", a catchword indicating the first word of the following page.</note>

BOOK ONE. 3

<margin>On Observations.</margin>

*Describe for me the first of these, the Historical?*
<note>The text uses "Historical" in the classical sense of 'historia,' meaning a systematic account or report of observed facts rather than just a timeline of events.</note>

The historical branch first records how the face of the world appears to us, what changes in it daily, what changes annually, or through longer cycles of time; what different things appear in various places on the Earth and sea, and what things remain the same. And indeed, it draws rarer or more notable events, such as eclipses of the Sun and Moon and significant conjunctions <term>conjunctions: when two or more celestial bodies appear close together in the sky from the perspective of Earth</term>, from historical records. However, it gathers into one collection the more precise observations of individual stars taken from the books of trustworthy craftsmen—from Hipparchus, Ptolemy, Albategnius, Arzachel, and others whom these authors cite—adding also those things which the present age has observed. In this task, Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish astronomer whose massive trove of data provided the empirical foundation for the laws of planetary motion.</note> was engaged with incredible diligence beyond all others, leaving behind thirty-eight years of his own most abundant, nearly continuous, and highly reliable observations.

Therefore, observations of this kind must be skillfully compared with one another and arranged into specific classes through specific cycles of time, so that like may be fitted with like. This is done in almost the same way that Aristotle, when about to explain the nature of animals, first established a most skillful "history of animals," reviewing in summary all the species established under the same genus and what they had in common.

<margin>On Hypotheses.</margin>

A 2 Describe

It compares this empirical method to Aristotle’s biological classifications, emphasizing the need for organized data before forming theories.</summary>

4 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

->Describe also the second part of the Astronomical
Duty?<-

The second part is <term>Optical</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Optics" in astronomy referred to the study of how light and perspective create the "appearances" we see from Earth, versus the actual physical positions of stars.</note>. Having considered these variations in observations and the agreement of different observations in certain respects, it strives to penetrate to the causes by which it is brought about that images <note>original: *species*</note> arise before the eyes of men that are far different from the truth. Astronomers call these images **APPEARANCES**, or in Greek <term>Phenomena</term> <note>original: *Φαινόμενα*</note>. In this pursuit, according to the strength of each person’s intellect, they "save" <note>original: *salvat*; a technical term in historical astronomy meaning to provide a mathematical model that matches observed data, even if the physical cause isn't fully understood yet.</note> and account for the many diversities of appearances through a single, consistently uniform form of motions or the shape of the bodies. The astronomer adapts their entire method of demonstration to laws and theorems that are both Geometric and Optical (the latter being subordinate to Geometry). Thus, by devising these types of forms for motions, one person may arrive closer to the actual **Nature of things** than another. Therefore, although in this difficult and blind grasping for causes it may happen that those who study Nature err from the truth in some parts of their theories, they may nevertheless "save" the appearances through them—

<summary>This page defines the "Optical" branch of astronomy, which focuses on explaining why celestial observations (phenomena) often differ from physical reality. It describes the astronomer's goal: using geometry to create models that "save the appearances" and bring us closer to understanding the true nature of the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Optical astronomy, Phenomena, saving the appearances, celestial motions, geometry, laws of nature, appearances vs. truth</keywords>

# Book One. 5

## On the causes of Hypotheses.

### What is the third part of the Astronomer’s Task?

The third part, *Physics*, is commonly not considered necessary for an *Astronomer*, even though it pertains most greatly to the purpose of this part of *Philosophy*, nor can it be completed by anyone but an *Astronomer*. For there ought not to be mere license for *Astronomers* to imagine whatever they please without reason; rather, it is necessary that you can also provide probable causes for your *Hypotheses*, which you present as the true causes of the *Appearances* <note>In this context, "Appearances" (apparentiarum) refers to the observed movements of celestial bodies as seen from Earth, which may differ from their actual physical paths.</note>, and thus you must first establish the principles of your *astronomy* in a higher science, such as *Physics* or *Metaphysics*. 

Yet, you are not excluded from those *Geometric, Physical,* or *Metaphysical* arguments supplied to you by the very systematic investigation <note>original: "diexodo" (from the Greek *διέξοδος*), meaning a passage through, a thorough treatment, or a logical unfolding</note> of your own discipline regarding matters belonging to those higher sciences, provided you include no begging of the question <term>Begging the question (Petitio Principii): A logical fallacy where the conclusion of an argument is already assumed in the starting premises.</term>. In this way it happens that the *Astronomer* (having so far achieved his purpose of devising causes for motions that are consistent with reason and capable of producing everything contained in the record of *Observations*) now [brings] into a single view...

<summary>This page argues that an astronomer must provide physical and metaphysical justifications for their theories, rather than just creating mathematical models that fit observations. It emphasizes that astronomy is a branch of philosophy that requires a rational search for the true causes of celestial movements.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, physics, metaphysics, hypothesis, logic, celestial mechanics, scientific method</keywords>

6 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

### On Tables.

*What does the Astronomer deal with in the fourth place?*

The fourth and fifth parts refer to that lower objective, namely to utility in common life. For the fourth part, which I have called **Arithmetic**, applies the discovered causes of motions to numbers, teaching a method by which the apparent face of the sky and the arrangement of the stars may be computed for any time, whether past or future. From this are born the **Astronomical Tables**, by which the method just mentioned is made easier and shorter; for this reason the Greeks call them <term>Handy Tables<note>original: "Κανόνας προχείρους" (*kanonas procheirous*). These were intended for quick calculation without needing to redo the complex geometry.</note></term>; of which kind are the **Tables of Ptolemy**, which the **Alfonsine Tables** <note>Compiled in the 13th century under Alfonso X of Castile.</note> improved 400 years ago, and the tables of **Copernicus** 80 years ago, which **Reinhold** made more exact and more extensive, naming them the **Prutenic Tables** <note>The *Tabulae Prutenicae* (Prussian Tables) were based on Copernican theory and used widely until Kepler's own work.</note>. Truly, since all the tables of his predecessors are prone to error, the **RUDOLPHINE TABLES** <note>Named in honor of Kepler's patron, Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II.</note> promise to <term>set the finishing touch<note>original: "colophonem imponere"</note></term> upon them; these were so designated by **TYCHO BRAHE**, and having been worked upon, they now await publication.

Therefore, this part supplies Chronologists, Astrologers, Weather-watchers, Physicians, Sailors, and Farmers with the principles necessary for each of their arts.

### BOOK ONE. 7

First, it serves the Historical part: because for the Observations—which are the foundations of Astronomy—to be exquisite and of sufficient precision, the eyes must be aided by instruments. With these, they may both aim more surely and measure more minutely without error <note>original: "hallucinatione," referring here to visual errors or illusions</note>. In this category, therefore, there exists the book by Tycho Brahe called *The Mechanics of Restored Astronomy* <note>original: "Astronomiæ instauratæ Mechanica," published in 1598, which described his advanced instruments</note>, which displays a great abundance of the most exquisite instruments. The design of these apparatuses lends the highest credibility to the observations made through them and recorded by Brahe.

Now, concerning the parts that follow: models must be made of wood, metal, paper, and similar materials, through which we may express astronomical hypotheses and place them before the eyes. This serves either to teach the unskilled and the beginners <note>original: "tyrones," a term for students or novices</note>, or to lighten the labor of calculation. In this category are the **MATERIAL SPHERE** <term>Material Sphere: A three-dimensional physical model, such as an armillary sphere, used to represent the circles of the heavens</term> and **THEORIES** <note>In this context, "theories" refers to physical models or diagrams that demonstrate planetary motion</note>. Or, we prepare delights for Great Lords or the wealthy, which is the purpose of Celestial Automata. These imitate the heavens themselves to a certain extent by an ingenious motion implanted within them; sometimes, beyond mere delight, they also have their own utility, especially when the sky is cloudy. Or again, we build observatory instruments, related to those mentioned first, but for the sake of common and popular use.

From this has arisen an infinite variety of instruments, as craftsmen compete with the skill of their hands against the most ingenious demonstrations of Geometers. The principal instruments, however, agree on this point: that while celestial motions and appearances are spherical and curved, we inhabitants of the earth have a flat horizon spread beneath us, and our walls are erected perpendicular to it. Finally, most bodies that we handle with our hands are either bounded by mere flat surfaces or at least by a mixture of straight and curved. Therefore, those instruments are easier for us to handle in which the Curve is changed into a straight line. Among the primary examples of this type are Rulers engraved with the divisions of a circle, called **GEOMETRIC SQUARES**, **ASTROLABES**, and, because of the flat walls of buildings, **SCIATERICA** <term>Sciaterics: The science of sundials or instruments that use shadows to tell time or track the sun’s position</term>, an instrument which finds use...

      There is none of these five parts <note>Kepler refers to the five traditional divisions of astronomy: historical, optical, physical, arithmetical, and mechanical.</note> that this *Epitome* does not touch upon. It presents the doctrine of **Eclipses** of the Sun and Moon, and the configurations of the **Planets** with each other and with the **Luminaries** <note>The Sun and Moon.</note> (in which the influence of the planets over these lower realms <note>The "sublunary" world, or the Earth.</note> consists). It teaches the method of calculation by which both the **Rudolphine Tables** <note>The highly accurate astronomical tables published by Kepler in 1627, named for his patron, Emperor Rudolf II.</note> and the positions of the Planets themselves without tables, and finally the laws for constructing instruments, have been or can be computed.

      The **World** is commonly thought, following the lead of the eyes, to be a vast building consisting of two primary parts: **Heaven** and **Earth**.

->*What do men think about the shape of the Earth?*<-

      The Earth appears to extend as a very wide plain in a circle toward all regions around the observer; hence, in **Homer**, it is called "wide-breasted" <note>original Greek: εὐρύστερ[νος] (*eurysternos*); a traditional Homeric epithet describing the broad expanse of the Earth.</note>

->*What do they think is the center of the circle of the earth?*<-

Any nation, if it has not been educated in the knowledge of the globe, thinks by the instinct of nature and sight that its own fatherland is in the center or middle of this flat circle. Even today, the common people among the Jews believe that Jerusalem, the ancient homeland of their race, is situated in the middle of the World.

->*But what do men think about the Waters?*<-

Because men, traveling as far as they can from the Land, eventually encounter the Ocean, some therefore think that the earth floats on the waters like a disc, and that the waters are contained in the lower part of the sky as if in a vessel. Hence the poets make the Ocean the "father of things"; others, on the contrary, conceive of another rim of Earth surrounding the lands beyond the Ocean, which contains the Ocean so that it does not flow out; these same people also lay beneath it the ear... <note>The text ends mid-word: *ter-* likely continuing to *terram* (earth/ground)</note>

*What then of the other part of the world, namely, of the Sky and its magnitude?* <note>The Latin "coelum" refers to both the physical sky and the celestial heavens.</note>

People believe the Sky is not much larger than the circle of the Earth, being joined to the lands and the Ocean at the outermost edge, so that it bounds the lands; they think that if one could travel that far, they would encounter the outermost edges of the sky, which would prevent further progress. Holy Scripture also accommodates itself to this human imagination: *If you were scattered even to the ends of the sky, from there I will gather you.* <note>original: "Si fueritis dispersi usq́; ad extrema coeli, inde vos recolligam." cf. Nehemiah 1:9</note> *His going forth is from the end of it, and his circuit even to its end.* <note>original: "Ab extremitate egressio ejus, & occursus ejus usq́; ad extremitatem ejus."</note> *Ps. 19.*

Thus the poets said that Mount Atlas, the highest mountain on the edge of Africa, carries the sky on his shoulders; and Homer places the Ethiopians at the extremes of the Sunrise and Sunset, believing that because of this proximity of the Sky and Earth, the Sun becomes so close to them that it scorches their skin.

*What shape do they think the Sky has?*

Our eyes attribute to the sky the shape of a tent, stretched out over our heads and over the Sun, Moon, and stars; or rather the shape of a vault <term>fornicis</term> <note>A "fornix" is an architectural arch or vault; the author uses this to describe the "dome" of the sky.</note> resting upon the Earth’s plain with a gently rising arch: such that the part of the sky directly overhead is much closer to the observer than the parts touching the mountains.

*What do people conceive regarding its motion?*

Whether the sky moves or remains at rest cannot be discerned by sight, since the thinness of its substance escapes the eyes—except for the fact that things which present no variety to the eyes seem to be at rest. The various positions of the Sun, Moon, and stars at the visible edges of the Lands strike the eyes. For the Sun seems to emerge with a certain effort from between the sky and the immobile mountains or Ocean, and to go out as if from a bridegroom’s chamber; <note>A reference to Psalm 19:5, comparing the sun to a bridegroom leaving his wedding canopy.</note> and having traversed the vault of the sky in the same way, it hides itself again in the opposite region. So too the Moon, the planets, and all the rest of the host of stars: as if they proceeded in a drawn-up and well-guarded battle line, the first...

Therefore, since the Ocean meets the furthest reaches of the land, common people believe that the Sun plunges into the Ocean and is extinguished, and that every day a new Sun emerges from the opposite side of the Ocean. This is the idea that poets imitate in their fictions. Indeed, even certain philosophers have claimed that on the furthest shores of Lusitania <note>modern-day Portugal</note> one can hear the hissing of the Ocean as it extinguishes the flames of the Sun, as Strabo <note>an ancient Greek geographer</note> records.

*What do common folk think about the size of the stars?*

Their size is not always thought to be the same. For when the Sun rises or sets, it appears huge; therefore, in its departure and at the start of its course, it is compared to a "Giant" in Psalm 19 <note>Psalm 19:5 describes the sun as a strong man or giant running a race</note>. Likewise, when the Moon rises with a full face, it seems to equal the roundness or base of a large vessel. When the Sun and Moon are nearer the peak of the sky <note>the zenith</note>, they appear to be about the width of a human face, equal to one another, and shaped like a flat circular disk. Similarly, the size of constellations or <term>asterisms</term> <note>identifiable patterns of stars</note> looks immense when they are near the mountains—so much so that they are hardly recognized—yet after they have risen high, they seem to shrink to a contemptible narrowness.

Regarding Orion, Virgil wrote:
*As great as Orion, when he walks on foot through the deepest waters of the mid-ocean, cutting a path, his shoulder towers above the waves.*
<note>original Latin: "quam magnus Orion, Cum pedes incedit medij per maxima Nerei Stagna viam ſcindens, humero ſupereminet undas." — Aeneid, Book 10</note>

The bodies of individual stars, however, are considered to be like points. They differ from one another in brightness and the extent of the light they cast, and they even vary individually as the atmosphere changes. Some are seen to shoot across very quickly and appear to fall to the earth <note>a reference to meteors or "shooting stars"</note>.

[they] are seen in that place from which they rush, before they begin to cross over, nor after the crossing has ceased are they seen any longer in that place to which they arrived; whereas, on the contrary, true stars are perennial <note>original: *perennes*; meaning eternal or enduring</note>. That motion of crossing is also extremely fast, and thus unlike other motions which do not strike the eyes in such a way. From this speed of motion, we rightly conclude that they are not among the true stars in the ether <note>original: *aethere*; in traditional cosmology, the "ether" was the pure, unchanging substance that filled the heavens above the Moon</note>, but are ignited and extinguished in the lowest region of the world <note>The "sublunary" region, or the Earth's atmosphere</note>; therefore, we give them the name **SHOOTING STARS**, or **FALLING STARS**, and having excluded them from Astronomy—as they have no law of motion—we pass them over to Physics <note>original: *Physicam*; at this time, "physics" referred to natural philosophy, which included the study of weather and atmospheric "meteors"</note>.

Next, among those which are durable to the senses, this distinction is perceived: that the greatest part of them perpetually maintain the same order among themselves, and being thus preserved, they rise and set daily in the same places within the span of a single century. But a few others—that is, five, plus the Moon as the sixth, and the Sun itself as the seventh—even though they also rise and set daily with the former, yet by comparison over many days, they are found not to maintain the same position, neither among themselves nor toward those former stars, nor do they always rise and set in the same places on the Horizon. Therefore, those are called **fixed**, and these **wandering** or **Planets**.

In both kinds, certain "adulterous" <note>original: *adulterinæ*; meaning imitation or false stars that appear temporarily</note> stars mix themselves in: among the planets, the "Hairy Stars" commonly called **COMETS**; among the fixed stars, stars so similar to the rest that they are hardly distinguished even by the most skilled Astronomers. They are discerned, however, by the fact that they eventually disappear; and lest they seem to be hidden and return like the others, they have no rule for their appearance, no order, and are seen most rarely after intervals of many years or even centuries. Because these show some regularity of motion and are not distinguished by their regions from true stars, and yet they perish and arise like shooting stars, they belong by equal right to Physics and to Astronomy.

...the day, while the Moon tempers the night with her light, and they cause shadows. **Fourthly**, the planets usually exceed the fixed stars in magnitude <note>In historical astronomy, "magnitude" referred to the apparent size or brightness of a star as seen from Earth.</note>.

**Fifthly**, the planets do not twinkle as the fixed stars do; they either do not twinkle at all, or very little, or in another different way that can be easily discerned.

**Sixthly**, the planets do not always maintain the same visible magnitude as the fixed stars. Indeed, the diameters of the Sun and Moon are found—through the use of subtle instruments—to increase and decrease. The Moon and Venus even change their "countenance" <note>original: "vultum". This refers to their phases, such as the crescent or full phase.</note>; the other five planets, when positioned opposite the Sun, pour out the fullest light and appear at their largest, while at other times they appear smaller.

->*I would like you to explain more clearly this difference between*<-
->*the motion of the fixed stars and the motion of the planets,*<-
->*as it appears to the eyes.*<-

While any fixed star, within the span of a single human life, crosses the face of the Earth daily along the same path, the planets, by contrast, sometimes cross in a low and short arc, and soon after in a long one near the zenith <term>vertici: the point in the sky directly overhead</term>, notably changing their points of rising and setting.

This change is first very conspicuous in the Sun, which Venus and Mercury perpetually accompany. For in summer, to those turning their faces toward the south, the Sun rises from the left and from behind; it passes at its highest point and strikes the lands from on high, stirring up heat and lengthening the day; then to the right it sets again behind the back. In winter everything is the opposite, and with a still face, both its rising and its setting can be observed. The Moon undergoes this cycle in a monthly space of time, Mars in two years, Jupiter in twelve years, and Saturn in thirty.

14 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

*How many types of motion should the astronomer consider?*

Two. The First and the Second.

*What do they call the First Motion?*

The daily motion—in Greek called the <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>original: νυχθήμερον; a term referring to the full 24-hour cycle of day and night</note>—which causes the fixed stars, the planets, the Moon, and the Sun, and indeed anything else in the heavens, to rise from one region of the horizon and set in the opposite. For those of us in this part of the world, if we turn our faces toward the East, this motion moves from the rising point toward the right. By this single motion alone—if no second motion interfered—any given star would rise every single day at the exact same point on the horizon, climb to the same height above the visible plane of the horizon, and set again at that same point.

*What do they call the Second Motions?*

Those slower motions <term>proper</term> <note>Meaning the motion unique to each specific celestial body, as opposed to the general rotation of the whole sky.</note> to the individual planets. These are what cause the planets not to rise and set at the same point of the horizon every day like the fixed stars do. Because of these motions, the planets do not always reach the same height when they arrive at the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>The meridian, or the highest point a star reaches in the sky each day.</note>, nor do they keep the same position relative to each other or to the fixed stars.

And for us in this part of the world, if we turn our faces toward the West, these motions appear to move from the setting point toward the left. I say they "happen" even though they are not as obvious to the eyes as the First motion. The First motion is the only one that reveals itself to the simple experience of most people; it actually disturbs our observation of the Second motions by sweeping those moving bodies along with it. However, we can understand the Second motions by mentally setting aside the First motion and comparing evening observations made over many different days.

*How many parts of astronomy are there then?*

Two. The Spherical Doctrine and the Theoretical Doctrine.

BOOK ONE. 15

*From where are they named?*

<term>Spherical astronomy</term> <note>original: "Sphærica"; refers to the study of the celestial sphere and the positions of stars.</note> is named from the instrument—namely, the **armillary sphere** <note>A model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings, centered on Earth or the Sun, that represent lines of celestial longitude and latitude.</note>—which is used to explain the **primary motion** <note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note>. **Theoretical astronomy**, however, comes from "theories": this is the name given to the flat instruments <note>Often paper diagrams or "volvelles" with moving parts used to calculate planetary positions.</note> which we use to explain the **secondary motions** <note>The slower movements of the planets, Sun, and Moon along the zodiac.</note>.

*How many books does the entire Epitome consist of?*

Seven. Three on spherical doctrine; three others on theoretical doctrine; and one on both combined, or on the motion of the **Eighth Sphere** <note>In traditional cosmology, the sphere of the fixed stars.</note>.

*Review the subjects of the books on spherical doctrine?*

This **first** book, after the general matters explained so far, next contains the principles by which spherical doctrine was handed down by **Copernicus**, as well as their proofs and the refutations of opposing arguments.
The **second** explains the origin, causes, and divisions of the circles and other parts of the sphere, and the instrument by which spherical doctrine ought to be taught.
The **third** delivers the spherical doctrine itself in its specific parts.

*State the subjects of the following books pertaining to theoretical doctrine?*

For theoretical doctrine, following the same method as the spherical doctrine, three books have likewise been made: the fourth, fifth, and sixth.
For the **fourth** contains the principles by which Copernicus handed down theoretical doctrine, reviewing and proving the arrangement of the whole world and its internal parts, and the motions of those parts, while dissolving objections.
The **fifth** proposes the origin and causes of the **eccentric circles** <note>A circle whose center is off-set from the center of the Earth or Sun, used to explain why planets seem to speed up or slow down.</note> in the "theories," explaining why there is a need for these figures—

### PART ONE.

*How, indeed, can the Order of the Heavens be known, and its principles be explained on Earth?*

IF first the true shape of the Earth, and thus of the whole world, is investigated.

*Is the earth, then, not flat, or extended downwards with an infinite root, as it commonly seems?*

Rather, it is a body composed of land and water joined together, separated from the heavens on all sides, and turned back upon itself; finally, it is round in every direction, in the shape of a ball, a globe, or a regular sphere: which can be proven both from its individual parts and from the constitution of the whole itself.

*Prove from the parts of the watery surface that they present a convex figure?*
<note>original: "gibbam figuram"; literally a "humped" or bulging shape, referring to the curvature of the horizon.</note>

Concerning the parts of the watery surface, that is, the Seas, we are taught by nautical experiments <note>Common "nautical experiments" in this period included observing ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon or seeing land from the masthead before it was visible from the deck.</note> that they are curved into an arc.

18 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

For when those traveling on the deep sea see nothing except the sky and the waves, spread around them in a perfectly flat circle; yet even the highest mountains of continents and islands that are not very far away remain hidden, as if submerged beneath the flattened waves. It happens that as they progress by sailing, those mountains seem to emerge from the waves and suddenly raise themselves to a visible height.

[A diagram showing the curvature of the Earth's surface. A mountain labeled 'D' is on the right. Two tangent lines of sight are drawn: 'BC' tangent at point 'A', and 'FD' tangent at point 'E'. Other labels include 'f', 'a', 'e', 'c', 'b'.]

*Let **D** be the mountain, the first location **A**, its line of sight or Horizon **BC**, a straight line touching the waves at **A**. With this line continued toward **C**, it passes above **D**, so that **D** cannot be seen from **A**. Now let a movement be made from **A** to **E**, so that the line of sight or Horizon of location **E** is the straight line **FD**, touching the waters at **E**; this line, when continued, falls upon the mountain **D**, so that whatever part of it stands out above **FD** can all be seen from **E**.*

But if the surface of the water were truly extended into a mere flat plane, no mountain rising above it would be hidden from a sight positioned upon it, unless, as one receded by an immense distance, the shape of the mountain itself along with its size gradually vanished. Conversely, as one approached, the mountains would by no means appear suddenly and after a short interval—having not been seen before—but an immense journey would be required for this to happen.

*As if the surface of the water were extended along a straight line **DF** into the infinite, and mountain **D** stood above it: because that same line **DF** would also be the line of sight, always falling upon mountain **D**, whether the eye were at **E** or at **F**, or at any other very remote point on this line.*

Next, ships or mountains are seen first from the top of the mast, when they cannot yet be seen from its base, even when the waves are not roughened by any swells at all, solely by the obstruction of the water's curvature <note>original: "tumor," literally a swelling or bulge, referring here to the physical curve of the Earth's surface</note>.

## Proof regarding the entire surface of the water?

Modern experience has taught the same concerning the whole world: namely, that it is a perfected globe—that is, a sphere turned back upon itself in every direction. Ferdinand Magellan, setting out from Spain, sailed toward the West. Having discovered the strait <note>The Strait of Magellan at the southern tip of South America, which connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.</note>, he passed from the Atlantic Ocean into the Eastern Ocean <note>original: "Eoum"; referring here to the Pacific Ocean.</note> and reached the Moluccas <note>The "Spice Islands" in modern-day Indonesia.</note>. From there, a single ship <note>The *Victoria*, the only vessel from Magellan's original fleet of five to complete the first circumnavigation of the globe.</note> continued in a constant and direct course—by no means turning back—always toward the West. By traveling through the Indian and Atlantic Oceans, it returned home to the place from which it had departed, appearing as if it had come back from the East.

It appears, therefore, that the surface of the Water and the Earth returns into itself, drawn in a circle, and is not fixed or attached to the floor of the heavens.

**These points concern the Water; but does the same hold true for the Continents?**

Since the Ocean is poured between the lands from the East to the West, and back to the East again, and its two great bodies of water meet at two straits—one to our West, called the Strait of Magellan, and the other to the East, between New Guinea and the Moluccas—the Earth is divided by the Ocean into a known Northern part and an unknown Southern part, which we similarly call "Magellanic" <note>The *Terra Australis Incognita* or "Unknown Southern Land." In the 16th century, it was often called "Magellanica" because it was believed the Strait of Magellan separated South America from a massive southern continent.</note>.

### 20 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

Furthermore, the Ocean flows through the Northern Land beyond **Tartary** <note>A historical name used by Europeans for the vast region of North and Central Asia stretching from the Caspian Sea to the Pacific Ocean.</note>, dividing it into two Continents: the Old and the New, which we call **America**. Thus, the Ocean flows around three Continents of the Earth as if they were three vast Islands.

Thirdly, although these Continents are very large, the Ocean winds its way into them in such parts that they are divided almost into Peninsulas, barely held together by very narrow **Isthmuses** <note>A narrow strip of land with sea on either side, forming a link between two larger areas of land.</note>. In this way, America is nearly split into a Southern and a Northern part (of which the former is called **Peru**, and the latter **New Spain** <note>original: "nova Hispania" — referring generally to Mexico and Central America</note>). In ancient times, however, the known continent was divided into **Europe, Africa, and Asia** by the Mediterranean, Ionian, Euxine <note>The Black Sea.</note>, and Red Seas, which are like gulfs of one and the same Ocean. Therefore, in no part of the Earth are the gulfs of the single, continuous Ocean very far away.

Given these facts, consider the Seas: where they come closest to one another, separated only by Isthmuses, experience proves that they maintain almost the same height; this is true of all shores everywhere. Next, consider the origins of the **Rivers** which empty into these Seas; they are mostly found in the highest mountains of the interior Continents. Frequently, the sources of several rivers that flow toward very different regions are located close to one another, with only a modest mountain ridge standing between them. Thus, no part of the land is much higher than the highest sources of the rivers.

If, therefore, the sources are not much higher than the shores, then the peaks of the highest mountains will also not greatly exceed the height of those same shores and of the sea itself, which is poured around everywhere.

Next, let it be considered that the greatest rivers of the whole world, and those which measure out the most land, are stagnant for the greater part of their course and move most slowly, being pushed along almost entirely by the column of water following from behind: so the Ganges, so the Nile through all of Egypt, so the Danube through Hungary and almost all of Thrace, all the way into the Euxine Sea <note>original: "pontum Euxinum," the ancient name for the Black Sea</note>. If in any place they roll forward with a swift descent, that does not last longer than until they have exited narrow and rough places, hemmed in by rocks on both sides.

From this it follows that a river is not easily found whose sources are elevated even one German mile <term>German mile: a historical unit of distance, significantly longer than a standard mile, measuring approximately 7.5 kilometers or 4.6 miles</term> above the surface of the sea, even if it traverses a distance of a thousand miles.

*It has been demonstrated that the surface of water is convex; and that the surface of the Earth does not assume a much different shape than the waters: but how is it proven that this shape is entirely round, since there are many convex shapes—Oval, Cylindrical, lumpy, swollen, and the like?*

It is certainly conceded regarding the surface of the Earth that it is not perfectly round, but bulges into mountains here and there: but regarding the waters of the Ocean, when they are calm, a complete roundness is proven by arguments drawn as much from Nature as from the senses.

*State the Argument from Nature?*

We see that there is a physical force within the bodies of the Earth and Water for uniting any bodies to themselves and attracting them—a force which is commonly called "gravity." Since, therefore, this entire globe of the Earth is surrounded on all sides by waters, a fluid material that does not limit itself at the sides; nor <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the page concludes</note>

22 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,
it is not improbable that the Earth is even internally passable everywhere by huge pipes, and thus perhaps the Earth is like a perforated pot, consisting of continents as shells, filled with water inside: certainly, all the parts of the water all around will be unable to form any other shape for the whole than a round one. This is because the power of uniting <note>original: "vis vniendi"; Kepler is describing a force of attraction or cohesion that we would now recognize as a precursor to the theory of gravity</note> in the waters—unimpeded by itself or by the Earth—produces a shape that is most unified, which is the round shape, having nothing outside of itself. Hence it happens that no prominence of the waters remains suspended in a heap above the roundness, nor do any waves of the Ocean; for water is spread out to establish a total uniformity, and the waves yield to the side and give place to what flows down, being pushed out by the greater weight of those flowing down.

*Could the same not also be said concerning the nature*
*of the earth?*

Indeed, the Earth, when it was first created by God, was either itself a certain fluid and soft mass and later hardened (and then the same things are true of the earth which were said of the waters), or it was created in its original solidity and hardness; and then even so it is not likely that any other shape was bestowed upon it than that which it would have received from itself if it had been soft at the beginning. For although it is hard, it is nevertheless a body or <term>matter</term> <note>the physical substance that makes up the world</note>, just like water; and when soaked with moisture or melted by fire, it can be made fluid in its parts like water. It is therefore right that it also received the shape proper to fluid matter, which is round.

*Why then is the earth not perfectly round*
*like the Ocean?*

The most wise Creator balanced the shape of the Earth with the most deliberate proportion between the nature of Matter and the use of Living Creatures, for whose sake the hard Earth was made. Thus, mountains might be raised somewhat for the continuous pouring out of waters <note>referring to the belief that mountains were the sources of springs and rivers</note>, and valleys might be depressed for receiving them. Yet, to the senses, when the whole sphere with its prominences comes into view at once, nothing would seem to be lost from its perfect roundness.

->*What arguments do you have from the senses for the roundness of the Earth, and thus of the entire globe consisting of land and water?*<-

First, if the Astronomer assumes that the Earth is round, and does not use different diameters for the Earth based on the diversity of mountains and valleys, but instead uses the same diameter everywhere in geometric computations; his operation usually results in sums that are consistent with astronomical experience: that is, they follow the <term>celestial phenomena</term> <note>The observable movements of the stars and planets.</note>. However, they would not follow if he did this while the Earth actually had different and sensibly distinct diameters—that is, if it were not round.

Next, as often as we travel by land or sea in equal distances directly toward the North; we find equal increases or decreases in the heights of the sun and stars at midday in Astronomy. Again, as often as we travel equal distances to the East or West under one and the same <term>parallel</term> (about which we speak in Book III); we count an equal number of more or fewer hours and minutes at the beginnings or ends of Lunar Eclipses.    Finally, it is obvious to the eye, without the need for lengthy reasoning, that the boundaries of the Earth’s shadow as it falls upon the body of the failing Moon <note>The "failing Moon" refers to a lunar eclipse.</note>, whether those edges are toward the North, the South, the East, or the West, are arcs of a perfect circle. As the science of optics teaches, a body whose shadow is bounded by a circle when placed before a round sun must necessarily be circular in the section from which the shadow falls. Since, therefore, with the passage of time and the occurrence of many lunar eclipses, all the boundaries of the Earth's body cast such shadows, the Earth is therefore round in every direction to the senses.

   Both the nature of water and experience deny this. ...tion, but you will always detect some slight downward slope; and it will appear that the waves do not overhang the lands, but rather sink below them.

*Explain the causes of this error in judgment?*

The sense of sight inspects the outermost parts of the sea with higher <term>visual rays</term> <note>original: "radijs visivis." Early modern science often modeled vision as literal rays connecting the eye to the object.</note> than those used for nearby parts. If those outermost parts were to become closer while remaining on these higher visual rays, they would be rendered altogether higher in appearance. We *think* those parts are nearby, and therefore we think they are higher than the parts close to us. We think they are nearby because we look at them obliquely; consequently, we do not correctly grasp the long sequence of intervening matter—from which alone the distance of the furthest points ought to be gathered. We mistakenly believe that we are encompassing the same amount of the water's surface with the angles of the higher rays as we encompass with the equal angles of the lower rays.

->[A diagram appears here: An observer stands at point **A** on a shore. Lines of sight (rays) extend to a flat water surface marked **B**, **C**, **D**, and **E**. To illustrate the illusion of curvature, points **F** and **G** are plotted vertically above **D** and **E**.]<-

*A spectator on the shore; **B E** is the flat surface of the water. **AB**, **AC**, **AD**, **AE** are the rays to the eye at **A**. **BC**, **CD**, **DE** are the intercepted surfaces, which are highly unequal. Therefore, the spectator, thinking that **CD** and **DE** are equal to the nearby **BC** because the angles at the eye are equal, thinks that along the same ray **AD**, he sees **F** instead of **D**, and along the same ray **AE**, he sees **G** instead of **E**, so that **BC**, **CF**, and **FG** are made equal. In this way, the flat surface **BCDE** appears to curve upward and be **BCFG**.*

[The number] nine hundred <note>This likely refers to a ratio or specific measurement calculated on the preceding page.</note> has no sensible proportion [to it]. Such indeed is found to be the <term>Semidiameter</term> <note>The radius of a circle or sphere.</note> of the globe of the Earth.

->*How can the size of this*<-
->*Semidiameter be investigated?*<-

Since the Earth is round, it is necessary that <term>plumb lines</term> <note>Weights hung from a cord to determine a perfectly vertical line.</note> hung in different places should incline toward each other [at the center]; towers erected perpendicularly should lean away from each other at their tops; that is, they should be further apart at the top. Since this is the case, it is easy to examine the plumb lines from two mountains—from one of which the other is visible—relative to a shared line of sight. From this, the angle is made known which is formed by the two lines of the two plumb lines, continued by imagination all the way to the center of the Earth. Therefore, since the distance between those two places is a part of the circumference of the whole globe, just as the angle at the center is a part of <term>four right angles</term> <note>360 degrees.</note>, the length of the entire circumference is easily investigated in the same measurement from the known length of that part. Or, from the known distance of the two places, as if from the base of a triangle, and from the known angles, the length of the two "legs" or lines meeting at the center of the Earth from the plumb lines—which is the size of the Earth's semidiameter—is computed through geometric principles.

[Diagram showing a triangle with vertices A, B, and C. Point A represents the center of the Earth, while B and C are points on the surface (a mountain and a citadel). Perpendicular lines from B and C extend downwards to meet at A, and upwards to show their divergence. Arcs are drawn at B and C to indicate angles.]

->*Teach me the process*<-
->*By an example?*<-
*Let two places, B and C, be distant by five common German miles* <note>original: "milliaribus quinq; Germanicis communibus." A German mile was a historical unit roughly equal to 7.5 kilometers.</note>, *B being a mountain and C a citadel. Let the angle at B on the mountain be found to be 89 degrees, 46 minutes; the other at the citadel C, 89 degrees, 55 minutes. Therefore, the angle BAC <note>The angle at the center of the Earth.</note> will be 0 degrees, 19 minutes. Since there are 360 degrees or 21,600 minutes in four right angles. If that part of the Earth's circumference between the mountain and the citadel, which is 19 minutes, is worth 5 miles of that place: Therefore, the 21,600 minutes of the entire circumference will be worth 5,684 of such miles.*

...form a perpendicular, and the line of sight is extended to the furthest waves. In this way, a triangle is formed with a right angle at the furthest waves, where the Cathetus <note>The vertical leg of a right-angled triangle.</note> is the line of sight, the Base is the line from the center of the earth to the furthest waves, and the Hypotenuse <note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.</note> is the line from the center of the earth to the peak of the promontory and the viewer’s eye. Therefore, since the Table of Sines <note>Trigonometric tables used by astronomers to calculate distances and angles.</note> provides for every angle of a Quadrant <note>A 90-degree arc or one-fourth of a circle.</note> the proportion of the Hypotenuse or Secant to the Base or Radius, and the amount by which the former exceeds the latter—which corresponds to the height of the observation point above the surface of the sea—it is easy, given this height in German miles, to also determine the number of miles in the Radius, or semi-diameter.

[A geometric diagram showing a right-angled triangle with vertices labeled C, G, O, and A. A curved line represents the surface of the earth, with A at the center, O on the surface directly below the observer at C, and G at the horizon point.]

*Give an example?*
*Suppose the height of the promontory CO is one Italian mile, or a quarter of a German mile <note>In the 17th century, a German mile was roughly 7.5 kilometers, much longer than an Italian or Roman mile.</note>, and let G be the furthest point of the sea visible from height C. If the angle GCO is found to be 88 degrees and 37 minutes, then since CGA is a right angle—because CG touches the surface of the globe GO at point G, and GA is drawn from the contact point G to the center A—the angle GAC will therefore be 1 degree and 23 minutes. The hypotenuse or secant AC of this angle is 100,029. Therefore, if the excess of CO over the radius OA or GA—which excess is 29—is equal to one quarter of a German mile, then the total GA or OA will be 863 miles.*

*Explain also the other form of Clavian <note>Referring to Christoph Clavius (1538–1612), a highly influential Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who helped refine the Gregorian calendar.</note> measurement?*

This form does not require climbing a mountain but instead requires knowledge of both the height of mountain CO and the distance of a ship G from mountain C. For the square of this distance GC, divided by OC, produces the entire diameter of the watery globe, increased by OC.

*By what method are astronomers accustomed to*
*measuring the globe of the Earth?*

Astronomers employ the heavens—that is, the altitude of the Pole <note>The "altitude of the Pole" refers to measuring the angle of the North Star (Polaris) above the horizon to determine a location's latitude.</note> in two locations situated under the same Meridian—and by that, they first measure the circumference of the Earth; from the circumference, they then derive its diameter. However, this first requires knowledge of the <term>Doctrine of the Sphere</term> <note>A traditional branch of astronomy dealing with the mathematical properties of the celestial and terrestrial spheres.</note>, which will finally be handed down in the following sections.

*Yet, can you show this with an example?*
*At Prague, the altitude of the Pole is 50° 6'.*
*At Linz, under the same meridian, it is 48° 16'.*
***
*The difference is 1° 50'.*

*Now, from Linz to Prague, the distance is commonly reckoned as 26 miles. If, therefore, 1 degree and 50 minutes is worth 26 miles, the entire circumference of 360 degrees will be worth 5,105 miles. But the circumference is to the diameter as 22 is to 7 <note>This is the classic Archimedean approximation for the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter (Pi).</note>. If, therefore, a circumference of 22 is worth 5,105 miles, a diameter of 7 will be worth 1,615 miles, and the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> will be 807 miles.*

*What is the radius of the Earth considered*
*to be today?*

Commonly today, 15 average <term>German miles</term> <note>A German geographical mile was much longer than a modern mile, roughly 7.5 kilometers.</note> are counted for each single degree, so that the entire circumference comes to 5,400 miles, and the radius to nearly 860.
Furthermore, we calculate 4 <term>Italian miles</term>—or 4,000 <term>Geometric Paces</term>—into one German mile. Each pace consists of 5 feet, and 1 foot consists of 4 palms. There are 8 <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, often translated as a "furlong."</note> in an Italian mile, and 32 in a German mile, each one being 125 paces. Thus, according to modern thinkers, one degree occupies 480 stadia, and the entire circumference is 172,800 stadia.

32 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

->What did the Ancients report about this?<-

The Ancients were less accurate during the dawn of Astronomy. For Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BCE) and chief librarian at Alexandria; he is the first known person to calculate the Earth's circumference.</note>, who lived before Christ, reported 250,000 <note>The OCR reads "2540000," but the internal logic of the text and historical records confirm 250,000 or 252,000.</note> stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance based on the length of a sports stadium; it is roughly 157 to 185 meters.</note>.

His reasoning was as follows: In Syene <note>Modern-day Aswan, Egypt.</note>, the Sun at the summer solstice <note>The longest day of the year, when the sun reaches its highest point in the sky.</note> illuminates the bottoms of wells at the noon hour; it is therefore exactly vertical there. But at Alexandria at that same time, it is distant from the vertical by one-fiftieth part of a circle, which is 7 degrees and 12 minutes. Now, the travel distance between both places is estimated at 5,000 stadia, which, when taken fifty times, equals 250,000.

Posidonius <note>A Greek Stoic philosopher and astronomer (c. 135–51 BCE).</note>, around the time of Christ, removed a twenty-fifth part, so that there are 240,000 stadia. His reasoning is very similar to the former. In his age, the star Canopus <note>The second brightest star in the night sky.</note> just grazed the horizon on the island of Rhodes and did not rise any higher. At Alexandria, however, it rose to the fourth part of one sign <note>One "sign" of the zodiac is 30 degrees; a fourth part is 7.5 degrees.</note>, that is, 7 degrees and 30 minutes, which is the forty-eighth part of the total circumference. Now, the travel distance—or the space of sea between both places—is estimated at 5,000 stadia, which, when taken forty-eight times, equals 240,000.

But Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), whose geocentric model dominated astronomy for over a millennium.</note>, who lived after Christ, comes closer to us; for he assigns 500 stadia to one degree, which, when taken three hundred and sixty times, equals 180,000.

On the authority of Al-Farghani <note>original: "Alphragano"; a 9th-century Persian astronomer.</note>, in the time of Al-Ma'mun <note>original: "Almeonis"; the Abbasid Caliph (r. 813–833 CE) who sponsored major scientific efforts.</note>, the Arabs compared their findings and determined that 1,360,000 palms <note>An ancient unit based on the width of a hand.</note> correspond to one degree of the great circle on Earth. Six of these make a cubit <note>An ancient unit based on the length of the forearm.</note>. Of these, four are reckoned by us as a foot, and twenty as a "geometric pace." Thus, there come to be 68,000 paces for each degree, which is 17 German miles <note>A "German mile" was significantly longer than an English mile, roughly 7.5 kilometers.</note> and 544 stadia. Thus, the total circumference would be 196,440 stadia <note>The OCR reads 19644, but the math 360 x 544 suggests 195,840.</note>.

Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategnius"; a 9th-century Arab astronomer and mathematician.</note>, or Muhammad of Ar-Raqqah, estimates half a degree to be a day's journey for a swift man, or 42 Arabic miles of his century.

BOOK ONE. 33

**Why is the measurement of the Earth—a geographical matter—included here, when we are occupied with Astronomy?**

Although it is the task of Geography to measure the circuit of the lands, the distances of places, the convex area of the terrestrial surface, and the very bulk of the entire globe: nevertheless, **Astronomy cannot do without this knowledge.**

For **1.** according to the number of degrees of longitude and latitude of the Earth, celestial phenomena <note>The "appearances" or positions of stars and planets as seen from the ground.</note> vary in different locations on the lands. Indeed, the number of degrees of longitude and latitude can be gathered from travel distance, if we have the total circumference of the greatest terrestrial circle known in that measure.

**2.** Since the Earth is our dwelling place, we use the radius <note>original: *semidiametro*</note> of the Earth as a <term>ten-foot rod</term> <note>original: *decempedâ*; a standard Roman surveying tool used as a metaphor for a base unit of measurement.</note> to measure the celestial bodies and their distance from the Earth. It is therefore right that our measure be known to us—that is, weighed against the magnitude of stature, the <term>fathom</term> <note>original: *orgyæ*; the distance between outstretched arms.</note>, the cubit, the foot, the <term>span</term> <note>original: *spithamæ*; the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger.</note>, the palm, the thumb, and the finger in our own small bodies.

**3.** In this very place, however, the method of demonstration required this reasoning of measurement to be inserted, because through it the **perfect roundness of the earth** was examined and proven.
