54 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,

# Principles of Spherical Doctrine

### PART TWO

# On the Shape of the Heavens.

*What, then, should be held regarding the shape of the Heavens?*

Since we are unable to observe the matter of the ethereal air <note>original: "aurae aethereae." At this time, it was believed that a thin, fluid substance called "ether" filled the space between stars and planets.</note> with our eyes, nothing prevents us from believing, in the meantime, that it is spread through the whole vastness of the World and surrounds the elementary sphere <note>The "elementary sphere" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, composed of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> on all sides.

But that the host of stars surrounds the Earth on all sides—and thus forms a kind of curved vault of a complete spherical shape—is evident from the fact that since the Earth is round, wherever people travel, they see the stars above their heads in the same way as we do. Furthermore, even for those remaining in one place, the entire army of stars is made visible in the space of a few days; so that those stars with which we began seem to be joined by and followed by those we see last. Therefore, the order of the stars returns into itself, drawn in a circle around the earth.

*Do you think, then, that the centers of the stars are arranged on the same spherical surface?*

This is indeed uncertain. For since some are small and others large, it is not unlikely that the small ones appear so because they have retreated far into the high ether, while the large ones appear so because they are closer to us. Nevertheless, it is not absurd to think that two fixed stars <note>original: "fixas." Stars that do not move relative to each other, forming the constellations, as opposed to the "wandering" planets.</note> of unequal apparent size could be at an equal distance from us.

But regarding the planets, it is certain that they are not on the same spherical surface as the fixed stars, but are lower <note>In this context, "lower" means closer to the center of the system (the Sun or Earth).</note> than the fixed stars; for they sometimes hide the stars from view, and in turn, the planets are never hidden by the fixed stars.

*If about*

He provides evidence that planets are closer to us than the stars because they can pass in front of them (occultation).</summary>

*What argument do you have for this matter?*

If the region of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *fixarum*. These are the stars that appear to remain in a permanent, "fixed" pattern relative to one another, unlike the planets.</note> were sown with stars in the same way everywhere, even in the neighborhood of our moving world, so that the location of our world and sun had no special boundary compared to the location of any other fixed star: then only a few massive fixed stars would be visible to us. Kepler famously attempted to relate the orbits of the planets to these "Platonic solids."</note>) could all be at the same distance and size from us. Those following these, not many more in number, would then be at twice the distance of the nearest ones; others further out would be at triple the distance, and so on, following an ever-increasing multiple.

And since even the largest stars appear so small that they can barely be recorded or measured with instruments, those that were twice or three times as far away would appear two or three times smaller, assuming their actual physical sizes were the same.

*The force of this argument seems to be weakened if one assumes that those stars which are further from Earth are generally larger? and its circle is indeed of unequal width, yet nonetheless it is not very different from itself all around. Therefore, the <term>Milky Way</term><note>Latin: *via lactea*</note> notably marks the location of the Earth and the <term>mobile world</term><note>The part of the universe containing the moving planets, as opposed to the stationary stars.</note>, above all other places, in the region of the fixed stars.

For suppose the Earth stood to the side, by one semi-diameter of the Milky Way; then this Milky Way would appear to it as a small circle, or a small ellipse, entirely declining to the other side; and at one glance it would be visible in its entirety, whereas now only half can be seen at any moment.

Again, suppose the Earth were indeed in the plane of the Milky Way, but near to its circumference on one side or the other: then that part of the Milky Way would appear huge, while the opposite part would appear narrow.

Thus the sphere of the fixed stars is bounded towards us below not only by the Orb of stars, but also by the circle of milk <note>The Milky Way</note>.

*Is the region of the fixed stars, therefore,*
*infinite upwards?*

Here Astronomy pronounces nothing: for at such a height it is destitute of the sense of the eyes. Astronomy teaches only this: that the space is finite as far as the stars, even the smallest ones, are discerned.

*Could not some of the visible stars be*
*distant from us by an interval*
*actually infinite?*

No: For what is discerned is discerned by its boundaries. Therefore, a visible star has boundaries all around. But if a star had receded into an actually infinite space, even these boundaries would be distant from one another by infinite spaces: for all of them together—that is, the whole body of the star—would participate in this infinite height: and so, while the angle of vision remained the same, the diameter of the star (which is the line between its boundaries) would be increased proportionally with its distance. Just as the diameter of an object twice as far becomes twice as long as the diameter of one closer, so also the diameter of something at a finite distance is finite; when a body is assumed to take on an infinitely multiplied distance, it would itself also become infinitely greater than itself.

40 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,
But these things are mutually contradictory: to be infinite and yet to be bounded; and it is equally contradictory to be infinite and yet to have a certain—that is, a finite—proportion to another infinite thing. Therefore, nothing visible is at an infinite distance from us.

_What if there are some stars, finite in their physical bodies, but scattered through spaces that are infinite upwards, which are not seen by us due to such a great distance?_

First, if they are not seen, they have nothing to do with astronomy <note>Kepler defines astronomy as the study of observable celestial phenomena; if it cannot be seen, it falls outside the scientist's preview.</note>. Second, if the region of the fixed stars is bounded on one side—namely, downwards towards our mobile world—why should it lack a boundary on the upper side?
Third, although it cannot be denied that there may be many stars which are not seen, either due to their smallness or their great distance, infinite space cannot be established by them. For if each individual star is finite in size, they must all together be finite in number. Otherwise, if they were infinite in number, no matter how tiny they were, as long as they had some size, they could constitute one infinite whole. This would be a body extending in three dimensions and yet still be infinite, which implies a contradiction: for a thing is called "infinite" because it lacks an end and a boundary, and therefore lacks dimension <note>In Aristotelian logic, which Kepler uses here, "dimension" implies a measurable beginning and end. Thus, an "infinite dimension" was seen as a logical impossibility.</note>. Thus, every actual number of things is finite, by the very fact that it is a number. Therefore, a finite number of finite bodies does not create an infinite space, as if accumulated by the multiplication of a multitude of finite spaces.

_Will you not at least concede that space is actually infinite upwards?_

If we are talking about a vacuum—that is, a thing of nothing, which was neither created, nor **EXISTS** <note>original: E S T</note>, nor can resist another so that it may **BE** <note>original: S I T</note> there—then the status of the question changes; something that is plainly nothing cannot "actually" exist. 
But if space exists because of the bodies placed within it <term>Relational Space: the idea that space only exists because objects exist to define it, rather than being an empty "container" that exists on its own</term>, it has already been demonstrated that neither is any locatable body actually infinite, nor can bodies of finite size be infinite in number. Therefore, there is no necessity for space to be infinite for the purpose of placing bodies. Moreover, there cannot even be an infinite line between only two bodies—

# BOOK TWO 41

...[the] line [is] actually infinite. For again these ideas conflict: that a thing could be actually infinite, and yet be bounded on both sides by individual finite bodies—as if by points—which are the boundaries of a line. <note>The author is pointing out the logical contradiction in saying a line is "infinite" if it has specific endpoints or "points" where it begins and ends.</note>

*What should I hold regarding the potential infinite; and can at least an infinite space or number be thought?*

The term "potential infinite" <term>potential infinite (infinitum in potentia): something that is not infinite in its current state, but has the capacity to increase or be divided without ever reaching a final end.</term> is used in two senses. For it is either understood in the way that the division of a quantity is called "infinite in power"—meaning that there are infinite sections that *could* be made within that quantity; yet whichever of those sections were actually made, each would be finite in itself, consisting of finite parts. Or, the "potential infinite" is understood in such a way that this "power" refers to the very magnitude of the whole infinite. In the former sense, it is true that no space and no number has ever been thought of, nor ever will be thought of, than which a larger cannot be imagined; yet there will always remain infinite numbers not yet even thought of, any of which could be thought of later. In this latter sense, however, there is no "infinite in power"—meaning that an infinite space or infinite numbers could be thought of all at once and at the same time, or that the infinite could be exhausted by thinking. For whatever is thought, by the very fact that it is thought, is finite. Nor do we grasp with the mind what the word "infinite" suggests to us in any other way than as a thing of which only a certain part shines in the mind, while the rest exceeds the mind's thought. In this way, it refers back to the first sense, and the concept is merely nominal. <note>The author argues that the human mind cannot "think" infinity all at once because the act of thinking a concept defines and limits it. We only call things "infinite" when we realize there is always more to the thing than we can currently hold in our minds.</note>

With what else but the Spherical?

There are almost no astronomical arguments; but there are two metaphysical ones especially. The first is drawn from the World itself, and the other from its Archetype. <note>original: "Archetypo". In 17th-century science, the "Archetype" refers to the divine blueprint or the ideal geometric patterns God used to create the universe.</note>

*State the first?*

We are debating the figure that encloses the World from the outside. Therefore, everything is inside that figure, and nothing is outside. If all...

Thirdly, if the surface also flows uniformly outside itself to the side, a body is born, and specifically a **parallelepiped**; and if the angle of flow is a right angle, it is also called **columnar**.

### BOOK TWO. 45
#### How does the third kind arise through composition?

All remaining plane figures consist of triangles, which are the components of <term>parallelograms (four-sided shapes with opposite sides that are parallel)</term>, provided that each side of a pair of triangles has the same length. In this way, all many-sided bodies <note>In modern terms, these are polyhedra.</note> are composed of the previously mentioned **Prisms** or **Tetrahedrons** <note>original: "Tetraedris"; a pyramid with four triangular faces.</note>, which are the primary parts, provided that the individual planes of a pair of Tetrahedrons match up. Among these composite shapes, the simplest are the **quadrangular Pyramids** just mentioned, because each consists of only two Tetrahedrons; Prisms, however, consist of three, and other shapes consist of more.

*I understand the origin of these other figures; it seems, therefore, that the **Sphere** is among the primary shapes, for it is born from the movement of a semicircular line around immobile poles and an axis. Would it follow then that the circular line exists before the sphere itself?*

[An illustration of a hemispherical dome structure supported by two vertical pillars.]

This method of creating the Sphere is merely a geometric—or rather, a mechanical—instruction used by Geometers to help beginners understand. However, it is not at all suitable when considering the actual Nature of the Sphere or its <term>metaphysical (the philosophical study of the fundamental nature of reality)</term> reality. For when a semicircle is rotated, certain points (as we have said) remain still, those closest to the center move slowly, and the points in the middle move with the greatest speed. Yet the Sphere itself is perfectly uniform and similar to itself in every part. Furthermore, in the origin of the "primary" shapes <note>These are simpler geometric forms that the author considers less perfect than the sphere.</note>, which are of a lower rank, there was a perfectly uniform movement <note>original: "fluxus"; the "flow" or path traced by a point to create a line, or a line to create a surface.</note> of all points. <margin>*Prove this secondary nature of the semicircular line?*</margin>

A circular line is understood to arise in two ways: the first is common and mechanical, which is when one leg of a compass remains stationary while the other revolves until it returns to its own tracks. However, this method is foreign to the nature of a circle, for it begins at a specific point, whereas there is nothing in a circle that possesses the quality of a beginning. Therefore, a circular line cannot exist in this way without a flat surface <note>a plane</note> in which it resides; a surface cannot be created without a straight line, a line cannot exist without a point, a point cannot exist without a position in a place, and a place cannot exist without a figure that contains that place—and the kind of figure that circumscribes a place is the Sphere. Therefore, the point, the line, the plane surface, and the circular line all take their beginning from the Sphere.

The second method is metaphysical and suited to the nature of quantities, by which a circular line is generated through the sectioning of a Sphere by a plane. Therefore, once again, both the plane and the sphere must pre-exist the circular line as the subjects and instruments of its creation. Thus, the Sphere is prior even to the circle.

<margin>*Is the Spherical figure therefore completely uncreated?*</margin>

It is called "uncreated" <note>original: "ingenita"</note> in respect to the other figures because it is generated by none of those methods; rather, it provides the points and the place for the others to be generated. Truly, in itself, it has a far different mode of generation—not from something else, but from its own innermost point, about which we will speak below.

48 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY,
*How will you prove that the Sphere is sufficient for itself and for others?*

Other figures, as I have said, are described, enclosed, and bounded by planes; planes by lines; and lines by points. Points, however, require a specific location in space: yet space itself requires being defined by something surrounding it. The Sphere, resting upon itself, requires nothing outside of itself that is not part of itself; for it is bounded by itself, and by 그 very fact, it encloses a space within itself. Within this space, points, lines, surfaces, and bodies can be established once a starting point is given.

*But will you also establish this figure as the creator and sustainer of all others?*

Geometers certainly know this: that every beauty of similarity in other figures, every beauty of logic, and every beauty of perfection exists within them only as something derived from the sphere. 

For all the planes of a single <term>regular body</term><note>Kepler is referring to the five Platonic Solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron), which are the only perfectly symmetrical 3D shapes.</note> must fit perfectly into the same circle, and a circle is derived from a sphere, as has been said. Furthermore, all the <term>solid angles</term><note>A corner where three or more faces of a 3D shape meet.</note> of any perfect figure must be at an equal distance from the center of that figure; that is, they must all touch the surface of the same sphere. Therefore, the sphere is the cause of perfection and the Standard for other figures; it possesses the character of <term>form</term><note>In the Aristotelian sense, 'form' is the essential nature or blueprint that gives a thing its identity.</note>. 

The comparison of the sides of a figure to its other diameters, and the comparison of several bodies to one another, cannot be done except by placing them within a sphere. In this sphere, all bodies are contained, and the sphere's diameter is divided according to certain ratios. Therefore, the sphere is the cause and the standard of definition, of scientific description, and of proportions for the other figures. 

Even the beauty of these proportions themselves cannot be established or understood except through the benefit of the circle; geometers themselves call this the <note>original: "Divinam eam proportionem"</note> Divine Proportion <note>Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio, which Kepler believed God used to design the universe.</note>.

*Show that there is within the Sphere an image of the adorable Trinity.*

*The Sun, Moon, and Planets appear in the form of a circular disk; therefore, they are not solid spheres.*

It does not follow that they are therefore truly flat disks. For experts in optics <note>original: "Optici"; referring to those who study the physics of light and vision</note> demonstrate that even solid globes, if viewed from a great distance, are seen as circular disks.

## tude of the Air, surrounding the Earth and

*Since the globe of the Earth is separated from the highest heaven by a very long distance: I ask, what fills that interval?*

The Air <note>Latin: *Aer*</note> closely encloses and surrounds the Lands and the Seas interspersed among the Lands; its highest altitude barely exceeds the highest peaks of the mountains. But above the Air, the ethereal Ether <note>Latin: *Aura ætheria*</note> immediately follows, spread through the entire universe, such that the Planets and Comets are carried through it and the remaining fixed celestial bodies are scattered, each circumscribed within its own Regions.

*By what distinction are the Ether and the Air separated from each other?*

Both are fluid, both are transparent <term>pellucidus (transparent): the quality of a substance that allows light to pass through so that objects behind it can be seen</term>, and both are of variable purity depending on the variety of places and times: yet they differ by manifest and perceptible degrees of transparency.

*Explain this distinction of transparency through its causes.*

The science of <term>optics</term> <note>original: "Optica scientia"; the study of light and vision, which in the 17th century was deeply concerned with how light traveled through different celestial and earthly substances</note> teaches three causes of transparency:
1. internal unity, 2. subtlety <note>original: "tenuitatem"; referring to the lack of density or the "fineness" of a substance's particles</note>, and 3. purity from the contamination of colors.
In the first cause, therefore, Air and <term>Ether</term> <note>original: "Æther"; the "fifth element" or the subtle fluid believed to fill the heavens beyond the Earth's atmosphere</note> are almost equal in degree; for the fluidity common to both causes internal unity, provided that no foreign material <note>original: "heterogeneum"</note> is mixed in.
However, dry exhalations and smoke are more frequently and abundantly mixed with Air, dividing the internal unity of the moist Air. Ether, diffused through vast spaces, is more rarely contaminated by foreign materials, and only in those few parts where it most closely touches the celestial spheres <note>original: "globos"; referring to the planets or stars themselves</note>.
In the second cause, there are degrees in a continuous series, such that the density of Water is greater, that of Air is moderate, and that of Ether is nonexistent—instead, its subtlety is inestimable and pure.
In the third cause, the distinction is this: that Air, by reason of its own matter and in proportion to its density, even possesses a blue color; Ether, when considered in its own proper matter, possesses no more color than it does density.

58 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY
<note>original: EPITOMES ASTRONOMIÆ</note>
...a certain flow out of the body into the region opposite the Sun, drawn out through the sun's rays which permeate the body, similar in motion to those flashes which here in the vicinity of our air show the appearance of a burning sky and <term>chasms<gloss>Kepler refers to "chasms" (chasmata), a term used in his era to describe atmospheric phenomena like the Aurora Borealis or deep openings in the clouds.</gloss></term>.

*Enough of the ethereal breeze; I ask now about the Air: by what shape is its surface bounded?*

It is bounded much more perfectly than the Ocean, with a spherical surface, for the same reasons; specifically because, just as it follows after Water in density, so also it holds the next place in weight. It only deserves to be called "light" in comparison to Water; otherwise, if it were absolutely light, tending by its own nature upward away from the center of the Earth, it would completely desert the earth. It happens, therefore, as in waves, by the equilibrium of its parts, that it turns out perfectly round. This must be understood, however, regarding calm Air.

*By what arguments do you prove that air is denser than ether?*

Mainly by two: 1. Because that which astronomical experience denies happening <margin>in</margin> in the ether above the air, is testified to happen entirely on the curved surface of the air itself: namely, that the Sun's rays, which are otherwise straight lines, when they fall obliquely <note>obliquely: at an angle</note> on the surface of the air, are refracted <note>refracted: bent as they pass from one medium to another</note> entirely downward and inward; which <term>optics<gloss>The study of light and vision.</gloss></term> teaches happens in a denser medium.

<margin>2.</margin> 2. Because the Air, illuminated by the Sun's rays, surrounds us with such splendors that we have day even when the sun has not yet risen, and we are unable to see the stars. Once the sun has risen, no room is so dark, provided it admits air through even the smallest hole, that it does not shine inside with the light of the air, even if it is not open to the sun's rays. This borrowed brightness, according to optical experts, is an argument for density and the <term>impurity of colors<gloss>original: "colorum fæculentiæ." Kepler means the air contains "feculence" or sediment-like particles (dust, vapor) that catch and scatter light.</gloss></term>.

# ->BOOK ONE 19<-

*Recount several instances from which it has been understood that the rays of the stars and the Sun are <term>refracted<note>original: "refringi"; the bending of light as it passes from the vacuum of space into the denser air of the Earth's atmosphere.</note></term> at the surface of the atmosphere, and reach the eye in a bent state.*

I. In certain lunar eclipses, when the center of the earth and the centers of the <term>luminaries<note>original: "luminarium"; a traditional term for the Sun and the Moon.</note></term> are in a single straight line, yet both bodies are seen above the horizon at the same time—just as if they were not in <note>In astronomy, "opposition" means the Sun and Moon are on exactly opposite sides of the Earth.</note> opposition, but both together in the upper hemisphere.

[A woodcut diagram illustrating an eclipse. It shows the Sun (A) with a face, the Earth (H) with its atmosphere (B, D), and the Moon (C) within the Earth's shadow. Rays of light are shown refracting through the atmosphere to an observer (O) on the Earth's surface. Dashed lines indicate the apparent positions (E, F) of the Sun and Moon above the horizon.]

*Here A, H, and C are the centers of the Sun, Earth, and Moon in one straight line; therefore, the Moon is in the Earth's shadow. O is the eye on the surface of the Earth; B and D represent the atmosphere around the Earth. The ray AB is bent downward at B and becomes BO; likewise, the ray from C at D becomes DO. Therefore, the eye—seeing through the bent rays OB and OD and not knowing they were refracted at B and D—imagines them to continue in a straight line without any bending, and judges the Sun (A) to be at E, and the Moon (C) to be at F. Thus, both appear to be above the horizon.*

But if EO and FO were actually straight lines, they would not be able to reach both bodies A and C simultaneously even then, because the observer (O) is outside the direct line AC; therefore, the observer would either see neither body, or only one of them.

II. In these same lunar eclipses, it appears very clearly that the shadow cast by the combined spheres of the earth and the atmosphere is diluted at its edges by a certain uneven reddish light. Thus the moon—especially when it grazes the edges of the shadow—even though it is entirely within the shadow, often glows so red that it appears to still be shining in some part of its body as if placed in the sun's light. This continues until, as the moon begins to exit the shadow, that reddish appearance is overtaken by the arrival of pure, direct solar light.

It also describes the "blood moon" effect, where the Earth's atmosphere bends and filters sunlight into the shadow, tinting the eclipsed Moon red.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the optical properties of light in the atmosphere, specifically focusing on the phenomenon of refraction and its effects on astronomical observations.</meta>

60 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

Indeed, this light, which is spread so unevenly, cannot come from anywhere else but from rays that have undergone a double <term>refraction</term><note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one substance into another, such as from the vacuum of space into the Earth's atmosphere.</note>, namely upon entering the air and upon exiting it.

For if B O D were a single straight line, and several other lines passed above O through the air, then by the same paths through which the light of the sun and the moon is carried to the eye at O—namely through A B O and C D O—the light of the sun is also carried to the Moon, through A B D C. This illuminates the moon slightly, even though it is kept within the shadow of the entire globe B C.

### III.
The Dutch who spent the winter beyond Tartary<note>This refers to the 1596–1597 expedition led by Willem Barentsz, where the crew was stranded on the Arctic island of Novaya Zemlya.</note>, after a night three months long, began to see the sun at midday during a time of year when the sun should not yet have been able to reach the horizon by several degrees. It follows, therefore, that the rays of the sun—which was still positioned below the earth—hit the air and, while they were meant to pass far above the heads of the Dutchmen, they were bent downward by <term>refraction</term> so that they struck the eyes of the Dutch.

### IV.
When the sun is sufficiently high, its body is round, and its diameters are all equal to one another, as is easy to explore with suitable instruments. But when the sun first rises, its vertical diameter appears shorter than its horizontal diameter through precise instruments; and to one contemplating the appearance of the sun accurately, it seems compressed, in some way imitating the shape of an egg. This, therefore, is caused by the refraction of the rays. For the study of optics teaches us that refractions are not perceptible when the sun is at a great height, but finally become perceptible when the sun is near the horizon. 

Thus, the lower any given point is, the more its ray is refracted; and this makes the point appear higher than it truly is. Since the upper edge of the sun appears only slightly higher than it truly is, but the bottom edge appears much higher than it truly is, the bottom will seem to approach the top through this refraction. Therefore, the distance from the top to the bottom—that is, the vertical diameter—appears contracted, while the horizontal diameter does not change, because the ends of the horizontal diameter are elevated equally.

V. Tycho Brahe revealed a method for observing refractions daily, especially using the fixed stars. For example, the "tail of Leo" <note>original: "cauda Leonis"; refers to the star Denebola</note> and "Spica" <note>the brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> are always separated from one another by the same arc of a great circle, which is 35 degrees and 2 minutes. We detect these distances with instruments whenever they <term>culminate|reach their highest point in the sky</term>, and likewise when they set, because they set at nearly the same time. 

But when the tail of Leo reaches an altitude of 34 and a half degrees in the eastern part of the sky, Spica already begins to be seen on almost the same vertical line, as if it were rising; even though in reality it is still below the horizon, because it is more than 34 degrees and 30 minutes—specifically 35 degrees and 2 minutes—distant from the tail of Leo. The reason for this, once again, is that the light ray from the tail of Leo is hardly refracted <note>bent by the atmosphere</note> at all, due to the star's sufficiently high altitude above the horizon. However, the ray from Spica is refracted significantly because, as it rises, it shines into the sphere of air <note>the atmosphere</note> at a very oblique angle; it therefore appears to be raised high above its true position, and thus seems to approach the tail of Leo standing above it.

[A geometric diagram illustrating atmospheric refraction. It shows a cross-section of the Earth with an observer at point 'A' on the surface. A curved line represents the atmosphere. Dashed lines indicate apparent positions 'q' and 'p'. The center of the Earth is labeled 'o'.]

Let **A** be the eye of the observer on Earth, and **A E C** the line of the Horizon. Nevertheless, it is seen through **A E** and is thought to be at **C**, because **G E** is refracted <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium, like the vacuum of space, into another, like the Earth's atmosphere.</note> at **E**, and the refracted ray **E A** reaches the eye at **A**. That eye assumes **AE** and **EG** form a single straight line **AEC**. Thus, instead of the true angle **HAG**, a smaller angle **HAC** is perceived.

### From where did astronomers first learn the height of the atmosphere?

From comparing the amount of **Refraction** when a star rises against when it is raised to a certain altitude.

### What optical principles must be known beforehand so that this method can be explained?

**First**, the more a ray of the sun or a star is inclined <term>inclined: the angle at which a ray hits a surface</term> upon the surface of the air (as a denser <term>medium: the substance, like air or water, through which light travels</term>), the more it is refracted. Therefore, a ray that grazes the sphere of air is refracted the most at the point of contact. However, all rays cross each other at the point of refraction; those that were higher in the thin medium <note>the vacuum of space</note> become the lower rays once refracted in the dense medium <note>the atmosphere</note>.

**Second**, the ratio between two angles of **Refraction** is composed of two other ratios: one between the angles of **Inclination** (which cause the refractions) established within the dense medium, and the other between the <term>secants: a trigonometric function related to the angle of the light</term> of those angles. Thus, if the **Refraction** for one specific inclination is known, the refractions for all other inclinations are also provided. 

**Third**, since the **Sphere of Air** surrounds the globe of the Earth, one and the same ray is tilted differently upon the Earth than it is upon the inner <note>concave</note> surface of the air. A ray that grazes the Earth—namely, the ray of a rising star—cuts through the surface of the air. 

**Fourth**, when we observe the refractions of rays, we do not measure their inclinations relative to the air (since its surface is invisible and far above us), but relative to the Earth where we stand. Therefore, we must afterwards investigate the tilt of the refracted ray relative to the curved inner surface of the air.

Show the method for calculating the height of the air <note>original: "altitudinem aeris"; the author is referring to the thickness of the atmosphere</note>, based on the given inclination of a light ray <term>inclination: the angle at which a ray of light strikes a surface, such as the ground or the edge of the atmosphere</term> both upon the earth and upon the inner curved surface of the air: and conversely, how to find the angle from the height.

A triangle is formed using the known radius of the earth, the radius of the sphere of the air, and the path of the light ray. In this triangle, the angles at the ends of the ray—meaning the angles of inclination—are known. Therefore, as the sine of the angle of inclination upon the inner surface of the atmosphere relates to the radius of the earth, so the sine of the angle of inclination upon the earth relates to the radius of the sphere composed of both earth and air. Thus, the amount remaining after subtracting the radius of the earth is the atmospheric height we are looking for.

**Example.**

*How can the refractions of other angles of inclination be computed from the refraction that occurs at one specific inclination of a ray as it falls upon the air? And conversely, how can the inclinations of other refractions [be found]?*

One must use the <term>Rule of Five<note>Also known as the compound rule of proportions; a mathematical method used to find an unknown value when five related quantities are known.</note></term>, or the rule of proportions, by multiplying each inclination by its own secant.

*Example.*
Let the inclination of a ray in a dense medium upon the surface of that medium be 89 degrees and 20 minutes, the <term>secant<note>In trigonometry, the secant is the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side of a right triangle.</note></term> of which is 85.94561. Let the refraction for this inclination be 40 minutes. (For refraction is never greater than the complement of the inclination upon the dense medium, and is almost always less.) Now, the refraction is sought for another inclination of 60 degrees <note>original: "p. 60." likely referring to "partibus," a common term for degrees.</note> for ray AI, the secant of which is 200,000. Therefore:

### What is the manner of the rising and setting of the signs through those positions of the sphere?

From the equator all the way to the polar circle, all signs <note>Referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note> rise, and indeed in their correct order. The horizon intersects the **Ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note> within the tropics twice at right angles—specifically, whenever its pole <note>The pole of the ecliptic, rather than the north/south celestial pole.</note> enters the horizon. Beneath the Tropic, this happens once; beyond the Tropic as far as the polar circle, the intersection becomes more and more oblique <note>Slanted or at an angle, rather than perpendicular.</note>. Beneath the Arctic Circle, the Ecliptic is joined...

The remaining semicircle, through which the Sun is thought to descend from Cancer through Libra into Capricorn <note>The signs of the Zodiac marking the transition from the summer solstice through the autumn equinox to the winter solstice.</note>, descends at that same moment. At the same time, in the northern intersection of the Horizon and the Meridian <term>Meridian: the great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a specific location</term> marked **R**, it begins to rise in the correct order. This continues until the entire equator has revolved and its end—that is, 30 degrees of Sagittarius—comes to the very point of the midday line **H**, as if it were about to ascend into the Horizon. Thus, the rising of this half of the Ecliptic <note>The "Ecliptic" is the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky.</note> has the entire equator rising along with it.

But within the polar circle, since near the lower solstitial point <note>The point of the winter solstice.</note> a certain arc <note>A segment of a circle.</note> never rises but remains always below the Earth; and near the upper solstitial point <note>The point of the summer solstice.</note>, another arc is always above, never setting, being always larger the closer the pole is to the zenith <note>The point directly overhead.</note>, until under the pole itself each arc becomes a semicircle. The intermediate arcs do indeed rise and set, but the one containing the spring equinox (in our Hemisphere) rises in a reversed order; the other, containing the autumnal equinox, rises in the correct order. These have the whole equator rising with them, though the former has a larger part of it rising in inverse order.

The rising amplitude <term>Rising Amplitude: the angular distance along the horizon from the true East point to the point where a celestial body actually rises</term> itself also follows this same variation. For between the Equator and the polar circle, this rising amplitude expands itself little by little from the Equinoctial rising point **Q**, toward the north **R** and the south **H**. The parts ordered from Cancer through Libra into Capricorn have their regions of rising from the northern parts of the Horizon **R** toward the south **H**; from there, from Capricorn through Aries into Cancer, they move in a retrograde <note>original: "retrogrado" — meaning moving backward or in reverse of the usual order.</note> order from the south **H** toward the north **R**, initially in small intervals. This continues until, under the polar circle itself and toward the interior, this rising amplitude traverses the entire semicircle of the Horizon, from the very northern point of the Horizon **R**, through the rising point **Q**, all the way to the very southern point **H**. But within the Polar circle, no such retrograde transposition of risings from south to north occurs from the opposite arcs, but the arcs of both semicircles... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>

Within the Polar circle, the addition of the oblique ascension of the arc rising in reverse order establishes the oblique ascension of the equal opposite arc.

Therefore, by comparing the <term>Nonagesimal</term> <note>The Nonagesimal (from the Latin *nonagesimus*, meaning ninetieth) is the point on the ecliptic that is exactly 90 degrees from where the ecliptic intersects the horizon; it is the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon at any given moment.</note> of the Ecliptic, **N**, and the point **M** "mediating the heavens" <note>original: *cœlum mediante*; this refers to the Midheaven or Medium Coeli, the point where the ecliptic intersects the local meridian.</note> with one another, the intercepted arc **NM** becomes known.

Secondly, in this triangle, the side on the Meridian **VM**—between the zenith **V** <note>original: *verticem*; the point directly overhead.</note> and the Ecliptic **M**—is investigated. For when the point **M** of the Ecliptic mediating the heavens is given, its declination **AM** is also given. If this declination is northern, it is subtracted from the altitude of the pole **VA**; if it is southern, it is added to it. This calculation establishes the distance of that Ecliptic point from the zenith, **VM**. Furthermore, the angle at the Nonagesimal of the Ecliptic, **VNM**, is a right angle. Therefore, with three parts given, the fourth can also be obtained: specifically, the side on the vertical circle, or the distance of the Nonagesimal from the zenith, **NV**. The complement of this, **NH**, is the altitude of the Nonagesimal above the Horizon, which is the measure of the sought angle **MOH**.

274 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY <note>original: "EPITOMES ASTRONOMIÆ"</note>

*How do you define the civil or political year?*

It is a span of time, or a specific number of whole days, toward which the motion of the Sun or the Moon (or both luminaries) points from a distance; it is adopted by the common institution of any given nation.

*Which form of the civil year is the most convenient of all for the discipline of astronomy?*

The Julian year of the Old Calendar <note>The "Old Calendar" refers to the Julian system, which was being replaced by the Gregorian calendar during Kepler's lifetime</note>, consisting of 365 days and adding one day every four years, so that after three "simple" years, the fourth consists of 366 days. This is the mean measure among astronomical years; this has been the at least implicit counting of time for all nations; and among us, it has been practiced and maintained by continuous observation since the time of the Caesars. An astronomer must repeatedly return to this form of the year, regardless of whatever other style more familiar to his own country he may have at hand.

*How do astronomers define the year?*

For them, the year is the span of time within which the Sun appears to complete its circuit in the sky; this is actually caused—as will be explained in the *Theories* <note>Kepler refers to the "Theories of the Planets," the section of his book dealing with physical causes</note>—by the circuit of the Earth's center around a truly immobile Sun.

*How many types of years are recognized by astronomers?*

Two types, based on the two different "finish lines" of the Solar revolution: the Sidereal and the Tropical (or Turning) year.

*What are the markers of the sidereal year?*

A point on the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path against the background of stars</term> onto which a great circle descends from the pole of the Ecliptic through a specific fixed star, such as Sirius, or the Horn of Aries, etc.

Days <margin>Days</margin>

*What are the boundaries of the Turning Year?* <note>original: "anni Vertentis." This refers to the Tropical year, the time it takes for the Sun to return to the same seasonal point, such as an equinox.</note>

These are the points on the Ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> where either the Celestial Equator or one of the two **colures** <term>colures: two principal circles on the celestial sphere which pass through the celestial poles and either the equinoxes or the solstices</term> intersects it. *Should we not then hold some prior knowledge regarding the apparent motion of the Sun or the Earth's own motion to understand this?*

Indeed, for a perfect explanation of the Turning Year, quite a few things must be drawn from Theoretical astronomy.

*Why, then, is it discussed within the spherical doctrine?*

The turning year can be viewed in several ways: we either divide the Sun’s circuit (which creates the year) by its natural boundaries derived from the "primary motion" <note>the daily rotation of the heavens</note> and investigate the various conditions of those parts—such as the differences between days and nights—and thus it belongs to **spherical doctrine**; or we measure the varying lengths of both the whole year and its individual parts. The causes of this variation must be sought from **Theoretical doctrine**.

*How many meanings does the word "Day" have among astronomers?*

Primarily two. For it either means the same as what the Greeks call a **Nychthemeron** <note>original: "Νυχθήμερον," a term combining the words for "night" and "day" to describe a full 24-hour cycle.</note>, which is the span of time in which one day and one night are completed—this is usually called a **natural day**. <margin>Just as a house, a ship, a chest, and a table all belong naturally to a single category of things because they are made of wood, but craft <note>The Latin "ars" (from which "artificial" is derived) refers here to human skill, categorization, or "artifice" as opposed to raw nature.</note> creates the distinction between the woods so that one becomes a ship and another a table; and just as there is one species for all human beings, from which the name "Man" applies to them, but the mind, custom, and the institutions of nations—which are added onto nature—distinguish people by distributing different duties and names among them (so that one is a king, another a bishop, and another a shepherd <note>original: "Opilio"</note>, though all are humans of the same nature): so the one and same **Nychthemeron** <note>original: "Νυχθήμερον"</note> arising from Nature is shaped in different ways into unequal segments of day and night across different horizons—that is, through the different perspectives of different viewers—one way here, and another way there.</margin>

*How do astronomers count hours and days?*

Either from midnight to the first of the twenty-four hours of the following midnight, as in the Pruthenic Tables <note>The *Tabulae Prutenicae* (1551) were astronomical tables based on the calculations of Nicolaus Copernicus.</note>. Or from Noon, counting again twenty-four hours until the following Noon; the day is sometimes called "complete" and sometimes "current," of which the expressed hours are parts.

*How many types of hours are there?*

As many as there are types of days: for some are called Equinoctial <note>original Greek: ἰσημέρινοι (*isēmerinoi*)</note>, and others are called Temporal <note>original Greek: Καιρικαὶ (*Kairikai*); these are also known as "unequal" or "seasonal" hours which vary in length depending on the time of year</note>, because they obtain a varying length according to the proportion of the seasons throughout the whole year.

*What is an equinoctial hour?*

It is the twenty-fourth part of the day-and-night <note>original Greek: τοῦ νυχθημέρου (*tou nychthēmerou*)</note>, or the natural day and night joined together.

*How is the Equinoctial Hour divided astronomically?*

It is divided like the 360 degrees of a circle, or like Time, into sixty minutes, such that 15 minutes make up a quarter of an hour. One minute passes into 60 seconds, one second into 60 thirds <note>In historical astronomy, subdivisions continued in base-60: minutes, seconds, thirds, fourths, etc.</note>; and so on continuously, as far as is necessary.

*Compare the divisions of the Equinoctial Hour with the human pulse?*

In a healthy, robust man of mature age, of a melancholic <term>melancholic: one of the four "humors" or temperaments in ancient medicine, associated with a slow, steady nature</term> temperament or an aging man, there are almost individual beats of the artery for every single second, with no distinction between the contraction <note>original: *systolen*</note> and the expansion <note>original: *diastolen*</note>; thus there would be sixty in one minute...

*What causes the unequal additions?* <note>The author uses "additions" to refer to the extra amount of time or rotation added to a 24-hour cycle to account for the Sun's movement. Today, we relate this to the "Equation of Time."</note>

There are two causes. The first is found in theoretical principles and the unequal <term>proper motion of the Sun</term> <note>The Sun’s apparent daily movement along the ecliptic, which is not constant because the Earth's orbit is elliptical.</note>, which causes the daily arcs of the Sun on the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The annual path of the Sun across the sky.</note> to be unequal to one another. For today, after the Summer Solstice, the Sun completes 57 minutes and 5 seconds in one day; but after the winter solstice, it completes 61 minutes and 21 seconds. The causes of this inequality are explained differently according to the varying opinions of authors, as is taught in the appropriate place. Furthermore, a small daily motion has a small <term>Right Ascension</term> <note>The distance measured along the celestial equator; the celestial equivalent of longitude.</note>, all else being equal, while a large motion has a large one.

The second cause is specific to this subject: even if the arcs of the Sun's daily motion were equal to one another, they would still have different, and thus unequal, Right Ascensions at different points on the Ecliptic. Furthermore, the Right Ascensions are not perfectly equal in those same Ecliptic locations across all centuries, because of the variation in the <term>obliquity of the Ecliptic</term> <note>The angle of the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit.</note>, about which some things were said above, and more will be said below in Book VII.

*How many types of additions are there among astronomers?*

Two types: 1. *Temporal* <note>original Greek: Καιρικὰ (Kairika)</note>, which are truly different at different times, now smaller and now larger. <margin>diverse / natural</margin> 2. And *Uniform* <note>original Greek: ὁμαλὰ (homala)</note>, which are the average (mean) between the larger and smaller, created by astronomers for the sake of measurement; these are equal.

*How do astronomers establish the mean or equal additions?*

Because in the 365 days and a quarter of the year, one whole extra revolution of the equator accumulates through the sum of the additions, <margin>entire / days</margin> astronomers divide that revolution by the 365 days and a quarter of the year, and that portion...

### 284 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

...they call one [rotation] the **Equal Addition**; this is equal to the Sun's average daily motion along the Ecliptic, specifically 59 minutes and 8 seconds. <note>The author is explaining that because the Sun moves slightly each day along its path (the ecliptic), the Earth must rotate slightly more than a full 360-degree circle for the Sun to return to the same spot in the sky.</note>

**How many types of Day-and-Night cycles <note>original Greek: *Nychthemera*</note> or natural days are there?**
According to the rule of additions, some are **apparent** or **True**; others are **equal** (mean) in quantity. These mean days are conceptual tools created by astronomers, which consist of the fixed "addition" mentioned above.

**How long is the Mean Natural Day, and how long is its hour?**
The length of a mean natural day consists of 360 degrees <note>original: *tempora*, referring to degrees of the celestial equator used as a measure of time</note> and 59 minutes, 8 seconds. Its hour, therefore, is worth nearly 15 degrees, 2 minutes, and 28 seconds.

**By how much time do True natural days differ from one another?**
The difference between any two consecutive days is impossible to observe. Even if one of the shortest days is compared directly to one of the longest, it does not produce a very large difference. However, when many days are added together in sequence during one part of the year and compared to a similar group of days in another part of the year, they become shorter or longer by a quite obvious difference. <note>This describes the "Equation of Time," the cumulative discrepancy between a sundial (true solar time) and a mechanical clock (mean solar time) over the course of a year.</note>

In other centuries, however, this could exceed a full hour by a further third of an hour. This should be understood as the entire span of the **Turning Year**, divided between two classes of days, of which some [require] fewer... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the page concludes.</note>

Through the elongation <term>elongation: the angular distance between two celestial bodies</term> of a star from the Meridian at night, the elongation of the Sun itself from the same Meridian is also sought.       5. This elongation of the Sun, since it is an arc of the celestial equator intercepted between the circle of declination of the Sun (or star) and the Meridian, is converted into hours. This is done by taking 15 degrees <note>original: "15. 2. 30. Temporibus"</note> for every one hour, provided that the **Right Ascension** of the place the Sun held or will hold at noon is known.       6. Therefore, during the day, while the Sun is still rising, these hours are subtracted from 12 to know how many hours have elapsed since midnight. But when the Sun is already setting, no subtraction is necessary; for the hours that result are numbered from noon, according to the **Astronomical custom**. <note>Unlike civil time, which often started at midnight or sunrise, astronomers traditionally began their "day" at noon.</note>

### 290 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

## Concerning Artificial Days and Nights; and the Alternation of Heat and Cold.

<margin>What specifically is an **artificial day** or **night** according to astronomers?</margin>

The **Artificial Day** is the span of time during which the center of the Sun can be observed above the **rational horizon** <term>rational horizon: a mathematical horizon passing through the center of the Earth, rather than the "sensible" horizon seen by an observer on the surface</term> with its rays free and non-refracted. **Night** is the duration the Sun remains below that horizon, even if there is significant light from **twilight** <note>original: *Crepusculi*</note> at the edges of the night that is almost equal to daylight.

<margin>Are these, then—the **artificial day** and **night**—parts of a single **Natural Day**?</margin>

Speaking accurately, one artificial day—in which the Sun rises and sets—is divided at its very midpoint between two **natural days** <note>A "natural day" refers to the full 24-hour rotation of the Earth relative to the Sun, traditionally measured from noon to noon in Kepler's time.</note>. One of these natural days began at the preceding noon, while the other ends at the following noon. The **artificial night**, however, is a part of only one of these two natural days: the preceding night belongs to the preceding natural day, and the following night belongs to the following one. Therefore, in those regions and times where the Sun is able to rise and set, the artificial day is certainly shorter than the natural day, and serves as a portion of it, no less than its companion, the artificial night.

Second, consider this: that the Earth's axis in the meantime is shifted a little, and thus is now inclined slightly differently toward the Sun than it was at the start of one rotation; by which means, as we learned in the second part, the Sun is rendered a little closer to one of the poles. ->BOOK THREE. 299<-

...of natural <term>days</term><note>A "natural day" (dies naturalis) refers to a full 24-hour cycle of day and night.</note>, are cut by the Horizon: or all points of the Ecliptic rise and set, and the Sun in all of them.

2. That under the polar <insert>circle</insert> the longest day increases to 24 hours, as does the longest night.

For if the <term>Zenith</term><note>original: "Vertex"; the point directly above the observer.</note> falls upon the polar circle, the pole of the Ecliptic then reaches the Zenith, and the Ecliptic is joined to the Horizon at the moment when the <term>solstitial colure</term><note>The great circle on the celestial sphere that passes through the celestial poles and the two solstices.</note> coincides with the Meridian. Thus, one of the two solstices does not rise, and the other does not set; one of the two <term>Tropics</term><note>The circles of latitude 23.5 degrees north or south of the equator.</note> remains entirely hidden, and the other stands entirely above the horizon. The former measures the longest night, the latter the longest day.

In this way, with one half, the entire Equator ascends; with the other half, nothing [ascends]. The Sun, therefore, moving within the common boundaries of these halves, creates in one a day equal to a natural day with no night, and in the other, the opposite.

3. That within the polar circle, several natural days—though not all—merge into a single <term>artificial day</term><note>An "artificial day" (dies artificialis) refers specifically to the period of sunlight, from sunrise to sunset.</note> or night; at the pole, an entire six-month period merges into one.

Because the Zenith (the pole of the Horizon) is within the polar circle, it is therefore sometimes positioned between the pole of the Equator and the pole of the Ecliptic. Thus, the pole of the Ecliptic is then lower toward the South; for this reason, the arc of the Ecliptic around one solstice at the Meridian is below the Horizon, and therefore the opposite arc under the pole of the equator does not rise, but stays above the Horizon and does not set. There, entire circles of natural days remain hidden; here, they are fully visible. The intermediate circles, however, are cut by the Horizon. At the pole, clearly none are cut, but half of them remain hidden and half are visible.

Thus, when the Ecliptic is cut by such a Horizon into four arcs: the upper does not set, the lower does not rise, and the intermediate arcs rise and set, as does the Sun moving within them.

4. That under the equator, all days are equal to their nights.

Because the centers of the circles of the natural days are on the axis of the World, and the axis there is on the horizon, the Horizon therefore cuts all those circles into equal segments.

*Thus the ascensions of semicircles starting from anywhere are all equal to each other; therefore, the semicircle before the Sun—representing the night—always rises in an equal time with the semicircle after the Sun—the indicator of the day.*

5. That outside the equator, only two days of the year are equal to their nights; of the rest, some are longer than the nights and some shorter; and the shortest day for us occurs in Capricorn, and the longest in Cancer. <note>In the Northern Hemisphere, the Sun enters Capricorn at the winter solstice and Cancer at the summer solstice.</note>

*For only the equator has its center in the plane of the horizon, passing through two opposite points of the ecliptic; therefore, only the equator is cut into equal halves by the horizon. The centers of all the other parallel circles are either above or below the equator, because the axis of the world is bisected by the equator, which holds those centers; therefore, the greater part of the former circles is above the horizon, and the greater part of the latter is below. The circle whose center is furthest from the equator on the axis—and thus is either the most elevated or the most depressed—contains the longest or shortest day.*

*Thus, in an oblique sphere <note>A view of the heavens where the celestial pole is at an angle, as seen from anywhere between the equator and the poles.</note>, only those halves of the ecliptic have equal ascensions <term>Ascension: the time it takes for a specific arc of the zodiac to rise above the horizon.</term> which begin from the equinoctial points; those starting elsewhere are unequal. Indeed, semicircles whose beginnings are near us in the north have larger ascensions, because the ascensional difference of the beginning is subtracted, while that of the end is added. The semicircle that begins from the start of Cancer has the greatest ascension, because the ascensional difference is at its maximum there.*

6. That two days, when the Sun is located at points equally distant from the Solstice, are equal to each other, and their nights are likewise equal.

*Because the same parallel circle <note>A circle of constant declination, marking the sun's daily path.</note> passes through such twin points.*

*Similarly: Because the ascensions of the semicircles starting from such twin points are equal.*

7. That one summer day has an equal winter night when the Sun is equally distant from one of the equinoctial points.

*For at such points, the circles decline equally to either side of the equator; they are therefore cut by the horizon in alternating fashion.*

### 8. That the increases of days or nights are fastest at the equinoxes and slowest at the solstices.

Because the Ecliptic is at its most oblique at the intersections <note>The equinoctial points where the Ecliptic crosses the Celestial Equator.</note>, the <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note> increases most rapidly there; however, at the <term>solstices</term><note>original: "Solstitijs", meaning "sun-standstill."</note> it lingers hesitantly, until the increase turns into a decrease. # BOOK THREE. 303

There also arose the custom of counting the hours of the day from sunrise; to ensure that noon always held the same position at the sixth hour and did not wander through the hours, it was necessary for the hours of each day to be twelve in number. <note>This refers to "unequal hours," a system where the period of daylight was always divided into 12 hours regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" was longer in summer than in winter.</note>
But among us Europeans, since the differences in day lengths are more evident—and in the North, across even short distances of land, they vary greatly—and because on certain days there is no convenient sunrise or sunset <note>A reference to the Arctic regions where the sun may not set or rise for days</note>, the method of counting hours from noon and midnight seemed better, and to use equal hours throughout the year; for this is more universal, easy to observe, and of great use in calculating the length of day and night. Then came the invention of automatic clocks <note>Mechanical clocks</note>, which indicate equal hours more easily than unequal ones; since all Europe is filled with such machines, equal hours have become the established custom, while unequal hours have fallen into disuse.

->*Why, however, were both day and night divided into 12 parts,*<-
->*rather than some other number?*<-

It is fitting that the first authors of this system wished to imitate the nature of the year, in which twelve months are constituted by nearly as many lunar cycles. For from the same source, it came about that the Zodiac was divided into twelve signs, and the <term>As</term> <note>A Roman unit of weight or currency</note> into as many parts or ounces <note>original: "uncias"</note>; as was mentioned in Book II. Added to this is the convenience of the number twelve, which has whole parts: a half, a third, a fourth, a sixth, and a twelfth—namely 6, 4, 3, 2, and 1.
Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure often credited with the origins of Egyptian and Greek science</note> is said to have chosen this number because the Apis Bull, whom the Egyptians worship as a deity, would urinate twelve times daily; and from this, "hours" <note>original: "ὥρας" (hōras)</note> were named from "to urinate" <note>original: "οὐρεῖν" (ourein)</note>. <note>This is a humorous but incorrect folk etymology popular in early modern texts.</note>
Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, the astronomer and teacher of Johannes Kepler</note> thinks the custom was taken from roosters, because they distribute their songs, both by night and day, into twelve intervals.

*You appeared to establish different beginnings for the day; can you therefore review the customs of nations, and the reasons each has regarding the start of the day?*

Although by nature there is no single starting point for the day within the heavens themselves, there are nevertheless clear distinctions on Earth between light and darkness, the presence and absence of the Sun, and the transition from one to the other. People often embrace and observe these transitions as natural markers.

Therefore, the Jews begin their day from the Evening, following nature while also observing the order of creation. For when the World was first founded, darkness still prevailed, which was then followed by light; thus, out of Evening and Morning, one day was made. <note>original: "ex Vespera & Mane dies unus." This refers to the Biblical account in Genesis 1:5.</note>

The same practice is attributed to the Athenians. I believe this was because the night was spent by the magistrates—who were rotated daily—in meditation upon those matters which they were to enact on the following day of their <term>prytany: a period of office held by a specific division of the Athenian council</term> <note>original Greek: πρυτανίας</note>. Alternatively, it may be because they conducted the days of the month according to the Moon, which begins to appear in the evening as the Sun sets.

The Italian and Bohemian clocks also reflect this same custom, as they count 24 equal hours from the beginning <note>The "Italian hours" or "Bohemian hours" system counted 24 hours starting from sunset, rather than two 12-hour cycles starting at noon/midnight.</note>

It also mentions the surviving "Italian" and "Bohemian" timekeeping systems that follow this sunset-to-sunset model.</summary>

->*You spoke of the distribution of the days of the week*<-
->*among the Planets. I would like to hear the method*<-
->*for this which the Chaldeans*<-

Since there are twelve hours of the day, and just as many for the night, and there are seven planets in this order: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—for they were numbered in this way by the ancients—they began, therefore, from the first day of the Jewish week. They assigned the first hour of that day to the Sun, the author of the day; the second to Venus, the third to Mercury, and the fourth to the Moon. Then, returning to Saturn, they assigned the <term>fifth hour</term> <note>The "Chaldean Order" of planets is based on their perceived speed/distance from Earth: Saturn (slowest/farthest), Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon (fastest/closest).</note> to him, and so on in succession. Thus, the twelfth and final hour of the day also fell to him, which is why the first hour of the night fell to Jupiter. In this way, it happened that the last hour of the night fell to Mercury. The entire day up to this point was named after the Sun, as the one to whom the first hour of that day was given. After Mercury, since the Moon follows, the first hour of the following day was given to the Moon, from which the name of that entire day is derived. By this reasoning, it happened that every fourth Planet from the previous one gave its name to the following day <note>This "Rule of Four" explains the jump from Sunday (Sun) to Monday (Moon) to Tuesday (Mars), etc.</note>. The first day was the Sun’s, the second the Moon’s, the third Mars’s, the fourth Mercury’s, the fifth Jupiter’s, the sixth Venus’s, and the seventh and last—which was holy and solemn to the Jews—belonged to Saturn, the first and highest of the Planets. This was celebrated with all the greater pleasure because the Jews, by divine precept, spent that day in rest and cessation from work, and Saturn was also the slowest of all the Planets, taking thirty years to complete his circuit. Thus, finally, the Jews—having received the knowledge of the Planets from the Chaldeans <note>Kepler refers to the ancient Babylonians, often called Chaldeans in early modern texts, who were famous for their astronomical and astrological systems.</note>—gave Saturn a name derived from rest and the Sabbath.

*and each is divided into 12 equal hours—*

# 308 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

## ON TWILIGHTS,
->An occurrence of the <term>artificial night|The period of total darkness between the end of evening twilight and the beginning of morning twilight.</term>.<-

*How do we investigate the length of Twilight?*

It is necessary that the altitude of the pole PR <note>The "pole" here refers to the Celestial Pole, and its altitude above the horizon equals the observer's latitude.</note>, the <term>declination|The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</term> of the Sun ST, and the depth of the Sun below the Horizon OS from which twilight begins be given. This depth is established as 16, 18, or 19 degrees, as was stated in the first book, and will be discussed further in the fifth part <note>Modern astronomy typically defines "astronomical twilight" as beginning or ending when the Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon.</note>. BOOK THREE. 309
->What is the variety of twilights across places and times, with respect to astronomical causes?<-

1. In a **right sphere** <note>original: "sphæra recta"; this refers to locations on the Earth's equator where the celestial poles lie on the horizon</note> twilights are the shortest, and throughout the whole year—at least regarding celestial causes—they are almost equal. For during the **equinoxes**, the Sun rises according to the straightness of the vertical circle, which coincides with the equator; thus the ascent of the arc of the **Ecliptic** <note>the Sun’s apparent path across the sky</note> between the Horizon and the Sun is equal to its depth below the horizon.

2. In **oblique spheres** <note>original: "obliquis"; locations at latitudes between the equator and the poles</note> summer twilights are the longest and winter twilights are the shortest; both the inequality between them and the length of each increase along with the altitude of the Pole <note>the observer's latitude</note>. For a right-angled triangle is formed from the circle of the natural day, the Horizon, and the Vertical, where the arc of the circle subtended by the right angle <term>QOS</term> <note>a geometric reference to a diagram likely appearing on a previous page</note> is greater than the arc of the Vertical OS, or the depth. And just as in our region the Sun in the summer signs slowly reaches a depth of 16, 18, or 19 degrees <note>the depth below the horizon at which total darkness begins</note>, but in the winter signs it does so quickly; so also in the other hemisphere, this occurs in those same parts of their own year, which nevertheless coincide with the opposite parts of our year. Therefore, in the summer signs, the Sun is slow to reach such a depth that it extinguishes the light of twilight, while in the winter, it does so quickly.

3. At a polar altitude <note>latitude</note> of 47, 48, or 50 degrees, the twilights of the **Solstice** last all night. For if 19, 18, or 16 degrees are subtracted from 66.5°—which is the **complement** <note>the remaining angle needed to reach 90 degrees</note> of the Sun’s maximum declination of 23.5°—those arcs of the polar altitudes remain. This happens much more evidently and for a longer duration at even higher polar altitudes.

Thus the shortest twilight in the whole world, according to these astronomical positions, lasts 1 hour and 4, 12, or 16 minutes. The longest twilight, however, has no limit <note>referring to the "midnight sun" or permanent twilight at the poles</note>.

310 - EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

# On Climates.

<margin>*What is the primary use of the teaching regarding artificial days?*</margin>

Astronomers, and the geographers who follow them, divide the surface of the Earth into **Climates** according to the increases in the length of the day. They relate celestial appearances to these zones, recording which phenomena differ as one moves from one Climate to another. For while in the more technical branches of Astronomy we speak of being "under this or that polar altitude" <note>This refers to what we now call latitude, measured by how high the North or South Star appears above the horizon</note>, astronomers and geographers use more popular language when speaking to the general public, saying instead "in this or that Climate."

<margin>*What is the origin of this name?*</margin>

**Climates** <note>original Greek: Κλίματα (klimata)</note> are so called because they represent "inclinations" <note>The author references the Greek verb *klinein*, to slope or lean; the OCR text "ἀκλίνειν" is likely a misspelling of "κλίνειν"</note>. They refer to those regions of the Earth which seem to slope away from the Equator toward either pole. At the Equator, the Earth is like a straight and level plane where both poles sit exactly on the horizon; however, as one moves toward the poles, the Earth seems to tilt so that one of the poles is seen to be elevated above the observer.

<margin>*What, then, is a Climate?*</margin>

<summary>This page defines "Climates" as latitudinal zones used by geographers to categorize the Earth based on the length of daylight and the elevation of the poles. It explains that the term "Climate" is a more accessible way to describe latitude, derived from the Greek word for the Earth's "inclination" or slope toward the poles.</summary>

BOOK THREE. 311

*Is it not enough to divide the entire surface of the Earth into five Zones?*

Zones, separated from one another by four primary <term>parallels</term> <note>Lines of latitude that run parallel to the Equator</note>—namely the two Tropics and the two polar circles—cover a vast width, as will be discussed in what follows. The ancients, therefore, setting aside the distinction of the Zones, divided all that width between the equator and the polar circle more precisely by this new method. Furthermore, while the Zones divide the entire surface of the Earth and are more a matter of astronomical consideration, <term>Climates</term> <note>In historical geography, a "climate" refers to a specific latitudinal band of the Earth characterized by the length of its longest day, rather than modern weather patterns</note> were more familiar to geographers. These were observed only in the small portion of the Earth known to the ancients, which did not exceed a semicircle in longitude or a quadrant in latitude.

*By how many parallels is each climate described?*

By three; for two always mark the boundaries of any given climate, while one passing almost through the middle of the climate has a day length halfway between the lengths at the beginning and the end. Nevertheless, one and the same parallel is always the start of one Climate and, at the same time, the end of another.

*Are the climates of equal width?*

Not at all; for those that are closer to the equator are always wider. <note>Because the Earth is a sphere, the physical distance between lines of latitude representing equal changes in day length decreases as one moves toward the poles</note>

312 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

It is no wonder that the number of <term>Climates<note>In ancient and Renaissance geography, a "Climate" was not a weather pattern, but a horizontal zone of the Earth defined by the length of its longest day of the year.</note></term> varies among different authors. Ptolemy, in the beginning, arranged the <term>parallels<note>Lines of latitude running east-west around the Earth.</note></term> by differences of half-hours in the duration between day and night—that is, by quarter-hour increments of the longest day. His goal was for each Climate to increase the difference between day and night by one full hour. By this method, when he reached the fourteenth parallel and the Climates began to have less than half the width of the first ones, he suddenly set the following increments to be double the previous ones (specifically, half-hours), so that the Climates would again have the width of the first ones. At the nineteenth parallel, the Climates were again reduced to half the previous width; therefore, between this and the twentieth, he again set the increment to be double the previous, namely one full hour.

The same author continued the number of Climates in the Northern Hemisphere up to the seventh, at which point he had begun to expand the parallels.

More recent authors, however, retaining the distance of one quarter-hour, count 48 parallels from the equator to the pole, and 23 Climates.

->*Where is the center of the first Climate placed?*<-

The first Climate has in its center a difference of two hours between the longest day and the shortest night; the second has three hours, the third four, and so on sequentially.

->*Why did they not begin at the equator, placing the center of the first Climate where the difference between day and night is one hour, just as in each following Climate this difference is increased by one hour?*<-

The first portion of this uniform progression by whole hours of difference between the longest day and the shortest night, on both sides of the equator (as also the middle...

314 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY
->What is the use of the doctrine of climates?<-

The primary use of this doctrine is found in explaining and understanding the writings of ancient Astronomers, Geographers, and Physicians. <note>Ancient authorities like Ptolemy divided the known world into seven "climates" based on the length of the longest day, rather than using degrees of latitude.</note> Today, their use is not so frequent; for instead of mentioning this or that <term>Climate</term><note>A latitudinal band of the Earth defined by the duration of its longest day.</note>, we more commonly express the altitude of either Pole itself.

->How is the altitude of the Pole investigated from a given Climate?<-

Given the Climate, the difference between the day and the shortest night is given. For in the first Climate, this difference is two hours; in the second, three; and so on. Let there be the seventh Climate: the difference is eight hours, such that the shortest night has eight hours, the longest day sixteen, and the semi-diurnal time <note>The time from sunrise to noon, or noon to sunset.</note> is eight hours. Therefore, the excess above the equal period (of 6 hours) is two hours, or 30 degrees of the equator. <note>Since the Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, 2 hours equals 30 degrees.</note> From those principles handed down above, the <term>Ascensional Difference</term><note>The difference between the time a celestial body rises at the equator versus its rising time at a specific latitude.</note> is 30 degrees. Thus, the same triangle *Q T S* is formed as was shown above on page 235, comprised of the Horizon, the equator, and the <term>colure of the solstices</term><note>One of the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere, passing through the celestial poles and the points of the solstices.</note>, upon which the Sun falls when it creates the longest day. The rest of the factors are as above: the specific process is as follows:
