BOOK THREE. 317

...in the cold regions, than in either the temperate or the torrid regions, the heat is nevertheless greater in the torrid zone.

*What then is the genuine celestial cause of Heat and cold, and thus of summer and Winter?*

The sun's approach to the zenith <note>original: *verticem*; the point in the sky directly above the observer</note> during the midday hours is the cause of summer, and its retreat from the zenith during the midday hours—even when it is at its closest possible point to the Zenith—is the cause of winter.

*From where does this approach and retreat of the Sun come?*

From the tilt <term>obliquity: the angle of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</term> of the Ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path through the stars over the course of a year</note> along which the Sun is seen to travel. For its semicircle turns from the equator toward the north by 23.5 degrees, while the other half is cast down by the same number of degrees to the south below the equator. The sum of both, 47 degrees, causes the variation of the Sun's Midday altitudes, which is more than half of a right angle <note>a right angle is 90 degrees; 47 degrees is slightly more than the 45-degree midpoint</note>.

*Why, however, does a Sun that is high and near the Zenith heat more than one that is low and approaching the horizon?*

Because the higher it is, the more directly its rays strike the surface of the Earth, and therefore the more strongly. However, a low Sun illuminates the lands from an oblique angle; this radiation—just as with physical blows or strikes—is rendered ineffective and weak because of the steepness of the incline.

*How are the four parts of the year—Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter—described and defined?*

Spring in the temperate Zone is that span of time in which the Sun rises from the Equinox to the solstice; Summer is from the Solstice to the autumnal Equinox; Autumn...

### 318 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY
...Autumn from that point to the other winter Solstice, and Winter from the winter Solstice to the vernal equinox.

*In this context, what do you call a solstice, and what an equinox?*

As mentioned above in Book 2, these were the four cardinal points of the Ecliptic <note>the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky</note>. But here, "Solstice" signifies the time, or those days of the year, in which the Sun's declination <note>the Sun's distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> from the equinoctial line seems to stand still; or rather, that moment when the center of the Sun reaches the Solstitial points, where it reaches its maximum declination and begins to return toward the equator. The Equinox, however, is that moment when the Sun's center occupies the Equinoctial points, making the preceding day equal to the following night, or vice versa.

The Greeks name the Solstices with a more descriptive term, *the turnings of the sun* <note>original: "τροπὰς ἡλίου" (*tropas heliou*)</note>, for the turnings of the Sun occur in an instant. They also call them the four Centers or Points, a term transferred from the points of the sphere to the corresponding Seasons of the year; to the Hebrews, they are the *Thecuphae* <note>original: "Thecuphæ"; referring to the *Tekufot*, the four turning points or seasons in the Hebrew calendar</note>. In common Latin usage, when the "Solstice" is mentioned, the high <note>summer</note> solstice is understood; the low <note>winter</note> solstice is called *Bruma* <note>term for the winter solstice or the shortest day</note>. The Greeks are accustomed to speak of the summer or winter "turning."

*It seems that summer is not correctly defined. For if the Sun's altitude determines the heat, why is the summer quarter not measured from the middle of Taurus through Cancer to the middle of Leo? In that way, the maximum altitude of the Sun—and thus the greatest heat—would be in its middle, and the ends of the quarter would have equal solar altitude on both sides.*

### BOOK THREE. 319

Here, the sluggishness of Matter <note>The author is describing what we now call "thermal inertia"—the way large objects like the Earth take time to heat up or cool down.</note> has the greatest effect. For even though the Sun is at the same height when it is in the middle of Taurus as when it is in the middle of Leo, the thick body of the Earth only begins to grow warm while the Sun is moving through Taurus. But once the Sun has passed into Leo, the heat has already lasted for three months; and because the Earth was already heated before, new heat is added to it daily, and the heat that lingers for some time is accumulated within the matter. This is also the reason why the day is hotter two hours after noon than at the hour of noon itself.

The reasoning regarding winter is the same. For even though the quadrants <note>The four 90-degree divisions of the Sun's path through the year.</note> of autumn and winter are equal in terms of the Sun’s low position, there is still some heat during autumn. In winter, there is pure cold: because as the Sun gradually moves away from our Hemisphere after the equinox, the earth—retaining some heat from the summer—needs time to be cooled down. In winter, however, the earth is already sufficiently chilled and covered with crusts of snow and ice; it cannot be so easily stripped of these, revived, and heated by the rays of the sun, even though the sun gradually raises itself from the lowest point of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path across the sky throughout the year</term> through the same degrees of altitude that it held during the Autumnal quadrant. Therefore, Astronomers are correct in defining the seasons by their qualities within the boundaries of the Cardinal Quadrants, rather than at the intermediate points.

Now indeed in the <term>Frigid Zones</term>, which the polar circle circumscribes, there is no place that does not lack the sun for some days of the year, as was demonstrated in the third part. Rightly, therefore, are these Zones named "Frigid" from the cold, and "Torrid" from the heat by which it is scorched. It remains, then, that the **Temperate Zones** are compared to the temperate parts of the year; because they are enclosed between the tropics and the polar circles, they never experience the Sun directly overhead, yet they are never without the sun for an entire natural day.

In the Torrid Zone, the <term>solstices</term> <note>the two times a year when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point at noon</note> only show the Sun at its highest point at the zone's boundaries <note>meaning exactly on the Tropic lines</note>. Since the maximum height of the sun at midday defines the beginning of summer, and the minimum height defines the beginning of winter: summer does not begin here from either solstice, except at the edge of the Zone, under the Tropic. Other intermediate places in the Torrid Zone, speaking by analogy, have two summers, when the Sun passes through the zenith; and two winters, when the sun is at the solstices, at which time it turns away as far as possible in the midday hours from their zenith toward either side of the world. The remaining Zones have a single summer and a single winter in each year, beginning the former from the "high" solstice and the latter from the "low" solstice.

*You Arabs have come into a world unknown to you,*
*Marvelling that the shadows of the groves do not move to the left.*
<note>original Latin: "Ignotum vobis Arabes venistis in orbem / Vmbras mirati nemorum non ire sinistras." This is a quote from the Roman poet Lucan’s "Pharsalia," describing how people from the southern tropics were surprised by the movement of shadows in the north.</note>
For Arabia Felix <note>Latin "Arabia Fœlix," meaning "Happy" or "Fertile" Arabia, referring to the southern Arabian Peninsula, largely modern-day Yemen.</note> is situated in the Torrid Zone <note>The tropical region between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</note>, where the Sun not only casts shadows to the North during the winter solstice, but also to the South during the opposite solstice. Therefore, since the shadow proceeds in a path opposite to the Sun—namely, as the sun is moved toward the west, the shadow itself tends toward the east—someone looking at their own shadow will see a northern shadow move toward the right (exactly as it appears to Us), but a southern shadow will move toward the left; a movement of shadow which we lack. 

For among the Temperate Zones, each has only one or the other shadow: the Northern Zone has a rightward shadow, and the Southern has a leftward one. They would therefore more correctly be called <term>Hekateroskioi</term> <note>From the Greek ἑκατερόσκιοι, meaning "shadowed on both sides." These are people whose shadows can fall both north and south depending on the season.</note>.
The inhabitants of the Frigid Zones are also themselves <term>Hekateroskioi</term>, but authors have preferred to designate them by a peculiar property as <term>Periscii</term> <note>From the Greek περίσκιοι, meaning "shadows all around."</note>, because for them, as the Sun does not set, the shadows are driven all the way around through every region of the horizon.

This subject belongs properly to <term>Gnomonics</term> <note>The art and science of constructing and using sundials.</note>, and it produced for us the doctrine of conic sections in Geometry. At this vertex is another Cone, which the plane of the horizon cuts; the section is circumscribed by the moving tip of the shadow. 

Therefore, the path of the equinoctial shadow in all Zones is a straight line, except under the Pole, where the line of the shadow’s projection is parallel to the Horizon, and thus it does not fall upon it.

BOOK THREE. 329

The path of the other shadows, which they mark with their extremities, is a <term>Conic section: a curve (like an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola) created by the intersection of a plane and a cone</term>. Of these, there are three types: finite ones like the **Ellipse** or circle; infinite ones like the **Hyperbola** (or opposite sections); and the **Parabola**, which is between them, appearing to aim for finiteness even though it is also infinite. Therefore, it is only in the Frigid Zones <note>The Arctic and Antarctic regions near the poles</note> that all these shapes can exist. The Ellipse is characteristic of these zones; directly at the Pole, it becomes a perfect circle. Or rather, these paths are spirals that resemble a circle or Ellipse, if you consider the combined path over several days during which the Sun does not set. This occurs because the plane of the Horizon then cuts through both sides of the cone of light.

On the day when the Sun just grazes the Horizon at natural midnight—signaling that it will begin to set in the following days—the path of the shadow is a **Parabola**. This happens because the plane of the Horizon is parallel to the upper side of the Cone, specifically when the Sun's <term>declination: the angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator</term> equals the altitude of the pole. This Parabola appears only on the single day of the Solstice at the polar circle: just as the Frigid Zone ends there, so too do the Ellipse and the Parabola end their appearance.

Once day and night begin to alternate by turns—in the Frigid as well as the Temperate and Torrid Zones—the shape of the shadow’s path is a **Hyperbola**, or opposite sections. This is the common shape for shadows in all Zones. In these cases, the plane of the Horizon cuts the axis of the Cones (that is, the axis of the World) outside of the cones' vertices <note>The "vertex" is the point or tip of the cone</note>. The specific differences between these opposite sections in any given Zone are explained more thoroughly in works on <term>Gnomonics: the science of using shadows to measure time, as with sundials</term>.

*perfectly upright move* **backward**?

In that case, as the Sun rises on this side of the Equator, a man’s shadow is carried to the right from the winter sunset toward the equinoctial sunset, and there for some

->### On the causes of the number and width of the Zones.<-

*So that I may understand that such a great variety of seasonal temperatures, and of days and nights—on which the Zones depend—arises from the single inclination of the Axis around which the Earth rotates: tell me, what would it be like then if the Axis of the Earth were not inclined?*

If that axis stood at right angles to the plane of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky, which is actually the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>, and the Earth rotated around it just as it does now, and at the same time was carried around the Sun as it is now, with this constant right angle: Then the Sun would indeed seem to travel through the fixed stars in its annual period and rise and set every single day, but there would be no division of the Ecliptic into halves, quarters, or signs <note>Referencing the Zodiac signs used to mark the seasons.</note>; there would be no distinction of the year through the different qualities of heat and cold; all days would be equal to all nights, and there would be no distinction on the globe of the Earth, except according to "more" and "less" <note>Meaning the climate would change only by latitude, with no seasonal change at all.</note>. For since the Axis of the Earth would thus be set parallel to the axis of the Ecliptic, the imaginary poles of the World would also coincide with the poles of the Ecliptic. Therefore, there would be two points on the Earth's surface where the body of the Sun, halved by the horizon, would circle around in eternal rotations, never raising itself and never sinking. From these poles, the closer one moved toward the equato- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "equator."</note>

BOOK THREE. 331

As one moved toward the equator, the Sun would become higher at midday, but it would remain at a constant altitude throughout the entire year; until one reached the equator, where the Sun, through the perpetual alternation of days and nights, would always pass directly overhead <note>Latin: *verticem*, the zenith</note> at noon. Thus, there would be a supreme, unique, and perpetual summer there, and a supreme, unique, and perpetual winter at the poles. The Sun would also rise and set in any given place just as some fixed star does now, always observing the same regions of the Horizon. Therefore, there would only be some change on Earth in terms of day and night, but no change in terms of the year; for it would be exactly as if the Earth did not travel around the Sun in its annual motion—except for the fact that it would see different stars at different times of the year, just as it does now.

      *What if the Earth’s axis lay totally inclined,*
      *lying within the very Plane of the Ecliptic <note>The "Ecliptic" is the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky</note>,*
      *meanwhile retaining a parallel position*
      *while the Earth revolves around the Sun?*

      Then there would indeed be changes, not only of days and nights through the revolution of the Earth around its axis, but also of the seasons of the year through the Earth’s circuit; however, these changes would be disproportionate and in some way common to all places on earth. For the poles of the Ecliptic would seem to revolve in the equator, and the Poles of the World <note>The North and South Poles</note> would be located on the Ecliptic—specifically at the start of <term>Cancer and Capricorn</term> <note>These represent the points of the summer and winter solstices</note>. Therefore, in summer, the Sun would reach the upper pole of the World, and in winter, the lower one. There, for those living under the pole, it would create a day six months in length, and in the middle of that period, it would scorch them most violently; indeed, it would strike at right angles (as it does now in the <term>torrid zone</term> <note>The tropical regions near the equator</note>) and simultaneously never set (as happens now during the "long day" of the <term>frigid zone</term> <note>The polar regions</note>), and furthermore without moving from its place. In winter, by contrast, those under the pole would freeze just as they do now, but they would have a night that was pure and deepest, diluted by no <term>twilight</term> <note>Refracted light that provides visibility even when the sun is below the horizon</note> as it is now. Thus, through the summer they would be killed by flames and parched heat <note>original: *squallore*</note>, and through the winter by ice and darkness: extreme opposites would rush upon a single place.

332 AN EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

On the other hand, for those living at the equator, the Sun would pass directly through the zenith <note>the point in the sky directly above an observer</note> at the equinoxes, just as it does now. However, at the solstices, the Sun would sink all the way down to the horizon. There, in a single spot on the horizon, it would seem to spin like a lathe, showing different parts of its surface to the observer.

In this way, all the characteristics of every climate zone would combine in every intermediate location between the poles and the equator. These places would have the Sun directly overhead during two summers each year, continuous daylight during one of their "winters," and continuous night during the other. Those closer to the pole would experience both a continuous day and a Sun that stays directly overhead for a considerable amount of time.

*Tell me also, what would happen then if—assuming the Earth's axis kept a constant tilt—the axis did not remain parallel to itself during the Earth’s orbit, but instead always pointed directly toward the Sun?* <note>Kepler is asking what would happen if the Earth were "tidally locked" or if its north pole always bowed toward the Sun as it moved.</note>

What would happen if the tilt were set at a right angle <note>original: "recto inclinationis angulo"</note> was discussed at the beginning: there would be no change in seasons. The same result would follow if the axis, projected onto the plane of the ecliptic <note>the path of the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note>, remained constantly facing the Sun. The only difference is that in the first case, the celestial poles coincide with the poles of the ecliptic; whereas in this case, they would travel around the ecliptic itself in an annual motion, with all the consequences that follow. However, if the axis is tilted so that it maintains a constant oblique <note>slanted</note> angle with the line connecting the centers of the Sun and the Earth (yet remains in a plane perpendicular to the ecliptic), then the variations and changes usually associated with that specific tilt would no longer occur throughout the year. Instead, different parts of the Earth would be affected by a far greater diversity: places that the Sun now leaves once a year would then be eternally deprived of sunlight, while those that currently have a sun that does not set once a year would then see it...

### BOOK THREE. 333

...they would enjoy a constant view of the Sun; not under the equator, but under the tropic, or (if the axis were completely laid flat in the Plane of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky as seen from Earth</term>, pointing toward the Sun) they would have the Sun directly overhead at the World Pole itself. The fixed stars would appear to traverse the entire Zodiac in the space of a year, while the Pole of the Earth—whether sitting right on the Ecliptic or on another parallel line—completed its annual circuit. In this way, the fixed stars (which provide our sense of place) would not seem fixed, and the Sun (the object located there) would be considered fixed. Indeed, at opposite parts of the year, the Sun would appear to travel in contrary paths in its daily motion; there would be a great confusion of movements and it would be most difficult to understand. 

Nor would anything else follow if the angle between the Earth's axis and the line connecting the centers of the Earth and Sun were in a plane oblique to the Ecliptic: except that the Sun would then not be guided through the beginnings of Cancer or Capricorn <note>These are the traditional starting points of the Summer and Winter solstices in the Zodiac.</note> under the tropic circle, but under some interior circle; and (with the Axis then lying down in the Plane) the Sun would seem to move again in a wide, wandering path across the Tropic. Everywhere there is a lack of either the change of the seasons of the year, or a distinction of the Climate Zones suited to those changes, or both.

*Since, therefore, a right angle (90 degrees) of the axis with the plane of the Ecliptic has been rejected—lest there be no change of seasons—and a total inclination (0 degrees), or a mere projection of the axis onto the plane of the Ecliptic, has been rejected—lest the change be too extreme—why was a middle angle between 90 and 0, namely 45 degrees (a semi-right angle), not chosen?*

If that angle were semi-right (45 degrees), there would only be three Zones: one Torrid and two Frigid. At the very point where the Sun ceases to be directly overhead in the summer, it would also cease to rise at the Winter Solstice <term>Solstice: the time when the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky, marking the longest or shortest day</term>. The contrary qualities of summer and winter would have the globe of the Earth distributed between them in such a way that no middle and temperate region would come between them; whereas in all other things, Nature naturally allows these qualities to have a middle ground.

334 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY

*From what source, then, do you think the most wise Creator derived the measure of the angle by which the Earth’s axis is inclined, or—which is the same thing—the tilt of the Ecliptic?* <note>original: "declinationis Eclipticæ". Kepler is asking why the Earth is tilted at roughly 23.5 degrees rather than some other number.</note>

Truly, I pray with a pure mind that, by His favorable divinity, His grace, and the dictation of His spirit, we may be able to discuss the secrets of His counsels. I believe it is both right and just to modestly inquire into the Numbers, measures, and weights <note>Kepler is referencing the Biblical idea from the Book of Wisdom that God "ordered all things by measure and number and weight."</note> according to which rules He Himself established all things. For He made the knowledge of these things common to man as to Himself, and in that regard, He placed no small part of His own image within man <note>The "Imago Dei" or Image of God, which Kepler believed was expressed through the human capacity to understand geometry.</note>, proving what He had made to be "exceedingly good." He will be even more pleased if, by the light of this image, we bring into the light of understanding the use of numbers, weights, and measures which He Himself demonstrated in the act of creation.

For these are not the kind of secrets from which we are forbidden to search; rather, they are placed before us like a mirror, so that through their explanation, we may to some extent behold the Goodness and wisdom of the Creator.

Since there are two primary kinds of causes which the Creator—the Best and Greatest—is found to have followed everywhere: the **formal**, or the beauty of the <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original blueprint or mathematical model in the mind of God.</note>; and the **final**, or the utility for living creatures.

Therefore, I believe that if the Creator, in this arrangement, had looked to the beauty of demonstrable figures, He would not have chosen the <term>Quindecagon</term> <note>A 15-sided polygon. If you divide a 360-degree circle by 15, you get 24 degrees, which was an early estimation of the Earth's tilt.</note>, the side of which cuts off 24 degrees of a circle—which is the amount of the tilt of the Ecliptic observed by the Indians, and slightly less by Eratosthenes <note>A Greek scholar who first calculated the Earth's circumference and tilt; his measurement was 23° 51'.</note>, namely 23° 51'. For although the Quindecagon is a demonstrable figure, its geometric proof is a far degree removed from equality; it is, in a way, accidental to the Quindecagon as such, and belongs instead to the Triangle and the Pentagon, from whose power and properties this demonstration is derived.

Indeed, this somewhat external demonstration does nothing to help the Quindecagon <note>A 15-sided polygon.</note> in the construction of a regular solid, whereas the other demonstrable figures assist this construction and "body-making" <note>original: Σωματοποίησιν (sōmatopoiēsin) — the process of forming three-dimensional solids from two-dimensional shapes.</note> in various ways.

Therefore, the beauty of these figures has its place elsewhere, specifically in the shaping of the celestial Orbs. In the distribution of the Zones, the needs of the living creatures who were to inhabit them had to take precedence. Regarding that utility, it has already been stated that there needed to be a certain variety and change. For since the Sun possesses heat and the Earth cold—by the very nature of matter—and since the Earth is an opaque and round body, the Sun certainly could not warm the whole of it from every side without some intervening motion. For this reason, the daily rotation of the Earth around its axis seems to have been decreed, as was discussed above in the first book.

Furthermore, because the Earth was intended to be a home for things coming into being and passing away <note>A reference to the Aristotelian concept of "generation and corruption," describing the cycle of life and decay in the physical world.</note>, it was not appropriate for every single part of the earth to be affected by the Sun equally at all times, each according to its own measure. Thus, because a simple revolution—with the axis standing straight relative to the plane of the Ecliptic <note>The "Ecliptic" is the path the Sun appears to follow across the sky; a "straight" axis would mean no seasons.</note>—would mean the poles and the regions near the poles would be abandoned by the heat, it was necessary for the axis to be tilted. This allows those parts to be turned toward the Sun alternately. Finally, with a simple revolution and a straight axis, as said above, Cold would be observed at only two points, while heat would be confined to a single line <note>The Equator.</note> that has no width. The entire surface of the sphere would have had the boundaries of heat and cold confused, without any clear distinction. But it pleased the Creator to distinguish light from darkness, and likewise to distinguish the boundaries, regions, and tracts of light and shadow, heat and cold. For these reasons, it was necessary for the axis to be tilted.

Thirdly, since even the simple turning of the Earth—with an axis straight to the plane of the Ecliptic—establishes certain marks for cold under the two poles, and for heat under the equator, the tracts of the Frigid Zones at the poles, and the Torrid <note>The "Torrid Zone" refers to the tropics, the warmest part of the Earth.</note>...

336 ABRIDGMENT OF ASTRONOMY

...the Torrid zone surrounds the equator; [it was determined that] there should be two frigid zones because of the two poles, and one Torrid zone.

Fourth, since it was not good for extremes to be joined without a middle ground, it was necessary for two temperate zones to come between them.

Fifth, these practical reasons having been considered, let a regard for beauty now provide the finishing touch <note>original: *colophonem imponat* — literally "to put the finishing stroke," a metaphor from book printing.</note>. For nothing in Geometry is more beautiful than equality, provided nothing stands in its way. It is therefore not unlikely that the Creator, from the beginning, ordained that the latitudes <note>The "width" or extent of the zones from north to south.</note> of the five Zones should be equal.

However, when a Meridian <term>Meridian</term> <note>A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a given location.</note> drawn through the poles cuts the Torrid and the temperate zones in opposite places, there result six portions of the Meridian; to these are added the individual sections of the two frigid zones, and they become eight portions in total. BOOK THREE. 337

*Do you seem to present a width of the <term>Zones</term><note>The five traditional climatic divisions of the Earth: one Torrid, two Temperate, and two Frigid.</note> that is far from the truth?*

Truly, the width of the Torrid Zone is double the <term>obliquity of the Ecliptic</term><note>The angle at which the Earth's axis is tilted relative to its orbit, which creates the seasons. The author notes this angle changes over centuries.</note>, namely 47 degrees and 3 minutes, or 706 miles today; so great also is the width of the two frigid zones combined. There remains for the temperate zones a width of 42 degrees and 57 minutes, or 644 miles, because the declination of the Ecliptic is 23 degrees, 31 and a half minutes <note>original: "sem:" for "semis", meaning one half</note> today. But just as in the past it was found to be greater—namely 23 degrees, 51 and a half minutes—so also before those times it could have been smaller, perhaps 22 degrees and 30 minutes at the creation of the world, and increased from there by one and a half degrees. Therefore, let this speculation be left to our descendants to be further proven.

*Does no other equality appear here, besides only the parts of the Meridian or the width of the Zones?*

Indeed, this also should be considered: if the obliquity of the Ecliptic were 24 degrees, 17 minutes, and 42 seconds—which is as much greater than it was in the time of <note>Eratosthenes was a Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BCE) who first accurately measured the Earth's tilt.</note>Eratosthenes as it is almost smaller today than of old (a value that is not absurd to think it once held)—then the surface area of the Torrid Zone, together with the surface areas of the two frigid zones, would have precisely as great an area as the two temperate zones have together. In this way, the surface of the Earth would be most equally distributed between the Extremes <note>The very hot and very cold regions.</note> and the Temperate regions. 

But if the declination were 23 degrees and 35 minutes, as <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 CE), an influential Arab astronomer known in Latin as Albategnius.</note>Albategnius found 730 years ago, then the Torrid Zone would be to one of the temperate zones as 4 is to 3.

# BOOK THREE. 339
## OF BOOK III.
### PART V.

->On the appearance and disappearance of the stars throughout the different parts of the year.<-
->On the Sidereal Year.<-

*So far we have discussed the "turning" or Tropical year <note>original: "anno vertenti"; the tropical year is measured by the sun's return to the same seasonal point, such as an equinox</note>; now let us also deal with the Sidereal year <term>sidereal year: the time it takes for the sun to return to the same position relative to the "fixed" stars</term>, concerning which I first ask: is it not of the same length as the Tropical year?*

It is not of the same length, but a little longer. The stars that we establish as the goal-marker <note>original: "meta," referring to the turning post in a Roman racecourse</note> for this year gradually change their locations relative to the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the apparent path of the sun against the background of stars</term>. Consequently, the circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic and a star intersects the ecliptic further and further from the point where the ecliptic crosses the equator.

*I used to think that the "fixed stars" in the Copernican system were truly what they are called: fixed. Are they, then, also in motion?*

Not in the least. Instead, the starting point for numbering the parts of the Zodiac—that is, the intersection of the ecliptic with the equator at the spring equinox—moves backward. Therefore, the specific point on the ecliptic where a perpendicular arc descends from a fixed star is always the same physical point in reality, but it is not always numbered as the same degree, because of the changed... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the next page likely completes the thought regarding the "changed equinox."</note>

<summary>This page explains the difference between a Tropical year (based on seasons) and a Sidereal year (based on stars), noting that the latter is longer due to the "precession" or backward movement of the equinoxes.</summary>

340 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

...and by its magnetic fibers, around which it revolves in its daily motion as if they were immobile, the Earth is tilted gradually from one fixed star toward another; as was begun to be stated in the first book, and often repeated since. Here, then, as long as the axis points toward the same fixed star or the same point under the stars within the space of a single year, it causes the fixed stars along the <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky throughout the year.</note></term> to appear as if they do not move. However, insofar as it gradually leaves its original fixed star or point over the course of centuries and nods toward other neighboring stars, it creates the illusion that the Pole of the World or of the sphere is passing toward that star. Now, it was already stated in the second book that the <term>Colures<note>Great circles on the celestial sphere that pass through the poles; specifically the solstitial colure mentioned here connects the celestial poles and the points of the summer and winter solstices.</note></term> of the solstices are carried through the poles of the Ecliptic and the World. Therefore, as the poles of the world move around the poles of the Ecliptic with a very slow motion, the colure follows them. But the intersection of the solstitial colure with the Ecliptic is considered the "beginning of Cancer." For this reason, the beginning of Cancer—due to the tilting of the Earth's axis—appears to move beneath the fixed stars. Consequently, the beginning of Aries, located a quarter-circle away (which is the intersection of the Equator and the Ecliptic where the counting of the Ecliptic's parts begins, as stated in the second book), also moves. Thus, it happens that the degree-number of some point on the Ecliptic—which is in reality stationary—is increased, and so that point appears to move forward.

*Of what use to us is this knowledge in this place?*

The writings of the Ancients regarding the rising and setting of the stars cannot be understood unless we know how great a difference has been created between us and them regarding the <term>sidereal years<note>The time it takes for the Earth to orbit the Sun relative to the fixed stars.</note></term> compared to the same number of <term>Tropical years<note>The time it takes for the Sun to return to the same position in the cycle of seasons, such as from one spring equinox to the next.</note></term>.

*How long is the Tropical year and how long is the sidereal year? What is the excess of the latter over the former, and over the Julian year? And what is the excess of the Julian over the Tropical year? Finally, what portion of the circle corresponds to the space of the intervening years?*

The mean and uniform length of the Tropical or "turning" year...

->BOOK THREE. 341<-

...of the turning <note>The "turning" year refers to the Tropical year, from the Greek *tropos* (turn), measured from one equinox or solstice to the next.</note> (for they are not all entirely equal in every respect, as will be discussed in the Theory of the eighth sphere <note>The "eighth sphere" in pre-modern astronomy was the realm of the fixed stars, beyond the spheres of the planets.</note>) it has been found to contain 365 Days, 5 Hours, 49 minutes, 15 seconds, and 46 thirds, based on the calculations of Copernicus and the **Prutenic Tables** <note>The Prutenic (or Prussian) Tables were astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551, based on the Copernican heliocentric model.</note>. Thus, it falls short of six hours—or a full day every four years, which is the **Julian year**—by 10 minutes, 44 seconds, and 14 thirds annually. However, as for the average length of the **sidereal year** <note>The sidereal year is the time it takes for the Sun to return to the same position relative to the fixed stars, rather than the seasons.</note>, as far as astronomers have been able to determine through diligent effort, they have judged it to add 9 minutes and 39 seconds beyond the six hours. Therefore, the difference between the **Tropical** and **sidereal year** is 20 minutes, 23 seconds, and 14 thirds every year. And in sixty years, it amounts to the same number of hours. Thus, in 70 years and two-thirds <note>original: "cum besse"</note>, a difference of almost one full day occurs; in 707 years, ten days; in 1413 years (which is nearly the time elapsed since the century of **Ptolemy**), twenty days; and in 1767 years (the time since **Hipparchus**), 25 days, during which the Sun completes the same number of degrees beneath the fixed stars, minus 22 minutes. Consequently, the **Julian years** are longer than the **Tropical years** by 13 days, while the **sidereal years** are longer than the **Julian** by 12 days.

*How were Astronomers able to observe the*
*length of both the Tropical and sidereal*
*year, since we can see neither the Tropical*
*points, nor the fixed stars when the Sun is*
*present and approaching*
*them?*

The length of the **Tropical year** is easily observed by those methods we were taught above for observing the meridian altitude of the Sun, the altitude of the pole, and finally the declination of the Sun. For the length of the **Tropical year** is considered exact when the Sun again reaches the same maximum declination from the equator—of the same quality—or again reaches the midpoint between both maximums <note>This refers to the Sun returning to the solstices or the equinoxes.</note>.

The length of the **sidereal year** requires a more subtle observation, and the matter has been attempted in more than one way.

The ancient inhabitants of **Egypt**, since they enjoyed a constant serenity...

342 SUMMARIES OF ASTRONOMY

continual; because Egypt is flat and possesses very high Pyramids, they observed the rising of the greatest among the fixed stars, which they usually call the Dog Star, Sirius <note>original: "Canem Sirium"</note>, diligently noting when it was first seen in the early morning before the sun, and from there counting the days until it again emerged in the morning from the rays of the Sun.

      Since this observation can only take place at the rising of the Sun, the Greeks, lacking so many advantages, turned to the contemplation of Lunar Eclipses, noting with which fixed stars the Moon appeared while it was lingering in the shadow of the earth: for then they knew that the Sun was in the region of the fixed stars directly opposite.

      Others first learned to compute the position of the Moon, which is assigned to <term>theoretical doctrine<note>original: "doctrinam Theoricam"; this refers to the mathematical models and calculations used to predict celestial positions rather than direct observation</note></term>. Then they observed when the Moon would cover some fixed star <note>this event is known as an occultation</note>: for however far they calculated the Moon to be from the Sun by their own computation, they established the fixed star to be that same distance from the Sun. And if this is done twice with the same fixed star, with a proper space of years intervening, it reveals the time of the Sun’s return to that same distance from that fixed star.

      HIPPARCHUS <note>a Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) considered the father of trigonometry and discoverer of the precession of the equinoxes</note>, not trusting the calculation of the Moon's motion, began to compare the Moon itself directly to the Sun and to the fixed stars. For during the day, when the Sun was just about to set, he measured with instruments how great an arc of the Ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> the Moon was distant from the Sun. After an hour, when the Sun had already sunk and the fixed stars were revealed, he consulted how great an arc of the Ecliptic that same Moon was distant from one of the fixed stars; the distance there from the Sun and here from the fixed star being merged into one, it indicated the Sun's distance from the fixed star. By this method, repeated after several centuries, the sought-after value is again revealed.

      This method of observing, in order to achieve its due precision, has need of many precautions, and there is always some tiny thing left in uncertainty. Therefore Tycho Brahe <note>a Danish nobleman (1546–1601) known for his incredibly accurate astronomical observations</note> and others in this century employed Venus instead of the Moon, because Venus, just like the Moon, may sometimes be seen during the day; yet it is not subject to so many complexities, nor is its course so swift or so changeable from hour to hour as that of the Moon.

THIRD BOOK. 343

*What then is the beginning of the sidereal year?*

Nature does not point to a beginning for the sidereal year <term>sidereal year: the time it takes for the Sun to return to the same position relative to the fixed stars, rather than the seasons</term> any more than it does for a circle; for any fixed star can be established as the starting point. This is true unless, by chance, certain specific stars are positioned at the Cardinal points <note>The equinoxes and solstices</note> at a given time; these are the points Nature recommends to us so that we may mark the start of the Tropical year <term>Tropical year: the year defined by the cycle of the seasons (from equinox to equinox)</term>. However, in this arrangement, the fixed stars would be observed for the sake of the Tropical beginning, and not truly for the Sidereal beginning as such.

Nevertheless, the providence of the Supreme Architect <note>A common Renaissance term for God as the creator of the geometric universe</note> has granted to our judgment certain aids for choosing one star over another, since all parts of the sky are distinct from one another due to the diversity of the arrangement of the fixed stars.

Thus, it was done in ancient times: the Egyptians began their year with the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: "Canis"; referring to Sirius</note> because it fell in the summer, and the Achaeans <note>The Greeks</note> from the rising of the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergiliarum"</note>; but this was a matter of political observation.

*Into what classes were the stars anciently divided?*

First, following the outlines of the various arrangements of the stars, men distributed the entire host of the heavens visible in our temperate zone into forty-eight Images <term>Images: the traditional constellations</term>.

Then, astronomers created six classes of stars scattered throughout the whole sky—not based on their location or configuration, but based on their Magnitude <note>Brightness</note>. The largest of these they called "of the first magnitude," the smallest "of the sixth," with the others placed in the same order in between.

*What are those 48 Images?*

Twelve fall in a certain way along the length of the Zodiac; these were mentioned above in the first book. The rest are located in the Hemispheres distinct from the Zodiac: twenty-one in the Northern Hemisphere and fifteen in the Southern.

*How do Astronomers define the longitude of a star?*

It is the arc of the Ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: the apparent path the Sun follows across the sky over the course of a year</term> counted according to the sequence of the [zodiacal] signs and intercepted between the Equinoctial point <note>The vernal equinox, the starting point of the celestial coordinate system</note> and the semi-circle of latitude that is drawn through the star: for this arc shows how much the star recedes from the beginning of the Ecliptic toward its end, according to the longitude of the sphere.

*What is the latitude of a star?*

The arc of the circle of latitude intercepted between the Ecliptic and the star; for it shows how far the star has moved away from the Ecliptic toward the sides of the World <note>meaning toward the north or south celestial poles</note>, by the shortest path.

*Compare longitude with Right Ascension, and latitude with declination?*

Longitude and Right Ascension begin from the same starting point; but longitude is reckoned on the Ecliptic, while Ascension is on the equator: the former is bounded by the circle of latitude, the latter by the circle of declination: of which the former is drawn through the poles of the Ecliptic, the latter through the poles of the equator.

*How is the longitude and latitude of any fixed star investigated?*

### 350 EPITOMES OF ASTRONOMY

What is the <term>mediation of the heaven</term>? <note>original: *Cœli mediatio*. This refers to the point where a celestial body or a point on the ecliptic crosses the local meridian—its highest point in the sky.</note>

It is the arc of the Ecliptic between the beginning of Aries <note>the vernal equinox</note> and the circle of declination drawn through the star.

*How, once the star’s Right Ascension and declination*
*are known, are its*
*longitude and latitude found?*

The angle between the Ecliptic and the Meridian serves this purpose. For, once the Right Ascension of the star is given, one seeks—either by calculation or from a table—the point on the Ecliptic having the same right ascension; such that it reaches the right Horizon and the Meridian at the same time as the star, and thus "mediates the heaven." The declination of that point on the Ecliptic is sought, again either by calculation or from a table, together with the angle which the Ecliptic makes with the Meridian at that point, which is called the angle of latitude.

Then, this declination of the point is compared with the declination of the star: For if they are of different denominations <note>meaning one is North and the other is South</note>, they are added to one another; but if they are of the same name, the smaller is subtracted from the larger; thus the arc of the circle of declination between the star and the Ecliptic is made clear, which can be called the <term>Base of latitude</term>; for it is opposite the right angle between the Ecliptic and the star’s circle of latitude. From this base and the angle of latitude, therefore, the latitude itself is computed, as well as the arc between the star and the point of the Ecliptic co-ascending with it.

Latitude is indeed computed thus: multiply the sine of the base of latitude by the sine of the Angle of latitude: having discarded the last 5 digits <note>a mathematical adjustment used in early modern trigonometry to manage large integer sines before the common use of decimal points</note>, the result is the sine of the latitude. But if the star and the point of the Ecliptic had declinations of the same name, and if the star's declination was simultaneously greater, the latitude retains the denomination of the point of the Ecliptic: but if there were either contrary declinations, or if the star's was smaller: the latitude of the star takes on the contrary denomination to the point of the Ecliptic.

Longitude is computed thus: multiply the Tangent of the base of latitude by the sine of the complement of the angle; the result is the Tangent of a small <term>prosthapharetic</term> arc. <note>An adjustment or "correction" arc used to find the true position from an intermediate calculation.</note>

**Midheaven** of this star **S** ends. **NS** is the **declination** of the star, and **ND** is the declination of the co-ascending point **D**. **SD** is the **base of latitude**: **NDO**, or **SDI**, is the **angle of latitude**. **ESI** is the **circle of latitude**, **SID** is a **right angle**, **SI** is the **latitude**, and **ID** is the **prosthaphæretic arc** <note>original: "arcus prosthaphæreticus"; a term from Greek meaning 'addition and subtraction,' used here for a corrective arc in calculation</note>; at **I** the **longitude** of the star **S** ends. But if **O** were the beginning of Aries, and **ODIC** followed the sequence of the signs, then **OI** would be the longitude of the star; Examples will follow below.

*Can this calculation not also be done without the table of the aforementioned angle?*

There is indeed a way, most frequently used by **Tycho Brahe** <note>A famous Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his accurate and comprehensive astronomical observations</note>, which does not use this angle; but it is long and more difficult; in which, for the triangle **DSI**, the triangle **PSE** is used, where **P** is the **Pole of the World** <note>The North Celestial Pole</note>, **E** is the **pole of the Ecliptic**; **EPC** is the **solstitial colure** <note>One of the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere</note>, **PS** is the **Complement of the Declination** **SN**; **PE** is the distance between the Poles, which is equal to the **obliquity of the Ecliptic**, and the Angle **EPS** is known from the measurement of its arc **NOQ**.

**THIRD BOOK.** 359

*To what end is it useful to investigate the locations of the fixed stars according to longitude and latitude?*

There are three principal uses for this matter. The first is in the part of spherical doctrine <note>The study of the "celestial sphere," an imaginary sphere of which the observer is the center and on which all celestial objects are considered to lie.</note> already taught, so that through the observation of fixed stars we might know what hour of the night it is, and consequently describe the appearance of the entire sky at any moment, by erecting a "theme" <note>original: "themata vel figura coeli," referring to the casting of a horoscope or a detailed map of the celestial positions at a specific time.</note> or figure of the heavens. For this reason, the locations of the fixed stars are inserted into the Rete <term>Rete: the pierced, "web-like" rotating plate of an astrolabe that shows the positions of the fixed stars.</term> of the astrolabe.

The second use is in theoretical doctrine, so that by comparing the Planets to the fixed stars, we can know their locations at any moment, provided we have first learned the locations of the fixed stars through which the Planets pass. For unless the Planets had been previously observed as to which locations they occupied at certain times, the "ratios" <term>Rationes: the mathematical proportions or underlying logic governing orbital motion.</term> of their motion could not be brought to light.

The third and most powerful use of this subject is this: because the rising and setting of the constellations mark certain seasons of the year. Indeed, ancient farmers—and, following their traditions, writers on rural matters, as well as doctors, poets, and historians—used these signs, and they cannot be understood without this part of the doctrine.

*Would it not be sufficient to refer the stars to the equator?*

Not at all. For 1. The Equator is not celestial in origin, but only a terrestrial circle, as has been said above in several places. 2. The distance of the fixed stars from the equator, or their "declinations" <term>Declination: the angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator, similar to latitude on Earth.</term>, change quite noticeably over the course of centuries; however, the latitude—or distance from the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; in early astronomy, it was considered a more stable reference point for stars than the Earth's equator.</note>—remains almost exactly the same through all ages. 3. The apparent progress of the fixed stars according to the longitude of the equator is found to be unequal in different centuries; whereas the progress according to the Ecliptic...

# 360 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

...it observes a far more perfect uniformity. 4. What is most important in this place: if I have the **Right Ascension** and **Declination** of a star, I can indeed compute its **Rising** above any given **Horizon**, and its **Setting** below it; but I cannot yet determine its **Apparition** <note>Also known as heliacal rising, when a star first becomes visible in the dawn sky after being lost in the sun's glare.</note> and **Occultation** <note>Heliacal setting, when a star is last seen in the evening before the sun's light hides it.</note> under the rays of the sun (which travels along the **Ecliptic**), unless I also relate that star to the **Equator**; where every position of the sphere has something unique. But if the locations of the fixed stars are described by the **Ecliptic**, a **Standard and Rule** is established that passes through the middle of them, accounting for all variations across the different positions of the sphere. 5. The locations of the other **Planets** are also perpetually arranged on this side and that of the **Ecliptic**, and they depart from the **Equator** along with the arcs of the **Ecliptic** itself. It is therefore expedient to reduce all the stars to the single **Ecliptic** as if into a common order.

->On the points of the Ecliptic that rise together.<-

*How is it known with which degree of the Ecliptic*
*any given star rises and*
*sets?*

One must first know the altitude of the pole <note>The observer's latitude.</note>, the **Declination**, and the **Right Ascension** of the star; and through these, from the second part <note>Referring to an earlier section of Kepler's textbook.</note>, the <term>ascensional difference</term> <note>The difference in time/angle between a star's rising on the equator versus its rising at a specific latitude.</note>; which, when added to or subtracted from the **Right Ascension** (depending on whether the declination is Southern or Northern), constitutes the star's **Oblique Ascension**.
Once the star's **Oblique Ascension** is given, the point of the **Ecliptic** rising together with this **Oblique Ascension**—and thus also with the proposed star—is easily found either from tables or from the doctrine of the second part; or, if it is a setting, the point descending with it.

# BOOK THREE. 36r

->On Horizontal variations, Refraction, and Parallax.<-

*What happens to stars as they are rising or setting?*

The refraction of rays, which at the very moment of rising or setting lifts the celestial bodies (as it appears to the eye) within the vertical circle by 30 minutes <note>Refraction makes objects near the horizon appear higher than they actually are. 30 minutes of arc is roughly the apparent diameter of the full moon.</note>. This amount decreases rapidly, so much so that at an altitude of 20 degrees, it vanishes entirely.

*What effect does this refraction of altitude have on oblique ascension and declination, and on longitude and latitude?*

It decreases the ascension <term>Ascension: The position of a star measured along the celestial equator</term> and latitude during rising, and it decreases the southern declination and latitude. Conversely, it increases the descent and longitude during setting, as well as the northern declination and latitude. By shortening distances in proportion to how perpendicular they are to the horizon, if we use the location of one fixed star as a "certain" and un-refracted point, it introduces the aforementioned errors into any calculation prepared from that distance.

*How do we learn through calculation how much any given refraction of altitude affects longitude and latitude, so that a star's position, distorted by refraction, may be corrected?*

The general method is by using the primary oblique-angled triangle of the "first motion" <term>Obliquangulum primi motus: A spherical triangle used by early astronomers to calculate the daily rotation of the heavens</term>, designated as VPS. On its side VS, which is the arc of the Vertical circle, let a higher mark **R** be chosen to represent the refracted position of the star **S**. Then, an arc is drawn from the Pole **P** through **R** and continued, and a perpendicular line **SI** is dropped down to it. Therefore, in [triangle] PVR...

362 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

In triangle **PVR**, the sides are known. For, given the quantity of refraction **RS** <note>original: "refractionis"; the bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, making stars appear higher than they actually are.</note>, the distance **VR** of the star from the vertex <note>The "vertex" or zenith is the point directly above the observer.</note> is given: or its complement, the altitude **RO**, to which that quantity applies. From the altitude affected by refraction (or the *refracted* altitude, as Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used to revolutionize planetary theory.</note> calls it), the calculation described in the first part provides the refracted declination **PR**, and the angle **PVR** at the star's refracted position **R**. Therefore, by dropping a perpendicular from **S**, the unrefracted position, onto the circle of refracted declination **PR** continued, 

-> [A circular diagram showing arcs and points labeled with letters P, V, R, S, I, representing a spherical triangle or celestial sphere.] <-

two right-angled triangles are formed, **RIS** and **PIS**. In the lower one, **RIS**, the angle at **R** is given together with the base **RS**, which is the quantity of refraction: therefore the sides can also be computed. One is **RI** on the circle of Declination, which is the refraction of the declination; the other is **IS** on the dropped perpendicular, the argument <note>In this context, "argument" refers to a value used to find another in a table or calculation.</note> of the refraction of the Right Ascension <note>Right Ascension and Declination are the two coordinates that pinpoint a star's location on the celestial sphere, similar to longitude and latitude on Earth.</note>. This is more nearly equal to the value it indicates the smaller the star's declination is. But if the declination is large, one moves to the second right-angled triangle **PIS**, whose sides are known: the arc of the declination circle **PI** (increased by the discovered refraction **RI**) and this perpendicular **IS**. Through these, one seeks the angle **P** at the pole, which is the corrected refraction of the Right Ascension.

**The shortest process.** Multiply the sine of arc **RS** (or rather the arc itself, because it does not differ from a straight line by any sensible amount) by the sine of angle **IRS** or **VRP**; after discarding the last 5 digits <note>This refers to the practice in 17th-century mathematics of using large integer tables for sines rather than decimals; "discarding digits" is equivalent to dividing by the table's radius.</note>, the sine of arc **IS** (or the arc **IS** itself) is produced. Then, divide the secant of arc **RS** (extended by 5 zeros) by the secant of arc **IS**. This produces the secant of arc **RI**, which when added to **PR** makes **PI**. Finally, divide the tangent of **IS** (or even the arc **IS** itself) extended by 5 zeros by the sine of arc **PI**; this produces the Refraction of the Right Ascension.

Therefore, from the corrected Declination <note>Declination: The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator.</note> and Right Ascension <note>Right Ascension: The celestial equivalent of longitude, measured along the celestial equator.</note>, both the longitude and latitude free from refractions will result.

*But what if the Right Ascension and declination of a star are not given, but rather its longitude and latitude? Must we always follow these circuitous routes? That is: must we return to Right Ascension and declination?*

If the longitude and latitude of the star are given; from the position of the Sun and the hour, the Nonagesimal <term>Nonagesimal: The point of the Ecliptic that is exactly 90 degrees from the points where the Ecliptic intersects the horizon; it is the highest point of the Ecliptic at any given time.</term> of the Ecliptic and its altitude must be sought; let P be the pole of the Ecliptic, PR and PS be circles of latitude; then RI will be the refraction of latitude, and IPS the refraction of longitude, and the process will remain the same in the rest as before.

->*What is related to Refractions?*<-

The Parallaxes <note>Parallax: The apparent shift in the position of an object when viewed from two different points. In historical astronomy, this correction was vital for the Moon, which is close enough to Earth for its position to shift depending on where the observer stands.</note> of certain celestial bodies, about which we treat in the sixth book: For once the parallax of any altitude is given, it is separated into longitude and latitude by the same method exactly, but with the opposite effect; for where refraction decreases <note>Refraction bends light, making objects appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note>, Parallax (if there is any) increases it, and vice versa: therefore, before everything else, the smaller should be subtracted from the larger, and one must proceed with the remainder—which retains the nature of the larger value—just as we have done so far with either of its elements. Understand this as applying to celestial bodies that have Parallax.

*Is there any advantage here if the stars are near the equator or the Ecliptic?*

If a solitary parallax is proposed, there is a certain shortcut, so that there is no need for the angle to the celestial body: but since parallax chiefly concerns the Moon—which is always found near the Ecliptic, especially during Solar Eclipses when Parallax is most needed—therefore this shortcut is deferred to the [section on] the motions of the Moon.

*What then are the most significant differences between Refractions and Parallaxes?*

The first difference in effect has already been stated: **Parallax** depresses <note>original: "deprimit" — makes the object appear lower than it truly is</note>, while **Refraction** raises <note>original: "attollit" — makes the object appear higher</note>. 2. All stars experience the refraction of altitude equally, whichever of them—on the same day or different days of the same atmospheric quality, in the same place on the Horizon or one of the same quality—comes to the same altitude; because the cause of Refractions is near us in the air <note>Kepler correctly identifies that atmospheric refraction is a local phenomenon caused by Earth's atmosphere, whereas parallax depends on the object's distance from Earth</note>. Only the Moon and some Comets produce a perceptible and constant diurnal <term>Parallax|The apparent shift in the position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth's surface.</term>; Mercury, Venus, the Sun, and Mars are indeed under suspicion of parallax, but the possession of it is controversial and no sensory perception of it exists <note>In the early 17th century, instruments were not yet precise enough to measure the tiny parallaxes of the sun and inner planets</note>. Regarding the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, there is not even a suspicion of any perceptible parallax, much less for the fixed stars. 3. Refractions quickly cease to be noticeable at an altitude of 20 or 30 degrees, as can be seen in the first book; portions of Parallaxes remain all the way up to the <term>Zenith|The point in the sky directly above the observer.</term> itself, proportional to the sines of the distance from the Zenith.

->*What about the locations of the two interior figures?*<-

Even though the **Octahedron** shares the nature of the **Cube** (whose parts are considered first), and the **Icosahedron** shares the nature of the **Dodecahedron** (whose parts are considered last), the place immediately following the Dodecahedron did not belong to the Octahedron. This is for two reasons.

First, the two classes of figures are in a certain way opposite to one another; it was therefore fitting that the starting point for their placement should also begin from opposite ends. Since the "first" place for the outer figures was considered to be the one that tended furthest toward the exterior <note>Saturn, the outermost planet</note>, it followed that the "first" place for the inner figures should be the one that tended furthest toward the interior, toward the center <note>Venus and Mercury</note>.

Secondly, it was more in harmony with the nature of similar shapes—the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**—and more suited to their mutual <term>inscription</term> <note>the geometric property where one shape fits perfectly inside the symmetry of another; these two shapes are "duals" of each other</note>, that they should follow one another as closely as possible, with only a single circuit or sphere <note>the Earth's orbit</note> coming between them.

->*If the intervals come so close to the proportions of the figures, why then does some discrepancy remain?*<-

1. Because the <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "archetypus"—referring to God's original blueprint for the universe</note> of the moving world consists not only of the five regular figures, by which the tracks of the planets and the number of those traveling them would be defined; but also of **Harmonic proportions**, by which the paths themselves were to be tempered toward a certain Idea, as it were, of celestial Music or a Harmonic concert of six voices. Since, however, this musical adornment required a distinction of motion in any one planet, from the slowest to the fastest—which distinction is achieved by the variation of the interval between the planet and the Sun—and since a different quantity or proportion of this variation was required in different planets: hence it was necessary that something very small be taken away from these geometric intervals (which are presented as uniform by the figures without variation) and left to the freedom of Harmony for representing the Harmonies of the motions.

2. Nor, however, was the property of the regular figures neglected, even in this so very small discrepancy. For just as the proportion of the spheres of the **Tetrahedron** is perfect—that is, simply expressible <note>original: "effabilis"—a mathematical term meaning the ratio can be expressed as a rational number</note>—while those of the **Cube** and the **Octahedron** are semi-perfect—that is, expressible in power <note>meaning the squares of the values are rational</note>, but inexpressible in length—and those of the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron** are plainly imperfect—that is, thoroughly inexpressible <note>original: "ineffabiles"—referring to irrational numbers like the Golden Ratio, which defines these two shapes</note>; so also the proportion of the Tetrahedric planets <note>the planets associated with the tetrahedron: Jupiter and Mars</note> imitates the figure very exactly, that is, almost at the very limits of the intervals. The proportions of the Cubic and Octahedric planets are less exactly like the figures, because the extreme intervals recede from them, though the intermediate ones align. But the entire spaces of the Dodecahedric and Icosahedric planets have deserted their figural proportions, although no other figures approach them more closely. 

For behold, how the minimum interval of Jupiter is, very exactly, one third part of the longest interval of Mars, just as in a **Tetrahedron** the interior sphere is one third of the exterior. Thus, with the corners of the Tetrahedron placed in the innermost path of Jupiter, the Tetrahedral planes touch, in a certain way, the outermost path of Mars. 

Behold again, how when the corners of the **Cube** are placed in the innermost paths of Saturn, and those of the **Octahedron** in the innermost paths of Venus, the planes of the figures are indeed submerged into those regions—the former into Jupiter’s, the latter into Mercury’s—yet they do not transcend them entirely, but penetrate approximately to the middle. 

Behold finally, how when the corners of the **Dodecahedron** are placed in the innermost paths of Mars, and those of the **Icosahedron** in the innermost paths of the Earth, the planes of the figures in no way reach the regions below them—the former that of the Earth, the latter that of Venus. Yet, in the meantime, no other intervals of the planets come closer to the smallest proportions of these figures. 

See concerning these things my *Harmonies of the World*, Book 5, Proposition 49, and throughout; where the causes are drawn forth not only for the exact quantity of the proportions between pairs, but also for the individual intervals of each solitary planet at its extremes.

BOOK FOUR. 473

**Can any evidence regarding the placement of the geometric figures also be drawn from the lengths of the orbital periods?**

To be sure, all proportions of time <note>original: "proportiones temporariæ"—referring to the ratios of the planets' orbital periods</note> are greater than the proportions of their orbits <note>meaning the ratio of the time spent orbiting is larger than the ratio of the distance from the Sun</note>, and thus also greater than their geometric proportions, as will be explained in the second part of this book. Nevertheless, the specific characteristics of the geometric figures can still be recognized among those periods without difficulty.

For just as there are three classes of geometric proportions—the greatest, which is unique; the middle; and the smallest, both of which are paired—specifically, the first comes from the single **Tetrahedron**; the second from both the **Cube** and the **Octahedron**; and the third from both the **Dodecahedron** and the **Icosahedron**.

In the same way, the proportion of time between **Jupiter** and **Mars** is the greatest and is unique, being nearly 6 to 1; that is, 12 years to slightly less than 2 years, which is evidence of the **Tetrahedron** placed between them.

However, between **Saturn** and **Jupiter**, and between **Venus** and **Mercury**, the proportion of time is smaller, and nearly the same in both cases. This is evidence of the related figures placed there—the **Cube** in the former and the **Octahedron** in the latter—which produce the same proportion in their respective spheres. For just as the 30 years of **Saturn** relate to the 12 years of **Jupiter**, so very nearly do the 225 days of **Venus** relate to the 88 days of **Mercury**.

Finally, between **Mars** and the **Earth**, and between the **Earth** and **Venus**, the proportion of time is the smallest, and again is almost the same on both sides. This is evidence of the figures placed there—the **Dodecahedron** in the former and the **Icosahedron** in the latter—which are related bodies and share the same proportion. For just as the 687 days of **Mars** relate to the 365 and a quarter days of the **Earth**, so 365 and a quarter days relate to 194 days. Since **Venus** has 225 days instead of 194 <note>meaning Venus takes slightly longer to orbit than the perfect geometric ratio would suggest</note>, it creates the smallest temporal proportion of all. The causes of such a slight discrepancy are explained in *The Harmony of the World*, Book V.

*Why was special consideration given to the placement of the Earth?*

Certainly, it is not by chance that for the Earth—the middle planet—the average distance from the Sun is found to be quite precisely the geometric mean <term>proportional</term> <note>A value that sits exactly in the middle of a geometric ratio, where A is to B as B is to C</note> between the shortest distance of Mars (the lowest of the "superior" planets) and the longest distance of Venus (the highest of the "inferior" planets). For as was said above, the space between Mars and Venus was left undefined and loose by the nesting of the geometric figures <note>Kepler’s theory that the five Platonic solids are "inscribed" or nested between the spheres of the planets</note>. It was thus left free so that, by dividing it with the orbit of the Earth, this proportion or any other could be expressed, had another been better. Therefore, this middle wall between the classes of figures—serving as the midpoint between the superior and inferior planets—ought also to act as a geometric mediator.

*What, then, defined that space which the nesting of the figures did not?*

Although there is a certain "augmented" figure—namely, the **spiked dodecahedron** <note>original: "Dodecaedron scilicet aculeatum." This refers to the stellated dodecahedron, a star-shaped solid Kepler described in his work "The Harmony of the World."</note>—which is found to define this space as accurately as the space between Jupiter and Mars is defined by the **Tetrahedron**; and although the association of that "imperfect" figure with its relatives, the **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**, seems to have its own logic; nevertheless, neither these nor any other figures define these spaces exactly on their own. Instead, this task was left to the **Harmonic adornment** of the motions, which required for itself some freedom in defining these spaces exactly <note>Kepler argues that while geometry provides the rough "skeleton" of the universe, the need for the planets to move in musical/harmonic ratios "fine-tunes" their actual distances.</note>.

*What cause do you judge there to be for the size of the Solar body?*

The following points persuade us that the globe of the Sun is the first of all the world's bodies in the order of creation—at least in the <term>Archetypal</term> <note>original: "Archetypali." This refers to the mathematical blueprint or "Idea" in the mind of God before the physical world was made</note> sense, if not also in the temporal sense. 1. Now indeed, the first body, by the very fact that it is first, received no proportion to the things that follow: but rather the following things received their proportion to it as the first. Therefore, there is no archetypal cause for the size of the Sun <note>Kepler argues the Sun's size is a fundamental constant, not a result of a ratio</note>: nor was there to be another globe twice as large as it is now; for indeed, the rest of the entire universe, and man within it, would also have had to be twice as large as they are now.

**I**n this way, then, will be the <term>semidiameter: the radius of a spherical body, or half its diameter</term> of the Earth **T**. *You are stating nearly triple the quantity that the Ancients <note>Kepler refers to the Greek astronomical tradition, specifically Ptolemy, whose measurements stood for over a millennium</note> attributed to the maximum distance of the Sun from the Earth; they established it as less than 1,200 semidiameters of the Earth. Not at all. For the Ancients made the Sun so near that it ought to have produced a <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different points</term> of three minutes of arc. From this, Tycho Brahe <note>A famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose precise data Kepler used to discover the laws of planetary motion</note> reasoned that the parallax of Mars—since it is closer to the Earth than the Sun—ought to be observed as much greater than three minutes. Yet I have observed that the parallax of Mars is not detectable at all. Therefore, the distance of Mars is greater, even when it is closest to us, and the distance of the Sun is also greater than 1,200 semidiameters.

In one's own proper measurement, it is right to obtain the ratio of equality as the first and primary principle, if nothing stands in the way.

*Do observations also support this*
*distance between the Moon and the Earth?*

Absolutely, to a hair <note>original: "ad unguem," meaning perfectly or precisely</note>: for <term>Brahe: Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose precise observations provided the data for Kepler’s laws</term> found the distance of the Moon at <term>perigee: the point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth</term> to be a little less than 54 <term>semidiameters: the radius, or half the width of a celestial body</term> of the Earth. In the <term>quadratures: the Moon's first and last quarter phases</term>, he found the distance at <term>apogee: the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</term> to be greater than 59 and a little less than 60; whereas from these principles, the former is indeed calculated as 54, and the latter as 59.

*How then, from the established axioms and*
*conclusions—which rival the axioms—should the*
*quantity of the Moon's semidiameter be derived?*

1. If the Moon's semidiameter (L) is set at 100,000 units, so that the interval (TL) between the centers of the Moon and Earth is 22,918,166 such units: the cube of 100,000 (which is 1,000,000,000,000,000) must be multiplied by the distance number 22,918,166; and the <term>biquadrate root: the fourth root (the square root of the square root)</term> of the result must be extracted. This will be 389,085, showing the size of the Earth's semidiameter (T) in those same units. For just as the Earth's semidiameter (389,085) is contained within the Moon's distance (22,918,166) almost 59 times, so also the cube of 389,085 will contain the cube of 100,000 almost 59 times; and thus the globe of the Earth contains the globe of the Moon. Therefore, the semidiameter of the Earth's body (T) will contain the semidiameter of the Moon's body (L) a little less than four times.

2. In another and simpler way, from the latter conclusion: seek the square root of 3,469 and one-third (namely, the distance of the Sun), which will be slightly less than 59. This is the distance TL (the Moon's distance) in units where the Earth's semidiameter is 1. Then, by dividing the cube of the Earth's semidiameter (1) by 59, and taking the cube root of the quotient, the semidiameter of the Moon’s body is revealed in that same dimension.
