*What is the mutual proportion of the planetary*
*globes among themselves?*

Nothing is more consistent with Nature than that the order of magnitudes should be the same as the order of the spheres. Thus, among the six primary planets, **Mercury** should have the smallest body, because it is the innermost and occupies the narrowest orbit. **Venus** should be the next largest, but still smaller than the Earth, because it travels in a narrower orbit than the Earth, yet a wider one than Mercury. The globe of **Mars** should be the next larger than the Earth, because its orbit is now further out and more ample, being the lowest of the <term>superior planets: the planets whose orbits lie outside the Earth's orbit (Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn)</term>. Again, the globe of **Jupiter** is larger, being the middle of the superior planets; and finally, the globe of **Saturn** is the largest of the moving bodies, because it is the highest.

However, since there are three dimensions of bodies—either according to their **diameters**, their **surfaces**, or the spaces contained by those surfaces (their **corpulence** <note>original: "corpulentiam," referring to volume or three-dimensional mass</note>)—and since the proportion of surfaces is the square of the diameters, and that of bodies is the cube; it is reasonable that one of these three proportions of the globes should be adapted to the proportion of their intervals <note>their distances from the Sun</note>. For example: since Saturn is nearly ten times higher from the Sun than the Earth is, either the diameter of Saturn will be ten times the diameter of the Earth (making its surface a hundred times that of the Earth, and its body a thousand times the body of the Earth); or Saturn’s surface will be ten times the surface of the Earth (so that the proportion of the bodies becomes <term>sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2, or 1.5 times</term> the proportion of the intervals, and Saturn would be thirty times larger than the Earth, just as it is thirty times slower); or finally, the bodies themselves have the same proportion as the intervals, so that Saturn is at least ten times larger than the Earth just as it is ten times higher, while in the surfaces there is preserved a <term>bes: a ratio of two-thirds (2:3)</term>

Of these three modes, the first is rejected without controversy both by archetypal reasons <note>the geometric and harmonic principles Kepler believed God used as a blueprint for the universe</note> and by observations of the diameters made with the instruments of the Belgian telescope <note>the "Dutch telescope," recently invented; Kepler refers to it as Belgian as the Netherlands were often called the Belgic Provinces</note>. Indeed, if a body equal to the Earth were seen from the distance we attribute to the Sun—3,469 Earth radii—it would appear with a diameter of 2 minutes. But now, at that proximity of Mars, the same body (equal to the Earth) would be seen to occupy more than 5 minutes, thus equaling six Jupiters. Therefore, by as much as the diameter of the Martian globe is larger than the diameter of the Earth, its appearance will be that much increased. Thus, we should not make the diameter of the Martian globe more than perhaps a sixth part larger than the diameter of the Earth, which occurs in the third mode.
From archetypal reasons, however, this argument will perhaps not fight ineptly: that just as before we made the proportion of the bodies of the Sun and Earth, and of the Earth and Moon, the same as that which existed between the Earth's radius and the radii of the spheres, so now the proportion of the planetary bodies is established as the same as that which exists between the radii of the orbits. Thus, Saturn in the mass of its body <note>original: "mole corporis," referring to its volume</note> will be a little less than ten times larger than the Earth, Jupiter more than five times, Mars one and a half times, but Venus a little less than three-quarters <note>original: "dodrante," a Roman unit for 3/4</note> of the Earth's body, and Mercury a little more than a third <note>original: "triente," a Roman unit for 1/3</note> of the same.

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s argument that Earth serves as the fundamental unit of measurement for the physical dimensions of the universe. He is refuting the idea that all planets follow a single, uniform scaling law relative to the Sun, using his recent telescopic observations of Saturn to prove that Earth is the unique "starting point" for these proportions.</meta>

486 EPITOME OF ASTRONOMY

*Should not the bodies of all the planets be adjusted to the body of the Sun according to the same laws as the Earth, just as the Earth's body is?*

Not at all. For if we were to follow this rule, the bodies of the planets would follow an order of size contrary to the order of their spheres <note>meaning their orbital distances</note>; that is, Mercury would be the largest and Saturn the smallest, with a diameter less than one-third the diameter of the Earth. However, that contradicts both the **archetypal reasons** <note>Kepler's theory that the universe was designed according to a geometric blueprint</note> already mentioned and the **observations of the diameters**. 

For Saturn at opposition <term>acronychus|when a planet is directly opposite the Sun from Earth's perspective, making it closest and brightest</term>, when it is nine times higher than the Sun, occupies about 30 seconds <note>arcseconds, a unit of angular measurement where 60 seconds make one minute and 60 minutes make one degree</note>; therefore, if it stood at the same proximity as the Sun, it would occupy four and a half minutes. Meanwhile, the Earth, if viewed from that same distance, would occupy only 2 minutes. Therefore, the diameter of Saturn is more than double the diameter of the Earth.

And this is what I said right at the beginning of this section: it becomes most evident from the facts themselves that the starting point for establishing proportions was made from the Earth. For observations of the Moon and of Eclipses testify to the equality of two proportions: one between the bodies of the Moon and the Earth, and the other between the diameters of the Earth and the orbit of the Moon. We cannot in any way resist this certainty of observation. 

Now, it was indeed very likely that the Earth would also be adjusted to the Sun by those same laws. When we established this, we then found that even observations made from a distance <note>original: "eminus"</note> were in agreement here; for those observations do not support a distance to the Sun of 1,200 Earth radii, but instead require double or triple that amount; and indeed, this "adjustment" of proportions required a triple distance <note>Kepler correctly suspected the Sun was much further away—about 3,600 Earth radii—than the traditional distance of 1,200 used since antiquity</note>. 

The Earth, therefore, is certainly the measure of both the bodies of the Sun and Moon, as well as their spheres. In this way, the body of Saturn (or any other planet) can by no means become the measure of both things; regarding this, we have again brought forward the evidence of certain observations of the diameters. Therefore, the Earth alone is such a measure: and the nature of dimensions requires that the starting point of the physical formation <note>original: "conformationis"</note> be made from a measure.

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s investigation into the physical makeup of the planets. BOOK FOUR. 487

*Regarding the rarity and density of these six globes, what should be held as true?*

**First**, it is not consistent with reason that the density of matter is the same in all of them. For where a certain multitude of bodies is necessary, there also a variety of conditions must be applied to distinguish them, so that they may truly be many. Indeed, the primary condition of bodies as physical objects is the internal arrangement of their parts. For inequality of mass occurs in a certain way to the bodies themselves because of their surfaces, which define their bulk; yet the internal part of one body does not differ from the part of another simply by this boundary of mass. Indeed, the principal argument for the dissimilarity of materials is drawn from the contemplation of **periodic times** <note>orbital periods—the time it takes for a planet to complete one circuit around the Sun</note>: for the math does not work out if we make the density of the globes the same, as we shall hear below.

**Second**, it is consistent with reason that as each body is closer to the Sun, it is also denser. For the Sun itself is the densest of all bodies in the entire world, a fact to which its immense and manifold power <note>Kepler believed the Sun’s physical "virtue" or force moved the planets; a denser Sun could hold more of this power</note> bears witness, which cannot exist without a proportionate subject. Furthermore, the very places near the center carry a certain idea of "narrowness," such as occurs in the condensation of much matter into a narrow space.

**Third**: nevertheless, rarity is not to be measured proportionally to the size of the bodies, nor density to their smallness. For example, the distance and simultaneously the size of the globe of Saturn is, based on what was said above, to the distance and size of the globe of Jupiter roughly as 10 is to 5. I say that the density of matter in the globe of Saturn, compared to the density in the globe of Jupiter, is not to be established in that same proportion which exists between 5 and 10.

For if anyone were to follow this, he would then sin against another law of variety by introducing a quantity of matter that is not unequal, but rather the same across all planets. For if the mass of Saturn (10) were multiplied by the density (5), it would pro-

[density] would result in a **quantity of matter** <term>quantity of matter: what we now call "mass"</term> of 50; that is, exactly as much as if you had multiplied the bulk of Jupiter, 5, by its density, 10.

But it seems more excellent and elegant that neither the bulks of the globes themselves (being of different density) should be equal to each other, nor should the density in the unequal bulks of the globes be the same, nor even that the quantity of matter should be distributed in equal portions through all the globes, which are already distinct in bulk and density. Rather, it is better that all these things vary. Just as the mobile globes follow one another in a certain order from the center <note>the Sun</note>, in that same order (order, I say, not necessarily the same ratio) we should measure out to them not only the physical space of their bodies and their rarity, but also the quantity of matter itself.

For example, if Saturn had a quantity of matter of 50, let there be assigned to Jupiter less than 50, but more than half of that (25)—perhaps, say, 36. For in this way, the bodies [volumes] will be in a ratio of 50 to 25; the quantity of matter as 50 to 36; the rarity as 50 to 36 (or 36 to 25); or the opposite density as 25 to 36 (or 36 to 50).

Furthermore, when I previously followed the idea of an **equality of material quantity** <note>the theory that every planet contains the same total amount of "stuff," just packed differently</note>, I was forced to assign to the size of the bodies the same proportion as their periodic times. Thus, just as Saturn’s year is 30 years and Jupiter’s is 12, the size of the Saturnian globe compared to the Jovian would have been as 30 to 12. However, my own observations of their diameters, and those of Remus <note>Georg Galgemair, an astronomer and student of Tycho Brahe who used the name "Remus Quietinus"</note>, refuted this proportion as being too large.

**Fourth**: The following reasons suggest that the proportion of the quantity of matter should be established as precisely half the proportion of the bulks or sizes (and thus 1.5 times the ratio of the diameters of the globes, and 0.75 times the ratio of their surfaces).

First, this ensures that both this proportion of quantity and that of density are each half the proportion of the planets' distances from the Sun. Thus, they meet each other in equal portions of that proportion: on one hand, the quantity of matter is greater [in the outer planet], while on the other, the density in that same large body is lesser. This is the best possible mediation of all factors. Namely, Saturn will be twice as "high" as Jupiter <note>twice as far from the Sun</note>, one-and-a-half times heavier [in total mass], and one-and-a-half times <margin>rarer</margin>

...rarer, or Jupiter one-and-a-half times <note>original: "sesquiplo"</note> denser; and by a comparison of the proportions of a single planet, Saturn will be twice as lofty <note>referring to its volume or "rarity"</note> as it is heavy, and twice as spacious as it is rare.

This same principle regarding the half-proportion of the distances is established by this geometric elegance <note>original: "concinnitate," a term Kepler often used to describe the "fittingness" or harmony of the universe's design</note>: that just as previously, between the distances of two planets from the Sun (for example, let them be 1 and 64 for the sake of easy numbers), two **geometric means** <term>geometric mean: a value between two numbers that maintains a constant ratio, used here to find proportional steps between distances</term> had to be established—4 and 16—specifically to shape the two remaining dimensions of the bodies. In this way, the bodies <note>the volumes</note> of the moving globes themselves would be to each other as 1 to 64; while the surfaces of the globes would be as 1 to 16 (or 4 to 64); and finally their diameters as 1 to 4 (or 4 to 16, or 16 to 64).

So now, between the distances of those same two planets from the Sun (1 and 64), let one **geometric mean** be established—8—specifically to physically shape the matter within the bodies, which is a single thing <note>Kepler treats "quantity of matter" as a single attribute, unlike volume which has three dimensions</note>. Thus, once again, the actual spaces <note>volumes</note> of the globes are as 1 to 64, while the **abundance of matter** <term>abundance of matter: Kepler's "copia materiae" is an early conceptualization of mass</term> [is as 1 to 8]...

*Finally, what do you determine to be the proportion of magnitude between those three primary regions of the world: the space in which the Sun resides, the space or Region of the moving bodies <note>the planets</note>, and the space of the entire world or the Region bounded by the sphere of the Fixed Stars?*

Even though observations do not reach the altitude of the fixed stars—not even those calculations of Copernicus—so that their height seems similar to infinity; and indeed, compared to that distance, the entire interval between the Sun and the Earth (which in the judgment of the Ancients comprises 1200, but by our own reasoning 3469 **semidiameters** <term>semidiameter: the radius of the Earth, used as a standard unit of astronomical measurement</term> of the globe of the Earth) is imperceptible; nevertheless, reason, insisting on the paths already begun, opens a way to penetrate even to this threshold.

And at the beginning, we must look to the example of the Earth and the orbits of the Moon and the Sun, because the proportions of the entire world are derived from the Earth’s own proportions: and the region described by these three bodies and their courses is, as it were, a certain "small world" <note>original: "parvus mundus," or microcosm</note>. For what the Sun is in the region of the fixed stars according to Copernicus, the Earth is in appearance within the sphere or region of the Sun—and according to Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, who proposed a system where the Sun orbits the Earth while other planets orbit the Sun</note>, this is even so in truth. And just as the Sun is in the center of the fixed stars, itself immobile in an immobile dwelling; so too, with respect to the motions of the Moon, the Earth is immobile in the center of the Sun's sphere, as if it were immobile. For just as the region of the moving bodies is arranged around the Sun, so also the orbit of the Moon is led around the Earth: there, the fixed stars are to the Planets as here the Sun itself is...

It is consistent, therefore, that just as the orbit of the Moon was made a proportional mean <term>proportional mean: a middle value in a geometric sequence, where the first is to the second as the second is to the third (A:B = B:C)</term> <note>original: "medium proportionale"</note> through necessary logic between the apparent orbit of the Sun and the body of the Earth at its center; so too the region of the moving bodies <note>the planets</note>, or the outermost circuit of Saturn, should be the proportional mean between the outermost sphere of the Fixed Stars and the body of the Sun at the center of the world.

Furthermore, this same conclusion is reached even without looking at the "small world" <note>the Earth-Moon system</note>, but from considering the "great world" <note>the universe</note> itself. For moving bodies, on one hand, strive for the immobility of the surrounding body <note>the physical space or "ether"</note> that provides their location; as they resist motion, they do not move with as much speed as the mover <note>the Sun’s force</note> desires. On the other hand, they receive motion from that mover to a certain extent. Thus, in the moving bodies, motion from the mover and rest from the space they occupy are mixed together. Therefore, if we may express physical realities in mathematical terms, the moving bodies can most fittingly be called a proportional mean between the body that is the source of motion <note>the Sun</note> and the immobile body that provides the location <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>.

Since this is true both physically and spatially (for the source is within, the locator is without, and the moving bodies are in the middle), nothing is more likely than that the radius <term>semidiameter: the distance from the center of a sphere to its edge</term> of the region of moving bodies is the proportional mean between the radius of the Sun's body and the radius of the sphere of the fixed stars. Thus, just as the globe of the Sun relates to the spherical system of all the planets, so this planetary system relates to the spherical body of the whole world, which is bounded by the region of the fixed stars. *How large, by this reasoning, does the Sphere of the*
*fixed stars become?*

Just as the diameter of Saturn—the outermost sphere of the moving bodies—contains within itself the diameter of the Solar body about two thousand times: So too the diameter of the sphere of the fixed stars would contain the diameter of Saturn within itself almost two thousand times. Thus, the diameter of the fixed stars will contain within itself about forty hundred thousand <note>4,000,000</note> diameters of the solar body. In terms of the diameters of the Earth (according to the proportion between the bodies of the Sun and Earth believed by the ancients), it would be five times more, i.e., two hundred hundred thousand <note>20,000,000</note> more; and according to our own calculations, it would be triple that: namely, six hundred hundred thousand <note>60,000,000</note>.

*This size for the Sphere of the fixed stars is truly*
*incredible; you make it two thousand times larger*
*than the Sphere of Saturn, whereas among the*
*ancients, the stars stand immediately above Saturn.*

On the contrary, the speed of the fixed stars and Saturn in the ancient system is much more incredible. Since it is necessary to establish one of these two things, it is more probable that the sphere of the fixed stars is two thousand, or even a thousand times, larger than the ancients said, than that it is twenty-four thousand times faster than Copernicus established. For in the former case, in a subject that is most vast and which is similar to the infinite <note>the outer shell of the universe</note>, no motion exists; in the latter case, in the modest orbit of Saturn, a motion would be established that is "similar to the infinite" <note>meaning impossibly fast</note>. By itself, such a vast size neither contradicts the observations of Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used</note>, nor is it inconsistent with reason that things at rest should be separated from moving things by an immense interval.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 492, where Kepler is defending his calculation of the immense distance to the fixed stars. He is using the principle of geometric analogy: the Sun is to the planets as the planets are to the stars.</meta>

...whereas the distance of the Sun from the Earth, according to the opinion of Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish nobleman and astronomer whose highly accurate observations provided the foundation for Kepler's laws</note>, is only about 1,150 Earth-semidiameters. But listen to the reason for this proportion.

### ON THE MAGNITUDE OF THE SPHERE OF THE FIXED STARS

*What is the reason for this proportion, which seems to expand the universe so vastly?*

The reason is derived from the very harmony and physical symmetry of the world. For as the Sun, the source of light and life, is to the orbits of the planets, so is the entire region of the planets to the sphere of the fixed stars. The Sun is a small, central body compared to the vast space in which the planets move; therefore, the planetary system itself should be like a small, central point compared to the immense thickness of the celestial sphere. <margin>The harmony of proportions</margin> 

*Does this not create a massive, empty void between Saturn and the stars?*

It is not a "void" in the sense of being wasted space, but a necessary distance to maintain the dignity of the stars. Just as there is a proportion between the size of a king’s palace and the king himself, so there must be a proportion between the Creator’s heavens and the bodies within them. Furthermore, this distance explains why the stars show no <term>parallax: the apparent shift of an object's position when viewed from two different locations, such as the Earth at opposite sides of its orbit</term>. If the Earth's orbit were not like a mere point in comparison to the stars, we would see the stars shifting as we move around the Sun.

->THE MEASURE OF THE STARS<-

*If the distance is so great, how large must the stars themselves be?*

If we follow this proportion, the fixed stars do not need to be of an incredible or impossible size. If a star of the third magnitude <note>an ancient way of ranking star brightness; first magnitude is brightest</note> were placed at this distance, it would have a diameter roughly equal to that of our Sun. Thus, the stars are not monstrously large; they are simply very far away, each one a sun in its own right, though we see them only as tiny sparks due to the immense interval.

<column-break/>

*Is this distance confirmed by any other observation?*

Indeed, it is confirmed by the very nature of sight and the lack of observable movement. If the sphere of the fixed stars were closer—for example, if it were only 2,000 or 4,000 times the distance of the Sun—then the motion of the Earth would cause the constellations to change their shapes throughout the year. Because the constellations remain fixed and their angles unchanged, the "bottom" of the universe <note>the inner boundary of the star sphere</note> must be pushed back to this incredible distance.

<summary>Kepler defends his model of a vast universe by arguing that the distance between Saturn and the fixed stars must be proportionally as large as the distance between the Sun and Saturn. This scale explains why astronomers cannot detect any apparent shift (parallax) in the stars' positions as the Earth orbits the Sun.</summary>

## BOOK IV
## PART II.

-> On the motion of the world-bodies. <-

I. How many and what kind of motions there are.

<margin>What does Copernicus think about the motion of bodies; what for him moves, and what remains at rest?</margin>

There are two species of local motion: for either the whole is turned while remaining in its place, with the parts indeed following one after another; this motion can be called *Dinesis* <note>original: Δινήσεως</note>, or Spinning, or Whirl-turning, by similarity to a lathe, or Rotation from the instrument called a pivot: or the whole itself is also carried from place to place in a circle; which motion the Greeks call *Phora* <note>original: Φορὰν</note>, and the Latins generally call a circuit, or a "carrying-around," or an orbit; however, both are commonly called a revolution.

Therefore, Copernicus posits that the Sun stands at the center of the world, immobile in respect to the whole (that is, its center and axis); yet, in respect to the parts of its body, we have recently perceived by our senses that it is turned around its own center and axis, which I had long ago asserted through reasoning; indeed, with such speed that one rotation is completed in the space of 25 or 26 days <note>Kepler is referring to the then-recent discovery of sunspots by astronomers like Galileo, Scheiner, and Fabricius. By tracking these spots, astronomers proved the Sun rotates on its axis, a fact Kepler had previously predicted on physical grounds.</note>.

Now, as each of the primary bodies <term>Primary bodies (primarii): Kepler refers here to the planets, which move around the Sun, as opposed to secondary bodies like the Moon which move around other planets.</term> is closer to the Sun, so it is carried around the Sun in a shorter period, certainly under the same common circle of the Zodiac, and all into that same direction in which the parts of the Sun's body move forward; Mer- <note>The text breaks here; it is the start of the word "Mercury."</note>

## PART II (Continued)

### II. On the cause of the planetary proportions.

<margin>By what logic the Creator assigned speeds to the heavens.</margin>

We must now consider why the planets are moved at these specific intervals. For the Creator, the Divine Architect, did not distribute these speeds by chance, but according to the laws of geometry and music. For instance, the motion of **Venus** is found in a **nine-to-eight ratio** <note>original: "ſeſquiocto-", meaning the sesquioctave ratio (9:8), which corresponds to a whole tone in musical harmony.</note> to the other spheres, a proportion that ensures the concord of the world-soul. There are **two** <note>original: "duo-"</note> primary factors that determine the length of a planet's year: the distance from the Sun and the density of the body itself. There are likewise **two** <note>original: "duo-"</note> ways in which the solar virtue acts upon these bodies, pushing them forward while they resist with their own natural inertia.

<column-break/>

In **each of the two** <note>original: "vtra-" / "vtraque"</note> motions—both the rotation of the planet on its axis and its revolution around the Sun—we see the same physical principle at work. The **Argument** <note>original: "Argu-" / "Argumentum"</note> for this is derived from the nature of the solar species <term>Solar species (species immateriata): Kepler’s theory of an immaterial force, similar to light or magnetism, that radiates from the Sun and physically sweeps the planets along their orbits.</term>.

As the power of the **Sun** <note>original: "ſo-" / "solis"</note> emanates outward, it is attenuated by the vastness of space. Consequently, the measurement **of time** <note>original: "tempo-" / "temporis"</note> required for a journey increases not just because the path is longer, but because the moving force is weaker. This is achieved through the marvelous **art** <note>original: "arte-" / "artificis"</note> or skill of the Creator, who balanced the weights and distances of the planets so that their motions would create a perpetual, silent song.

*How does the proportion of the periodic times,*
*which you have assigned to the moving bodies, relate to*
*the previously mentioned proportion of the orbits in*
*which they are carried?*

The proportion of the times is not equal to the proportion of the orbits, but is greater than it; and indeed, in the primary planets, it is precisely the **sesquialterate** <note>original: "sesquialtera"; this refers to the ratio of 3:2, or the power of 1.5. This is the first statement of Kepler's Third Law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance.</note> of that. That is, if you take the cube roots of the 30 years of Saturn and the 12 years of Jupiter, and you square those roots; in these squared numbers will be the genuine proportion of the orbits of Saturn and Jupiter. This is also the case if you compare orbits that are not next to each other. For example, Saturn has 30 years. The Earth has one year. The cube root of 30 is approximately 3 and 11 hundredths. But the cube root of 1 is 1. The squares of these roots are 9 and 672 thousandths, and 1. Therefore, Saturn's orbit is to the Earth's orbit as 9672 is to 1000: and a more accurate number results if you assume more accurate times.

*What is gathered from this?*

Not all planets are carried with the same speed, as Aristotle wished—otherwise the times would be as the orbits and their diameters—but as each one is higher and more remote from the Sun, so it completes less space in one hour in its mean motion. Saturn indeed (according to the size of the Sun's sphere believed by the ancients) covers 240 German miles, Jupiter 320, Mars 600, the center of the Earth 740, Venus 800, Mercury 1200. Although according to the distance of the Sun demonstrated by me in the previous sections, the number of miles will have to be tripled everywhere.

*State also the opinion of Aristotle, how*
*he himself thinks the planets go around.*

Aristotle, believing the heavens to be packed with solid spheres (though of an equivocal <note>Aristotle believed celestial matter, the "quintessence," was fundamentally different from the four earthly elements</note> matter), and the later philosophers, whom the Arabs seem to have followed, and after them Purbach <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), a key astronomer whose "Theoricae Novae Planetarum" updated medieval planetary theory</note> the author of the *Theories*: these men, I say, first gave credit to astronomy regarding the number of circles necessary to demonstrate the appearances <note>The "appearances" refer to the observed motions of planets, such as retrograde motion, which astronomers sought to explain through geometry</note>; thus Aristotle believed Eudoxus and Callippus regarding the 25 spheres. To these he assigned as many moving intelligences, which would carry in their minds the time of the period and the region of the world toward which they must strive. However, since it was likely that all should look back to the same principle, Aristotle judged that another 24 spheres should be interposed between these 25, which he called *unrolling* <note>original Greek: ἀνελίττοντας (anclittontas)</note> or **Revolving** spheres: namely, so that each lower sphere—which was liable to suffer the dragging force of the sphere above it due to the contact of their surfaces—might be set free by the interposed revolving sphere. This intervening sphere would strive in the opposite direction of the one above for an equal time, and by that resistance, it would provide the appearance of a resting place; in this seemingly immobile place, the lower sphere could lean and complete its own peculiar period. Thus, the mover of each sphere was established to provide a most uniform motion to its own sphere and to all the lower ones it embraced, within the higher sphere that touched it most closely. And since it pleased that philosopher that motion should be from eternity, he also established that the movers were eternal and immaterial, because material things were not capable of infinity: it followed, therefore, that the movers were separate and immobile principles. Furthermore, since this eternal duration of the celestial essence seemed to him to be the goodness and perfection of the whole world—inasmuch as it was opposed to destruction, which was something evil—he also attributed the highest perfection to those principles, and the understanding of it; and from the understanding of the good, the will—

*What do you think of this Philosophy?*

In response, I object to him not so much on the authority of Christian teaching, but rather on the very absurdity of the doctrine itself. It invents Gods whose duties are derived from the works of nature, and meanwhile ascribes to them from eternity such things as must necessarily have proceeded from a single first principle of all things at the beginning of time. Since this reasoning cannot do without such Theology: if the gods are denied, the whole system collapses. Furthermore, solid spheres cannot be granted, as was proven above. Yet this Philosophy relies on solid spheres, and once they are undermined, it falls. For Aristotle would easily concede this: that a body cannot be transported from place to place by its own soul if it were deprived of the instrument of a sphere—which must be stretched out through the entire circuit to be completed—and if there were likewise no immobile body upon which the sphere might rest.
Then, even if we were to grant the existence of solid spheres, there are nevertheless immense gaps between them. Those spaces will either be filled with a useless sphere that contributes nothing to the circumstances of motion—which is most absurd—or, if there are no solid spheres through those intervals, then the spheres do not touch or carry one another.
Finally, this reasoning fails itself; while it looks out for the spheres and how each might rest upon another, it forgets the lowest one.
For even if we grant that spheres are supported by spheres and are contiguous to one another, what then supports the final sphere of the Moon? Or upon what columns does it rest against the Earth, which is—as they think—at rest? Since across the entire surface of the Earth, no solidity is encountered anywhere? Winds, clouds, and birds pass through most freely and easily in every direction. Why does the immense weight of the heavens not occasionally sink down near us, especially in the denser parts of the spheres? <note>The author is challenging the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic model of the universe, which imagined the planets embedded in physical, crystalline spheres. He points out the mechanical impossibility of these heavy "solid" spheres resting on nothing but the thin air surrounding the Earth.</note>

*If there are no solid spheres, it will seem all the more necessary that Intelligences <note>In this context, "Intelligences" refers to spiritual beings or angels thought by ancients to guide the stars.</note> are needed to administer the motions of the heavens, even if they are not Gods: For what if they are angels or some other rational creature?*

There is no need for these, as shall be proved, nor is it possible for a planetary globe to be driven around by an intelligence alone. For first, a mind destitute of animal power <note>Kepler distinguishes between "mind" (reason) and "animal power" (the physical ability to move a body).</note> sufficient to induce motion possesses no motive force in its mere will; it can neither be heard nor perceived by a brute globe; nor, if it were perceived, would a material globe have the faculty of obeying it and moving itself. On the contrary, however, natural powers implanted in the bodies of the planets themselves can provide for this: that the planet be transferred from place to place.

But granted that it were sufficient for motion that an intelligence *willed* to move into this or that region; the discovery of the figure in which the line of motion is ordained would then become absurd. Conversely, the elliptical shape of the planetary path, and the laws of motion by which such a shape is produced, savor more of the nature of a balance <note>statera: a reference to mechanical equilibrium or physical scales</note> or material necessity, rather than the conception and intention of a Mind, as will be shown below. Then, even if we grant that an Idea other than that of a circle shines forth in the moving Mind: the question remains by what means the Mind can apply either this or that shape to the regions of the world. A circle is described by one certain center, but an ellipse—which is the shape of the planetary orbits—is described by two centers.

What seat, therefore, will you give to the Mind, so that it may measure out a circle or an elliptical orbit in the liquid fields of the ether? Do you locate it in that center? You would then be placing it in the ethereal air, which differs in no way from the rest of the world's space, because the orbit of the planet is eccentric <note>off-center</note> from the body of the sun. But this is quite absurd, since elsewhere the principle of individuation for souls is assigned to matter and to the body to which the soul is joined—which differs in place, time, and many other marks from the remaining matter of the world. Certainly, no other position is suitable for a soul or a mind except through its own body, which it informs <note>gives form and life to</note>. And by what force shall the Mind be moved from place to place in a small little circle around the center of the world, so that it may stay with the centers of the planetary orbits through the passing of ages, if the Mind lacks a body—if, just as it cannot be positioned, it is not movable by itself? By what means will the Mind maintain its position and its distance from the center of the world?

But even suppose it were provided with a seat in the center; how would it then manage to make a planet, located very far away, arrange its orbit around this center? If it held the planet tied with a small cord, it might perhaps fly around based on the connection to the center. Perhaps the Mind, looking out from the center, could perceive—especially if it were equipped with bodily eyes—whether the planet were moving in a circle, namely if it were always viewed at an equal angle. But if the planet went off course, by what path would the Mind lead it back, if it could not see the orbit itself?

But how will a mind perceive an orbit that is not specifically marked out by some physical body?       But if you place the motive mind outside the center of the orbit, its condition will be even worse. Or the mind will be in the globe of the planet itself: then in either case the question arises, by what means does the mind know where the center is, around which the planet's orbit must be arranged, and how far it and its globe are distant from that point? For Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose works on Aristotelian philosophy influenced medieval and Renaissance science</note> rightly judged that the Mover of a planet, if it is a mind, requires knowledge of the center and of its own distance from it. For a circle is both defined and completed by these same things: a center and an equal curvature around it—that is, an equal distance of the circumference from that center. Therefore, however much you exalt the motive mind, a circle is not anything else, even to God, than what has already been said: and the same must be understood, in its own measure, concerning the elliptical figure.

<note>original: "LIBER QVARTVS"</note>

It rests in every place where it is set down in isolation. Indeed, for it to be moved from its position and its state of rest, it has need of some power which is something more than its own matter and naked body, and which overcomes this natural inertia of its own. For such a faculty is already above the character of nature, a child of form, or an indicator of life.

->*From what do you prove that the matter of celestial bodies resists its movers, and is overcome by them, just as in a Balance, weights are overcome by their motive faculty?*<-

This is proved, first, from the periodic times of the revolution of individual globes around their own axes, such as the Earth in its daily time, or the Sun in the time of about 25 days. For if there were no inertia in the matter of the celestial globe—which is to it like a certain weight—there would also be no need for power to move the globe; and if even the smallest power for moving were posited, there would then be no reason why the globe should not be turned in an instant. Now, however, since the revolutions of the globes take place in a certain time, which is longer in one planet and shorter in another, it appears from this that the inertia of matter is not related to the motive power as "nothing" is to "something." Therefore, the inertia and thus the resistance of celestial matter is not non-existent.

The same is proved, secondly, from the carrying-around of the globes about the sun, when they are considered together. For a single mover, by a single rotation of itself, moves six globes, as we shall hear below. But if the globes did not have a natural resistance of a certain proportion, there would be no reason why they should not follow the whirling of their mover exactly, and thus be turned with it at one and the same time. Now, however, all indeed go into that region toward which the mover is whirled, yet none fully attains the speed of its mover, and one follows more sluggishly than another. Therefore, they mix with the speed of the mover their own inertia of matter in a certain proportion.

*In order that I might more correctly understand the force of the Sun’s rotation, tell me what you think would have happened if the Sun did not rotate?*

Just as a magnet does not stop attracting another magnet turned toward it with its friendly part until it brings it to the point of physical contact and unites it entirely to itself—and either turns a magnet presented to it with its hostile part and attracts it once it is turned, or, if it cannot turn it, repels it and leaves it no place within the sphere of its power (provided it is not hindered)—so also must we think concerning the Sun. *carrying power: does the proportion of the power*
*to the body of the planet therefore not*
*remain constant?*

Certainly not, if we consider the parts of a single revolution; and for that reason, the same planet becomes faster in one part of its revolution, as above at E <note>E refers to the perihelion, or the point closest to the Sun</note>, than in the other at A <note>A refers to the aphelion, or the point farthest from the Sun</note>, as will be stated below. But notwithstanding this, the total carrying power collected through all those degrees into which the planet comes within one revolution is always of the same quantity in every return.

*How can it happen that the power emanating*
*from the body of the Sun is weaker at a*
*greater distance at A, than near the Sun*
*at E? What affects it or renders*
*it weak?*

Because that power is corporeal <note>original: "corporea"; Kepler argues that the force is physical rather than purely spiritual or mathematical</note> and partakes of quantity: therefore it can be scattered and thinned out. Since, therefore, there is just as much power diffused into the very wide orbit of Saturn as there is collected in the very narrow orbit of Mercury: it is therefore very thin in its parts within the orbit of Saturn, and for that reason very weak; but it is very dense near Mercury, and for that reason very strong.

*If we were dealing with the body of the Sun itself,*
*I could grant it this natural power of*
*moving: but you lead this material power*
*out from the body, and place it without*
*a subject in the vast ether; does this*
*not seem absurd?*

BOOK FOUR. 523

It is clear that this should not seem absurd, as shown by the example of the magnet, against which the same objection could be raised. But in neither case is this force without an analogous subject <note>In 17th-century physics, a "subject" is the underlying substance or medium that carries a property or force.</note>. For just as in the source itself, the subject for that natural faculty is the body of the Sun, or the fibers stretched out from its center to its circumference; so also in this very outflow, I think a rational distinction should be made between the immaterial species <note>original: "speciem... immateriatam." In Kepler's physics, a "species" is an image or influence radiating from a body that allows it to act at a distance.</note> of the Solar body, flowing out as far as the planets and beyond, and its force or energy, which grasps and moves the planet at close range. Thus, the former is the subject of the latter, even though it is not a physical body, but an immaterial species of a body.

*Could you give an example of this?*

A genuine example is found in the light and heat of the Sun. There is no doubt that just as the Sun is entirely luminous, it is also entirely ignited, and because of the density of its matter, it is altogether comparable to a glowing mass of gold, or something even denser. Now, from that light of the Sun, there goes out and descends to us a non-corporeal, non-material species, which we call the light or rays of the Sun; yet this species receives quantities and accidents. Indeed, it flows out in straight lines, it can be condensed or thinned out, and it is entirely divisible by <margin>continuation of the word "refraction" from the following lines</margin> mirrors and glass—namely, through reflection and refraction—as we are taught in Optics. And yet this species of Solar light also carries heat itself, and according to the ratio of its strength, greater or lesser, by which it falls upon bodies capable of being illuminated, it also heats them more or less. <margin>Mercury</margin> Therefore, just as that species, or light—which we know for certain flows down from that light of the Sun—is the subject of the heat-producing faculty, likewise extended from the Sun through the species; so also the immaterial species of the Sun's body, having descended as far as the planets, has as its companion the species of that energetic virtue in the body of the Sun, which strives to unite similar things to itself and repel dissimilar things.
The example is even more evident in that same light when, passing through glass or colored cloths, or upon colored <margin>Absurdity</margin> surfaces—

*State the reasons for this distinction of the*

1. It is necessary that the matter of the solar body be something distinct from the light within it. For the motion of the rays of light in a straight line happens in a moment, but the rotation of the solar body occurs over time. But if we were to establish that the naked species of light were the subject and vehicle of the power of grasping, the single light of the sun would claim for itself the entire essence of its body. For that which is found in the species of a thing is originally the same as that in the thing itself.
2. Quantities belong to the light that has fallen down, undoubtedly not entirely according to the intimate essence of light, but according to something diverse from the light itself; namely, because it exists in a body with magnitude, and because the joined species of both the body and the light fall down together.

<margin><unclear>The surface of the body is considered, and it possesses the same properties as other surfaces in motion and impact; however, it suffers nothing from the body that is illuminated within the surface, because it does not descend from the internal bulk of its source.</unclear></margin>surface is considered, and it possesses the same properties as other surfaces in motion and impact; however, it suffers nothing from the body that is illuminated within the surface, because it does not descend from the internal bulk of its source. The power of grasping a body <note>Kepler uses the term "vis prensandi" to describe a quasi-magnetic force that "grabs" the planets to move them</note> must necessarily descend from a body, so that the moving cause is analogous to its mobile object. Therefore, it also admits the dimensions of a body and moves bodies: not only according to the surface, but by insinuating itself into their very matter.

4. Hence, no matter of an opposing surface prevents light from illuminating that surface in an instant. However, that which does obstruct light—namely, an opaque object—obstructs it perpetually and is never overcome, so long, that is, as it remains opaque. But the power of grasping does not overcome the whole mass: for the resistance of the matter in the body of the planet obstructs and detracts from it. By this resistance, it happens that the planet does not exactly follow the grasping force as it is moved forward, but is left behind and abandoned by it; in this mutual struggle, there is a place for time <note>Kepler argues that while light is instantaneous, the physical movement of planets takes time because of the "laziness" or inertia of matter</note>.

5. This diversity arises from the same cause: that light is terminated and hindered by the opaque surfaces of bodies, preventing it from penetrating further to other bodies positioned in the same straight line. But this force, which leads the planet around by grasping it, is not hindered by its surface, but penetrates into the body which it grasps; and through that body, it even penetrates into the body of a further planet, if it should happen that two planets fall into a straight line with the Sun. Thus, the motion is in no way disturbed by the interposition of bodies. But if the motion proceeded from the illumination of light, this absurdity would occur: that as often as a superior planet was eclipsed by an inferior one, its motion would cease for as long as it took for the inferior one, by its own speed, to rescue itself from that line.

6. Finally, that the motion of the planets does not necessarily come from the bare light of the Sun is evident from examples of other things, where a motion similar to that of the heavens occurs without light. This can be seen in the Magnet, and will be made clear below by the example of the Moon, which is moved by the Earth, a body that is not at all luminous. Even if then its own...

      *What is the similarity between the species of light and*
            *this power of grasping?* <note>original: "virtutis prensandi" - Kepler's term for the sun's ability to "grip" and move the planets.</note>

   The similarity is most absolute in the very origin and conditions of each species: the descent of both from a luminous body occurs in a moment; both pass through a medium, whether large or small, without loss or "toll"; nothing perishes on the journey from its source, and nothing is scattered between the source and the object to be illuminated or moved.
   Therefore, both outflows are immaterial—not like odors, which involve a diminution of substance, nor like heat from a glowing furnace, or anything similar by which media are filled. For that species is nowhere except in the body that is opposite and encountered: in the case of light, upon its opaque surface; but in the case of the motive power, within the entire body. In the intermediate space between the sun and the surface, it is not present, but rather *was* present <note>Kepler argues that the force exists only as a transition between the source and the target, not as a lingering substance in the vacuum.</note>. But if a concave spherical surface of an opaque body were encountered, both solar species, with the full forces by which they had departed from the body of the sun, would be dispersed into that concavity, so that there would be just as much of it in a large and more remote sphere of this kind as in a narrow and nearby one. And since the proportion of convex orbs is double the proportion of the diameters <note>Kepler is referring to the surface area of a sphere increasing with the square of the radius.</note>: therefore, this species would be made twice as thin in unequal orbs as it is more remote; and again, because the proportion of circles is the same simple one as that of the diameters: therefore, in length, the species is thinner in the same proportion as it is more remote from the source.

*But Light is attenuated in the double proportion of the intervals <note>original: "dupla intervallorum proportione"; this refers to the inverse square law where intensity decreases by the square of the distance</note>, that is, in the proportion of the surfaces; why therefore is the moving Power not also made weaker in the double proportion rather than in the simple proportion?*

Because the moving power has as its subject the emanation <note>original: "speciem"; Kepler uses this to mean a physical species or radiating image</note> of the solar body, not as it is merely a body, but as it is established in motion, revolving around its own axis and immobile poles.
Therefore, although the emanation of the solar body is attenuated in length and breadth no less than light: nevertheless, that attenuation contributes to weakening the moving power only by reason of its length; for the local motion, which the Sun imparts to the planets, occurs only in length <note>referring to the orbital path along the ecliptic</note>, in which direction the parts of the Sun's body are also mobile, and not in breadth toward the poles of the body, in respect to which the Sun is immobile.

*Yet even the mobile bodies <note>the planets</note> have breadth no less than length; therefore they are carried by this power, as much as it possesses length and breadth: why then would the moving power not also be weakened in breadth, and thus in the double proportion of the intervals?*

Indeed, the bodies of the planets have not only these two dimensions, but also a third of thickness or height, and they occupy this power in a clearly threefold manner: and for that reason, the grasping, carrying, and moving power of a single planet is not a single circle lacking breadth, but consists of infinite, as it were, parallel circles in breadth and in height: but it does not follow from this that the attenuation of this power occurs either in the double or triple proportion of the intervals—

For just as elsewhere in geometry the proportion of equal multiples is the same, so also here in physics: as one minimal physical line (as a part of the planetary body) relates to the thinness of a single circle of force <note>Kepler uses "virtuous circle" to mean a circle of power or influence</note> established by the simple proportion of the intervals, so also do infinite minimal physical lines (as all parts of the planetary body, arranged in both breadth and depth) relate to as many circles of motive power. These circles, each and all, have the power of moving only in length <note>along the path of the orbit</note>, and none in breadth or depth—neither individually nor joined together. Therefore, just as the individual lines or fibers of two separate planetary bodies would be moved by individual circles of motive power in the simple proportion of their distances, so also the entire fibers of the planetary globe joined together are moved by the entire circles of power joined together in that same simple proportion. This is because that breadth and depth of the motive power is not of its own essence, but is accidental to the mobile object.

*Are these things—concerning the species of the solar body and its power driving the planets (especially the Earth) around—more difficult to believe than those earlier ideas of the philosophers regarding intelligences, motive souls, and solid spheres?*

It does no harm for things to be difficult to believe, provided they are easier to understand, and that nothing can be objected against them (as was objected against the spheres and intelligences) or anything else by which impossibility might be proven.       Four causes concur to establish the length of a periodic time. For just as it happens in a Mill, whose wheel is driven by the force of a river—where the wider and longer the wings, boards, or oars you attach to the wheel, the greater the force of the river (spread through the width and depth of the rushing water) you divert into the machine—so it also happens in this celestial vortex of the Solar species rushing in a circuit, which causes motion

->*Proof: In the comparison of two planets, is the weakening of the moving power exactly balanced by the size with which the movable bodies of the planets occupy it?*<-

The masses or volumes of the bodies are in a simple and direct proportion to their distances, as was demonstrated above. That is, as the distance SA is to SD, so is the mass of the planet's body at A to the mass of the other planet at D. Now, indeed, the moving power <note>Latin: *virtus motrix*; Kepler's concept of a physical force emanating from the sun</note> is also dense and strong in a simple but inverse proportion to those same distances; for as the same distance SA is to SD, so is the strength of the species <note>Latin: *species*; here referring to the "emanation" or "image" of the solar force</note> at CA to the strength of the species at FD. Therefore, by the same proportion that this power is weakened, it is in turn occupied; for example, Saturn is carried by a power ten times weaker than the Earth, but in turn, by its own body, it occupies ten times more of the power of its region than the Earth occupies of the power of its region with its body. And if the total power which Saturn occupies with its mass were divided into ten parts, which are equal in space to the total power the Earth occupies, each of these parts or spaces of power has only a tenth part of the strength of that which the one space occupied by the Earth has. Therefore, those ten parts, with their ten tenths collected into one, are equal in power to that single one by which the Earth is carried. Thus, if in that greater size of the thinner globe of Saturn there were no more matter than in the narrowness of the denser body of the Earth, the globe of Saturn would be carried forward through as much space of its orbit in one year as the length of the Earth's entire orbit, and thus it would complete its own orbit in ten years. But as it is, it has about three times more matter and weight than the Earth; therefore it requires three times longer, namely: thirty years.

*What was the need to teach this compensation? *What then is the cause why, the further any of the equal arcs of the eccentric <note>The "eccentric" refers to the off-center circular path used in older astronomy to model elliptical orbits.</note> is distant from the Sun, the longer the delays the planet weaves into it, and that in the very same proportion as the distances?*

It is, without doubt, that very weakening of the moving power <note>original: "virtutis motricis"</note>. For here the three remaining causes are lacking to us. For the arc or the path is supposed to be of the same length on both sides, such as DH and AI; the density of the body remains the same, and the size of its shape likewise, because FD and CA here represent one and the same planet. Only the strength of the power remains. But more on this in what follows.

✠ from the rotation of the Solar body in that space, and plainly removes the truth of the station and retrogradation of the planets, and excuses it through a mere deception of sight: these questions must be carefully distinguished. 1. Whether the Sun remains fixed in the center of the world. 2. Whether all five orbits of the planets, and that of the Earth in their midst, are led around the Sun, so that the Sun is in the embrace of them all. 3. Whether the Sun occupies the very center of the entire planetary system, or whether it stands near it. 4. Whether this very center of the system, and the Sun within it, moves in an annual motion, or rather, while the Sun remains immobile, the Earth has an annual motion through the opposite parts of those signs under which the Sun is thought to be located at any given time.

*You proved above that the Sun is 1. in the center of the sphere of the fixed stars: now prove also that it is 2. within the embrace of the planetary orbits?*

That the Sun is in the middle of the planetary circuits is proved first by an accident of this motion, namely: by the appearance of stations and retrogradations <note>Stationary points and retrograde motion occur when a planet appears to stop or move backward in the sky; Kepler argues this is an optical illusion caused by the Earth's own movement.</note>, which is a fallacy of sight; or even when the planets appear faster in their direct motion than they truly are.

For to begin with the lower planets, for many centuries following Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy was the 2nd-century astronomer who argued for a geocentric (Earth-centered) universe.</note> (to say nothing now of the most ancient Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (3rd century BCE) was the first known proponent of a heliocentric model.</note>), it occurred to authors such as Martianus Capella, Campanus, and others, that it could not be otherwise—that the Sun, Venus, and Mercury have the same period of time, namely a year—unless they also shared the same path, and the Sun held the center of the two orbits of Venus and Mercury, and they ran their courses around the Sun. By this reasoning, it happens that these planets, when they appear retrograde, are not actually retrograde, but continue the same path under the fixed stars by circling the Sun: a thing which was more consistent with the nature of celestial bodies.

2. A few years ago, Galileo confirmed this line of reasoning with a most brilliant demonstration, having

->[An astronomical diagram showing the phases of Venus as it orbits the Sun. The Sun is at the center, depicted with a face and rays. Venus is shown in eight positions around the Sun, exhibiting phases from full to crescent. Lines of sight originate from a small figure representing Earth at the bottom. detected through the Telescope the illumination of Venus. When it is in direct motion and near the Sun, it has a round shape; when it is retrograde <note>appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, it appears crescent-shaped. From this, it is most certainly proved both that its illumination comes from the Sun, and that when it appears round and moves directly, it is above the Sun; but when it is crescent-shaped and retrograde, it is below the Sun, and thus it revolves around the Sun. For the sake of clarity, the demonstration of this matter should be joined with the demonstration of the Moon's illumination. Regarding Mercury, Marius <note>Simon Marius, a contemporary German astronomer</note> puts forward similar findings by the service of the same Telescope, having observed a weakening of the light as the planet descends toward the Earth. This is an indication that the appearance of its illumination changes and the light is thinned into a horn-shape <note>a crescent</note>, so that it strikes the eye less from a nearby position than from a far distance. Without this thinning into a crescent, such a thing would be absurd; for otherwise, nearby objects appear larger than if they had moved further away.

BOOK FOUR. 537

Now, as far as the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are concerned, Aristarchus, Copernicus, and Tycho Brahe demonstrate that if we also arrange them around the Sun, and establish the Sun as the common center, as it were, of the five planets—so that the motion of the Sun, whether true or apparent, involves the entire orbits of the five planets—we are liberated from several complications. Just as we were previously freed from two unnecessary eccentrics <note>off-center circular paths</note> in the cases of Venus and Mercury, we are now freed in the superior planets from: 1. three epicycles <note>smaller circles moving along the circumference of larger ones</note>; 2. the blind and incredible coincidence of their real motion with the motion of the Sun; 3. and thus their stations and retrogradations <note>the appearance of a planet stopping or moving backward in the sky</note>—which, just as with Venus and Mercury, are actually non-existent in respect to the Sun which they orbit; 4. likewise, many intricacies in the motion of latitude are removed from theoretical doctrine; 5. finally, the causes are revealed for the difference of why the five planets become stationary and retrograde, while the Sun and Moon never do; and 6. why Saturn, the highest of the superior planets, has the smallest arc of retrogradation, Jupiter in the middle has a medium arc, and Mars, being the closest, has the largest. All of these matters will be explained below in Book VI. Truly, the causes of these appearances are utterly unknown among the ancient astronomers.

3. But even the secondary planets <note>moons</note> provide us with some testimony of this matter. For Marius <note>Simon Marius, a contemporary of Galileo</note> discovered in his *World of Jupiter* <note>original: "mundo Ioviali"</note> that the revolutions of the Jovian satellites around Jupiter are by no means regular in relation to the lines we project from the center of the Earth to Jupiter; they are, however, regular if compared to lines drawn from the center of the Sun through Jupiter. Surely this serves as a most significant argument that the orbit of Jupiter is arranged around the Sun, and that the distance of the Sun from the center of the Jovian orbit is certain and fixed in a way; whereas the Earth varies its distances from this center throughout the year.

Ptolemy, however, is held as the leader <note>original: "coryphæum"</note>. The second and third systems are ascribed to more recent authors, although the second, named after Copernicus, is the most ancient <note>Kepler refers to the heliocentric idea's roots in ancient Pythagorean thought</note>. The author of the third is Tycho Brahe.

      Ptolemy, therefore, treats each of the wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the planets</term> at least separately, and assigns the apparent causes of all their motions, retrogradations, and stations to each within its own individual spheres. He does this in such a way, however, that he places in each one a certain sphere that completes its period with respect to the motion of the Sun. Ptolemy does not explain the reasons why this happens, except that Latin writers attribute some obscure force to certain rays of the Sun, being fascinated by mere ignorance of those Rays.

      The remaining two authors compare the planets with one another, and whatever commonalities are detected in their motions, they deduce them from the same common cause. This common cause (which makes the planets appear stationary and retrograde in a certain configuration of the planet with the Sun) is still attributed by Brahe to the real motion of the entire planetary spheres; by Copernicus, however, it is removed entirely from the planetary spheres themselves.

      For Brahe teaches that all five spheres of the primary planets are connected at some common point, which is not far from the center of each individual sphere (as if they were all described here on a common circular table B). <margin><unclear>S n v</unclear></margin> And he teaches that this, as if a common node, actually goes around in a year's time together with the Sun, and indeed very close to it (in the little circle A marked with dots), and carries the entire spheres around with it, displacing them, as it were, from their spaces in the world. This is done in the same manner as grain-cleaners <note>original: "pollinctores," likely referring to those who winnow or sift</note> turn a sieve with their hands while grasping one part of the rim, shaking it: so that the position of the entire planetary system is, for example, in the month of June according to circle B, in August according to C, in October according to D, in December according to E, in February according to F, in March according to G, and from there again according to B. Meanwhile, the planet is not at all disturbed by this displacement of its sphere within the <margin>x</margin> sphere,

Copernicus, however, leaves the centers of the orbits—as far as the annual period is concerned—entirely fixed, and also places the fixed center of the Sun in the vicinity of these said centers. He ascribes the annual motion around the Sun to the Earth, and thus to our own sight. From this it follows that while our sight considers itself to be at rest, the Sun appears to move with an annual motion, and all five planets appear at times to stand still, at times to travel in the opposite direction <note>retrograde motion</note>, and at times to proceed very quickly on a direct path.

Therefore, all five lines of altitude <note>the apsidal lines or lines of eccentricity</note> perpetually meet in the center of the Sun. Look at the diagrams on pages 455 and 454.

    2. From the motion of the latitude of the planets. From the same state of affairs—namely, from observations—we learn that the orbit of each primary planet is intersected by the ecliptic at locations opposite to one another from the center of the sun, and not from any other nearby point.

Second, because the moving force <note>term: "vis motrix" - Kepler's concept of a physical force, similar to gravity or magnetism, that drives planetary motion</note> cannot reside in a mathematical point, but requires a body, namely the heart of the world, the sun. Third, because the moving force altogether demands for itself the center of the world, in which the Sun itself is; just as rest belongs to the surface of the world, and motion to the intermediate [parts]...

First, however, the following point must be wrested from the Brahean opinion** <note>Referring to Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer who proposed a system where the Earth is stationary and the Sun orbits it, while other planets orbit the Sun.</note> **and demonstrated: that the center of the region of moving bodies does not differ from the center of the Sun. For if Brahe follows this path, he will be forced to assign one motion to the Sun, and yet another different motion to this center of moving bodies; by which motion it would happen that the Sun sometimes precedes this center, sometimes follows it, sometimes stands above it, and sometimes below; and yet both would always have the exact same period of time.**

**6. Furthermore, something absurd and miraculous would happen to Brahe’s system. The motions of all the other primary planets agree in this: that the points around which their motions appear uniform differ in position from the common center of the region of moving bodies. Only the Earth would observe this very point as the rule of its motion, if the Sun were not in the very center of the region of moving bodies. But what would be the cause of this diversity?**

**8. Finally, the reason why Copernicus and Brahe made those two centers differ is not sufficient, nor is it astronomical enough. For they were driven to that point only because, in their types of hypotheses, they wanted to express a total equivalence to the Ptolemaic form.** <note>The ancient system where everything revolves around the Earth in perfect circles.</note> **And yet it was not necessary for them to follow so closely in the footsteps of Ptolemy. Indeed, Ptolemy did not build all parts of his hypothesis from observations, but founded many things upon this preconceived false opinion: that one must presuppose the motions of the planets to be uniform throughout the entire circle—which is demonstrated to be false by observations. He who desires to solidly understand these astronomical arguments, here placed under a single view, should consult my commentaries on the motions of the star Mars.** <note>A reference to Kepler's seminal work, *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note>

### *By what arguments, finally, do you prove that the center of the Sun—which is in the middle of the planetary spheres, carrying their entire System—does not revolve with any annual motion, as Brahe maintains, but according to Copernicus, remains immobile in one place, while the center of the Earth revolves with an annual motion?*

Even if by demonstrating one point, the other necessarily follows, some arguments nevertheless pertain more closely to the Sun itself, some to the Earth, and some equally to both.

First, the same argument serves here which we just used to claim for the Sun the center of the spheres: namely, the removal of a superfluous multitude of spheres and motions. For just as it is much more probable that there is one single system of solar spheres, common both to the center of the sun and to that "knot" of the five spheres according to Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) proposed a geo-heliocentric system where the Sun orbits the Earth while the other planets orbit the Sun.</note>, rather than believing Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose geocentric model required complex epicycles for every planet.</note>—who held that in every one of the five planets, besides the spheres regarding their own proper motions, there existed an additional entire system of spheres exactly like the sixth system of the Sun—so also it is now much more probable that the center of the single Earth revolves with an annual motion while the Sun remains at rest according to Copernicus, than that the same annual motion (besides the other motions proper to each) should belong to that "knot" of five systems along with the spheres and the planets themselves and the sixth sun, according to Brahe. 

For although Brahe removed those five superfluous theories of Ptolemy (which were similar to the Solar theory) from the genuine systems of the planets, and traced them back to that common knot of systems, hiding them and fusing them into one; he nevertheless left the physical reality that was produced by those theories in the world: namely, that any planet, besides that motion which must truly be granted to it, is even now moved additionally by the motion of the sun itself, mixing both into one. From this mixture, since solid spheres <note>The traditional belief that planets were carried on physical, crystalline shells, which Kepler and Brahe eventually helped disprove.</note>...

If there were no solid spheres <note>referring to the ancient belief in physical crystalline shells carrying the planets</note>, the spirals created in the space of the world would become most entangled. See the diagram of this entanglement in the commentary on Mars, folio 3.
      Copernicus, on the other hand, completely strips the five planets of this extraneous motion of the Sun through a single simple motion of the center of the Earth. He ensures that the centers of the six primary planets—namely, the Earth and the remaining five—each describe a single, simple orbit, or a line very close to a circle, in the space of the world, which is perpetually consistent with itself.
      The second argument is from the motion of latitude. If the epicycles <note>small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones</note> go around while the Earth stands still—either according to Ptolemy or according to Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, who proposed a geo-heliocentric system</note>—it would be necessary for those epicycles, especially those of the lower planets <note>Mercury and Venus</note>, to shake their sides as well as their heads and feet in various ways; that is, to be balanced in a twofold manner. But with the Earth moving, all the orbits remain most constantly inclined toward the Ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note>. See Book VI, Part III, regarding the latitudes of the lower planets, which provide a most evident argument for the motion of the Earth.
      Thirdly, just as above in the spherical doctrine, by granting the diurnal <note>daily</note> revolution of the Earth, the immense sphere of the fixed stars was liberated from a daily motion of inestimable speed; so now also, by granting the same Earth an annual motion after the example of the other planets, we account for that most slow motion of the fixed stars, which is called the "precession of the equinoxes" by Copernicus. See Book VII concerning these matters. For it is much more credible that these things are attributed to the axis of one small terrestrial body than to such a vast mass.
      Fourthly, the consideration of the proportion of the orbits fights on this side. For it is by no means probable that the center of a larger orbit should go around in a small orbit. Now, the proper orbits of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are much larger than the orbit of the Sun: Saturn's is almost tenfold, Jupiter's fivefold, and Mars's one-and-a-half times larger. Therefore, these five orbits are not carried around or displaced from their positions, but their centers remain almost fixed; and as a consequence, instead of this common motion of them and the Sun, the Earth goes around.

The seventh reason is taken from the causes of the intervals <note>The distances between planets</note> explained above in the first part of this book, which are disturbed and mutilated unless we also grant the Earth its own orbit, which Copernicus gives to it between the orbits of Mars and Venus. For even if the interval of Saturn and Jupiter could be deduced from the Cube, Jupiter and Mars from the Tetrahedron, and Venus and Mercury from the Octahedron—even in Tycho Brahe's arrangement—there would still remain only a single interval between Mars and Venus. Neither would that interval of Mars and Venus, which is in a ratio greater than double, fit one of these figures (namely the Dodecahedron or the Icosahedron); nor could it be deduced from two figures without some orbit coming between them.

Thus, by an absurd and improper reasoning, one would only hint at that same beauty from afar: namely, that the Earth would traverse a single orbit while remaining at rest.       The tenth argument, taken from the periodic time, is this: that the apparent motion of the Sun takes 365 days, which measure is the mean between the period of Venus (225 days) and that of Mars (687 days). Does not the nature of things, therefore, cry out with a loud voice that the circuit in which those 365 days are consumed is also in a middle location between the circuits of Mars and Venus around the Sun? And thus, this circuit does not belong to the Sun around the Earth (since around the Earth none of the primary planets have their ordered orbit, as <note>Tycho</note> Brahe concedes) but belongs to the Earth around a resting Sun, just as the other primary planets—namely these very ones, Mars and Venus—complete their periods by running around the Sun.

      The eleventh argument is taken from the moving causes (based indeed on the opinion of Brahe, although it is not conceded by everyone). For because there are no solid orbs <note>Kepler refers to the then-common rejection of "crystalline spheres" in favor of fluid heavens</note>, the moving powers can be placed nowhere else than in the moving bodies themselves. But in this case, the condition of the "moving souls" <note>term: moving souls (animae motrices).
